lessons.title: Long division, remainders, and factors
lessons.summary: Execute polynomial long division over a field, prove the remainder theorem, and use evaluation to decide divisibility by a linear factor.
objectives: Execute polynomial long division over a field, prove the remainder theorem, and use evaluation to decide divisibility by a linear factor.

content.markdown:
## Division turns a root into a factor

Evaluation says whether $p(\alpha)$ vanishes. Long division explains why that numerical fact is equivalent to the structural statement that $t-\alpha$ divides $p$.

## Reactivate the exact dependencies

Day 1 established polynomial equality by coefficient comparison. Week 1 established typed functions, so evaluation is taken in a declared field. A quotient-remainder equality is a polynomial identity over that field. The leading coefficient of the divisor must be invertible; over a field this is automatic for every nonzero divisor.

## The division algorithm

For $p,g\in K[t]$ with $g\ne0$, there are unique $q,r\in K[t]$ such that $p=gq+r$ and either $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$.

At each step, divide the leading term of the current dividend by the leading term of $g$, subtract the resulting multiple of $g$, and continue until the degree drops below $\deg g$.

content.title: Make the first division step
content.introMarkdown: Give the first quotient term and the new partial dividend after subtraction.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the divisor’s leading term was used to cancel the dividend’s leading term.

Every later subtraction depends on the first quotient term.

Restore the zero quadratic coefficient and realign the subtraction.

## Complete model: long division by a linear polynomial

Divide $t^3+2t^2-5t-6$ by $t+3$.

Display every quotient term and subtraction, then verify the quotient-remainder identity.

### Strategy

Cancel the current leading term successively with $t^2$, then $-t$, then $-2$.

### Hypotheses

The divisor $t+3$ is nonzero and monic in $K[t]$.

### Intermediate claims

Subtract $t^2(t+3)=t^3+3t^2$ to obtain $-t^2-5t-6$.

Subtract $-t(t+3)=-t^2-3t$ to obtain $-2t-6$.

Subtract $-2(t+3)=-2t-6$ to obtain $0$.

### Justification

Each subtraction cancels the current leading term, and the final remainder has degree below one.

### Conclusion

$t^3+2t^2-5t-6=(t+3)(t^2-t-2)$, with remainder $0$.

content.title: Complete a divisible cubic
content.introMarkdown: Find the quotient and remainder, then verify the product.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first subtraction whose signs do not match the multiple being removed.

A sign error can create a false nonzero remainder.

Multiply the divisor by each quotient term on a separate line before subtracting.

## Remainder and factor theorems

Divide $p(t)$ by $t-\alpha$. The remainder is a constant $r$, so $p(t)=(t-\alpha)q(t)+r$. Evaluating at $t=\alpha$ gives $p(\alpha)=r$.

Therefore $p(\alpha)=0$ exactly when the remainder is zero, which is exactly when $t-\alpha$ divides $p(t)$. This is the factor theorem.

content.title: Use evaluation as a remainder
content.introMarkdown: Determine the remainder without long division and decide whether $t+1$ is a factor.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether you evaluated at $-1$ rather than $1$.

The divisor $t+1$ corresponds to the root candidate $-1$.

Rewrite the divisor as $t-(-1)$ and repeat the single evaluation.

## Complete model: from evaluation to factor

For $p(t)=t^3-7t+6$, use the root $1$ to obtain a factorization.

Check the evaluation, divide by $t-1$, and verify the resulting identity.

### Strategy

First compute $p(1)$. Then use long division, retaining the missing $0t^2$ coefficient.

### Hypotheses

$p\in K[t]$ and $t-1$ is a nonzero linear divisor.

### Intermediate claims

$p(1)=1-7+6=0$, and division gives quotient $t^2+t-6$ with remainder $0$.

### Justification

The factor theorem licenses divisibility; multiplication verifies $(t-1)(t^2+t-6)=t^3-7t+6$.

### Conclusion

$p(t)=(t-1)(t^2+t-6)=(t-1)(t-2)(t+3)$.

content.title: Turn a root into a verified factor
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $t-2$ divides $p$ and compute the cubic quotient.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first missing coefficient in the cubic quotient.

The factor theorem proves existence, but the quotient still requires exact division.

Multiply your quotient by $t-2$ and correct the earliest mismatching coefficient.

## Write the algorithm before calling a computer

A reliable implementation stores coefficients in descending degree, inserts zeros for missing powers, and repeats the leading-term cancellation until the remainder is shorter than the divisor. A computer-algebra quotient is a later verification, not the first explanation.

content.title: Execute and specify the division algorithm
content.introMarkdown: Compute quotient and remainder manually, then give pseudocode precise enough to reproduce the calculation.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the degree of the remainder and the reconstruction identity.

An algorithm has not finished if the remainder is still divisible in degree.

Repeat leading-term cancellation until the remainder degree is below two, then verify.

## Boundary: the coefficient ring matters

The field hypothesis makes leading coefficients invertible. Long division in an arbitrary coefficient ring can fail in this form. Also, $p(\alpha)=0$ proves only that $\alpha$ is a root; it does not yet determine the root’s multiplicity.

## Course reference

Tomorrow repeats the factor theorem at distinct roots to prove the degree bound. The zero polynomial will be isolated before the proof begins.
Day 2 is complete when evaluation, divisibility, quotient, and remainder are connected by an explicit polynomial identity.

lessons.title: Why degree bounds the number of roots
lessons.summary: Prove by sequential factorization that a nonzero degree-$d$ polynomial over a field has at most $d$ distinct roots, transfer the bound to identity testing, and use the elementary factor definition of root multiplicity.
objectives: Prove by sequential factorization that a nonzero degree-$d$ polynomial over a field has at most $d$ distinct roots, transfer the bound to identity testing, and use the elementary factor definition of root multiplicity.

content.markdown:
## A finite coefficient list cannot hide infinitely many roots

The root-count theorem converts local facts $p(r_i)=0$ into a global restriction from degree. It is the first proof this week in which each repeated use of the factor theorem must be justified.

## Reactivate the factor theorem and proof structure

Day 2 established the factor theorem and exact quotient identity: $p(\alpha)=0$ implies $p=(t-\alpha)q$. Week 1 established typed domains and explicit proof hypotheses. Work over a field $K$ and assume $p\ne0$.

## Sequential factorization at distinct roots

Suppose $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ are distinct roots. The factor theorem gives $p=(t-r_1)q_1$. At $r_2$, the equation $0=(r_2-r_1)q_1(r_2)$ and $r_2-r_1\ne0$ imply $q_1(r_2)=0$. Thus $q_1=(t-r_2)q_2$.

Repeating this argument gives $p=(t-r_1)\cdots(t-r_m)q_m$. Because $p\ne0$, also $q_m\ne0$, so $\deg p=m+\deg q_m\ge m$.

content.title: Identify the indispensable hypotheses
content.introMarkdown: Explain which wording is mathematically sound and why the zero polynomial must be excluded.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the word “nonzero” appears before degree is used.

The zero polynomial has every field element as a root and is the decisive exception.

Rewrite the theorem with all hypotheses before analyzing the proof.

## Complete proof model: a cubic cannot have four distinct roots

Assume a nonzero cubic $p\in K[t]$ has four distinct roots $r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4$.

Derive a contradiction by applying the factor theorem sequentially.

### Strategy

Factor at one root, then prove each remaining root descends to the quotient before factoring again.

### Hypotheses

$K$ is a field, $p\ne0$, $\deg p=3$, and the four roots are pairwise distinct.

### Intermediate claims

$p=(t-r_1)q_1$.

Since $0=p(r_2)=(r_2-r_1)q_1(r_2)$ and $r_2-r_1\ne0$, $q_1(r_2)=0$.

Continuing at $r_3,r_4$ gives $p=(t-r_1)(t-r_2)(t-r_3)(t-r_4)q_4$.

### Justification

The field has no zero divisors, so each nonzero difference may be cancelled. The product of four linear factors has degree four, and $q_4\ne0$ because $p\ne0$.

### Conclusion

The right side has degree at least four, contradicting $\deg p=3$. Therefore a nonzero cubic has at most three distinct roots.

content.title: Descend a root to the quotient
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $r_2$ is a root of $q_1$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the nonzero factor $r_2-r_1$.

The second root descends to the quotient only because the roots are distinct.

Evaluate the factorization at $r_2$ and justify the cancellation.

## Generalize without skipping the descent step

For $m$ distinct roots, the proof needs $m-1$ descent arguments of the form $0=(r_j-r_i)q(r_j)$. Merely writing “factor all the roots” conceals the reason that a root of $p$ remains a root of the current quotient.

content.title: Plan the general degree argument
content.introMarkdown: State the induction invariant after $j$ roots have been processed.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your invariant says that unprocessed roots remain roots of the quotient.

Without that clause, the next factor-theorem application is unsupported.

Add the descent statement before advancing the induction index.

## Second model: the quadratic case

Let $q\in K[t]$ be a nonzero quadratic with distinct roots $a,b,c$.

Write a complete short proof that this assumption is impossible.

### Strategy

Factor at $a$, descend the root $b$, then descend $c$ once more.

### Hypotheses

$K$ is a field, $q\ne0$, $\deg q=2$, and $a,b,c$ are pairwise distinct.

### Intermediate claims

$q=(t-a)q_1$; evaluating at $b$ gives $q_1(b)=0$, so $q=(t-a)(t-b)q_2$; evaluating at $c$ gives $q_2(c)=0$.

### Justification

Distinctness makes $b-a$, $c-a$, and $c-b$ nonzero. The factor theorem then forces a third linear factor.

### Conclusion

$q$ would have degree at least three, contradicting $\deg q=2$.

content.title: Prove the root-count theorem
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $p$ has at most $d$ distinct roots.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first linear factor introduced without a descent argument.

The final degree inequality depends on every factor being justified.

Repair that evaluation step, then rebuild the product through all roots.

## Transfer the theorem to identity testing

If $p$ and $q$ have degree at most $d$, then $p-q$ also has degree at most $d$. Agreement at $d+1$ distinct inputs makes those inputs roots of $p-q$. The root bound then forces a sharp conclusion, provided the zero-polynomial case is stated correctly.

content.title: Deduce an identity from values
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $p=q$ as polynomials.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the root theorem was applied to a polynomial already known to be zero.

The theorem applies to the nonzero alternative; the zero alternative is the desired conclusion.

Split the proof into $h=0$ and $h\ne0$ before invoking the bound.

## Complete model: multiplicity before derivatives

Let $p(t)=(t-2)^3(t+1)$ over $\mathbb C$.

Prove the multiplicity of each root directly from the factor definition.

### Strategy

For each root $\alpha$, isolate the largest visible power $(t-\alpha)^m$ and evaluate the remaining factor at $\alpha$.

### Hypotheses

A root $\alpha$ has multiplicity $m$ when $p=(t-\alpha)^m q$ with $q(\alpha)\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

For $\alpha=2$, take $q(t)=t+1$ and observe $q(2)=3\ne0$. For $\alpha=-1$, write $p=(t+1)(t-2)^3$ and observe $(t-2)^3|_{t=-1}=-27\ne0$.

### Justification

The nonzero residual value proves that no additional copy of the corresponding linear factor divides $p$.

### Conclusion

The root $2$ has multiplicity $3$, while $-1$ has multiplicity $1$.

content.title: Read multiplicity from an exact factorization
content.introMarkdown: List every distinct root, prove its multiplicity from the factor definition, and reconcile the multiplicities with degree four.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first root for which the residual factor was not evaluated.

A visible power gives a lower bound on multiplicity; the nonzero residual proves it is exact.

Factor out the proposed maximal power and evaluate what remains at that root.

## Boundary: distinct-root count and multiplicity count answer different questions

The root-count theorem bounds distinct root values. Elementary multiplicity is already defined here by $p=(t-\alpha)^m q$ with $q(\alpha)\ne0$, and multiplicities sum to the degree when the polynomial splits. Week 3 will prove the derivative criterion $p(\alpha)=p'(\alpha)=0$ for detecting repetition; do not use that unproved criterion yet.

## Course reference

**Resource version:** Khan Academy Algebra 2, Course R registry snapshot 2026-07-28.

**Exact locator:** Polynomial factorization → factor and remainder theorems in Khan Academy Algebra 2 course index.

**Reading purpose:** Use the factor-theorem examples to check the first failed implication only. Return here for the full division-theorem proof and the zero-polynomial boundary.
Tomorrow uses coefficient comparison to derive Viète’s formulas and combines them with long division as a reversible cubic workflow.
The proof is complete only when every descended root, nonzero quotient, and degree equality is visible.

lessons.title: Viète’s formulas and a reversible cubic workflow
lessons.summary: Derive Viète’s formulas for monic quadratics and cubics, use long division to expose a remaining quadratic, and distinguish exact algebraic evidence from computation.
objectives: Derive Viète’s formulas for monic quadratics and cubics, use long division to expose a remaining quadratic, and distinguish exact algebraic evidence from computation.

content.markdown:
## Roots and coefficients are two views of one polynomial

Viète’s formulas do not add a new polynomial. They compare the coefficient representation with the factor representation and make the passage between them explicit.

## Reactivate expansion and long division

Day 1 established coefficient equality, and Day 2 established the quotient-remainder identity. Week 1’s typed-function discipline keeps the coefficient field and evaluation domain explicit. No appeal to decimal roots is needed.

## Derive the formulas

If a monic quadratic has roots $r,s$ and splits, then $(t-r)(t-s)=t^2-(r+s)t+rs$. Thus for $t^2+At+B$, $r+s=-A$ and $rs=B$.

For a split monic cubic, $(t-r)(t-s)(t-u)=t^3-(r+s+u)t^2+(rs+ru+su)t-rsu$. Therefore the three elementary symmetric sums are read from the coefficients with signs $-,+,-$.

content.title: Derive the quadratic relations
content.introMarkdown: Derive the relations between $A,B$ and $r,s$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sign of the linear coefficient after expansion.

The root sum is the negative of the monic quadratic’s linear coefficient.

Expand once more and align the coefficients of $t^2,t,1$.

## Complete model: a cubic from its roots

Construct the monic cubic with roots $1,-2,3$.

Compute all three elementary symmetric sums and verify the expanded polynomial.

### Strategy

Use the cubic Viète formula, then multiply one pair of factors as a check.

### Hypotheses

The polynomial is monic and is specified to split with the three listed roots.

### Intermediate claims

$r+s+u=2$, $rs+ru+su=-2+3-6=-5$, and $rsu=-6$.

### Justification

The coefficient signs in $t^3-e_1t^2+e_2t-e_3$ give $-2,-5,+6$.

### Conclusion

$(t-1)(t+2)(t-3)=t^3-2t^2-5t+6$.

content.title: Derive all cubic Viète relations
content.introMarkdown: Express $A,B,C$ through the roots.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first elementary symmetric sum whose sign is wrong.

The cubic alternates signs in $t^3-e_1t^2+e_2t-e_3$.

Write the full factor expansion before replacing it with coefficient symbols.

## Division exposes the residual quadratic

When one root $r$ of a cubic is known, divide by $t-r$. The quadratic quotient contains the other two roots when the cubic splits. Viète’s quadratic formulas then recover their sum and product without solving the cubic from scratch.

content.title: Trace the long-division invariant
content.introMarkdown: State an invariant relating $p,g,q_j,r_j$ and explain why the remainder degree decreases.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether $p=gq_j+r_j$ remains true after your proposed update.

The invariant is the proof that the algorithm has not changed the dividend.

Multiply the new quotient contribution by $g$ and recompute the remainder.

## Complete model: one root, then two

Let $p(t)=t^3-t^2-8t+12$ and use the root $2$.

Divide exactly and recover the other two roots through the quadratic quotient.

### Strategy

Verify $p(2)=0$, divide by $t-2$, then factor or use the quadratic sum and product.

### Hypotheses

$p$ is monic over $\mathbb R$, and $2$ is checked rather than assumed to be a root.

### Intermediate claims

$p(2)=8-4-16+12=0$ and $p=(t-2)(t^2+t-6)$.

### Justification

The quotient has root sum $-1$ and product $-6$, so its roots are $2$ and $-3$.

### Conclusion

$p=(t-2)^2(t+3)$; the cubic roots counted with multiplicity are $2,2,-3$.

content.title: Recover two roots from one
content.introMarkdown: Divide by $t-2$ and recover the remaining roots exactly.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the earliest mismatch between the quotient and its claimed roots.

The remaining roots must satisfy both their sum and product equations.

Refactor the quotient and verify both Viète relations.

## Evidence boundary for symbolic computation

A hand-written division algorithm proves what each step means. A computer-algebra expansion can verify the final identity, but a decimal root list does not establish exact factorization or multiplicity.

content.title: Run the complete exact cubic workflow
content.introMarkdown: Verify the root, divide, factor the quotient, and check all three Viète relations.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the product sign in the cubic relation.

For a monic cubic, the constant coefficient is the negative root product.

Recompute the three symmetric sums from the exact roots.

## Boundary: Viète requires the stated factorization

The formulas relate coefficients to roots in a splitting field and count roots with multiplicity. They do not prove that an arbitrary polynomial splits over $\mathbb R$. Week 3 moves to $\mathbb C$ and states the fundamental theorem of algebra explicitly.

activities.title: Derive the quadratic relations
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $t^2+At+B=(t-r)(t-s)$.

Derive the relations between $A,B$ and $r,s$.

Show the expansion and match coefficients in the basis $t^2,t,1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The sum and product relations have the correct signs.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: They are derived by expansion and coefficient comparison.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $(t-r)(t-s)=t^2-(r+s)t+rs$. Coefficient comparison gives $A=-(r+s)$ and $B=rs$, equivalently $r+s=-A$ and $rs=B$.

activities.title: Derive all cubic Viète relations
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $t^3+At^2+Bt+C=(t-r)(t-s)(t-u)$.

Express $A,B,C$ through the roots.

Display the expanded factor product and identify every sign.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Expansion gives $t^3-(r+s+u)t^2+(rs+ru+su)t-rsu$. Therefore $A=-(r+s+u)$, $B=rs+ru+su$, and $C=-rsu$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: All three elementary symmetric sums and signs are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The relations follow from a displayed expansion rather than memory alone.

activities.title: Trace the long-division invariant
activities.promptMarkdown:
During long division of $p$ by nonzero $g$, let $q_j$ be the accumulated quotient and $r_j$ the current remainder.

State an invariant relating $p,g,q_j,r_j$ and explain why the remainder degree decreases.

Give the stopping condition.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: At every stage, $p=gq_j+r_j$. Choosing the next quotient term to cancel the leading term of $r_j$ makes the new remainder have strictly smaller degree. Stop when $r_j=0$ or $\deg r_j<\deg g$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The invariant $p=gq_j+r_j$, degree decrease, and stopping condition are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The response connects the selected quotient term to cancellation of the leading term.

activities.title: Recover two roots from one
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $p(t)=t^3-4t^2+t+6$, and note that $p(2)=0$.

Divide by $t-2$ and recover the remaining roots exactly.

Use the quotient’s sum and product as a check.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Division gives $p=(t-2)(t^2-2t-3)=(t-2)(t-3)(t+1)$. The quotient roots have sum $2$ and product $-3$, matching the coefficients. The three roots are $2,3,-1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The quotient $t^2-2t-3$ and roots $2,3,-1$ are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope

activities.title: Run the complete exact cubic workflow

Verify the root, divide, factor the quotient, and check all three Viète relations.

The roots sum to $3$, their pairwise-product sum is $-4$, and their product is $-12$, matching coefficients $-3,-4,12$ through the signs. Decimal approximations can check plausibility but do not prove the exact factors or equality.

rubric.label: Justification and scope

objectives: Retrieve Week 1 function discipline after one week and synthesize expansion, division, factorization, Viète relations, and the root-count theorem in one exact cubic argument.

content.markdown:
## Make the polynomial workflow durable

A cubic will later be treated both as a function and as coefficient data. Today tests whether Week 1 typing survives inside Week 2 algebra and whether this week’s methods form one coherent chain.

## Required foundations

Day 4 assembled coefficient comparison, division, and exact factorization into a reversible polynomial workflow. Week 1 established that a polynomial formula becomes a function only with a domain and codomain, and distinguished the function from its graph and image. The one-week retrieval below is explicit rather than disguised as new teaching.

## The Week 2 chain

For a polynomial over a field: coefficient collection proves identities; division gives quotient and remainder; evaluation gives the remainder for a linear divisor; a zero remainder gives a factor; repeated factors control degree; and exact factors expose Viète’s symmetric sums.

content.title: Order the five polynomial steps
content.introMarkdown: Order coefficient comparison, evaluation, division, factorization, and Viète verification into a defensible workflow.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether each method was assigned an evidence role it actually supplies.

A workflow is reliable only when no step is asked to prove more than it can.

Separate evaluation, division, exact identity verification, and degree control.

## Deliberate one-week review of Week 1

Without notes, reconstruct the five pieces of function data. Then apply them to the same formula $p(t)=t^2$ viewed as $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and as $\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$.

content.title: Retrieve typed function data after one week
content.introMarkdown: Retrieve the Week 1 distinctions and decide surjectivity for both maps.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first missing item among domain, codomain, rule, graph, and image.

The one-week review tests whether typed function discipline survived the new polynomial context.

Write the two function signatures before revising surjectivity.

## Complete synthesis model

Analyze $p(t)=t^3-2t^2-5t+6$ using the root $1$.

Link evaluation, division, exact factorization, Viète checks, and the root-count boundary.

### Strategy

Verify the candidate root, divide, factor the quotient, and then check symmetric sums.

### Hypotheses

$p\in\mathbb R[t]$ is nonzero and monic of degree three.

### Intermediate claims

$p(1)=0$, division gives $t^2-t-6$, and $t^2-t-6=(t-3)(t+2)$.

### Justification

Thus $p=(t-1)(t-3)(t+2)$. The roots sum to $2$, their pairwise sum is $-5$, and their product is $-6$.

### Conclusion

The three distinct roots attain the degree bound. A fourth distinct root is impossible.

content.title: Diagnose a synthesis model
content.introMarkdown: Identify the earliest mathematical error and repair the Viète check.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sign connecting the root product to the cubic constant term.

A correct factorization can still be misread through a Viète sign error.

Write $t^3-e_1t^2+e_2t-e_3$ and substitute the exact roots.

## Complete model: recover and verify

Suppose $(T+S)(2T^2+uTS+vS^2)=2T^3+5T^2S+4TS^2+S^3$.

Recover $u,v$ and verify every coefficient.

### Strategy

Use the tuple $(2,u+2,v+u,v)$ and compare all four entries.

### Hypotheses

The equality is an identity of binary cubics over a field.

### Intermediate claims

$u+2=5$ gives $u=3$, and $v=1$ from the last coefficient.

### Justification

The remaining mixed equation gives $v+u=1+3=4$, so the system is consistent.

### Conclusion

The quadratic is $2T^2+3TS+S^2$.

content.title: Recover a factor independently
content.introMarkdown: Determine $u,v$ or prove that the displayed identity is inconsistent.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first coefficient equation contradicted by the forced values.

A proposed identity must satisfy every monomial coefficient.

List the complete coefficient tuple before concluding inconsistency.

## Independent weekly synthesis

The final problem begins with a binary factorization and ends with a univariate root statement. Keep the change of viewpoint explicit: dehomogenizing at $S=1$ produces a polynomial in $t=T/S$ only on that chosen chart.

content.title: Complete the Week 2 synthesis
content.introMarkdown: Expand $F$, factor $p$, identify all roots of $p$, verify Viète’s formulas, and use the degree bound to prove there are no other distinct roots.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the chart $S=1$ and the root-count hypothesis were both stated.

The final synthesis combines a projective-looking binary form with an affine univariate theorem.

Separate the dehomogenization sentence from the nonzero degree-three root argument.

## Boundary: review is not repetition without a purpose

The Week 1 checkpoint is repeated after one week in a new polynomial setting and with less scaffolding. The other four checkpoints collect new Week 2 evidence. Their targets are not paraphrases of the review.

activities.title: Diagnose a synthesis model
activities.promptMarkdown:
A solution claims that the roots $1,3,-2$ of $t^3-2t^2-5t+6$ have product $6$ and therefore confirm the constant term directly.

Identify the earliest mathematical error and repair the Viète check.

Then explain why three distinct roots do not leave room for a fourth.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The root product is $1\cdot3\cdot(-2)=-6$. For a monic cubic the constant coefficient is the negative of the product, so $-(-6)=6$. The polynomial is nonzero of degree three and already has three distinct roots; the root-count theorem excludes a fourth.

rubric.label: Mathematical content

activities.promptMarkdown:

Expand $F$, factor $p$, identify all roots of $p$, verify Viète’s formulas, and use the degree bound to prove there are no other distinct roots.

State exactly what changes when passing from the homogeneous binary form to the chart $S=1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The expansion, exact roots, Viète checks, and degree-bound conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $F=T^3+2T^2S-5TS^2+2S^3$. Hence $p(t)=(t-1)(t^2+3t-2)$. The remaining roots are $(-3\pm\sqrt{17})/2$. Their total sum with $1$ is $-2$, their pairwise-product sum is $-5$, and their total product is $-2$, matching $p=t^3+2t^2-5t+2$. These are three distinct roots, and the nonzero cubic has no fourth. Setting $S=1$ is a dehomogenization in one affine chart; it does not describe a possible root at $S=0$.

lessons.title: Exact complex arithmetic and polar form
lessons.summary: Compute exactly in Cartesian and polar form, track arguments modulo $2\pi$, and use polar form to take powers without replacing exact values by decimals.
objectives: Compute exactly in Cartesian and polar form, track arguments modulo $2\pi$, and use polar form to take powers without replacing exact values by decimals.

content.markdown:
## The complex plane makes all polynomial roots available

Week 2 treated roots over a chosen field. Moving to $\mathbb C$ will let every nonconstant polynomial split, but only if complex arithmetic and polar notation remain exact.

## Reactivate polynomial roots and Week 2 identities

A root of $p\in\mathbb C[t]$ is a complex number $z$ with $p(z)=0$. Recall that exact factorization is a polynomial identity; a rounded numerical residual is only evidence.

## Cartesian and polar data

Write $z=x+iy$ with $i^2=-1$. Its conjugate is $\bar z=x-iy$ and $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. If $z\ne0$, a polar form is $z=re^{i\theta}=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ with $r=|z|>0$.

The modulus is unique. The argument is defined only modulo $2\pi$: $\theta$ and $\theta+2k\pi$ describe the same number. Products multiply moduli and add arguments.

content.title: Compute exactly in Cartesian form
content.introMarkdown: Give each result as $x+iy$ and show how conjugation makes the quotient denominator real.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the first use of $i^2=-1$ or the conjugate denominator.

A single sign error changes every later polar check.

Expand the product and quotient numerator on separate lines.

## Complete model: locate, convert, and square

Let $z=-\sqrt3+i$.

Find an exact polar form and compute $z^2$ in exact Cartesian form.

### Strategy

Use the signs of the Cartesian coordinates to choose the quadrant, then apply the polar power rule.

### Hypotheses

$z\ne0$, so a polar form exists. Its point lies in quadrant II.

### Intermediate claims

$|z|=\sqrt{3+1}=2$ and one argument is $5\pi/6$, so $z=2e^{5\pi i/6}$.

### Justification

$z^2=4e^{5\pi i/3}=4(1/2-i\sqrt3/2)$.

### Conclusion

$z^2=2-2\sqrt3,i$. Direct Cartesian multiplication gives the same result.

content.title: Convert a quadrant-III number
content.introMarkdown: Give the modulus, one principal argument, and the full argument class.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the point was placed in quadrant III before choosing an angle.

The tangent ratio alone leaves a quadrant ambiguity.

Draw the coordinate signs and replace the argument representative.

## Arguments are congruence classes

An equation such as $\arg z=-3\pi/4$ names one representative. The full argument set is $-3\pi/4+2\pi\mathbb Z$. Quadrant information is the quickest protection against a sign error.

content.title: Diagnose an argument error
content.introMarkdown: Identify the first error and give a correct polar form.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the moment the argument was inferred from tangent without coordinates.

Opposite points have the same tangent but differ by $\pi$.

Use the signs of real and imaginary parts to select the correct class.

## Complete model: a high power without expansion

Compute $(1+i)^6$ exactly.

Use polar form and reduce the final argument before returning to Cartesian coordinates.

### Strategy

Write $1+i=\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}$, then raise modulus and argument separately.

### Hypotheses

De Moivre’s formula applies to integer powers of a nonzero complex number.

### Intermediate claims

$(\sqrt2)^6=8$ and $6(\pi/4)=3\pi/2$.

### Justification

$e^{3\pi i/2}=-i$.

### Conclusion

$(1+i)^6=-8i$.

content.title: Compute an exact fifth power
content.introMarkdown: Give the polar calculation and final Cartesian value.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the multiplication of the argument by five and its reduction.

A correct modulus cannot repair an incorrect angle.

Reduce $35\pi/6$ by an integer multiple of $2\pi$ before taking cosine and sine.

## Complete model: reverse a complex square

Solve $u^2=8i$ in $\mathbb C$.

Find every solution exactly, verify both values, and prove completeness from argument classes.

### Strategy

Write every argument of $8i$ before dividing the argument congruence by two.

### Hypotheses

$8i=8e^{i(\pi/2+2k\pi)}$ and a square root has modulus $\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$.

### Intermediate claims

$2\arg u=\pi/2+2k\pi$, so $\arg u=\pi/4+k\pi$. Modulo $2\pi$, the two classes give $u=2+2i$ and $u=-2-2i$.

### Justification

$(2+2i)^2=8i$ and $(-2-2i)^2=8i$. The two residue classes of $k$ modulo $2$ exhaust the argument solutions.

### Conclusion

The complete solution set is $\{2+2i,-2-2i\}$.

content.title: Solve an exact square-root equation
content.introMarkdown: Find every solution exactly and prove that the list is complete.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether $2k\pi$ was added before dividing the argument by two.

Dividing one representative alone loses one square root.

Solve the argument congruence and list its two classes modulo $2\pi$.

## Boundary: zero has no argument

Polar form with an argument applies only to nonzero complex numbers. The number $0$ has modulus zero but no distinguished direction. Never divide by a modulus or invoke an argument before checking nonvanishing.

lessons.title: Roots of unity and the usable fundamental theorem
lessons.summary: Derive all $n$th roots of unity and of a nonzero complex number, and use the fundamental theorem of algebra with its exact degree and multiplicity conclusion.
objectives: Derive all $n$th roots of unity and of a nonzero complex number, and use the fundamental theorem of algebra with its exact degree and multiplicity conclusion.

content.markdown:
## Rotational symmetry explains multiple choices of root

Every argument may be shifted by $2\pi k$ before division by $n$. Those shifts produce the regular $n$-gon of roots and, later, the three possible distinguished roots of a square-free cubic.

## Reactivate polar powers and degree

Day 1 established exact polar powers: powers multiply arguments and raise moduli. Week 2 established that a nonzero degree-$d$ polynomial has at most $d$ distinct roots.

## The complete root formula

The solutions of $z^n=1$ are $\zeta_k=e^{2\pi ik/n}$ for $k=0,\ldots,n-1$. They are distinct because two exponents differ by a multiple of $2\pi i$ only when their indices are congruent modulo $n$.

More generally, if $w=\rho e^{i\phi}\ne0$, then its $n$th roots are $\rho^{1/n}e^{i(\phi+2\pi k)/n}$ for $k=0,\ldots,n-1$.

The fundamental theorem of algebra says that every nonconstant $p\in\mathbb C[t]$ of degree $d$ factors into $d$ linear factors counted with multiplicity.

content.title: Verify one general root
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\zeta_k^n=1$ and state when $\zeta_j=\zeta_k$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the exponent after raising $\zeta_k$ to the $n$th power.

The congruence classification rests on exact exponential equality.

Reduce the exponent modulo $2\pi i$ and state the index congruence.

## Complete model: sixth roots of unity

Find all solutions of $z^6=1$.

List the exact roots, prove distinctness, and describe their geometry.

### Strategy

Set $6\theta=2\pi k$ and take one representative for each residue class modulo six.

### Hypotheses

Every solution has modulus one because $|z|^6=1$.

### Intermediate claims

$z=e^{k\pi i/3}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4,5$.

### Justification

The six argument classes are distinct modulo $2\pi$ and each sixth power is one.

### Conclusion

The roots are $1,(1+i\sqrt3)/2,(-1+i\sqrt3)/2,-1,(-1-i\sqrt3)/2,(1-i\sqrt3)/2$, the vertices of a regular hexagon.

List $k=0,1,2,3$ before translating to Cartesian values.

## Roots of an arbitrary nonzero number

For $z^n=w$, matching moduli gives $|z|=|w|^{1/n}$. Matching arguments gives $n\arg z=\arg w+2\pi k$. Taking $k=0,\ldots,n-1$ produces every distinct solution.

Return to $3\theta=\pi/2+2\pi k$ and solve for three classes.

## Complete model: roots become linear factors

Factor $t^3-1$ completely over $\mathbb C$.

Use the cube roots of unity and verify the factorization exactly.

### Strategy

Find the three cube roots of one and attach one linear factor to each.

### Hypotheses

$t^3-1$ is a nonconstant complex polynomial of degree three.

### Intermediate claims

The roots are $1,\omega,\omega^2$, where $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$.

### Justification

The monic polynomial with these roots has degree three and constant term $-1$; direct multiplication gives $t^3-1$.

### Conclusion

$t^3-1=(t-1)(t-\omega)(t-\omega^2)$.

Index the four solutions by $k=0,1,2,3$ and verify their fourth powers.

## Three roots counted with multiplicity

The fundamental theorem gives a degree-three complex polynomial three linear factors counted with multiplicity. It does not say the three root values are distinct. Distinctness is a separate condition studied tomorrow.

The theorem counts roots with multiplicity.

Add the no-repeated-root hypothesis at the exact step where factor roots become distinct.

## Boundary: degree counts multiplicity

The fundamental theorem supplies $d$ linear factors counted with multiplicity. It does not assert $d$ distinct points. Tomorrow proves an exact criterion for detecting when two or more factors coincide.

lessons.title: The repeated-root criterion
lessons.summary: For a nonzero complex polynomial, prove both directions of the repeated-root criterion and use it to detect repeated roots exactly.
objectives: For a nonzero complex polynomial, prove both directions of the repeated-root criterion and use it to detect repeated roots exactly.

content.markdown:
## The derivative detects a collision of factors

A repeated root is where at least two linear factors coincide. The derivative criterion packages that factor collision into two evaluations and later becomes the algebraic boundary between three distinct sheets and a degenerate fiber.

## Reactivate roots, factors, and exact division

Day 2 established exact complex-root enumeration and the fundamental theorem’s multiplicity count. Week 2 established the factor theorem: $p(\alpha)=0$ gives $p=(t-\alpha)q$.

## Multiplicity and the derivative

Let $p\in\mathbb C[t]$ be nonzero. A root $\alpha$ has multiplicity $m\ge1$ when $p=(t-\alpha)^mq$ with $q(\alpha)\ne0$. It is repeated when $m\ge2$.

If $p=(t-\alpha)^2r$, then $p'=2(t-\alpha)r+(t-\alpha)^2r'$, so $p(\alpha)=p'(\alpha)=0$.

Conversely, $p(\alpha)=0$ gives $p=(t-\alpha)q$. Differentiating gives $p'=q+(t-\alpha)q'$, hence $p'(\alpha)=q(\alpha)$. If this is zero, the factor theorem gives $q=(t-\alpha)r$, so $(t-\alpha)^2$ divides $p$.

content.title: Factor once at a root
content.introMarkdown: State the factorization supplied by the factor theorem and differentiate it.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the derivative of $(t-\alpha)q$ includes both product-rule terms.

The quotient value $q(\alpha)$ is the reverse proof’s hinge.

Differentiate first, then substitute $t=\alpha$.

## Complete proof model: both directions

Let $f\in\mathbb C[t]$ be nonzero and let $\beta\in\mathbb C$.

Prove that $\beta$ is repeated if and only if $f(\beta)=f'(\beta)=0$.

### Strategy

Use a square factor in the forward direction. In the reverse direction, factor once, differentiate, and evaluate to expose the quotient value.

### Hypotheses

$f$ is nonzero, so multiplicity is defined by a maximal finite exponent. The coefficient field has characteristic zero.

### Intermediate claims

If $f=(t-\beta)^2h$, then both $f(\beta)$ and $f'(\beta)$ vanish.

If $f(\beta)=0$, write $f=(t-\beta)q$.

Then $f'=q+(t-\beta)q'$, so $f'(\beta)=q(\beta)$.

### Justification

When $f'(\beta)=0$, the factor theorem applied to $q$ gives $q=(t-\beta)h$, producing the square factor.

### Conclusion

$\beta$ is repeated exactly when $f(\beta)=f'(\beta)=0$.

content.title: Prove the forward implication
content.introMarkdown: Prove $p(\alpha)=p'(\alpha)=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the common factor of $t-\alpha$ in the derivative.

The forward implication needs both derivative terms to vanish.

Write the product-rule expansion before evaluating.

## The reverse direction has a decisive evaluation

After writing $p=(t-\alpha)q$, the identity $p'(\alpha)=q(\alpha)$ is the hinge of the proof. A response that says only “differentiate and factor again” has not justified why the quotient has the root.

content.title: Complete the reverse implication
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $(t-\alpha)^2$ divides $p$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the second factor theorem was applied to $q$, not again to $p$.

The extra factor comes from the quotient having the same root.

Name $q(\alpha)=0$ explicitly and factor $q$.

## Complete model: two exact witnesses

Let $p(t)=(t-2)^2(t+1)$.

Verify the repeated root at $2$ by factorization and by the derivative criterion.

### Strategy

Use the displayed square factor, then differentiate the expanded polynomial as an independent check.

### Hypotheses

$p$ is nonzero and lies in characteristic zero.

### Intermediate claims

$p=t^3-3t^2+4$, so $p'=3t^2-6t=3t(t-2)$.

### Justification

$p(2)=0$ and $p'(2)=0$; the remaining factor $t+1$ is nonzero at $2$.

### Conclusion

The multiplicity of $2$ is exactly two.

content.title: Prove the full repeated-root criterion
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\alpha$ is repeated if and only if $p(\alpha)=p'(\alpha)=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first direction whose hypothesis or conclusion was not stated.

A biconditional requires two separate implications.

Label the directions and repair the quotient evaluation in the reverse one.

## Detect every repeated root of a polynomial

To find repeated roots, solve the simultaneous equations $p(\alpha)=0$ and $p'(\alpha)=0$ exactly. Factoring either polynomial can shorten the work, but both equations must be checked.

content.title: Detect all repeated roots exactly
content.introMarkdown: Find every repeated root and determine its multiplicity.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether multiplicity was inferred only from $p=p'=0$.

The criterion proves repetition, while exact multiplicity needs the remaining factor to be nonzero.

Use the displayed factorization to show that no third copy occurs.

## Boundary: exclude the zero polynomial

For the zero polynomial, every $\alpha$ satisfies $p(\alpha)=p'(\alpha)=0$, but no largest finite multiplicity exists. The nonzero hypothesis is part of the theorem, not a cosmetic convention.

lessons.title: Exact roots and cubic multiplicity patterns
lessons.summary: Classify a complex cubic as $1+1+1$, $2+1$, or $3$ using exact factors and the repeated-root criterion, while treating decimal roots only as numerical evidence.
objectives: Classify a complex cubic as $1+1+1$, $2+1$, or $3$ using exact factors and the repeated-root criterion, while treating decimal roots only as numerical evidence.

content.markdown:
## Multiplicity is an exact algebraic statement

A numerical solver may print nearby decimals for a repeated root or hide an exact radical relation. The later geometry depends on whether roots truly coincide, so classification must remain symbolic.

## Reactivate factorization and the derivative criterion

Day 2 established that a cubic over $\mathbb C$ has three roots counted with multiplicity. Day 3 proved that a root is repeated exactly when the polynomial and derivative both vanish there.

## The three cubic partitions

A nonzero cubic over $\mathbb C$ has exactly one of three multiplicity partitions: $1+1+1$ for three distinct roots; $2+1$ for one double and one simple root; or $3$ for one triple root.

The labels describe multiplicities, not numerical distances. Exact factorization gives the classification directly. The derivative criterion detects whether a repeated factor is present.

content.title: Factor before classifying
content.introMarkdown: List the exact roots and classify the multiplicity partition.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the grouping factor common to both pairs of terms.

A wrong common factor changes the entire root list.

Factor $(t-3)$ first, then factor the residual difference of squares.

## Complete model: all three cubic patterns

Classify $p_1=t^3-t$, $p_2=(t-2)^2(t+1)$, and $p_3=(t+3)^3$.

Give exact roots, multiplicities, and a derivative check for every repeated root.

### Strategy

Factor each polynomial exactly, then use $p'$ only where a multiplicity exceeds one.

### Hypotheses

All three are nonzero cubics over $\mathbb C$.

### Intermediate claims

$p_1=t(t-1)(t+1)$ has roots $-1,0,1$, and $p_1'(t)=3t^2-1$ gives $p_1'(-1)=2$, $p_1'(0)=-1$, and $p_1'(1)=2$.

$p_2'(t)=2(t-2)(t+1)+(t-2)^2=3t(t-2)$. Thus $p_2(2)=0$ and $p_2'(2)=0$, while $p_2(-1)=0$ and $p_2'(-1)=9\ne0$.

$p_3'(t)=3(t+3)^2$, so $p_3(-3)=0$ and $p_3'(-3)=0$.

### Justification

The exact exponents of the linear factors give multiplicities. The displayed derivative evaluations independently distinguish the simple roots from the repeated roots.

### Conclusion

$p_1$ has pattern $1+1+1$, $p_2$ has $2+1$, and $p_3$ has $3$.

content.title: Classify three exact cubics
content.introMarkdown: State exact root values and multiplicities for each cubic.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first exponent of a linear factor that was read incorrectly.

The exponent is the multiplicity.

Rewrite each cubic as a product of powers of distinct linear factors.

## Why decimals cannot certify multiplicity

The approximations $1.41421356$ and $1.41421357$ may represent one exact number with numerical error or two distinct exact numbers. Conversely, two printed values $1.000000$ may hide distinct nearby roots. Multiplicity is proved by exact factors or simultaneous zeros of $p,p'$.

content.introMarkdown: State what this output suggests and what exact evidence is still needed to claim pattern $2+1$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a decimal coincidence was treated as exact equality.

Multiplicity is unstable under rounding.

Replace the numerical claim with exact factorization or simultaneous-zero evidence.

## Complete model: keep radicals exact

Analyze $p(t)=(t^2-3)(t+1)$.

List exact roots and prove their multiplicity pattern without decimals.

### Strategy

Factor $t^2-3$ over $\mathbb C$ and compare the three exact root values.

### Hypotheses

$3\ne1$, so $\sqrt3\ne\pm1$.

### Intermediate claims

$p=(t-\sqrt3)(t+\sqrt3)(t+1)$.

### Justification

The roots $\sqrt3,-\sqrt3,-1$ are pairwise distinct; for example $\sqrt3=1$ would imply $3=1$.

### Conclusion

The multiplicity pattern is $1+1+1$.

content.title: Classify through exact division
content.introMarkdown: Divide by $t-1$, factor exactly, and classify the cubic.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the earliest mismatch in the quadratic quotient or derivative evaluation.

Both the factorization and derivative must support the same repeated root.

Multiply the exact factors and evaluate $p'$ at each root.

## Classify before approximating

When an exact factorization is available, read multiplicities from it and verify repeated roots with $p'$. Approximate only afterward if a geometric plot is useful.

content.title: Classify a radical cubic exactly
content.introMarkdown: Give every root exactly, prove the multiplicity partition, and then provide decimal approximations only as a labelled plotting aid.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether exact distinctness was replaced by decimal separation.

The classification is algebraic, while the decimals are only a plot aid.

Prove each necessary inequality by exact arithmetic before approximating.

## Complete model: turn exact roots into a geometric record

Draw the roots of $q(t)=(t^2+1)(t-2)$ in the complex plane.

Produce an exact coordinate record and a labelled sketch that preserves multiplicity.

### Strategy

Factor first, convert each root $a+bi$ into the point $(a,b)$, and mark repeated roots without plotting the same point several times.

### Hypotheses

The horizontal axis records real part, the vertical axis records imaginary part, and both axes use the same scale.

### Intermediate claims

$q=(t-i)(t+i)(t-2)$, so the exact roots are $i,-i,2$, each with multiplicity one.

The coordinate record is $i\leftrightarrow(0,1)$, $-i\leftrightarrow(0,-1)$, and $2\leftrightarrow(2,0)$.

Place and label these three points on equally scaled axes. The pair $i,-i$ is symmetric across the real axis because $q$ has real coefficients.

### Justification

The factorization proves completeness and multiplicity. The coordinate map $a+bi\mapsto(a,b)$ determines each plotted point exactly.

### Conclusion

The sketch contains three labelled simple-root points: $(0,1)$, $(0,-1)$, and $(2,0)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compare each plotted point with its exact $a+bi$ coordinate and factor exponent.

A sketch can look plausible while omitting a root or hiding multiplicity.

Refactor each cubic, list one coordinate per distinct root, mark its exponent, and redraw with equal scales.

## Boundary: three factors need not mean three points

A cubic always has three complex linear factors counted with multiplicity. Only the $1+1+1$ case gives three distinct root values and therefore three distinct choices of marked root.

objectives: Retrieve Week 2 coefficient and division methods after one week, then synthesize exact complex roots, the fundamental theorem, and repeated-root evidence into a complete cubic classification.

content.markdown:
## Link the algebraic and complex views

A complex-root argument is only as reliable as its polynomial arithmetic. The one-week review isolates coefficient and division evidence before the final cubic synthesis.

## Required earlier ideas

Days 2–4 established exact root enumeration, the repeated-root criterion, and cubic classification. Reactivate those alongside Week 2 factorization, long division, and coefficient comparison. Week 2’s focus itself depended on Week 1 algebra, so both earlier links remain visible.

## The Week 3 chain

Polar form enumerates exact root candidates. The fundamental theorem fixes the total number of linear factors. Exact factorization and $p,p'$ distinguish the partitions $1+1+1$, $2+1$, and $3$.

content.title: Classify from simultaneous zeros
content.introMarkdown: State the multiplicity partition and the number of distinct root values.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether repeated and exactly double were treated as the same claim.

The derivative criterion detects repetition, not the full exponent.

Use the displayed factorization to establish exact multiplicity.

## Deliberate one-week review of Week 2

Without notes, reconstruct the coefficient tuple $(ac,ad+bc,ae+bd,be)$ and explain why checking only three coefficients cannot prove a binary-cubic identity.

content.title: Retrieve the binary product formula
content.introMarkdown: Give the four coefficients and explain why a three-coefficient check is incomplete.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first mixed coefficient omitted from memory.

The one-week review tests the complete four-coordinate map.

Distribute the $aT$ and $bS$ rows separately, then collect.

## Complete model: a rotated root-of-unity cubic

Analyze $p(t)=t^3+1$ over $\mathbb C$.

Find every root exactly and classify the multiplicity pattern.

### Strategy

Solve $t^3=-1=e^{i\pi}$ through argument classes.

### Hypotheses

$p$ is a nonzero complex cubic.

### Intermediate claims

The roots have arguments $\pi/3,\pi,5\pi/3$, giving $e^{i\pi/3},-1,e^{5\pi i/3}$.

### Justification

The three argument classes are distinct and each cube is $-1$.

### Conclusion

$p=(t+1)(t^2-t+1)$ has pattern $1+1+1$.

content.title: Check a rotated cubic root set
content.introMarkdown: List the three roots and classify the cubic $t^3+8$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the argument $\pi+2\pi k$ was divided by three before listing roots.

The three classes determine both completeness and distinctness.

Index $k=0,1,2$ and convert each exact angle.

## Complete model: detect a double root

Analyze $q(t)=t^3-3t+2$.

Use exact factorization and the derivative criterion to classify it.

### Strategy

Test $1$, divide, and inspect the quadratic quotient.

### Hypotheses

$q$ is a nonzero complex cubic.

### Intermediate claims

$q(1)=0$ and division gives $t^2+t-2=(t-1)(t+2)$.

### Justification

$q=(t-1)^2(t+2)$ and $q'=3(t-1)(t+1)$, so $q(1)=q'(1)=0$.

### Conclusion

The pattern is $2+1$, with double root $1$ and simple root $-2$.

content.title: Detect a repeated root in expanded form
content.introMarkdown: Find exact factors and verify the repeated root with $p'$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first mismatch between the claimed factorization and $p'$.

A repeated-root classification should be supported by both exact witnesses.

Multiply the factors, differentiate the expanded cubic, and evaluate.

## Explain the distinguished-root count

The final answer must identify exactly which hypothesis turns three factors counted with multiplicity into three distinct choices. It must also explain what changes in the $2+1$ and $3$ boundary cases.

content.title: Complete the Week 3 synthesis
content.introMarkdown: Explain the possible numbers of distinct root choices and prove why a cubic with no repeated root has exactly three.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the fundamental theorem was asked to prove distinctness.

It counts factors with multiplicity; the derivative criterion excludes collisions.

Separate those two logical steps before counting choices.

## Boundary: “generic” is not yet a theorem here

This week proves the conditional statement: a cubic with no repeated root has three distinct root choices. Later algebraic-geometry weeks will make precise in what sense the repeated-root locus is exceptional. Do not use that later language as current evidence.

activities.title: Complete the Week 3 synthesis
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $p\in\mathbb C[t]$ be a nonzero cubic.

Explain the possible numbers of distinct root choices and prove why a cubic with no repeated root has exactly three.

Your answer must use the fundamental theorem of algebra, the repeated-root criterion, and the partitions $1+1+1$, $2+1$, and $3$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The fundamental theorem gives three linear factors counted with multiplicity. Their multiplicities form exactly one of $1+1+1$, $2+1$, or $3$, giving respectively three, two, or one distinct root values. If $p$ has no repeated root, no $\alpha$ satisfies $p(\alpha)=p'(\alpha)=0$, so neither $2+1$ nor $3$ can occur. Therefore the pattern is $1+1+1$ and there are exactly three choices of distinguished root.

lessons.title: Sets, products, and indexed notation
lessons.summary: Use extensional set equality, Cartesian products, set-builder notation, and indexed unions and intersections without confusing elements, subsets, and ordered pairs.
objectives: Use extensional set equality, Cartesian products, set-builder notation, and indexed unions and intersections without confusing elements, subsets, and ordered pairs.

content.markdown:
## Equations become objects only after their solution sets are named

The course will repeatedly move between formulas, maps, and the sets on which equations hold. Precise set notation prevents a point, a set of points, and a condition on points from being treated as interchangeable.

## Reactivate function data

From Week 1, a function has a domain and codomain. Today uses only that typed-set foundation. No topology, algebraic geometry, or scheme language is assumed.

## Membership, inclusion, and equality

A set is determined by its elements. Write $x\in A$ when $x$ is an element and $A\subseteq B$ when every element of $A$ belongs to $B$. To prove $A=B$, prove both inclusions.

For sets $A,B$, the union $A\cup B$ contains elements in at least one set; $A\cap B$ contains elements in both. Relative to a universe $U$, the complement is $U\setminus A$.

The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$. Order matters.

content.title: Distinguish membership from inclusion
content.introMarkdown: Decide the truth of $1\in A$, $2\in A$, $\{2\}\in A$, $\{2\}\subseteq A$, and $A=B$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether $2$ and $\{2\}$ were treated as the same object.

Set notation is typed: an element and its singleton are different.

List the two elements of $A$ explicitly before revising each relation.

## Complete model: an indexed family

For $n\ge1$, let $A_n=[-n,n]\subseteq\mathbb R$.

Compute $\bigcup_{n\ge1}A_n$ and $\bigcap_{n\ge1}A_n$ from the membership definitions.

### Strategy

Translate union membership as existence of an index and intersection membership as membership for every index.

### Hypotheses

The index set is the positive integers, and $A_1\subseteq A_2\subseteq\cdots$.

### Intermediate claims

For any $x\in\mathbb R$, choose an integer $n\ge|x|$; then $x\in A_n$.

An element belongs to every $A_n$ exactly when it belongs to the smallest set $A_1=[-1,1]$.

### Justification

The family is increasing, so the existential union expands without bound while the universal intersection is controlled by its first member.

### Conclusion

$\bigcup_{n\ge1}A_n=\mathbb R$ and $\bigcap_{n\ge1}A_n=[-1,1]$.

content.title: Compute an indexed union and intersection
content.introMarkdown: Compute $\bigcup_{n\ge1}B_n$ and $\bigcap_{n\ge1}B_n$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first use of “some $n$” where “every $n$” is required, or conversely.

Union and intersection have different quantifier structures.

Rewrite membership in each indexed operation as a quantified statement.

## Set-builder notation and products

Set-builder notation $\{x\in U:P(x)\}$ names the elements of a universe satisfying a condition. In two variables, $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ is a subset of the product $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$.

content.title: Enumerate and type a product
content.introMarkdown: List $C\times D$ and decide whether $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$ belongs to it.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the second coordinate of the disputed ordered pair.

Membership in a Cartesian product is coordinatewise and ordered.

Test the first coordinate against $C$ and the second against $D$.

## Complete model: order in a Cartesian product

Let $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{x,y,z\}$.

Enumerate $A\times B$ and $B\times A$, then compare them.

### Strategy

Fix the first coordinate and pair it with every allowed second coordinate.

### Hypotheses

The symbols $1,2,x,y,z$ are distinct.

### Intermediate claims

$A\times B=\{(1,x),(1,y),(1,z),(2,x),(2,y),(2,z)\}$, while $B\times A=\{(x,1),(x,2),(y,1),(y,2),(z,1),(z,2)\}$.

### Justification

Ordered pairs $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ are generally different.

### Conclusion

The products have the same cardinality six but are not the same sets.

### Use the feedback before continuing

An equation without a declared universe does not determine one set.

Add the ordered-pair universe before the condition.

## Translate a geometric description

A geometric object may be specified by an ambient product and one or more equations. The notation must state both: the equation alone is not a set until the allowed variables are declared.

## Boundary: the universe changes complements

The complement of $A$ is meaningless until the universe is fixed. For example, the complement of $[0,1]$ in $\mathbb R$ differs from its complement in $[0,2]$.

lessons.title: De Morgan’s laws by two inclusions
lessons.summary: Prove finite and indexed De Morgan laws by translating set membership into explicit logical equivalences and establishing both inclusions.
objectives: Prove finite and indexed De Morgan laws by translating set membership into explicit logical equivalences and establishing both inclusions.

content.markdown:
## Set proofs make logical structure visible

De Morgan’s laws are not symbol-moving rules. They express how negation changes “or” into “and,” and the proof works by tracking one arbitrary element.

## Reactivate universes and quantified membership

Day 1 established universes, finite set operations, and indexed membership; Week 1 supplies typed domain and codomain sets. Fix a universe $U$. Then $x\in A\cup B$ means $x\in A$ or $x\in B$, while $x\in A\cap B$ means both. Indexed union uses “there exists an index”; indexed intersection uses “for every index.”

## Prove equality through membership

For subsets of $U$, De Morgan’s laws are $U\setminus(A\cup B)=(U\setminus A)\cap(U\setminus B)$ and $U\setminus(A\cap B)=(U\setminus A)\cup(U\setminus B)$.

A two-inclusion proof starts with an arbitrary element of one side, expands membership definitions, applies the logical De Morgan law, and reaches membership in the other side. Then it repeats in reverse.

content.title: Translate one membership statement
content.introMarkdown: Translate this into a statement about membership in $A$ and $B$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether negating “in both” produced “outside at least one.”

The entire law depends on the correct logical negation.

Write the proposition with $P$ and $Q$, negate it, then translate back.

## Complete proof model: complement of a union

Prove $U\setminus(A\cup B)=(U\setminus A)\cap(U\setminus B)$.

Write both inclusions and expose every logical equivalence.

### Strategy

Choose an arbitrary element and translate complement, union, and intersection membership into logical statements.

### Hypotheses

$A,B\subseteq U$, and every complement is relative to the same universe $U$.

### Intermediate claims

If $x\in U\setminus(A\cup B)$, then $x\notin A\cup B$, so $x\notin A$ and $x\notin B$.

Thus $x\in U\setminus A$ and $x\in U\setminus B$, hence $x$ belongs to their intersection.

Conversely, membership in both complements implies membership in neither $A$ nor $B$, hence not in the union.

### Justification

The middle equivalence is the logical law $\neg(P\lor Q)\Leftrightarrow(\neg P\land\neg Q)$.

### Conclusion

Both inclusions hold, so the sets are equal.

content.title: Repair a missing inclusion
content.introMarkdown: Complete the reverse inclusion.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the inclusion direction that is still absent.

One inclusion proves only containment, not equality.

Start with an arbitrary element of the intersection of complements.

## Complement of an intersection

The second law uses $
eg(P\land Q)\Leftrightarrow(
eg P\lor
eg Q)$. The word “or” is inclusive: an element may lie outside both sets.

content.title: Prove the second finite law
content.introMarkdown: Give both inclusions through elementwise logic.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether “or” was incorrectly changed to “and.”

The complement of an intersection contains points missing from either set.

Rewrite the logical equivalence before continuing the set proof.

## Complete model: a countable interval family

For $n\ge1$, let $B_n=[-1+1/n,\,1-1/n]\subseteq\mathbb R$.

Prove $\mathbb R\setminus\bigcup_{n\ge1}B_n=\bigcap_{n\ge1}(\mathbb R\setminus B_n)$ and identify the common set.

### Strategy

First determine the union exactly. Then fix $x\in\mathbb R$, expand union membership as an existential statement, and negate that quantifier.

### Hypotheses

The index set is the positive integers. The intervals are nested and increase toward $(-1,1)$ without containing either endpoint.

### Intermediate claims

Every $B_n$ lies in $(-1,1)$. Conversely, if $|x|<1$, choose $n$ with $1/n\le1-|x|$; then $|x|\le1-1/n$, so $x\in B_n$. Hence $\bigcup_{n\ge1}B_n=(-1,1)$.

$x\in\mathbb R\setminus\bigcup_{n\ge1}B_n$ if and only if there is no positive integer $n$ with $x\in B_n$.

This is equivalent to $x\notin B_n$ for every positive integer $n$, hence to $x\in\bigcap_{n\ge1}(\mathbb R\setminus B_n)$.

### Justification

The decisive step is the logical equivalence $\neg\exists n\,P(n)\Leftrightarrow\forall n\,\neg P(n)$. Every step is reversible, so the chain proves equality rather than one inclusion.

### Conclusion

Both sides equal $\mathbb R\setminus(-1,1)=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$.

content.title: Prove indexed De Morgan for unions
content.introMarkdown: Prove $U\setminus\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i=\bigcap_{i\in I}(U\setminus A_i)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the point where “no index” should become “every index fails.”

Indexed De Morgan is a quantified law.

Write the existential union condition and negate it formally.

## Indexed De Morgan laws

For a family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$, negating “there exists $i$ with $x\in A_i$” gives “for every $i$, $x\notin A_i$.” This yields $U\setminus\bigcup_iA_i=\bigcap_i(U\setminus A_i)$. The dual law reverses union and intersection.

content.title: Prove indexed De Morgan for intersections
content.introMarkdown: Prove $U\setminus\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i=\bigcup_{i\in I}(U\setminus A_i)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether failure of “for every index” produced at least one witness index.

The union of complements requires an existential witness.

Name the index whose membership fails and finish the equivalence chain.

## Boundary: empty index sets

With the standard conventions, the union over an empty family is $\varnothing$ and the intersection is $U$. The indexed laws remain valid. State these conventions if an empty index set is allowed.

lessons.title: Images, preimages, and point inverse images
lessons.summary: For a typed function, distinguish the image of a domain subset, the preimage of a codomain subset, and the preimage of a point using exact set-builder notation.
objectives: For a typed function, distinguish the image of a domain subset, the preimage of a codomain subset, and the preimage of a point using exact set-builder notation.

content.markdown:
## The direction of a map controls the direction of a set operation

An image moves a subset forward through a function. A preimage pulls a subset or point condition backward. The notation looks similar, but the ambient sets and logical operations differ.

## Reactivate the full function signature

Day 2 established elementwise set proofs; Week 1 established typed functions. Let $f:X\to Y$. The domain $X$ tells us where input subsets live, and the codomain $Y$ tells us where target subsets and target points live.

## Three different constructions

For $A\subseteq X$, the image is $f(A)=\{f(x):x\in A\}\subseteq Y$. For $B\subseteq Y$, the preimage is $f^{-1}(B)=\{x\in X:f(x)\in B\}\subseteq X$.

For a point $b\in Y$, write $f^{-1}(b)$ as an abbreviation for $f^{-1}(\{b\})=\{x\in X:f(x)=b\}$. This notation does not assert that $f$ has an inverse function.

content.title: Type the three expressions
content.introMarkdown: State the ambient set of $f(A)$, $f^{-1}(B)$, and $f^{-1}(b)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether each input subset and target subset was placed on the correct side of $f$.

The function signature determines every ambient set.

Write $f:X\to Y$ above the three set-builder definitions.

## Complete model: one map, three set operations

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $f(x)=x^2$, let $A=[-2,1]$, and let $B=[1,4]$.

Compute $f(A)$, $f^{-1}(B)$, and $f^{-1}(4)$.

### Strategy

Track the direction: send every point of $A$ forward, then solve target membership conditions backward.

### Hypotheses

$A$ lies in the domain and $B,4$ lie in the codomain.

### Intermediate claims

The square on $[-2,1]$ ranges from $0$ to $4$, so $f(A)=[0,4]$.

$1\le x^2\le4$ gives $x\in[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]$.

$x^2=4$ gives $x=\pm2$.

### Justification

The image and both preimages are computed from their separate set-builder definitions.

### Conclusion

$f(A)=[0,4]$, $f^{-1}(B)=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]$, and $f^{-1}(4)=\{-2,2\}$.

content.title: Compute image and preimages of a shifted square

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first computation that sent a target condition forward instead of pulling it back.

Images and preimages solve different problems.

Rewrite each requested set from its definition before solving inequalities.

## Preimages preserve unions and intersections

For subsets $B,C\subseteq Y$, $f^{-1}(B\cup C)=f^{-1}(B)\cup f^{-1}(C)$ and $f^{-1}(B\cap C)=f^{-1}(B)\cap f^{-1}(C)$. These follow directly from membership logic.

Images preserve unions but need not preserve intersections as equalities; different inputs can have the same image.

content.title: Prove a preimage identity
content.introMarkdown: Prove $f^{-1}(B\cap C)=f^{-1}(B)\cap f^{-1}(C)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the intersection was translated before or after applying $f$.

A preimage preserves the logical “and” because it tests one value $f(x)$.

Start with an arbitrary $x\in X$ and write the full equivalence chain.

## Complete proof model: preimage of a union

Let $f:X\to Y$ and $B,D\subseteq Y$.

Prove $f^{-1}(B\cup D)=f^{-1}(B)\cup f^{-1}(D)$.

### Strategy

Translate membership in a preimage into membership of the function value.

### Hypotheses

$f$ is a function with codomain containing $B$ and $D$.

### Intermediate claims

$x\in f^{-1}(B\cup D)$ iff $f(x)\in B\cup D$, iff $f(x)\in B$ or $f(x)\in D$.

### Justification

The final disjunction is exactly $x\in f^{-1}(B)$ or $x\in f^{-1}(D)$.

### Conclusion

The two sets have the same members.

content.title: Find strict image-intersection containment
content.introMarkdown: Compare $f(A\cap C)$ with $f(A)\cap f(C)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the two distinct inputs that collide under $f$.

The counterexample depends on noninjectivity, not on unusual sets.

Compute $f(-1)$ and $f(1)$ before comparing the two sides.

## Use a noninjective map deliberately

The square map makes image and preimage asymmetry visible. A point may have two preimages even though $f^{-1}(b)$ is written with inverse notation.

content.title: Coordinate image, preimage, and point preimage
content.introMarkdown: Compute $h(A)$, $h^{-1}(B)$, and $h^{-1}(2)$, with the correct ambient sets.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check every open and closed endpoint against the original interval.

A single endpoint error changes the image or preimage set.

Test $-3,1,-2,-1,1,2$ individually, then restate the inverse-notation boundary.

## Boundary: $f^{-1}$ has two uses

When $f$ is bijective, $f^{-1}$ may name an inverse function. In $f^{-1}(B)$ it always denotes a set preimage and is defined for every function. The surrounding type determines the meaning.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-04, source lines 595 to 604.

**Resource version:** Book of Proof, third edition.

**Exact locator:** Section 12.6: Point inverse images within Image and inverse image (Book of Proof, third edition, §12.6).

**Reading purpose:** Use the exact image and inverse-image definitions to compare with the square, shifted-square, and absolute-value computations on this page.
Tomorrow packages simultaneous equations as the inverse image of one point, while explicitly postponing affine-variety and canonical fiber theory.
Day 3 is complete when the direction, ambient set, and meaning of every occurrence of $f^{-1}$ are explicit.

activities.title: Find strict image-intersection containment
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $f(x)=x^2$, $A=\{-1\}$, and $C=\{1\}$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Both sides are computed and strict containment is shown.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The failure is traced to noninjectivity rather than to a set-algebra error.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $A\cap C=\varnothing$, so $f(A\cap C)=\varnothing$. But $f(A)=f(C)=\{1\}$, hence $f(A)\cap f(C)=\{1\}$. Equality fails because distinct inputs have the same image; injectivity would prevent this collision.

activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $h:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be $h(x)=|x|$, let $A=(-3,1]$, and let $B=[1,2)$.

rubric.description: The image $[0,3)$, interval preimage, and two-point preimage are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $h(A)=[0,3)$: zero occurs, values up to $1$ occur on the positive side, and values below $3$ occur on the negative side, but $3$ does not. Also $h^{-1}(B)=(-2,-1]\cup[1,2)$ and $h^{-1}(2)=\{-2,2\}$. The last object is a subset of the domain containing all inputs sent to $2$; $h$ is not injective and has no inverse function on all of $[0,\infty)$.

lessons.title: Simultaneous equation sets as point preimages
lessons.summary: Package simultaneous equations as the point preimage $F^{-1}(0,0)$ using only elementary set and function notation, while treating affine-variety and canonical fiber language as previews.
objectives: Package simultaneous equations as the point preimage $F^{-1}(0,0)$ using only elementary set and function notation, while treating affine-variety and canonical fiber language as previews.

content.markdown:
## One map can carry several equations

A pair of equations can be combined into a single function with two output coordinates. The common solution set is then the preimage of one point. This notation will recur later, but today it remains elementary set theory.

## Reactivate the exact set-theoretic dependency

Day 3 established point preimages for typed functions. Use $F:X\to Y$ and that definition only. No quotient ring, Zariski topology, scheme, base change, or affine-geometric theorem is available or needed.

## Package a system into one function

Given functions $f_1,f_2:X\to\mathbb C$, define $F:X\to\mathbb C^2$ by $F(x)=(f_1(x),f_2(x))$. Then

$$F^{-1}(0,0)=\{x\in X:F(x)=(0,0)\}=\{x\in X:f_1(x)=0\text{ and }f_2(x)=0\}.$$

This is an equality of sets obtained by expanding the definition of an ordered pair.

content.title: Build the coordinate map
content.introMarkdown: Define one typed map whose zero point preimage is the common solution set.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether both equations became separate output coordinates of one typed map.

A point preimage in $\mathbb R^2$ encodes a conjunction of two scalar equations.

Write the source, target, and ordered pair before the set-builder line.

## Complete model: a system as one point preimage

Define $G:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ by $G(x,y)=(x+y,x-y)$.

Describe and compute $G^{-1}(1,3)$.

### Strategy

Expand equality of ordered pairs into two scalar equations and solve them simultaneously.

### Hypotheses

The input is an ordered pair in $\mathbb R^2$ and the target point is $(1,3)\in\mathbb R^2$.

### Intermediate claims

$G(x,y)=(1,3)$ means $x+y=1$ and $x-y=3$. Adding gives $2x=4$, so $x=2$ and $y=-1$.

### Justification

Substitution gives $G(2,-1)=(1,3)$.

### Conclusion

$G^{-1}(1,3)=\{(2,-1)\}$.

### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first algebraic step that does not satisfy both coordinate equations.

A point preimage solves the system simultaneously.

Substitute the proposed point into the original ordered pair.

## Preview boundary: later names, no later theory

Later in Course R, the point preimage $F^{-1}(y)$ will be called a fiber, and some polynomial equation sets will be studied as affine varieties. Those are vocabulary previews only.

Today’s legitimate conclusion is the set equality obtained from the definition of $F$. Do not infer dimension, smoothness, irreducibility, coordinate rings, or behavior under base change.

content.title: State the exact evidence boundary
content.introMarkdown: Identify which conclusion is justified and which conclusions are unsupported.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the first conclusion that goes beyond equality of sets.

Later geometric properties need definitions and theorems not yet taught.

Keep the set equality and remove every unsupported dimension or smoothness claim.

## Complete model: a zero set in three coordinates

Let $H:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ be $H(x,y,z)=(x+y+z-1,x-y)$.

Write $H^{-1}(0,0)$ in set-builder notation and parametrize it as a set.

### Strategy

Expand the ordered-pair equality, solve $x=y$, and choose one free parameter.

### Hypotheses

Only ordinary real linear equations and point-preimage notation are used.

### Intermediate claims

$x-y=0$ gives $y=x$, and $x+y+z-1=0$ then gives $z=1-2x$.

### Justification

Every $s\in\mathbb R$ gives a solution $(s,s,1-2s)$, and every solution has this form.

### Conclusion

$H^{-1}(0,0)=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x+y+z-1=0,\ x-y=0\}=\{(s,s,1-2s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

content.title: Describe a nonlinear zero preimage
content.introMarkdown: Compute $F^{-1}(0,0)$ exactly.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first solution of one equation that was not checked in the other.

The zero preimage is an intersection of conditions.

Use $x=y$ first, solve the remaining equation, and verify both points.

## The source exercise in five coordinates

For functions $f_1,f_2:\mathbb C^5\to\mathbb C$, define $F=(f_1,f_2)$. The notation $X=F^{-1}(0,0)$ abbreviates exactly two equations and nothing stronger at this stage.

content.title: Write the five-coordinate equation set
content.introMarkdown: Express the common zero set $X$ in set-builder notation and as $F^{-1}(0,0)$.

### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the learner-facing target accidentally treats preview vocabulary as mastered theory.

Week 4 owns elementary sets and preimages only.

Restate the conclusion as an equality of subsets of $\mathbb C^5$ and name the deferred claims.

## Boundary: a point preimage is not yet a geometric fiber theory

The notation $F^{-1}(0,0)$ is valid elementary set notation. The canonical Course R fiber concept is taught much later, after affine varieties. No checkpoint today awards evidence for that future concept.

## Course reference
