activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Assume $\sqrt2=m/n$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ne0$, and $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Squaring gives $m^2=2n^2$, so $m^2$ is even and the parity lemma gives $m=2k$. Substitution gives $4k^2=2n^2$, hence $n^2=2k^2$, so $n$ is even. Thus $2$ divides both $m$ and $n$, contradicting $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Therefore $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

lessons.title: Coprime divisibility in the Euclidean domain $\mathbb C[t]$
lessons.summary: Prove in $\mathbb C[t]$ that coprimality and $L\mid DQ$ imply $L\mid D$, then recover the syllabus case $D=\dot L$, using either evaluation for a linear factor or a valid Euclidean-domain Bézout identity.
objectives: Prove in $\mathbb C[t]$ that coprimality and $L\mid DQ$ imply $L\mid D$, then recover the syllabus case $D=\dot L$, using either evaluation for a linear factor or a valid Euclidean-domain Bézout identity.

content.markdown:
## Use the theorem only in a ring where it is valid

The syllabus points toward a divisibility step needed much later. This week teaches a safe univariate prototype in $\mathbb C[t]$. This ring admits Euclidean division, so coprime polynomials satisfy a Bézout identity.

The source exercise writes the third polynomial as $\dot L$. Here $D$ is a neutral name for that polynomial variation: setting $D=\dot L$ recovers the exact implication $L\mid\dot LQ\Rightarrow L\mid\dot L$. No derivative property is used in this proof.

No claim about arbitrary coprime binary forms in $\mathbb C[T,S]$ is made today.

## Reactivate the exact prerequisites

Week 5 supplies implication structure. A direct proof must preserve the ring in every line. From polynomial arithmetic, use evaluation and the factor theorem. Function and injectivity notation remain part of the course foundation but do not replace divisibility arguments.

## The univariate proposition

Let $L,Q,D\in\mathbb C[t]$ and suppose $\gcd(L,Q)=1$. Because $\mathbb C[t]$ is a Euclidean domain, there exist $A,B\in\mathbb C[t]$ with $AL+BQ=1$.

Concretely, repeated polynomial division computes the gcd, and back-substitution expresses that gcd as $AL+BQ$. When the gcd is $1$, this is the required Bézout identity.

If $L\mid DQ$, multiply the identity by $D$: $D=ADL+BDQ$. Both terms on the right are divisible by $L$, so $L\mid D$.

In particular, substituting $D=\dot L$ proves the exact syllabus implication. The generic letter $D$ makes clear that the argument uses only divisibility, not any special property of the dotted polynomial.

For a linear $L=t-a$, evaluation gives a shorter proof: $L\mid DQ$ implies $D(a)Q(a)=0$, and coprimality gives $Q(a)\ne0$, hence $D(a)=0$ and $L\mid D$.

## Verify an explicit Bézout identity

For $L=t-1$ and $Q=t^2+1$,

$$-\frac{t+1}{2}(t-1)+\frac12(t^2+1)=1.$$

The identity can be checked by expansion. It certifies coprimality in $\mathbb C[t]$ and may be multiplied by any polynomial $D$.

content.title: State the safe univariate proposition
content.introMarkdown: State the desired conclusion and the ring property that licenses Bézout.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the ambient ring was stated before the Bézout claim.

The proof route depends on a structural theorem that is false in the later multivariable setting.

Add $L,Q,D\in\mathbb C[t]$ and name Euclidean division before revising the proof plan.

## Evaluation proves the linear-factor case directly

If $(t-1)\mid D(t)(t^2+1)$, evaluate at $t=1$. The product value is $2D(1)=0$, so $D(1)=0$. The factor theorem gives $(t-1)\mid D$.

The nonzero value $Q(1)=2$ is the exact place where coprimality with the linear factor is used.

content.title: Verify and use an explicit identity
content.introMarkdown: Verify $-(t+1)L/2+Q/2=1$ and derive $L\mid D$ from $L\mid DQ$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sign when expanding $-(t+1)(t-1)/2$.

If the identity does not equal $1$, multiplying it cannot recover $D$.

Verify the identity independently before multiplying by $D$.

## Complete analogous model: evaluate at the root of $L$

Let $L=t+2$ and $Q=t^2+t+1$ in $\mathbb C[t]$. Suppose $L\mid DQ$.

Prove $L\mid D$ by evaluation and identify the coprimality check.

### Strategy

Evaluate the divisible product at the root $-2$ of $L$ and show the other factor does not vanish there.

### Hypotheses

$D,Q,L$ are univariate complex polynomials. One has $Q(-2)=4-2+1=3\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

Since $(t+2)\mid DQ$, the factor theorem gives $D(-2)Q(-2)=0$. Thus $3D(-2)=0$, so $D(-2)=0$.

### Justification

The field $\mathbb C$ has no zero divisors, and $Q(-2)$ is nonzero. The factor theorem then converts $D(-2)=0$ into $(t+2)\mid D$.

### Conclusion

The desired divisibility holds. Coprimality is used concretely through $Q(-2)\ne0$.

content.markdown:
## A plausible proof can fail at its first theorem

The pair $T,S\in\mathbb C[T,S]$ has no common nonconstant factor, yet no polynomials $A,B$ satisfy $AT+BS=1$. The univariate Bézout route therefore cannot be copied into two variables.

The later Week 23 theory will prove the relevant divisibility statement by unique factorization and multiplicities. That proof is deliberately not taught here.

## Reactivate the scope controls

A polynomial claim must name its ring. A proof may invoke a theorem only after checking its structural hypotheses. Week 5 supplies implication and negation; function and injectivity remain typed examples. Today polynomial evaluation at $(0,0)$ supplies the decisive contradiction.

## The ideal $(T,S)$ is proper

Every element of $(T,S)$ has the form $A(T,S)T+B(T,S)S$ and therefore vanishes at $(0,0)$. The constant polynomial $1$ does not vanish there, so $1\notin(T,S)$.

Hence $(T,S)\ne\mathbb C[T,S]$. Although $T$ and $S$ share no nonunit common factor, they do not generate the unit ideal.

## Refute the proposed identity by evaluation

Assume $AT+BS=1$ for some $A,B\in\mathbb C[T,S]$. Evaluating at $(T,S)=(0,0)$ gives $0=1$, a contradiction.

This refutes the identity for the explicit coprime pair. It does not refute the separate Euclid-style divisibility lemma in a unique factorization domain.

Substitute $T=0$ and $S=0$ into the complete claimed equality.

## Locate the imported assumption

In $\mathbb C[t]$, every ideal is principal and gcd $1$ implies the ideal $(L,Q)$ is the whole ring. In $\mathbb C[T,S]$, not every ideal is principal. The step ‘gcd $1$, therefore $AL+BQ=1$’ imports a principal-ideal-domain theorem without its hypothesis.

Week 23 will distinguish gcd, unit ideal, prime factors, and multiplicities.

## Complete analogous model: another proper two-generator ideal

In $\mathbb C[X,Y]$, consider the pair $X-Y$ and $Y$.

Show that they have no common nonconstant factor but cannot satisfy $A(X-Y)+BY=1$.

### Strategy

Use the linear forms' non-associate status for coprimality and evaluate at their common zero for the failed identity.

### Hypotheses

Both polynomials are irreducible linear forms and are not scalar multiples, so their only common divisors are units.

### Intermediate claims

At $(X,Y)=(0,0)$, both $X-Y$ and $Y$ vanish. Therefore every element of the ideal $(X-Y,Y)$ vanishes at the origin.

### Justification

If $A(X-Y)+BY=1$, evaluation at the origin gives $0=1$. Thus the ideal is proper despite elementwise coprimality.

### Conclusion

Coprime elements in a multivariable polynomial ring need not generate the unit ideal.

## Preserve the true claim boundary

The implication ‘$\gcd(L,Q)=1$ and $L\mid DQ$ imply $L\mid D$’ is true in a unique factorization domain under the standard gcd interpretation. The proof uses irreducible-factor exponents, not the false unit-ideal inference.

Because that factorization and multiplicity theory belongs to Week 23, today records the claim as deferred and assesses only diagnosis of the invalid Bézout route.

## Boundary: refuting a proof is not refuting its conclusion

The example $(T,S)$ refutes ‘coprime implies Bézout identity’ in $\mathbb C[T,S]$. It does not provide $D$ for which $T\mid DS$ but $T\nmid D$.

A valid alternative proof of the divisibility conclusion remains possible and is deferred.

## Retrieval should strengthen method selection

Complex-root calculations supply exact evaluation points. Quantifier logic supplies the implication and negation structure. The week's corrected algebra supplies a theorem whose ring hypothesis is explicit.

A root-of-unity calculation is a finite algebraic problem. A quantified theorem states which polynomial, factor, and witness choices are universal or existential. A proof method is valid only inside the declared ring.

The first two checkpoints are scheduled deliberate reviews; the final three combine the retrieved tools with Week 6 proof selection.

## Complete model: complex evaluation inside the safe ring

Let $L=t-i$, $Q=t^2+1+t$, and suppose $L\mid DQ$ in $\mathbb C[t]$.

Use evaluation to decide whether $L\mid D$, and explain the proof-method choice.

### Strategy

Evaluate at $i$, the root of $L$, and check that the second factor is nonzero.

### Hypotheses

$Q(i)=i^2+1+i=i\ne0$. All polynomials lie in $\mathbb C[t]$.

### Intermediate claims

Divisibility gives $D(i)Q(i)=0$, hence $iD(i)=0$ and $D(i)=0$.

### Justification

The field has no zero divisors and $i\ne0$. The factor theorem converts $D(i)=0$ to $(t-i)\mid D$.

### Conclusion

A direct evaluation proof is shorter than contradiction because the linear factor exposes the decisive nonzero value immediately.

For a linear factor, evaluation is usually the shortest route. For a general univariate polynomial, Bézout packages all irreducible factors and multiplicities.

Both routes are direct proofs. The decision is mathematical, not stylistic.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
In $\mathbb C[t]$, $L=t^2+1$ and $Q=t$ are coprime, with the explicit identity $1\cdot(t^2+1)+(-t)\cdot t=1$. Multiplying by $D$ gives $D=D(t^2+1)-Dt^2$. Since $L\mid DQ=Dt$, it also divides $t(Dt)=Dt^2$, and it plainly divides $D(t^2+1)$. Hence $L\mid D$.

This is an instance of the universal $\mathbb C[t]$ coprime divisibility theorem. In $\mathbb C[T,S]$, gcd $1$ does not generally produce a Bézout identity, as $(T,S)$ shows. The complex factor $t^2+1=(t-i)(t+i)$ uses the scheduled Week 3 retrieval, while the universal implication and its counterexample form use the scheduled Week 5 retrieval.

lessons.summary: Disprove five plausible polynomial or function statements with counterexamples that satisfy every hypothesis and violate the stated conclusion, including one repeated-root transfer.
objectives: Disprove five plausible polynomial or function statements with counterexamples that satisfy every hypothesis and violate the stated conclusion, including one repeated-root transfer.

content.markdown:
## One valid counterexample defeats a universal claim

A counterexample is not merely an unusual example. It must lie inside every stated hypothesis and make the conclusion false.

Polynomial boundary cases are especially productive: cancellation of leading terms, missing real roots, noninjective symmetries, and simple roots mistaken for repeated roots.

## Reactivate the exact prerequisites

A polynomial retains its coefficient field, degree, and factorization. A complex root solves the polynomial equation in $\mathbb C$. Repeated-root transfer uses the criterion $p(a)=p'(a)=0$. Week 6 supplies proof-method and hypothesis checking. A function counterexample must respect its declared domain and codomain.

## A counterexample protocol

Write the universal statement as ‘for every object satisfying $H$, conclusion $C$ holds.’ Choose an object, verify $H$ line by line, then compute a direct failure of $C$.

Five useful false claims are: quadratic sums keep degree $2$; a zero at $0$ is automatically repeated; every real quadratic has a real root; equal polynomial values force equal inputs; two prescribed zeros force the zero polynomial.

## Cancellation and field choice

For $p=t^3$ and $q=-t^3$, both inputs have degree $3$ but $p+q=0$, so the sum does not have degree $3$. For $r=t^4+1\in\mathbb R[t]$, positivity shows that there is no real root.

Each example attacks a different hypothesis boundary.

content.title: Test a proposed counterexample
content.introMarkdown: Decide whether the proposed pair is a valid counterexample.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether every proposed polynomial satisfies the stated degree restriction.

An object outside the universal domain cannot refute the claim.

Verify the hypothesis list before calculating the sum.

## Root multiplicity and function collisions

For $p=t-1$, one has $p(1)=0$ but $p'(1)=1$, so $1$ is simple rather than repeated. This is a transfer use of the repeated-root criterion, not scheduled retrieval.

For the even polynomial function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=x^4$, the values at $1$ and $-1$ agree, so the map is not injective.

content.title: Build two distinct counterexamples
content.introMarkdown: Give one exact counterexample to each and verify its hypotheses.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the second example is being evaluated in the real rather than complex universe.

$t^4+1$ has complex roots but no real roots.

Write the coefficient field and root universe beside the example.

## Complete model: audit every part of a counterexample

Disprove: every cubic polynomial in $\mathbb R[t]$ has exactly one real root.

Give one cubic, verify its degree, and exhibit all of its distinct real roots.

### Strategy

Choose a factored cubic with three distinct real linear factors.

### Hypotheses

Let $f(t)=t^3-t=t(t-1)(t+1)\in\mathbb R[t]$. Its leading coefficient is nonzero, so it has degree $3$.

### Intermediate claims

The exact factorization gives the three distinct real roots $-1,0,1$.

### Justification

The factor theorem verifies each root, and the three distinct factors show that the claimed uniqueness fails.

### Conclusion

The universal statement is false.

content.title: Transfer the three-root cubic model
content.introMarkdown: Verify degree and exhibit three distinct exact real roots.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether all three proposed roots are distinct and make the polynomial exactly zero.

A single root or approximate values do not refute the exact uniqueness claim.

Use the displayed linear factors to verify each root on a separate line.

## Three zeros do not determine the zero polynomial

The polynomial $t(t-1)(t+1)$ vanishes at $-1,0,1$ but is not the zero polynomial. Finite agreement never determines an arbitrary polynomial unless a degree bound supplies enough points.

The next task assembles all five counterexamples with distinct failure mechanisms.

content.title: Complete three boundary counterexamples
content.introMarkdown: Give a different polynomial or function for each claim.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the repeated-root example first: both value and derivative are needed.

A simple root satisfies the value equation but not the derivative equation.

Place each claim's hypotheses and conclusion in separate columns and verify every row.

## Boundary: the example must satisfy the hypothesis

The zero polynomial cannot refute a claim restricted to degree-$3$ polynomials because its degree is not $3$. A complex root cannot refute a claim about real roots unless the root is real.

For repeated roots, vanishing alone is insufficient; the derivative must also vanish.

content.title: Present five complete counterexamples
content.introMarkdown: For each claim, state the universal domain, verify the chosen object's hypotheses, and compute the failed conclusion.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first numbered example whose object falls outside its stated universal domain.

A disproof succeeds only when the counterexample satisfies every hypothesis.

Audit hypothesis membership before retaining the conclusion failure.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-07, source lines 628 to 637.

**Resource version:** Book of Proof, third edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 9, §9.1: counterexamples (book-of-proof-3e-ch9-section-9.1).

**Reading purpose:** Use §9.1 to compare the hypothesis-audit structure of a counterexample with the five polynomial and function disproofs.

## Next: prove a universal sequence by induction

Counterexamples defeat false universal claims. Tomorrow proves a true family of identities by establishing a base case and a step that reaches every later integer.
A counterexample is complete only after its hypothesis membership and conclusion failure are both proved.

Give one exact counterexample to each and verify its hypotheses.

activities.title: Present five complete counterexamples
activities.promptMarkdown:
Disprove the five false claims treated on this page: degree of a quadratic sum, real root of a real quadratic, zero implying repeated root, equal values implying equal inputs, and two zeros implying the zero polynomial.

For each claim, state the universal domain, verify the chosen object's hypotheses, and compute the failed conclusion.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
1. In $\mathbb C[t]$, $t^2$ and $-t^2$ both have degree $2$, but their sum is $0$.

2. In $\mathbb R[t]$, $t^2+1$ has degree $2$ and no real root.

3. The polynomial $t$ vanishes at $0$, but its derivative equals $1$ there, so the root is not repeated. This is transfer of the repeated-root criterion, not scheduled review.

4. The typed map $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ sends $1$ and $-1$ to the same output.

5. The nonzero polynomial $t(t-1)$ vanishes at both $0$ and $1$.

lessons.title: Induction and the binomial theorem
lessons.summary: Prove the binomial theorem for every nonnegative integer exponent using a verified base case, an explicit induction hypothesis, and Pascal's identity.
objectives: Prove the binomial theorem for every nonnegative integer exponent using a verified base case, an explicit induction hypothesis, and Pascal's identity.

content.markdown:
## Induction explains why one algebraic pattern persists

Checking several exponents suggests the binomial formula but does not prove the infinite family. Induction links each exponent to the next one.

The induction step must use the hypothesis for exponent $n$ to derive the exact formula for exponent $n+1$.

## Reactivate proof and polynomial algebra

Week 6 supplies direct proof structure. Polynomial multiplication and coefficient collection justify every equality. The induction statement is indexed by $n\in\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.

## Induction and the target identity

Let $x$ and $y$ be commuting indeterminates. The calculation takes place in the polynomial ring $\mathbb C[x,y]$.

For $0\le k\le n$, the binomial coefficient is $\binom nk=n!/[k!(n-k)!]$, with $0!=1$. It counts the ways to choose which $k$ of the $n$ factors contribute $y$ when $(x+y)^n$ is expanded.

The binomial theorem states

$$(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk x^{n-k}y^k\qquad(n\in\mathbb N_0).$$

The base case is $n=0$. In the step, multiply the induction formula by $x+y$, shift one summation index, and use Pascal's identity $\binom nk+\binom n{k-1}=\binom{n+1}k$.

## Base case and induction hypothesis

At $n=0$, both sides equal $1$. For the step, fix $n\ge0$ and assume the displayed formula holds for that $n$. This assumption may be used only inside the step.

The target is the same formula with $n+1$ in every exponent and binomial coefficient.

content.title: State the induction obligations
content.introMarkdown: Write all three formulas explicitly.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether every exponent and summation endpoint changed from $n$ to $n+1$ in the target.

An incomplete target cannot establish the next member of the family.

Copy the theorem once, then replace the index consistently.

## The summation calculation

Multiplication gives two sums:

$$(x+y)^{n+1}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nkx^{n+1-k}y^k+\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nkx^{n-k}y^{k+1}.$$

Set $j=k+1$ in the second sum. The interior coefficient of $x^{n+1-j}y^j$ becomes $\binom nj+\binom n{j-1}$.

For $1\le j\le n$, the factorial definition proves Pascal's identity:

$$\binom nj+\binom n{j-1}=\frac{n!(n+1-j)+n!j}{j!(n+1-j)!}=\frac{(n+1)!}{j!(n+1-j)!}=\binom{n+1}j.$$

The endpoints give $x^{n+1}$ and $y^{n+1}$ because only one original sum contributes at each end.

content.title: Align the two binomial sums
content.introMarkdown: Shift the second index and identify the coefficient of $x^{n+1-j}y^j$ for $1\le j\le n$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the exponent of $x$ after setting $j=k+1$.

Coefficients can be combined only when both sums refer to the same monomial.

Rewrite the second sum entirely in $j$ before adding coefficients.

## Complete analogous model: sum of the first odd numbers

Prove $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^2$ for every integer $n\ge1$.

Give the complete base case and induction step.

### Strategy

Verify $n=1$. Add the next odd number $2(n+1)-1=2n+1$ to the induction hypothesis.

### Hypotheses

At $n=1$, the left side is $1$ and the right side is $1^2=1$, so the base case holds. For the step, assume for a fixed $n\ge1$ that $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^2$.

### Intermediate claims

The sum through the next odd number is $n^2+(2n+1)=(n+1)^2$.

### Justification

The new summand is exactly the $(n+1)$st odd number, and the final equality is the binomial expansion of $(n+1)^2$.

### Conclusion

The base case and step prove the identity for all $n\ge1$.

content.title: Transfer the induction model
content.introMarkdown: Give the base case and the complete algebra of the step.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the new term is $n+1$ rather than $n$.

Adding the wrong term does not move from the $n$th sum to the $(n+1)$st sum.

Write the two consecutive finite sums before performing the algebra.

## Pascal's identity is the hinge

The two expanded sums contribute to the same interior monomial. Their coefficients add. Pascal's identity converts that sum into the coefficient required for exponent $n+1$.

The endpoints are handled separately because only one of the two sums contributes there.

content.title: Complete the endpoint calculation
content.introMarkdown: Assemble the full target sum from endpoints and interior coefficients.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a nonexistent coefficient such as $\binom n{-1}$ was introduced without a convention.

The written proof should not rely on an unstated extension of binomial coefficients.

Separate the two endpoints before combining the interior range.

## Boundary: a step without a base proves no starting case

The implication $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$ can hold even when every $P(n)$ is false. The base case anchors the chain.

Likewise, verifying $n=0,1,2$ without a general step proves only three cases.

content.title: Prove the binomial theorem
content.introMarkdown: Give the complete base case, induction hypothesis, two-sum calculation, index shift, Pascal step, endpoints, and conclusion.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing link among base case, hypothesis use, index shift, Pascal identity, and endpoints.

Each link is required to derive the exact $n+1$ formula.

Repair the earliest missing link, then recheck all exponent and index ranges downstream.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-07, source lines 628 to 637.

**Resource version:** Book of Proof, third edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 3, §3.6: the binomial theorem; Chapter 10, §10.1: proof by induction (book-of-proof-3e-sections-3.6-and-10.1).

**Reading purpose:** Use §3.6 for Pascal's identity and the coefficient formula, and §10.1 for the base-and-step proof architecture.

## Next: prove both directions of an equivalence

Tomorrow replaces the induction chain by two implication proofs. Each direction begins from a different hypothesis and may need a different method.
The induction proof is complete only when the base anchors the family and the algebraic step produces every term of the $n+1$ formula.

activities.title: Align the two binomial sums
activities.promptMarkdown:
Starting from the induction hypothesis, expand $(x+y)^{n+1}=(x+y)(x+y)^n$ into two sums.

Shift the second index and identify the coefficient of $x^{n+1-j}y^j$ for $1\le j\le n$.

State Pascal's identity at the decisive line and verify it from the factorial formula.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The two sums are $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^{n+1-k}y^k$ and $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^{n-k}y^{k+1}$. Setting $j=k+1$ in the second, the interior coefficient is $\binom nj+\binom n{j-1}$. For $1\le j\le n$, this equals $[n!(n+1-j)+n!j]/[j!(n+1-j)!]=(n+1)!/[j!(n+1-j)!]=\binom{n+1}j$.

activities.promptMarkdown:

State exactly which new summand is added.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: At $n=1$, both sides equal $1$. Assume $1+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2$. Adding the next summand $n+1$ gives $n(n+1)/2+(n+1)=(n+1)(n+2)/2$, which is the formula for $n+1$.

activities.title: Complete the endpoint calculation
activities.promptMarkdown:
After combining interior terms in the induction step, identify the terms for $j=0$ and $j=n+1$.

Assemble the full target sum from endpoints and interior coefficients.

Explain why Pascal's two-term addition is not used at the endpoints.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The first sum alone contributes $x^{n+1}$ at $j=0$, with coefficient $\binom{n+1}{0}=1$. The second sum alone contributes $y^{n+1}$ at $j=n+1$, with coefficient $\binom{n+1}{n+1}=1$. Together with the interior terms, these give $\sum_{j=0}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}j x^{n+1-j}y^j$. At each endpoint only one original sum has an in-range term.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Both endpoint terms and the complete target sum are correct.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary
rubric.description: The response explains the index-range reason for handling endpoints separately.

activities.title: Prove the binomial theorem
activities.promptMarkdown:
For commuting indeterminates $x,y$, prove $(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nkx^{n-k}y^k$ for every $n\in\mathbb N_0$.

Give the complete base case, induction hypothesis, two-sum calculation, index shift, Pascal step, endpoints, and conclusion.

Write a continuous proof rather than a list of formulas.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Every part of the induction proof and summation algebra is correct.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary
rubric.description: The proof uses the hypothesis only in the step, handles endpoints honestly, and invokes induction after establishing base and step.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
For $n=0$, both sides equal $1$. Assume the formula for a fixed $n\ge0$. Then

$$(x+y)^{n+1}=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^{n+1-k}y^k+\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^{n-k}y^{k+1}.$$

In the second sum set $j=k+1$. For $1\le j\le n$, the coefficient of $x^{n+1-j}y^j$ is $\binom nj+\binom n{j-1}=\binom{n+1}j$. The endpoint terms are $x^{n+1}$ and $y^{n+1}$. Therefore the expression equals $\sum_{j=0}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}j x^{n+1-j}y^j$. The induction principle proves the theorem for every $n\in\mathbb N_0$.

lessons.title: Equivalence requires both directions
lessons.summary: Prove a biconditional by separating its two implications, choosing a valid method for each, and keeping the hypotheses of one direction out of the other.
objectives: Prove a biconditional by separating its two implications, choosing a valid method for each, and keeping the hypotheses of one direction out of the other.

content.markdown:
## An equivalence is two theorems

The notation $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ abbreviates $P\Rightarrow Q$ and $Q\Rightarrow P$. The two directions may use different definitions or proof methods.

A proof that silently reuses the first direction's hypothesis in the second is circular.

## Reactivate the proof and polynomial prerequisites

Week 6 supplies direct and contrapositive methods. A proof states the assumption for the current direction. Polynomial division and evaluation support the factor-theorem equivalence.

## Organize the biconditional

Write ‘Forward’ and ‘Reverse’ as separate proof paragraphs. Under ‘Forward,’ assume $P$ and derive $Q$. Under ‘Reverse,’ discard that assumption, assume $Q$, and derive $P$.

For $(t-a)\mid p\Leftrightarrow p(a)=0$, factorization proves the forward direction. Euclidean division with remainder proves the reverse direction.

## Forward factor-theorem direction

Assume $(t-a)\mid p$. Then $p=(t-a)q$ for some $q\in\mathbb C[t]$. Evaluating at $a$ gives $p(a)=0$.

This direction uses only the definition of divisibility and evaluation.

content.title: Separate the two obligations
content.introMarkdown: Write the assumption and target for each direction.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the reverse direction truly begins from $p(a)=0$.

Reusing divisibility there would assume the desired conclusion.

Create two columns headed by their different assumptions.

## Reverse factor-theorem direction

Assume $p(a)=0$. Euclidean division by $t-a$ gives $p=(t-a)q+r$ with constant $r$. Evaluating at $a$ gives $r=p(a)=0$, so $p=(t-a)q$ and $(t-a)\mid p$.

The desired factorization is derived rather than assumed.

content.title: Prove the forward factor direction
content.introMarkdown: Prove $p(a)=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether divisibility was expanded into an existential quotient.

The evaluation step needs an actual factorization.

Write $p=(t-a)q$ before substituting $t=a$.

## Complete analogous model: divisibility by $6$

For $n\in\mathbb Z$, prove $6\mid n$ if and only if $2\mid n$ and $3\mid n$.

Give both directions with their distinct arithmetic justifications.

### Strategy

Use explicit divisibility in the forward direction. In the reverse direction, combine the two factors using coprimality of $2$ and $3$.

### Hypotheses

The universe is $\mathbb Z$. The integers $2$ and $3$ are coprime.

### Intermediate claims

If $n=6k$, then $n=2(3k)=3(2k)$. Conversely, if $n=2a=3b$, then $3\mid2a$ and coprimality gives $3\mid a$, so $a=3k$ and $n=6k$.

### Justification

The forward direction expands the definition. The reverse uses Euclid's lemma in $\mathbb Z$.

### Conclusion

Both implications hold, so the biconditional is proved.

content.title: Diagnose the divisibility-by-six model
content.introMarkdown: Give the decisive line in each direction.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the reverse direction justified why $5$ divides the quotient $a$.

The two separate divisibility witnesses do not automatically combine.

Apply Euclid's lemma to $5\mid2a$ and state $\gcd(2,5)=1$.

## Audit a two-direction proof

For each paragraph, underline its starting assumption and circle its conclusion. Neither paragraph may begin with both sides of the biconditional.

A shared definition can appear in both directions, but the logical data must restart.

content.title: Prove the reverse factor direction
content.introMarkdown: Prove $(t-a)\mid p$ by Euclidean division.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the remainder was declared constant before evaluation.

The equality $r=p(a)$ uses the degree bound from division by a linear polynomial.

State $\deg r<1$, then evaluate the division equation.

## Boundary: proving the converse is not repetition

The first direction may be immediate while the converse requires a theorem. Calling the reverse ‘similar’ without giving its argument leaves the equivalence unproved.

Conversely, two proofs of $P\Rightarrow Q$ do not supply $Q\Rightarrow P$.

content.title: Prove the factor-theorem equivalence
content.introMarkdown: Prove $(t-a)\mid p(t)$ if and only if $p(a)=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first direction whose stated assumption does not match its paragraph.

A biconditional fails if either implication is circular or missing.

Audit the forward and reverse paragraphs independently before joining them with ‘if and only if.’

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-07, source lines 628 to 637.

**Resource version:** Book of Proof, third edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.2: if-and-only-if proofs and equivalent statements (book-of-proof-3e-ch7-sections-7.1-7.2).

**Reading purpose:** Use §§7.1–7.2 to compare the two-direction structure with the factor-theorem and divisibility equivalences.

## Next: audit an invalid equality proof

Tomorrow follows an equality chain until a forbidden division occurs, then repairs the theorem by adding the missing nonzero hypothesis.
An equivalence is established only when each direction starts from its own assumption and reaches the other side by a valid argument.

In the reverse direction, identify the coprimality step.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $n=10k$, then $n=2(5k)=5(2k)$. Conversely, if $n=2a$ and $5\mid n$, then $5\mid2a$. Since $\gcd(2,5)=1$, Euclid's lemma gives $5\mid a$, so $a=5k$ and $n=10k$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Both divisibility directions are correct.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary
rubric.description: The reverse proof names the exact coprimality use and does not assume a common witness.

activities.title: Prove the reverse factor direction
activities.promptMarkdown:
Assume $p(a)=0$ for $p\in\mathbb C[t]$.

Prove $(t-a)\mid p$ by Euclidean division.

Name the degree of the remainder and compute it by evaluation.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The division statement, constant remainder, evaluation, and factor conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary
rubric.description: The proof begins only from $p(a)=0$ and derives rather than assumes divisibility.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Euclidean division gives $p(t)=(t-a)q(t)+r$ with $r\in\mathbb C$ because the divisor has degree $1$. Evaluating at $a$ gives $0=p(a)=r$, so $p=(t-a)q$ and $(t-a)\mid p$.

activities.title: Prove the factor-theorem equivalence
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $p\in\mathbb C[t]$ and $a\in\mathbb C$.

Prove $(t-a)\mid p(t)$ if and only if $p(a)=0$.

Write two labelled paragraphs and finish by identifying the theorem used only in the reverse direction.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Both directions of the factor theorem are complete and correct.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary
rubric.description: The assumptions restart between directions and the division algorithm is used only where needed.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Forward: if $p=(t-a)q$, then $p(a)=0$. Reverse: if $p(a)=0$, Euclidean division gives $p=(t-a)q+r$ with constant $r=p(a)=0$, hence $(t-a)\mid p$. The reverse direction uses the division algorithm; the forward direction needs only the divisibility definition and evaluation.

lessons.title: Locate and repair division-by-zero fallacies
lessons.summary: Locate the first illegal division or cancellation in a false proof, construct a boundary counterexample, and state and prove the corrected theorem with its nonzero hypothesis.
objectives: Locate the first illegal division or cancellation in a false proof, construct a boundary counterexample, and state and prove the corrected theorem with its nonzero hypothesis.

content.markdown:
## A false proof often has many correct lines before one illegal step

The task is to locate the earliest invalid transition. Later contradictions are consequences of that error, not separate mistakes.

Cancellation is a theorem with a nonzero or no-zero-divisor hypothesis. It is not a visual editing operation.

## Reactivate proof-method and scope controls

Week 6 requires every theorem hypothesis to be checked. Week 5 supplies implication scope. A function or polynomial equality preserves its declared universe. Injectivity is a valid cancellation property for maps; algebraic cancellation requires a nonzero factor in an integral domain.

## The classic false equality proof

Assume $a=b$. Then $a^2=ab$, so $a^2-b^2=ab-b^2$, and $(a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b)$. The next line cancels $a-b$ and concludes $a+b=b$.

But $a=b$ makes $a-b=0$. Cancelling that factor divides both sides by zero. Every earlier equality is valid; this transition is not.

## Repair the cancellation theorem

Over $\mathbb C$, if $ac=bc$ and $c\ne0$, then $(a-b)c=0$. Since $\mathbb C$ has no zero divisors and $c\ne0$, it follows that $a-b=0$, so $a=b$.

Without $c\ne0$, take $c=0$, $a=1$, and $b=2$.

content.title: Locate the first illegal cancellation
content.introMarkdown: Name the operation and the exact expression whose value blocks it.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the value of the factor being removed under the original hypothesis.

Cancellation is valid only after a nonzero condition is established.

Substitute $a=b$ into the factor before accepting the implication.

## Preserve lost solutions

From $x^2=x$, writing $x(x-1)=0$ gives two cases: $x=0$ or $x=1$. Dividing by $x$ discards the valid solution $x=0$.

Factoring exposes the boundary case that cancellation would erase.

content.title: Build the zero-factor boundary case
content.introMarkdown: Give a counterexample and state the corrected theorem.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proposed inputs are distinct while their products remain equal.

A boundary example must violate the conclusion while satisfying the hypothesis.

Set the common factor to zero first, then choose two distinct remaining factors.

## Complete model: find the exact break

Audit the chain from $a=b$ through $(a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b)$ to $a+b=b$.

Identify the first invalid transition, give a numerical boundary instance, and state the corrected cancellation rule.

### Strategy

Verify each equality in order and inspect the factor being cancelled.

### Hypotheses

The initial hypothesis gives $a-b=0$. Choose $a=b=1$ for a concrete instance.

### Intermediate claims

With $a=b=1$, the factored equation is $0\cdot2=1\cdot0$, namely $0=0$. Cancelling the zero factor would yield $2=1$.

### Justification

Division by zero is undefined. Cancellation from $uc=vc$ to $u=v$ is valid only when $c\ne0$ in a field.

### Conclusion

The first invalid transition is cancellation of $a-b$. Adding $a-b\ne0$ would contradict the original assumption $a=b$, so the false proof cannot be repaired without changing its setup.

content.title: Transfer the fallacy diagnosis
content.introMarkdown: Identify the first invalid transition and evaluate both sides before and after it.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the cancelled factor at the supplied value $x=3$.

The symbolic appearance of a common factor does not make its inverse exist.

Evaluate the line before performing cancellation.

## Audit equations by reversible steps

Addition, subtraction, and expansion are reversible equalities. Multiplication by a fixed nonzero scalar is reversible. Division by a variable expression is reversible only after proving that expression is nonzero.

When the divisor may vanish, split into cases instead.

content.title: Prove the corrected theorem
content.introMarkdown: Prove $a=b$ without using an unlabelled cancellation.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proof explicitly uses $c\ne0$.

A correct theorem hypothesis must do work in the proof.

Name the inverse $c^{-1}$ or the no-zero-divisor implication at the decisive line.

## Boundary: a true conclusion can follow from an invalid step

An invalid proof is not rescued when its final sentence happens to be true. Validity concerns the implication from hypotheses through every transition.

Likewise, one illegal cancellation may lose only a boundary solution rather than produce an obvious contradiction.

content.title: Audit a lost-solution proof
content.introMarkdown: Locate the invalid step, solve the equation correctly, and state the conditional version of the division.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether $x=0$ was tested in the original equation before division.

Division by a variable is an equivalence only on the branch where that variable is nonzero.

Factor first and split the zero and nonzero cases explicitly.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-07, source lines 628 to 637.

**Resource version:** Book of Proof, third edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 9, §9.1: counterexamples; Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.2: conditional and equivalent reformulations (book-of-proof-3e-sections-9.1-and-7.1-7.2).

**Reading purpose:** Use the counterexample and equivalence sections to diagnose a failed cancellation and state the corrected theorem with its exact hypothesis.

## Next: retrieve sets and the corrected $\mathbb C[t]$ proof

Friday returns to Week 4 set notation and Week 6 proof methods. The divisibility retrieval will use only the corrected univariate proposition.
A proof audit succeeds when it identifies the first invalid transition, supplies the missing hypothesis, and preserves every boundary solution.

Assume $a=b$ and consider $(a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b)\Rightarrow a+b=b$.

Name the operation and the exact expression whose value blocks it.

State why all earlier algebra may still be correct.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The implication cancels or divides by $a-b$. The assumption $a=b$ gives $a-b=0$, so the operation is division by zero. The earlier expansion and subtraction steps are valid equalities; the first failure occurs only at cancellation.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary

Give a counterexample and state the corrected theorem.

Use distinct $a,b$ and identify the missing hypothesis.

Take $a=1$, $b=2$, and $c=0$. Then $ac=bc=0$ but $a
e b$. The corrected theorem adds $c
e0$: if $ac=bc$ and $c

activities.title: Transfer the fallacy diagnosis
activities.promptMarkdown:
Assume $x=3$ and examine $(x-3)(x+4)=2(x-3)\Rightarrow x+4=2$.

Identify the first invalid transition and evaluate both sides before and after it.

State the corrected conditional cancellation rule.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Under $x=3$, the factored equality is $0\cdot7=2\cdot0$, so $0=0$. Cancelling $x-3=0$ yields the false equation $7=2$. The corrected rule allows cancellation only when $x-3\ne0$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary

activities.title: Prove the corrected theorem
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $a,b,c\in\mathbb C$, suppose $ac=bc$, and assume $c\ne0$.

Prove $a=b$ without using an unlabelled cancellation.

Use either multiplication by $c^{-1}$ or the no-zero-divisor property.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The corrected cancellation proof is valid.

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary
rubric.description: The nonzero hypothesis is used exactly where invertibility or no-zero-divisor reasoning requires it.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Subtracting gives $(a-b)c=0$. Since $c\ne0$ and $\mathbb C$ has no zero divisors, $a-b=0$, hence $a=b$. Equivalently, multiply $ac=bc$ by the existing inverse $c^{-1}$.

activities.title: Audit a lost-solution proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
A solution of $x^2=x$ divides by $x$ and concludes $x=1$.

Locate the invalid step, solve the equation correctly, and state the conditional version of the division.

Explain why the invalid route loses rather than invents a solution.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Writing $x^2=x$ as $x(x-1)=0$ gives $x=0$ or $x=1$. Division by $x$ is valid only in the case $x\ne0$ and then yields $x=1$. The original equation also permits $x=0$, so unconditional division discards that boundary case. It loses a solution rather than creating a false new one.

rubric.label: Mathematical content

rubric.label: Proof structure and boundary
rubric.description: The response distinguishes conditional division from unconditional cancellation and explains the lost-solution mechanism.

lessons.title: Scheduled retrieval and Week 7 synthesis
lessons.summary: Retrieve Week 4 sets after three weeks and the corrected Week 6 $\mathbb C[t]$ divisibility proof after one week, then synthesize counterexample, induction, equivalence, and proof-audit methods.
objectives: Retrieve Week 4 sets after three weeks and the corrected Week 6 $\mathbb C[t]$ divisibility proof after one week, then synthesize counterexample, induction, equivalence, and proof-audit methods.

content.markdown:
## Retrieval now tests proof boundaries

Week 4 supplies typed sets, preimages, and membership equivalence. Week 6 supplies method selection and the corrected coprime-divisibility proposition in $\mathbb C[t]$.

Repeated-root material is not scheduled review today. Any appearance belongs to Week 7 transfer and is labelled accordingly.

## Reactivate the full dependency chain

A function and its preimages are typed. Week 5 supplies quantifier scope. A proof checks every hypothesis. Injectivity is refuted by one collision. Polynomial divisibility remains in the declared ring.

## Four methods, four evidence shapes

A counterexample supplies one valid witness to failure. Induction supplies a base and a link between consecutive cases. Equivalence supplies two implication proofs. Proof audit locates the first invalid transition and repairs its hypothesis.

The first two checkpoints are the only scheduled retrievals on this page.

## Deliberate review: Week 4 Day 4 after three weeks

Use a new polynomial map to prove a zero set equals one zero-point preimage. State the function signature before the membership chain; ‘fiber’ remains later vocabulary for this set.

### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the target singleton belongs to the codomain $\mathbb C^2$.

A preimage is meaningful only for a subset of the codomain.

Write the function signature before the elementwise equivalence.

## Deliberate review: Week 6 after one week

Prove a new $\mathbb C[t]$ divisibility instance. Check the Bézout identity and explicitly exclude the false $\mathbb C[T,S]$ route.

content.title: Retrieve the corrected $\mathbb C[t]$ lemma
content.introMarkdown: Prove $L\mid D$ using an explicit Bézout identity.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the stated Bézout identity expands to $1$.

The retrieved proof must preserve the corrected algebra, not only its conclusion.

Verify the identity before multiplying it by $D$.

## Complete model: choose the evidence shape

Classify four tasks: disprove a universal polynomial claim; prove a finite-sum formula; prove a set equality; diagnose cancellation by a variable.

Match each task to counterexample, induction, two-inclusion equivalence, or boundary-case proof audit.

### Strategy

Read the quantifier and conclusion form before choosing any algebra.

### Hypotheses

A universal disproof needs one witness; an indexed identity needs a recurrence; set equality needs membership in both directions; variable cancellation needs a nonzero case split.

### Intermediate claims

The four matches are counterexample, induction, elementwise biconditional or two inclusions, and proof audit with a zero-factor boundary.

### Justification

Each method produces exactly the evidence demanded by its logical form.

### Conclusion

Method selection is a consequence of the target, not a memorized daily template.

content.title: Transfer the method-classification model
content.introMarkdown: Choose counterexample, induction, membership equivalence, or proof audit and state the first evidence needed.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the first method whose evidence shape does not match the target's quantifier.

A method can be mathematically respectable yet fail to prove the stated claim.

Rewrite the target as universal failure, indexed family, equivalence, or conditional cancellation before choosing again.

## Build one coherent final argument

The final task combines a corrected divisibility proof with a proof audit. It asks what is true in $\mathbb C[t]$, why the proof works there, and where a copied multivariable proof would fail.

No repeated-root criterion is presented as scheduled retrieval.

content.title: Distinguish incomplete proof structures
content.introMarkdown: State exactly what each draft establishes and what remains missing.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a valid partial argument was accidentally promoted to the full theorem.

Correct local reasoning does not supply a missing logical obligation.

List the acceptance obligations for each proof form and mark the absent one.

## Boundary: retrieval must preserve corrections

A spaced-review system should not faithfully repeat a known false statement. The Week 6 retrieval is keyed to the corrected $\mathbb C[t]$ proposition.

The multivariable unique-factorization proof remains deferred to Week 23.

content.title: Complete the Week 7 proof-boundary synthesis
content.introMarkdown: Verify the univariate proof, locate the invalid multivariable generalization, and state the exact theorem boundary.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the valid $\mathbb C[t]$ proof and invalid $\mathbb C[T,S]$ inference were separated.

A correct special case does not license a theorem after its structural hypothesis changes.

Annotate the ambient ring on every Bézout line, then retain only the lines valid in that ring.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-07, source lines 628 to 637.

**Resource version:** Book of Proof, third edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 9, §9.1; Chapter 10, §10.1; Chapter 3, §3.6; Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.2 (book-of-proof-3e-week-07-sections-9.1-10.1-3.6-7.1-7.2).

**Reading purpose:** Use the exact counterexample, induction, binomial, and equivalence sections to review the four distinct proof architectures synthesized here.

## Next week: functions, bijections, and proof capstone

Week 8 will combine typed maps with the proof methods developed here. You will need complete equivalence arguments and careful cancellation boundaries.
Week 7 is complete when you can choose the evidence shape from the logical target and preserve every hypothesis, boundary case, and scheduled-review label.

activities.title: Retrieve a zero-set point-preimage equality
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^2$ be $F(x,y,z)=(x+y+z,xy-z)$ and $X=\{(x,y,z):x+y+z=0,\ xy-z=0\}$.

Prove $X=F^{-1}(\{(0,0)\})$.

Give an elementwise biconditional and name the scheduled three-week Week 4 retrieval.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For every $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb C^3$, membership in $X$ is equivalent to $x+y+z=0$ and $xy-z=0$, equivalent to $F(x,y,z)=(0,0)$, equivalent to membership in $F^{-1}(\{(0,0)\})$. Thus the sets are equal. This is the scheduled three-week retrieval of Week 4.

State exactly what each draft establishes and what remains missing.

The forward implication proves only $P\Rightarrow Q$; it leaves $Q\Rightarrow P$ unproved. Neither draft establishes its advertised theorem.

Let $L=t-1$, $Q=t^2+1$, and $D\in\mathbb C[t]$ with $L\mid DQ$. A draft proves $L\mid D$ using $-(t+1)L/2+Q/2=1$, then claims the same Bézout step works for $T,S\in\mathbb C[T,S]$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The identity $-(t+1)(t-1)/2+(t^2+1)/2=1$ is correct. Multiplying by $D$ shows $D$ is a sum of two multiples of $L$, because $L\mid DQ$; hence $L\mid D$ in $\mathbb C[t]$.

The multivariable generalization fails at ‘coprime implies Bézout identity’: $T,S$ have no common nonunit factor, but $AT+BS=1$ is impossible because evaluation at $(0,0)$ gives $0=1$. This refutes the proof route, not the unique-factorization divisibility conclusion deferred to Week 23.

Today's scheduled retrievals are Week 4 set and point-preimage notation after three weeks and Week 6 proof methods after one week. Reading that point preimage as a set-theoretic fiber is a later transfer, not part of the Week 4 source claim. Repeated-root work appeared earlier this week as transfer and is not a scheduled review on this page.

lessons.title: Typed maps and the two identities of a bijection
lessons.summary: State the full data of a map, type-check both composites, and distinguish the injectivity and surjectivity consequences of left and right inverses.
objectives: State the full data of a map, type-check both composites, and distinguish the injectivity and surjectivity consequences of left and right inverses.

content.markdown:
## Why inverse proofs begin with types

The capstone theorem is short only after its maps are stated correctly. An identity such as $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}$ is incomplete until the domain of that identity is known. Writing the types first prevents a plausible calculation from proving the wrong statement.

This week culminates in a conditional theorem about supplied polynomial maps. The course does not yet possess formulas for the later space $X$, so the present task is to master the proof architecture that those formulas will eventually enter.

## Reactivate the proof language

Use three established facts. A function includes its domain and codomain. An injective map satisfies $f(x)=f(x')\Rightarrow x=x'$. A proof must state its hypotheses and justify every implication.

For maps $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$, the composite $g\circ f$ is a map $A\to A$, while $f\circ g$ is a map $B\to B$. Keep these two identity maps distinct.

## Bijections and two-sided inverses

A map $f:A\to B$ is bijective when it is both injective and surjective. Maps $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$ are mutual inverses when

$$g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A\qquad\text{and}\qquad f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_B.$$

The first identity makes $g$ a left inverse of $f$; it forces $f$ to be injective. The second makes $g$ a right inverse of $f$; it forces $f$ to be surjective. Together they prove that $f$ is bijective and that $g=f^{-1}$.

content.title: Type-check the inverse identities
content.introMarkdown: State the domain and codomain of each composite and write the only type-correct identity that each composite could equal.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the middle set in each composition before checking any formula.

The two equations live on different sets and have different logical consequences.

Write $A\to B\to A$ and $B\to A\to B$, then restore the matching identity subscripts.

## What each side proves

Assume $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A$. If $f(a)=f(a')$, applying $g$ gives $a=g(f(a))=g(f(a'))=a'$. Thus $f$ is injective.

Assume instead $f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_B$. For any $b\in B$, the element $a=g(b)$ satisfies $f(a)=f(g(b))=b$. Thus $f$ is surjective.

Neither argument supplies the other property. A one-sided inverse becomes two-sided only when an additional hypothesis closes the missing direction.

content.title: Derive the one-sided consequences
content.introMarkdown: Prove directly that $u$ is injective and state, without claiming more, what remains unproved.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first line where the hypothesis $v\circ u=\operatorname{id}_P$ should replace a composite.

Injectivity is a statement about equal inputs after equal outputs, not a statement about reaching every target.

Restart with two points of $P$ and stop after proving they are equal.

## Complete worked model

Let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $F(t)=3t-4$ and let $G:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $G(s)=(s+4)/3$.

Prove that $F$ and $G$ are mutual inverses, then extract injectivity and surjectivity from the appropriate compositions.

### Strategy

Write the types, compute each composite on a variable from its own domain, and only then invoke the two-sided-inverse definition.

### Hypotheses

Both maps are defined on all real numbers, and division by $3$ is valid because $3\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

For every $t\in\mathbb R$,

$$G(F(t))=\frac{(3t-4)+4}{3}=t.$$

For every $s\in\mathbb R$,

$$F(G(s))=3\frac{s+4}{3}-4=s.$$

### Justification

The first identity is on the domain of $F$ and proves that $F$ is injective. The second is on its codomain and proves that $F$ is surjective.

### Conclusion

Both identities hold, so $G=F^{-1}$ and $F$ is bijective.

content.title: Diagnose the proof model
content.introMarkdown: Explain why the first calculation proves injectivity of $F$ and the second proves surjectivity of $F$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your injectivity sentence starts with equal outputs and your surjectivity sentence starts with an arbitrary target.

The composite equations are useful because they discharge two different quantifier patterns.

Rewrite each sentence from its definition and insert the matching composite only at the decisive step.

## Boundary: one identity may hold on a proper inclusion

Let $i:\{0,1\}\hookrightarrow\{0,1,2\}$ be inclusion and define $r(0)=0$, $r(1)=1$, $r(2)=0$. Then $r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_{\{0,1\}}$, but $i\circ r$ sends $2$ to $0$. The inclusion has a left inverse and is injective, yet it is not surjective.

This example is finite and explicit. It shows exactly why a polished inverse proof must verify the identity on the larger set as well.

content.title: Check a left inverse that is not an inverse
content.introMarkdown: Compute $q\circ j$ and $j\circ q$ at every relevant element, and classify the properties of $j$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Evaluate the composite on $c$ before stating any conclusion about bijectivity.

The extra codomain element is precisely what the left-inverse equation cannot see.

Add the missing evaluation and weaken the conclusion to the property actually proved.

## Transfer to a new pair of formulas

A two-sided inverse proof must show that the formulas are defined on the declared sets, that both composites are type-correct, and that both identities hold for arbitrary inputs. The final question removes the worked model's affine constants and asks you to control a non-linear inverse.

content.title: Prove a non-linear bijection
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $H$ is bijective with inverse $K$, and identify separately the injectivity and surjectivity evidence.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the first composite whose variable or identity domain is missing.

A complete inverse proof needs two universal identities, not two untyped simplifications.

Restore the type and quantifier for that composite, then reread the conclusion property by property.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-08, source lines 638 to 649.

**Resource version:** Book of Proof, third edition.

**Exact locator:** 12.1 Functions; 12.2 Injective and surjective functions (Book of Proof, third edition, Chapter 12, §§12.1–12.2).

**Reading purpose:** Read the definitions of a function, injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity before comparing them with the typed composite proofs on this page.

## Next: equation-defined targets

Day 2 keeps the same two-identity architecture but replaces maps of the real line with polynomial parametrizations of a line and a parabola in the affine plane.
You are ready to continue when you can type both composites, prove the separate one-sided consequences, and refuse a bijectivity claim when one identity is absent.

activities.title: Type-check the inverse identities
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$ be maps.

State the domain and codomain of each composite and write the only type-correct identity that each composite could equal.

Then identify which identity is the left-inverse condition for $f$ and which is the right-inverse condition.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
$g\circ f:A\to A$, so its identity condition is $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A$. This makes $g$ a left inverse of $f$.

$f\circ g:B\to B$, so its identity condition is $f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_B$. This makes $g$ a right inverse of $f$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both composites have the correct source and target, and each is matched with the correct identity map.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The left- and right-inverse labels follow from the written order of composition.

activities.title: Derive the one-sided consequences
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $u:P\to Q$ and $v:Q\to P$ satisfy $v\circ u=\operatorname{id}_P$.

Prove directly that $u$ is injective and state, without claiming more, what remains unproved.

Your proof must begin with $u(p)=u(p')$ and show exactly where the composite identity is used.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The response proves injectivity from the left-inverse identity and does not infer surjectivity.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The equality chain begins with two arbitrary domain points and explicitly applies the supplied identity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Let $p,p'\in P$ and assume $u(p)=u(p')$. Apply $v$ to both sides. Then

$$p=(v\circ u)(p)=v(u(p))=v(u(p'))=(v\circ u)(p')=p'.$$

Hence $u$ is injective. The equation does not prove that every $q\in Q$ lies in the image of $u$, so surjectivity and bijectivity remain unproved.

activities.title: Diagnose the proof model
activities.promptMarkdown:
In the worked proof for $F(t)=3t-4$ and $G(s)=(s+4)/3$, the two calculations use different variables and identity maps.

Explain why the first calculation proves injectivity of $F$ and the second proves surjectivity of $F$.

Give the two short arguments from the definitions rather than repeating only the composite formulas.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
If $F(t)=F(t')$, applying $G$ gives $t=G(F(t))=G(F(t'))=t'$, so $F$ is injective.

For any $s\in\mathbb R$, choose $t=G(s)$. Then $F(t)=F(G(s))=s$, so $F$ is surjective.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The response derives both properties from their definitions and uses the correct composite for each.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument distinguishes equality of preimages from existence of a preimage.

activities.title: Check a left inverse that is not an inverse
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $j:\{a,b\}\to\{a,b,c\}$ be inclusion and define $q(a)=a$, $q(b)=b$, and $q(c)=b$.

Compute $q\circ j$ and $j\circ q$ at every relevant element, and classify the properties of $j$.

State the one identity that holds, the input where the other fails, and the strongest justified conclusion.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
$q(j(a))=a$ and $q(j(b))=b$, so $q\circ j=\operatorname{id}_{\{a,b\}}$.

However, $(j\circ q)(c)=j(b)=b\ne c$, so $j\circ q$ is not the identity on $\{a,b,c\}$. Therefore $j$ is injective and has a left inverse, but it is not surjective or bijective.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both finite composites are evaluated correctly and the failed identity is witnessed at $c$.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The classification stops at injectivity and does not promote a left inverse to a two-sided inverse.

activities.title: Prove a non-linear bijection
activities.promptMarkdown:
Define $H:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ by $H(x)=x^3-5$ and $K:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ by $K(y)=\sqrt[3]{y+5}$.

Prove that $H$ is bijective with inverse $K$, and identify separately the injectivity and surjectivity evidence.

Write the types and both composition identities. End by explaining why either single identity would leave one property unproved.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both real composite identities are correct, and the inverse and bijectivity conclusions follow.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof states domains, quantifies arbitrary inputs, and assigns the correct logical consequence to each identity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Both maps are defined on all of $\mathbb R$. For $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$K(H(x))=\sqrt[3]{x^3-5+5}=x,$$

so $K\circ H=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}$ and $H$ is injective. For $y\in\mathbb R$,

$$H(K(y))=(\sqrt[3]{y+5})^3-5=y,$$

so $H\circ K=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}$ and $H$ is surjective. Hence $H$ is bijective and $K=H^{-1}$. The first identity alone would not prove surjectivity; the second alone would not prove injectivity.

lessons.title: Polynomial parametrizations of a line and a parabola
lessons.summary: Verify mutual inverse polynomial maps for equation-defined subsets of the affine plane and use the defining equation at the decisive composite.
objectives: Verify mutual inverse polynomial maps for equation-defined subsets of the affine plane and use the defining equation at the decisive composite.

content.markdown:
## Why an equation matters in an inverse calculation

A parametrization sends a coordinate to a point satisfying an equation. Its proposed inverse often projects back to that coordinate. The easy composite returns the parameter; the other composite returns the original point only because that point obeys the target equation.

This distinction is the small-scale version of the later capstone. There will eventually be explicit formulas for a more complicated $X$, but this lesson uses only targets whose equations are fully supplied.

## Recall the two checks

A formula into an equation-defined set must first land in that set. A two-sided inverse proof must then compute one identity on the parameter space and one identity on the target set.

Use the function, proof, and injectivity concepts from earlier weeks. Do not use an unstated geometric theorem.

## From a parameter to an equation-defined line

Let $L=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y=2x+3\}$. The map $\alpha:\mathbb R\to L$, $\alpha(t)=(t,2t+3)$, lands in $L$ because its coordinates satisfy the defining equation. The projection $\beta:L\to\mathbb R$, $\beta(x,y)=x$, is defined on every point of $L$.

The composite $\beta\circ\alpha$ is visibly the identity on $\mathbb R$. For $(x,y)\in L$, the other composite is $(\alpha\circ\beta)(x,y)=(x,2x+3)=(x,y)$, where the final equality uses $y=2x+3$.

content.title: Verify that a parametrization lands in its target
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $a$ defines a map $\mathbb R\to M$ and state the natural projection $b:M\to\mathbb R$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether you actually substituted both coordinates into $v=4u-1$.

A formula is not a map into an equation-defined target until membership has been proved.

Write the coordinate substitution first, then state the projection with $M$ as its domain.

## Use the target equation in the harder composite

For the line model, $(\beta\circ\alpha)(t)=t$ uses only the formulas. The equation of $L$ enters in $(\alpha\circ\beta)(x,y)=(x,2x+3)=(x,y)$.

A proof that ends at $(x,2x+3)$ has not yet shown the identity on $L$. The decisive sentence names the membership hypothesis $(x,y)\in L$ and extracts $y=2x+3$.

content.title: Compute both composites on a new line
content.introMarkdown: Compute $b\circ a$ on $\mathbb R$ and $a\circ b$ on an arbitrary point of $M$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the equality where $(u,4u-1)$ should become $(u,v)$.

That equality is true on $M$, not on every point of $\mathbb R^2$.

Insert “since $(u,v)\in M$, $v=4u-1$” before the conclusion.

## Complete worked model

Let $P=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y=x^2+2x\}$, $\phi(t)=(t,t^2+2t)$, and $\psi(x,y)=x$.

Prove from the defining equation that $\phi:\mathbb R\to P$ and $\psi:P\to\mathbb R$ are mutual inverse polynomial maps.

### Strategy

Check target membership, compute the parameter-space composite, then compute the target-space composite on a general point of $P$.

### Hypotheses

The target is exactly the set of real pairs satisfying $y=x^2+2x$. Both formulas are polynomial in ambient coordinates.

### Intermediate claims

The point $(t,t^2+2t)$ lies in $P$. Moreover,

$$(\psi\circ\phi)(t)=t.$$

For $(x,y)\in P$,

$$(\phi\circ\psi)(x,y)=\phi(x)=(x,x^2+2x)=(x,y).$$

### Justification

The last equality uses the supplied equation $y=x^2+2x$. It is not an ambient identity on all of $\mathbb R^2$.

### Conclusion

The two typed identities prove that $P$ is polynomially parametrized by one affine coordinate in this explicit case.

content.title: Locate the hypothesis in the parabola proof
content.introMarkdown: Identify the exact hypothesis needed to replace this pair by $(x,y)$ and explain why the equality would fail for a general point of $\mathbb R^2$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your cited equality follows from membership in $P$.

Inverse formulas on an equation-defined set may rely essentially on its equations.

Write the membership equation and test your claimed ambient equality at $(0,1)$.

## Boundary: projection need not recover a point

On the full plane, the maps $t\mapsto(t,t^2)$ and $(x,y)\mapsto x$ do not give a two-sided inverse: projecting $(0,1)$ and parametrizing again gives $(0,0)$. The inverse statement becomes true only after restricting the target to the parabola $y=x^2$.

A restriction is part of the theorem. It cannot be inferred from a suggestive picture.

content.title: Find the correct target restriction
content.introMarkdown: State the largest equation-defined graph $C\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ suggested by these formulas for which $c:\mathbb R\to C$ and $p:C\to\mathbb R$ are mutual inverses.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your target equation makes the second coordinate of $c(x)$ equal to $y$.

The second composite is an identity only on points satisfying that equation.

Define the graph first, then recompute the composite on a symbolic point of it.

## Independent parabola proof

The final target changes both coefficients and notation. Your proof should still have four visible stages: well-definedness, the first composite, the second composite with its equation, and the mutual-inverse conclusion.

content.title: Prove an explicit parabola isomorphism
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\Phi:\mathbb R\to Q$ and $\Psi:Q\to\mathbb R$ are mutual inverse polynomial maps.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proof establishes that $\Phi(t)$ belongs to $Q$ before composing.

Well-definedness and the two identities are separate obligations.

Restore the earliest missing obligation, then check the final conclusion against both composites.
