## Next week: abstract vector spaces

Week 10 turns the concrete coordinate sets used here into vector spaces, defines subspaces, and proves results about bases and dimension.
Week 9 is complete when you can solve a concrete system, compute its kernel and image, and prove the full fiber formula without invoking untaught rank-nullity.

activities.title: Type a matrix function
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

State the natural source and target of $x\mapsto Ax$ and determine its image.

Give an arbitrary-target preimage rather than relying on a dimension count.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$. Its image is all of $\mathbb R^2$ because for arbitrary $(r,s)$, the input $(r,s,0)$ maps to $(r,s)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The map type and full image are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Surjectivity is proved by a preimage formula.

activities.title: Prove a composition is injective
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ and $B:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ are injective matrix maps.

Prove directly that $BA$ is injective.

Use equal outputs rather than citing a theorem name.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The two injectivity hypotheses are applied in the correct order.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof begins with arbitrary equal composite outputs and reaches equality of inputs.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $BAx=BAx'$, injectivity of $B$ gives $Ax=Ax'$. Injectivity of $A$ then gives $x=x'$. Hence $BA$ is injective.

activities.title: Verify an inverse matrix pair
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $N=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

Compute $NM$ and $MN$ and state the conclusion.

Name the identity matrix and the source on which each product acts.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $NM=I_2$ and $MN=I_2$. Both act on $\mathbb R^2$. Therefore the associated linear maps are mutual inverses, and each matrix map is bijective.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both products equal the $2\times2$ identity.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The two-sided inverse conclusion follows from both typed identities.

activities.title: Translate a solution set into fiber language
activities.promptMarkdown:
For $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ and $b\in\mathbb R^2$, suppose $Ax_0=b$.

State the fiber $A^{-1}(b)$ and its relation to $A^{-1}(0)$.

Use preimage notation and then translate it into kernel notation.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $A^{-1}(b)=\{x:Ax=b\}=x_0+\ker A$. Also $A^{-1}(0)=\ker A$. Thus a nonzero fiber is a translate of the zero fiber whenever it is nonempty.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both preimage identities and the translation statement are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer includes the nonempty-fiber hypothesis through the supplied $x_0$.

activities.title: Identify an empty matrix fiber
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$ be $A(t)=(t,2t)$ and let $b=(1,0)$.

Determine $A^{-1}(b)$ and explain why it is not a translate of $\ker A$ by a solution.

Use the two coordinate equations to prove inconsistency.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $A(t)=(1,0)$ would require $t=1$ and $2t=0$ simultaneously, which is impossible. Hence $A^{-1}(b)=\varnothing$. Although $\ker A=\{0\}$, there is no $x_0$ with $Ax_0=b$, so the translate theorem does not apply.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The fiber is correctly shown to be empty and the kernel is identified.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The missing existence hypothesis is explicit.

activities.title: Synthesize Week 9 on a new matrix fiber
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $b=(4,1)^T$.

Find the complete fiber $A^{-1}(b)$ as a base point plus the kernel and prove your formula.

Include dimensions, elimination, a verified base point, a verified kernel generator, and both set inclusions.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The map type, base point, kernel generator, and fiber formula are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Both inclusions are proved and the result is interpreted as a nonempty fiber.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The map is $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$. One solution is $x_0=(2,1,0)$ because $Ax_0=(4,1)$. The kernel equations give $\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{(2,-1,1)\}$. If $Ax=b$, then $A(x-x_0)=0$, so $x\in x_0+\ker A$. Conversely, $A(x_0+tv)=b$ for every kernel vector $tv$. Hence $A^{-1}(b)=(2,1,0)+t(2,-1,1)$.

lessons.title: Vector spaces and the subspace test
lessons.summary: Use the vector-space axioms through the subspace test, prove concrete sets are subspaces, and reject sets that fail closure or contain no zero vector.
objectives: Use the vector-space axioms through the subspace test, prove concrete sets are subspaces, and reject sets that fail closure or contain no zero vector.

content.markdown:
## Why many different objects obey the same algebra

Coordinate tuples, solutions of homogeneous systems, and polynomials can all be added and scaled. A vector space records the common laws, allowing one proof about span or basis to apply across these different objects.

The abstraction is earned by Week 9: kernels already behaved like sets closed under addition and scaling. Today we state the structure precisely.

## Reactivate concrete linear combinations

From Week 9, a homogeneous solution set is preserved by adding solutions and multiplying a solution by a real scalar. From the function concept, remember that addition and scalar multiplication must be defined on the declared set.

We work over a specified field $\mathbb F$, usually $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

## Vector spaces and subspaces

A vector space over $\mathbb F$ is a set $V$ with addition and scalar multiplication that satisfy the following laws for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$: addition is associative and commutative; there is a zero vector and every vector has an additive inverse; $1v=v$; $(ab)v=a(bv)$; $a(u+v)=au+av$; and $(a+b)v=av+bv$. Its elements are vectors, even when they are functions or polynomials rather than arrows.

A subset $W\subseteq V$ is a subspace when it contains $0$ and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Equivalently, a nonempty subset is a subspace when $au+bv\in W$ for every $u,v\in W$ and every $a,b\in\mathbb F$.

content.title: Apply the subspace test
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $W$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^3$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proof treats arbitrary $u,v$ and arbitrary scalars.

A subspace claim is universal; examples cannot establish closure.

Introduce symbolic vectors and compute the defining expression on $au+bv$.

## Matrix kernels are subspaces

For an $m\times n$ matrix $A$, define $\ker A=\{x\in\mathbb F^n:Ax=0\}$. If $u,v\in\ker A$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$, the distributive laws for matrix multiplication give $A(au+bv)=aAu+bAv=0$. Thus the kernel of a matrix is a subspace of $\mathbb F^n$.

This is the abstract form of Week 9's homogeneous-direction calculation. Week 11 will define general linear maps and show that the same argument applies to their kernels.

content.title: Prove a kernel is closed
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\ker E=\{p:p(1)=0\}$ is a subspace.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether evaluation was distributed across both scalar multiples.

The kernel proof depends on linearity of the defining map.

Expand $(ap+bq)(1)$ before using the two zero conditions.

## Complete worked model

Let $S$ be the set of real $2\times2$ symmetric matrices.

Prove $S$ is a vector subspace of $M_2(\mathbb R)$ and give a three-vector coordinate description.

### Strategy

Use transpose identities for closure, then write a general symmetric matrix in terms of three fixed matrices.

### Hypotheses

A matrix is symmetric when $A^T=A$. Transpose distributes over addition and scalar multiplication.

### Intermediate claims

If $A^T=A$ and $B^T=B$, then $(aA+bB)^T=aA^T+bB^T=aA+bB$. Every symmetric matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x&y\\y&z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

### Justification

The displayed matrix equals $xE_{11}+y(E_{12}+E_{21})+zE_{22}$, and the coefficients are uniquely read from its entries.

### Conclusion

$S$ is a subspace with coordinates $(x,y,z)$ relative to the displayed three matrices.

content.title: Audit a matrix-subspace model
content.introMarkdown: Explain what each part proves and why the coordinate coefficients are unique.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your uniqueness claim identifies how each coefficient is recovered.

A spanning expression alone does not prove unique coordinates.

Compare corresponding matrix entries in two proposed expressions.

## Boundary: natural-looking sets may fail

The set of polynomials of degree exactly $2$ is not a subspace: it excludes the zero polynomial, and $t^2+(-t^2)=0$ leaves the set. The affine plane $x+2y-z=1$ is also not a subspace because it does not contain zero.

Homogeneous constraints tend to define subspaces; nonhomogeneous constraints tend to define translates.

content.title: Find the first failed subspace condition
content.introMarkdown: Give two independent reasons that $D$ is not a subspace of $\mathbb R[t]_{\le3}$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your chosen polynomials both have exact degree $3$.

A closure counterexample must begin with elements of the set.

Use $t^3$ and $-t^3$, then test their sum against the definition.

## Independent subspace proof

The final target is a space of functions. Treat addition and scalar multiplication pointwise and prove the defining condition survives arbitrary linear combinations.

content.title: Prove a function set is a vector subspace
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $W$ is a subspace of $V$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first evaluation condition not checked for the linear combination.

Membership in $W$ requires both zeros simultaneously.

Write the calculations at $0$ and $1$ on separate lines before concluding.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Use the sessions to compare coordinate vector spaces with concrete subspaces defined by homogeneous conditions.

## Next: span, independence, basis, and coordinates

Day 2 asks when a list generates a vector space without redundancy and when every vector therefore has unique coordinates.
You are ready to continue when you can prove subspace closure for arbitrary linear combinations and can produce exact counterexamples when a condition fails.

activities.title: Apply the subspace test
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x+2y-z=0\}$.

Prove that $W$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^3$.

Use the one-step linear-combination form of the subspace test.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The zero vector and closure under arbitrary linear combinations are proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The defining homogeneous equation is used linearly rather than checked on isolated examples.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The zero vector lies in $W$. If $u=(x,y,z)$ and $v=(x',y',z')$ lie in $W$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, then the defining expression on $au+bv$ is $a(x+2y-z)+b(x'+2y'-z')=0$. Thus $au+bv\in W$, so $W$ is a subspace.

activities.title: Prove a kernel is closed
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $E:\mathbb R[t]_{\le3}\to\mathbb R$ be evaluation at $1$: $E(p)=p(1)$.

Prove that $\ker E=\{p:p(1)=0\}$ is a subspace.

Show explicitly how evaluation acts on $ap+bq$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel condition and closure calculation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof transfers the abstract subspace test to polynomial functions.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The zero polynomial satisfies $E(0)=0$. If $p(1)=q(1)=0$, then for scalars $a,b$, $E(ap+bq)=(ap+bq)(1)=ap(1)+bq(1)=0$. Hence $ap+bq\in\ker E$, so the kernel is a subspace.

activities.title: Audit a matrix-subspace model
activities.promptMarkdown:
The symmetric-matrix model uses both a closure argument and a coordinate expression.

Explain what each part proves and why the coordinate coefficients are unique.

Name the entry that determines each coefficient.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The transpose calculation proves closure under arbitrary linear combinations, hence the subspace property. In $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x&y\\y&z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, the $(1,1)$ entry fixes $x$, the off-diagonal entry fixes $y$, and the $(2,2)$ entry fixes $z$, so the coordinates are unique.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The closure and coordinate roles are correctly separated.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Uniqueness is justified entry by entry.

activities.title: Find the first failed subspace condition
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $D$ be the set of real polynomials of degree exactly $3$.

Give two independent reasons that $D$ is not a subspace of $\mathbb R[t]_{\le3}$.

Use the zero-vector condition and one explicit closure failure.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The zero polynomial does not have degree exactly $3$, so $0\notin D$. Also $t^3$ and $-t^3$ lie in $D$, but their sum is the zero polynomial, which does not. Thus $D$ fails both the zero and addition conditions.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both the missing zero vector and a valid addition counterexample are given.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer identifies exact defining conditions rather than saying only that degree can drop.

activities.title: Prove a function set is a vector subspace
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V$ be the real vector space of all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, and let $W=\{f:f(0)=f(1)=0\}$.

Prove that $W$ is a subspace of $V$.

Check both evaluation conditions for an arbitrary linear combination.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The zero function and both pointwise closure conditions are proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument is universal in the two functions and two scalars.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The zero function lies in $W$. If $f,g\in W$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, then $(af+bg)(0)=af(0)+bg(0)=0$ and $(af+bg)(1)=af(1)+bg(1)=0$. Thus $af+bg\in W$, so $W$ is a subspace.

lessons.title: Span, linear independence, basis, and coordinates
lessons.summary: Distinguish spanning from linear independence, prove a list is a basis, and compute unique coordinates relative to an ordered basis.
objectives: Distinguish spanning from linear independence, prove a list is a basis, and compute unique coordinates relative to an ordered basis.

content.markdown:
## Why a basis solves two problems at once

A spanning list is expressive enough to build every vector. An independent list has no redundant direction. A basis has both properties, so every vector has one and only one coordinate column.

Coordinates depend on the ordered basis. The vector is intrinsic; its coordinate column is a representation chosen for a calculation.

## Use the vector-space structure

A linear combination of $v_1,\dots,v_n$ is $a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n$. Their span is the set of all such combinations.

The list is linearly independent when $a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n=0$ forces every coefficient to be zero.

## Spanning and independence are separate

In $\mathbb R^2$, the vectors $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,1)$ span the plane but are dependent because $(1,1)-(1,0)-(0,1)=0$. The single vector $(1,0)$ is independent but does not span the plane.

A basis is an ordered list that spans and is independent. The standard ordered basis of $\mathbb R^2$ is $e_1=(1,0)$, $e_2=(0,1)$.

content.title: Separate span from independence
content.introMarkdown: Decide whether the list spans $\mathbb R^2$ and whether it is independent.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your dependence relation uses coefficients that are not all zero.

Only a nontrivial zero combination proves dependence.

Compute $v_1+v_2$ and compare it with $v_3$.

## Why basis coordinates are unique

If $v=\sum a_iv_i=\sum b_iv_i$ in an independent list, subtracting gives $\sum(a_i-b_i)v_i=0$. Independence forces $a_i=b_i$ for every $i$.

Spanning supplies existence of coordinates; independence supplies uniqueness.

content.title: Prove coordinate uniqueness
content.introMarkdown: Prove $a_i=b_i$ for all $i$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the two representations were moved to the same side.

Independence applies to a linear combination equal to zero.

Subtract term by term, then invoke independence on the resulting coefficients.

## Complete worked model

Use the ordered basis $B=((1,1),(1,-1))$ of $\mathbb R^2$.

Find the $B$-coordinates of $(5,1)$ and verify the reconstruction.

### Strategy

Solve $a(1,1)+b(1,-1)=(5,1)$ by comparing coordinates.

### Hypotheses

The two basis vectors are independent because $a+b=0$ and $a-b=0$ imply $a=b=0$, and they span by the same solvable system.

### Intermediate claims

The equations are $a+b=5$ and $a-b=1$. Adding gives $2a=6$, so $a=3$; then $b=2$.

### Justification

$3(1,1)+2(1,-1)=(5,1)$.

### Conclusion

The coordinate column is $[(5,1)]_B=(3,2)^T$.

content.title: Change coordinates in a new vector
content.introMarkdown: Compute its $B$-coordinate column and reconstruct the vector.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the first coordinate multiplies the first listed basis vector.

Changing the basis order changes the coordinate column.

Rewrite the ordered expansion before solving the two equations.

## Boundary: coordinates require a basis

The list $((1,0),(2,0))$ is dependent and does not span $\mathbb R^2$. Some vectors have no representation, and vectors on its line have many representations. Calling coefficients “coordinates” would hide both failures.

content.title: Diagnose a failed coordinate system
content.introMarkdown: Give one vector with no $L$-representation and one vector with two different $L$-representations.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your nonunique representations have different coefficient pairs.

Uniqueness fails only when the same vector has genuinely different columns.

Write both coefficient pairs and evaluate both combinations.

## Independent basis proof and coordinates

The final list lives in polynomial space. Prove spanning and independence separately, then compute a coordinate column in the stated order.

content.title: Prove a polynomial list is a basis
content.introMarkdown: Prove $B$ is a basis and find the $B$-coordinates of $p(t)=2+3t+t^2$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first coefficient equation that is inconsistent with the ordered list.

A triangular coefficient argument depends on resolving the highest degree first.

Compare $t^2$, then $t$, then constants, and rebuild both the general and specific calculations.

**Reading purpose:** Use the session to compare existence from spanning with uniqueness from independence.

Day 3 applies basis and coordinate ideas to degree-$d$ homogeneous polynomials in two variables and counts their monomials.
You are ready to continue when you can prove both basis properties and can explain why ordered-basis coordinates are unique.

activities.title: Separate span from independence
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider $v_1=(1,1)$, $v_2=(1,-1)$, and $v_3=(2,0)$ in $\mathbb R^2$.

Decide whether the list spans $\mathbb R^2$ and whether it is independent.

Give one spanning calculation and one nontrivial dependence relation.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $v_1$ and $v_2$ span because $(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{2}v_1+\frac{x-y}{2}v_2$. The three-vector list is dependent because $v_1+v_2-v_3=0$. Thus it spans but is not a basis.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ be a basis of $V$ and suppose $x=a_1v_1+a_2v_2+a_3v_3=b_1v_1+b_2v_2+b_3v_3$.

Name the exact basis property used after subtraction.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Linear independence, rather than spanning, is identified as the uniqueness property.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Subtracting the two representations gives $(a_1-b_1)v_1+(a_2-b_2)v_2+(a_3-b_3)v_3=0$. Since a basis is linearly independent, every coefficient is zero. Hence $a_i-b_i=0$ and $a_i=b_i$ for $i=1,2,3$.

activities.title: Change coordinates in a new vector
activities.promptMarkdown:
Keep $B=((1,1),(1,-1))$ and consider $(4,-2)$.

Compute its $B$-coordinate column and reconstruct the vector.

Show the two scalar equations.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The coordinates $(1,3)$ and reconstruction are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The coordinate order follows the declared ordered basis.

activities.title: Diagnose a failed coordinate system
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the ordered list $L=((1,0),(2,0))$ in $\mathbb R^2$.

Give one vector with no $L$-representation and one vector with two different $L$-representations.

Explain which basis property fails in each example.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $(0,1)$ has no representation because every combination of the listed vectors has second coordinate zero; spanning fails. The vector $(2,0)$ equals $0(1,0)+1(2,0)$ and also $2(1,0)+0(2,0)$; uniqueness fails because the list is dependent.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The no-representation and multiple-representation examples are valid.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each failure is matched to spanning or independence.

activities.title: Prove a polynomial list is a basis
activities.promptMarkdown:
In $\mathbb R[t]_{\le2}$, let $B=(1,t+1,t^2+t)$.

Prove $B$ is a basis and find the $B$-coordinates of $p(t)=2+3t+t^2$.

Use coefficient comparison for both independence and the coordinate calculation.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Independence, spanning, and the coordinate column $(0,2,1)$ are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Coefficient comparison is used to prove both basis properties, not only to solve the final example.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $a+b(t+1)+c(t^2+t)=0$, coefficient comparison gives $c=0$, then $b+c=0$ so $b=0$, then $a+b=0$ so $a=0$; the list is independent. For any $\alpha+\beta t+\gamma t^2$, choose $c=\gamma$, $b=\beta-\gamma$, and $a=\alpha-\beta+\gamma$, proving spanning. For $p$, $c=1$, $b=2$, and $a=0$, so $[p]_B=(0,2,1)^T$.

lessons.title: Binary forms and the concrete dimension $d+1$
lessons.summary: Write explicit bases for homogeneous binary forms and prove from unique coefficients that the degree-$d$ space has dimension $d+1$.
objectives: Write explicit bases for homogeneous binary forms and prove from unique coefficients that the degree-$d$ space has dimension $d+1$.

content.markdown:
## Why homogeneous coefficients form a vector space

A binary form of degree $d$ is a polynomial in $T,S$ whose every monomial has total degree $d$. Its coefficients can be added and scaled, so the forms constitute a concrete vector space.

The formal tensor-quotient construction of a symmetric power is postponed to Week 15. Today we prove the $d+1$ count directly from monomials and use symmetric-power notation only as a preview.

## Reactivate polynomials and bases

A polynomial is determined uniquely by its coefficients. A basis must span and be independent. From Week 9, coordinate columns provide a concrete model for finite-dimensional spaces.

The vector-space prerequisite is active; the polynomial concept is reactivated for this argument.

## The monomial list

Every homogeneous binary form of degree $d$ has a unique expression

$$a_0T^d+a_1T^{d-1}S+\cdots+a_{d-1}TS^{d-1}+a_dS^d.$$

The $d+1$ monomials $T^d,T^{d-1}S,\dots,S^d$ span by this expression. They are independent because a zero polynomial has every coefficient equal to zero.

content.title: List a homogeneous basis
content.introMarkdown: List the standard monomial basis in descending powers of $T$ and state its size.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sum of the exponents in the first questionable monomial.

Homogeneity is controlled by total degree, not by the degree in one variable.

List exponent pairs $(4,0)$ through $(0,4)$ before rewriting the monomials.

## Prove spanning and independence

Spanning is immediate from the general coefficient expression. For independence, suppose $\sum_{i=0}^d a_iT^{d-i}S^i=0$. Equality with the zero polynomial forces $a_i=0$ for every $i$.

Therefore the concrete space of binary degree-$d$ forms has dimension $d+1$. This proves the numerical statement without yet constructing the formal symmetric-power quotient.

content.title: Prove the cubic monomials form a basis
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$ is a basis of $B_3$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your proof contains both existence of an expansion and uniqueness of the zero expansion.

A monomial list is a basis only after both spanning and independence are established.

Separate the general form from the zero-combination argument.

## Complete worked model

Let $B_2$ be the homogeneous binary quadratics with ordered monomial basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$.

Prove the basis claim and compute the coordinate column of $q=3T^2-2TS+5S^2$.

### Strategy

Use the unique coefficient expansion for both basis properties, then read the ordered coordinates.

### Hypotheses

Every term of a binary quadratic has total degree $2$, and distinct monomials have independent coefficient positions.

### Intermediate claims

Every $q$ is $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$. A zero such combination forces $c=d=e=0$.

### Justification

The ordered coefficient column of the displayed $q$ is $(3,-2,5)^T$.

### Conclusion

$B_2$ has dimension $3$ and the stated coordinate column.

content.title: Read and reconstruct binary-form coordinates
content.introMarkdown: Reconstruct the binary quadratic and verify its total degree.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check which monomial receives the middle coordinate.

A coordinate column is meaningless without its ordered basis.

Write the ordered basis over the three entries before reconstructing the form.

## Boundary: degree at most and homogeneous degree are different

$\mathbb C[T,S]_{\le2}$ contains $1,T,S,T^2,TS,S^2$ and has six standard monomials. The homogeneous degree-$2$ subspace contains only $T^2,TS,S^2$.

The formal notation $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ carries a tensorial meaning and convention choices that are not established here. Only the concrete homogeneous-form model is assessed.

content.title: Distinguish two polynomial spaces
content.introMarkdown: State which belong to the degree-at-most-two space and which belong to the homogeneous quadratic space.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the total degree of the term $S$.

A homogeneous polynomial requires every nonzero term to have the same total degree.

Annotate each monomial with its exponent sum, then revise the classification.

## Independent degree-$d$ proof

The final proof must work for arbitrary $d\ge0$. Count exponent pairs, prove spanning, and prove independence from coefficient uniqueness.

content.title: Prove the dimension of binary degree-$d$ forms
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $(T^d,T^{d-1}S,\ldots,TS^{d-1},S^d)$ is a basis and conclude $\dim B_d=d+1$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first place where spanning, independence, or the count is asserted without its general argument.

A dimension theorem needs a proved basis, not a pattern from low degrees.

Write the indexed coefficient expansion and use it once for spanning and once for independence.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-10, source lines 660 to 668.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Exact locator:** Unit I, Session 9: Independence, basis, and dimension — basis counting method in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Use the basis-counting method for the concrete binary-form space; no ARTIN or formal symmetric-power source is claimed here.

## Next: replacement and equal basis size

Day 4 proves that finite bases cannot have different lengths by replacing spanning vectors with independent ones.
You are ready to continue when you can prove the $d+1$ result from monomial coefficients and can state exactly which symmetric-power structure remains a preview.

activities.title: List a homogeneous basis
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider homogeneous binary quartics.

List the standard monomial basis in descending powers of $T$ and state its size.

Explain why $T^3S^2$ is not on the list.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The basis is $(T^4,T^3S,T^2S^2,TS^3,S^4)$, with five elements. The monomial $T^3S^2$ has total degree $5$, not $4$, so it is not a binary quartic.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All five quartic monomials and the total-degree exclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The list is organized by the exponent pairs summing to $4$.

activities.title: Prove the cubic monomials form a basis
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $B_3$ be the space of homogeneous binary cubics.

Prove that $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$ is a basis of $B_3$.

Give separate spanning and independence paragraphs.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both basis properties and the dimension conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Coefficient uniqueness is explicitly used for independence.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every binary cubic has the form $aT^3+bT^2S+cTS^2+dS^3$, so the four monomials span. If that combination is the zero polynomial, uniqueness of polynomial coefficients gives $a=b=c=d=0$, so the list is independent. Hence it is a basis and $\dim B_3=4$.

activities.title: Read and reconstruct binary-form coordinates
activities.promptMarkdown:
In the ordered basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$, consider coordinate column $(4,1,-3)^T$.

Reconstruct the binary quadratic and verify its total degree.

State why changing the basis order would change the column.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The form is $4T^2+TS-3S^2$. Each monomial has total degree $2$. Coordinates are indexed by the ordered basis, so reordering the monomials reorders the entries even though the polynomial is unchanged.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The reconstructed quadratic and homogeneity check are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The dependence of coordinates on basis order is stated precisely.

activities.title: Distinguish two polynomial spaces
activities.promptMarkdown:
Compare $p(T,S)=T^2+S$ and $q(T,S)=T^2+TS+S^2$.

State which belong to the degree-at-most-two space and which belong to the homogeneous quadratic space.

Justify each answer term by term.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Both $p$ and $q$ have total degree at most $2$, so both lie in $\mathbb C[T,S]_{\le2}$. Only $q$ is homogeneous of degree $2$, because all its monomials have total degree $2$. The term $S$ has degree $1$, so $p$ is not a binary quadratic form.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Membership in both spaces is classified correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The explanation uses the degree of every term.

activities.title: Prove the dimension of binary degree-$d$ forms
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $B_d$ be the complex vector space of homogeneous polynomials in $T,S$ of total degree $d$.

Prove that $(T^d,T^{d-1}S,\ldots,TS^{d-1},S^d)$ is a basis and conclude $\dim B_d=d+1$.

State the boundary of the conclusion: the formal tensor-quotient construction of $\operatorname{Sym}^d$ is not being proved on this page.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The basis proof and $d+1$ count are correct for every $d\ge0$.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer clearly limits the claim to the concrete homogeneous-form space.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every homogeneous degree-$d$ polynomial has a unique expression $\sum_{i=0}^d a_iT^{d-i}S^i$, so the listed monomials span. If their linear combination is zero, uniqueness of polynomial coefficients forces every $a_i=0$, so they are independent. There are $d+1$ exponent pairs $(d-i,i)$, hence $\dim B_d=d+1$. This proves the concrete homogeneous-form statement; the formal symmetric-power quotient and its canonical identifications wait until Week 15.

lessons.title: Replacement and equality of finite basis sizes
lessons.summary: Prove the finite replacement lemma and use it in both directions to show that any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have equal size.
objectives: Prove the finite replacement lemma and use it in both directions to show that any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have equal size.

content.markdown:
## Why dimension must not depend on the chosen basis

A vector space can have many bases. Dimension is meaningful only if all finite bases contain the same number of vectors.

The replacement lemma proves this without determinants or rank-nullity: an independent list cannot be longer than a finite spanning list.

## Reactivate span and independence

A spanning list writes every vector as a linear combination. An independent list has no nontrivial zero combination.

The decisive replacement step expresses a new independent vector in the current spanning list and replaces one vector with a nonzero coefficient.

## One replacement step

Suppose $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ spans $V$ and $w\ne0$. Write $w=a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n$. Some $a_j\ne0$. Solve for $v_j$:

$$v_j=a_j^{-1}\left(w-\sum_{i\ne j}a_iv_i\right).$$

Therefore replacing $v_j$ by $w$ leaves a spanning list. The nonzero coefficient is what makes the rearrangement legal.

content.title: Perform one spanning replacement
content.introMarkdown: Show that $(w,v_2,v_3)$ still spans $V$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sign of $v_2$ when solving for $v_1$.

The new list spans only if it can reconstruct the removed vector.

Isolate $2v_1$ first, then divide by the nonzero coefficient.

## The finite replacement lemma

Let $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ span $V$ and let $(w_1,\dots,w_m)$ be independent. Insert $w_1$ and remove a $v_j$ with nonzero coefficient. At step $k$, the current list contains $w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$ and still spans.

Express $w_k$ in that list. At least one coefficient of a remaining $v$ is nonzero; otherwise $w_k$ would lie in the span of $w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$, contradicting independence. Replace that $v$. The process can run for at most $n$ steps, so $m\le n$.

content.title: Justify the nonzero remaining coefficient
content.introMarkdown: Prove that an expansion of $w_k$ must have a nonzero coefficient on at least one remaining $v_j$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your contradiction shows $w_k$ lies in the span of the earlier $w$ vectors.

That is precisely what independence forbids at step $k$.

Delete the remaining-$v$ terms under the zero-coefficient assumption and read the resulting equation.

## Complete worked model

In $\mathbb R^3$, start from $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and use $w_1=(1,1,0)$, $w_2=(0,1,1)$, $w_3=(1,0,1)$.

Replace one vector at a time and verify that the final list is a basis.

### Strategy

Use a nonzero coordinate to replace $e_1$ with $w_1$, then express $w_2$ in the new spanning list, and repeat for $w_3$.

### Hypotheses

The standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ spans $\mathbb R^3$. Because the scalar $2$ is nonzero in $\mathbb R$, the final recovery equation can be divided by $2$.

### Intermediate claims

$e_1=w_1-e_2$, so $(w_1,e_2,e_3)$ spans. Next $w_2=e_2+e_3$, so $e_2=w_2-e_3$ and $(w_1,w_2,e_3)$ spans. Finally $w_3=w_1-w_2+2e_3$, so $e_3=(w_3-w_1+w_2)/2$.

### Justification

Each replacement has a nonzero coefficient, so the displayed recovery equations prove that $(w_1,w_2,w_3)$ spans $\mathbb R^3$. For independence, suppose $\alpha w_1+\beta w_2+\gamma w_3=0$. Comparing the three coordinates gives $\alpha+\gamma=0$, $\alpha+\beta=0$, and $\beta+\gamma=0$. The first two equations give $\beta=\gamma=-\alpha$; the third then gives $-2\alpha=0$. Hence $\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0$, so the list is independent.

### Conclusion

$(w_1,w_2,w_3)$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^3$.

content.title: Audit the third replacement
content.introMarkdown: Verify the identity and solve it for $e_3$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the third coordinate after subtracting $w_2$.

The replacement is valid only if the removed vector is exactly recoverable.

Verify the vector identity coordinate by coordinate before dividing by $2$.

## Boundary: a zero coefficient cannot support replacement

If $w=v_1+v_2$ in a spanning list $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, the coefficient of $v_3$ is zero. Replacing $v_3$ by $w$ may lose the $v_3$ direction. The lemma requires replacing a vector whose coefficient in the expansion of $w$ is nonzero.

content.title: Reject an illegal replacement
content.introMarkdown: Prove the new list does not span and identify the legal replacement choices.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the coefficient of the vector the draft removes.

A zero coefficient gives no equation from which to recover that vector.

Write all three coefficients of $w$ and choose only a nonzero one.

## Equal size of finite bases

If $B=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ and $C=(w_1,\dots,w_m)$ are bases, then $B$ spans and $C$ is independent, so the replacement lemma gives $m\le n$. Reversing their roles gives $n\le m$.

content.title: Prove that finite bases have equal size
content.introMarkdown: Prove $m=n$ from the replacement lemma.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether each inequality names which list spans and which is independent.

One application gives only one inequality.

Write the two applications on separate lines and reverse the roles for the second.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-10, source lines 660 to 668.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Exact locator:** Unit I, Session 9: Independence, basis, and dimension — exchange and basis-size consequences in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Use the session to compare the exchange argument with the complete replacement proof developed here.

## Next: scheduled retrieval and Week 10 synthesis

Day 5 retrieves polynomial structure, proof boundaries, and concrete linear systems before consolidating basis and coordinate reasoning.
You have completed the theorem when the nonzero replacement coefficient is justified and the equal-size proof includes both inequalities.

activities.title: Perform one spanning replacement
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ span $V$ and suppose $w=2v_1-v_2+3v_3$.

Show that $(w,v_2,v_3)$ still spans $V$.

Solve explicitly for the removed vector $v_1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The solved expression for $v_1$ is correct and proves spanning.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The nonzero coefficient $2$ is identified as the legal basis for replacement.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $v_1=\frac12(w+v_2-3v_3)$. Thus the new list generates $v_1$ as well as $v_2,v_3$, so it generates every vector generated by the original spanning list. Hence $(w,v_2,v_3)$ spans $V$.

activities.title: Justify the nonzero remaining coefficient
activities.promptMarkdown:
At step $k$, a spanning list begins with $w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$ and continues with unreplaced vectors $v_j$.

Prove that an expansion of $w_k$ must have a nonzero coefficient on at least one remaining $v_j$.

Explain the contradiction if every such coefficient were zero.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The nonzero remaining coefficient is proved from independence.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The contradiction identifies the exact forbidden dependence relation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If every coefficient on the remaining $v_j$ were zero, the expansion would write $w_k$ as a linear combination of $w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$. Then $w_1,\dots,w_k$ would be dependent, contradicting the assumed independence of the full $w$-list. Hence some remaining $v_j$ has nonzero coefficient and can be replaced.

activities.title: Audit the third replacement
activities.promptMarkdown:
The model claims $w_3=w_1-w_2+2e_3$.

Verify the identity and solve it for $e_3$.

Explain why the coefficient $2$ is the decisive replacement coefficient.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $w_1-w_2+2e_3=(1,1,0)-(0,1,1)+(0,0,2)=(1,0,1)=w_3$. Hence $e_3=(w_3-w_1+w_2)/2$. The nonzero coefficient $2$ permits recovery of the removed $e_3$, preserving span.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The identity and solved expression for $e_3$ are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The nonzero coefficient is tied to reversibility of replacement.

activities.title: Reject an illegal replacement
activities.promptMarkdown:
In $\mathbb R^3$, let $w=e_1+e_2$. A draft replaces $e_3$ in $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ by $w$.

Prove the new list does not span and identify the legal replacement choices.

Give one vector that cannot be generated by $(e_1,e_2,w)$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every combination of $e_1,e_2,w$ has third coordinate zero, so $e_3$ is not generated and the list does not span $\mathbb R^3$. Since $w=1e_1+1e_2+0e_3$, one may legally replace $e_1$ or $e_2$, but not $e_3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The lost direction and the two legal replacements are identified correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Replacement legality is linked to nonzero expansion coefficients.

activities.title: Prove that finite bases have equal size
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V$ have finite bases $B=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ and $C=(w_1,\dots,w_m)$.

Prove $m=n$ from the replacement lemma.

State and justify both inequalities; do not cite rank-nullity or determinants.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both replacement-lemma applications and the equality conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The spanning and independence roles of each basis are explicit in both directions.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $B$ spans $V$ and $C$ is independent, the finite replacement lemma gives $m\le n$. Because $C$ spans $V$ and $B$ is independent, applying the same lemma with the roles reversed gives $n\le m$. Therefore $m=n$. Thus the size of a finite basis depends only on $V$.

lessons.title: Retrieval and synthesis: from polynomials and systems to bases
lessons.summary: Retrieve polynomial arithmetic, proof boundary checks, and linear-system directions at scheduled intervals, then synthesize them in a basis proof.
objectives: Retrieve polynomial arithmetic, proof boundary checks, and linear-system directions at scheduled intervals, then synthesize them in a basis proof.

content.markdown:
## Why the reviews converge on basis

Polynomial coefficient lists become coordinates, counterexamples test basis hypotheses, and homogeneous solution directions become kernels. The 8-, 3-, and 1-week retrievals each supply one part of the Week 10 synthesis.

## Prerequisite chain

Use Week 1 function data, Week 6 proof structure, polynomial arithmetic, and Week 9 concrete linear systems. These are mathematical prerequisites, separate from the scheduled review intervals.

## Deliberate review: Week 2 after eight weeks

Division by a monic linear polynomial gives $p(t)=(t-a)q(t)+p(a)$. Today the quotient coefficients and remainder are interpreted as a coordinate decomposition.

content.title: Recover a polynomial decomposition
content.introMarkdown: Write $p=(t-1)q+r$ and verify the remainder by evaluation.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the coefficient of $t$ after multiplying $(t-1)q$.

One coefficient error changes the coordinate decomposition.

Multiply the proposed quotient back before keeping the remainder.

## Deliberate review: Week 7 after three weeks

A universal claim about spanning lists can fail through one redundant example. The counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis and violate the conclusion.

content.title: Disprove a false basis claim
content.introMarkdown: Disprove the claim with an explicit list in $\mathbb R^2$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your example really spans the whole plane.

A counterexample must satisfy the claim's premise.

Use a list containing the standard basis, then add a redundant vector.

## Deliberate review: Week 9 after one week

A kernel parametrization supplies spanning directions. To call those directions a basis, check that their only zero combination is trivial.

content.title: Promote kernel directions to a basis
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $(2,1,0)$ and $(-1,0,1)$ form a basis of $K$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proof establishes every vector of $K$ has the displayed expansion.

Verified directions need not span the whole kernel.

Solve the defining equation for $x$ before testing independence.

## Synthesize coordinates across representations

A polynomial basis converts a function-like object into a coefficient column. A kernel basis converts a homogeneous solution into parameter coordinates. In both cases, spanning gives existence and independence gives uniqueness.

content.title: Compare two coordinate constructions
content.introMarkdown: State what spanning and independence contribute in each case.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the reconstruction of the first incorrect coordinate column.

Coordinates are verified by rebuilding the original vector.

Multiply each basis vector by its proposed coefficient and add.

## Boundary: correct size does not prove basis

Two vectors in $\mathbb R^2$ can still be dependent, and three polynomials in a three-dimensional polynomial space can still fail to span. Size becomes decisive only after a theorem combines it with independence or spanning.

content.title: Reject basis-by-counting
content.introMarkdown: Show that the list has the expected length but is not a basis.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your dependence relation is nontrivial.

The correct list length does not remove redundancy.

Compare $t+1$ with the sum of the first two vectors.

## Complete worked model

In $\mathbb R[t]_{\le2}$, use $C=(1,t-1,(t-1)^2)$.

Prove $C$ is a basis and compute coordinates by expanding around $t=1$.

### Strategy

Expand in the monomial basis to get a triangular coefficient system, then solve from the highest degree downward.

### Hypotheses

The ambient polynomial space consists of all degree-at-most-two real polynomials.

### Intermediate claims

$a+b(t-1)+c(t-1)^2=c t^2+(b-2c)t+(a-b+c)$. Zero coefficients force $c=0$, then $b=0$, then $a=0$; arbitrary monomial coefficients can be solved in reverse.

### Justification

Thus the list is independent and spanning.

### Conclusion

$C$ is a basis; its coordinates are Taylor-like coefficients around $1$ without invoking calculus.

content.title: Complete the Week 10 basis synthesis
content.introMarkdown: Prove $B$ is a basis and find the $B$-coordinates of $p(t)=t^3+3t^2+5t+3$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the highest-degree coefficient comparison that first differs from the triangular argument.

Resolving coefficients from degree three downward controls the entire proof.

Expand the four basis elements, repair that coefficient, and continue downward before reconstructing $p$.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-10, source lines 660 to 668.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Exact locator:** Unit I, Sessions 7–9: special solutions, independence, basis, and dimension in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Review how concrete homogeneous directions become basis vectors and how independence controls unique coordinates.

## Next week: linear maps and their matrices

Week 11 uses ordered bases to turn linear maps into matrices, composes those matrices, and changes coordinates for binary forms.
Week 10 is complete when you can prove subspace and basis claims, count homogeneous-form dimensions, and prove finite basis size is well-defined.

activities.promptMarkdown:
Divide $p(t)=t^3-2t+3$ by $t-1$.

Write $p=(t-1)q+r$ and verify the remainder by evaluation.

Give every coefficient of $q$.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
