Tomorrow we will express the image as a quotient of the source and read elementary exact sequences.
Day 2 is complete when you can reconstruct both halves of the rank–nullity proof and state exactly where finite-dimensionality enters.

activities.title: Read the theorem with the correct ambient dimension
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $T:V\to W$ be linear with $\dim V=7$ and $\dim\ker T=3$.

Determine the rank and state what can and cannot be concluded about surjectivity when $\dim W=5$.

Use the source dimension in rank–nullity, then compare the resulting rank with the target dimension.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Rank–nullity gives $\operatorname{rank}T=7-3=4$. Since $\dim W=5$, a four-dimensional image cannot equal $W$, so $T$ is not surjective.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The rank and nonsurjectivity conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The source dimension is used in the theorem and the target dimension only in the surjectivity comparison.

activities.title: Prove the spanning half
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the basis notation from the proof architecture.

Prove carefully that $T(v_1),\ldots,T(v_s)$ span $\operatorname{im}T$.

Start with an arbitrary image vector $T(x)$ and expand $x$ in the full source basis.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The arbitrary image vector is shown to be in the span.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof exposes the preimage and uses the vanishing kernel components.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $y\in\operatorname{im}T$, choose $x\in V$ with $y=T(x)$. Write $x=\sum_i a_i k_i+\sum_j b_jv_j$. Since $T(k_i)=0$, linearity gives $y=T(x)=\sum_j b_jT(v_j)$. Thus the displayed images span $\operatorname{im}T$.

activities.title: Prove the independence half
activities.promptMarkdown:
Return to the abstract extended basis $(k_1,\ldots,k_r,v_1,\ldots,v_s)$.

Prove that $T(v_1),\ldots,T(v_s)$ are linearly independent.

Translate a zero relation in the image into membership in the kernel, then use uniqueness of basis coordinates.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The image list is proved linearly independent.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Kernel membership is converted into a relation in the extended source basis.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $\sum_j b_jT(v_j)=0$, then $T(\sum_j b_jv_j)=0$, so $\sum_j b_jv_j\in\ker T$. Hence $\sum_j b_jv_j=\sum_i a_ik_i$ for some scalars. Rearranging gives a relation in the full basis; all coefficients vanish, so every $b_j=0$.

activities.title: Audit the theorem hypotheses
activities.promptMarkdown:
A proof says: “$T:V\to W$ is linear, so $\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T$.”

Identify the missing hypothesis for the numerical theorem used this week and explain where it enters the proof.

Point to the basis-extension and finite counting step.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The proof must assume that $V$ is finite-dimensional. Then a finite kernel basis extends to a finite basis of $V$, and counting the kernel vectors and added vectors yields the integer equality.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The missing finite-dimensional hypothesis is identified.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response locates the exact proof step that uses the hypothesis.

activities.title: Prove rank–nullity for a difference operator
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $\Delta:\mathbb R[t]_{\le4}\to\mathbb R[t]_{\le3}$ be $\Delta p(t)=p(t+1)-p(t)$.

Determine the kernel, prove that $\Delta$ is surjective, and verify rank–nullity.

Use leading terms to show that differences of $t,t^2,t^3,t^4$ span polynomials of degrees $0,1,2,3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel, surjectivity argument, and dimension check are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Leading terms establish the triangular independence and spanning argument.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The kernel consists of constant polynomials: a nonconstant polynomial of degree $m$ has difference of degree $m-1$ with nonzero leading coefficient. Moreover $\Delta(t^j)$ has degree $j-1$ and leading coefficient $j$, so the four differences for $j=1,2,3,4$ form a triangular spanning family of $\mathbb R[t]_{\le3}$. Thus rank $=4$, nullity $=1$, and $5=4+1$.

lessons.title: Quotient spaces and elementary exactness
lessons.summary: Interpret cosets in a quotient vector space and verify exactness by comparing an image with the next kernel.
objectives: Interpret cosets in a quotient vector space and verify exactness by comparing an image with the next kernel.

content.markdown:
## Remove precisely the information a map cannot see

Two source vectors have the same image exactly when their difference lies in the kernel. The quotient $V/\ker T$ packages this equivalence and leaves only the information visible to $T$.

## Reactivate subspaces and equivalence

For a subspace $U\subseteq V$, the coset $v+U$ contains every vector differing from $v$ by an element of $U$. Addition and scalar multiplication are performed on representatives and must be shown independent of that choice.

## The quotient vector space

The quotient $V/U$ is the set of cosets $v+U$. We declare

$$(v+U)+(w+U)=(v+w)+U,\qquad a(v+U)=av+U.$$

These operations are well-defined because changing $v$ or $w$ by elements of $U$ changes the result by another element of $U$.

content.title: Recognize equal cosets
content.introMarkdown: Decide whether $(2,0,1)+U$ equals $(1,-1,1)+U$ and justify the criterion you use.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Subtract the two representatives before comparing their coordinates.

Cosets can be equal even when their displayed representatives differ.

Compute the difference and express it as a scalar multiple of $(1,1,0)$.

## Why the induced map is well-defined

For $T:V\to W$, define $\bar T:V/\ker T\to\operatorname{im}T$ by $\bar T(v+\ker T)=T(v)$.

If two cosets are equal, their representatives differ by a kernel vector, so their images agree. The induced map is injective by the same criterion and surjective by the definition of the image.

content.title: Prove the induced map is an isomorphism
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\bar T$ is well-defined, linear, injective, and surjective onto $\operatorname{im}T$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check well-definedness before discussing injectivity or surjectivity.

A formula on cosets is not a map until it is independent of representatives.

Assume two representatives differ by a kernel vector, compare their images, and then prove the remaining properties.

## Complete worked model

Let $S:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $S(x,y)=x+y$ and let $U=\ker S=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1)\}$.

Describe $\mathbb R^2/U$ concretely and identify the induced isomorphism to $\mathbb R$.

### Strategy

Use $x+y$ as a coset invariant and choose $(s,0)$ as a representative of the coset with invariant $s$.

### Hypotheses

Two vectors have the same sum exactly when their difference belongs to $U$.

### Intermediate claims

Every $(x,y)+U$ equals $(x+y,0)+U$, and $\bar S((x,y)+U)=x+y$.

### Justification

The invariant is constant on cosets and every real number occurs.

### Conclusion

The quotient is one-dimensional and $\bar S:\mathbb R^2/U\to\mathbb R$ is an isomorphism.

content.title: Construct a different quotient coordinate
content.introMarkdown: Construct explicitly an isomorphism $\mathbb R^2/K\to\mathbb R$ and give a canonical representative for each coset.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check that adding a vector of $K$ leaves your proposed coordinate unchanged.

A quotient coordinate must be constant on each entire coset.

Use $x-y$, verify invariance under $(x,y)\mapsto(x+a,y+a)$, then find a representative with second coordinate zero.

## Exactness at one space

A sequence $U\xrightarrow{A}V\xrightarrow{B}W$ is exact at $V$ when $\operatorname{im}A=\ker B$.

For $T:V\to W$, let $\widetilde T:V\to\operatorname{im}T$ denote the same formula with its codomain restricted to the image. Then

$$0\longrightarrow\ker T\longrightarrow V\xrightarrow{\widetilde T}\operatorname{im}T\longrightarrow0$$

is short exact: the first map is injective, its image is $\ker\widetilde T=\ker T$, and $\widetilde T$ is surjective by definition. The separate inclusion $\operatorname{im}T\hookrightarrow W$ records how reachable outputs sit inside $W$. It is not appended after $T:V\to W$, because those two arrows are not composable.

content.title: Check exactness by two inclusions
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\mathbb R\xrightarrow{A}\mathbb R^2\xrightarrow{B}\mathbb R$ is exact at $\mathbb R^2$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether you proved only that the composite is zero.

$B\circ A=0$ gives only $\operatorname{im}A\subseteq\ker B$, not equality.

Take an arbitrary kernel vector and solve for the scalar whose image under $A$ equals it.

## Transfer: quotient structure and exactness together

The quotient $V/\ker T$ and exactness of $\ker T\hookrightarrow V\xrightarrow{T}\operatorname{im}T$ are two descriptions of the same information: the kernel is removed, and the remaining classes are identified with reachable outputs.

content.title: Analyze evaluation through a quotient
content.introMarkdown: Determine $\ker E$, construct the induced isomorphism $\mathbb R[t]_{\le2}/\ker E\to\mathbb R$, and write an exact sequence at the polynomial space.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the kernel contains exactly, rather than merely at least, the multiples of $t-2$.

The induced quotient map is injective only after the exact kernel is known.

Apply the factor theorem to $p(2)=0$, then prove well-definedness and surjectivity separately.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-12, source lines 677 to 684.

**Resource version:** MIT Differential Forms, 30 January 2019 edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 1 §1.2, pp. 4–8: quotient spaces, quotient maps, and induced maps; Chapter 5 §5.2, p. 183: exact and short exact sequences in MIT Differential Forms, 30 January 2019 edition.

**Reading purpose:** Read the quotient-map construction first, then use the exact-sequence definition to connect $V/\ker T$ with $\operatorname{im}T$.
Tomorrow the same dimension logic will be applied to the supplied differential of polynomial multiplication, without yet importing the later Jacobian theory.
Day 3 is complete when you can work with cosets, prove the induced quotient-to-image isomorphism, and verify exactness by equality of an image and a kernel.

activities.title: Recognize equal cosets
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $U=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0)\}\subseteq\mathbb R^3$.

Decide whether $(2,0,1)+U$ equals $(1,-1,1)+U$ and justify the criterion you use.

Subtract the representatives and test membership in $U$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The coset comparison is correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Equality is justified by the representative-difference criterion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The difference is $(1,1,0)$, which lies in $U$. Therefore the two cosets are equal. In general, $v+U=w+U$ exactly when $v-w\in U$.

activities.title: Prove the induced map is an isomorphism
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $T:V\to W$ be linear and define $\bar T$ as above.

Prove that $\bar T$ is well-defined, linear, injective, and surjective onto $\operatorname{im}T$.

Give one short argument for each property and keep the codomain equal to the image.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All four properties are proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each property uses the relevant definition and the correct codomain.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $v-v'\in\ker T$, then $T(v)=T(v')$, so the formula is well-defined. Linearity follows from the quotient operations and linearity of $T$. If $\bar T(v+\ker T)=0$, then $v\in\ker T$, so the coset is zero; hence $\bar T$ is injective. Every $y\in\operatorname{im}T$ equals $T(v)=\bar T(v+\ker T)$, so it is surjective.

activities.title: Construct a different quotient coordinate
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $D(x,y)=x-y$ and $K=\ker D=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)\}$.

Construct explicitly an isomorphism $\mathbb R^2/K\to\mathbb R$ and give a canonical representative for each coset.

Adapt the worked model without reusing its sum invariant.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The quotient map, representative, and isomorphism proof are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The difference invariant replaces the non-identical sum invariant from the model.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Define $\bar D((x,y)+K)=x-y$. It is well-defined because adding $(a,a)$ does not change the difference. Every coset equals $(x-y,0)+K$, so these vectors provide representatives. The map is linear, injective by the kernel criterion, and surjective because $\bar D((s,0)+K)=s$.

activities.title: Check exactness by two inclusions
activities.promptMarkdown:
Define $A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$ by $A(t)=(t,-t)$ and $B:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ by $B(x,y)=x+y$.

Prove that $\mathbb R\xrightarrow{A}\mathbb R^2\xrightarrow{B}\mathbb R$ is exact at $\mathbb R^2$.

Show both inclusions between $\operatorname{im}A$ and $\ker B$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The image and kernel are proved equal.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Both set inclusions are explicit and use the defining formulas.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every $A(t)=(t,-t)$ satisfies $B(A(t))=0$, so $\operatorname{im}A\subseteq\ker B$. Conversely, if $(x,y)\in\ker B$, then $x+y=0$, hence $(x,y)=(x,-x)=A(x)$. Thus $\ker B\subseteq\operatorname{im}A$, proving equality and exactness.

activities.title: Analyze evaluation through a quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $E:\mathbb R[t]_{\le2}\to\mathbb R$ be $E(p)=p(2)$.

Determine $\ker E$, construct the induced isomorphism $\mathbb R[t]_{\le2}/\ker E\to\mathbb R$, and write an exact sequence at the polynomial space.

Prove the kernel description by polynomial division and verify the induced formula on cosets.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel, quotient isomorphism, and exactness statement are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Polynomial division supplies the equality-of-cosets criterion and the proof does not omit well-definedness.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\ker E=(t-2)\mathbb R[t]_{\le1}$. The induced map $\bar E(p+\ker E)=p(2)$ is well-defined and bijective because equality of values at $2$ is equivalent to a difference divisible by $t-2$, and constants show surjectivity. The sequence $\ker E\hookrightarrow\mathbb R[t]_{\le2}\xrightarrow{E}\mathbb R$ is exact at the polynomial space and, since $E$ is surjective, also at $\mathbb R$ if followed by $0$.

lessons.title: Dimension counting for the multiplication differential
lessons.summary: Type the supplied linear map $dM_{(L,Q)}$, count source and target dimensions, prove a kernel lower bound, and state what remains unproved.
objectives: Type the supplied linear map $dM_{(L,Q)}$, count source and target dimensions, prove a kernel lower bound, and state what remains unproved.

content.markdown:
## A dimension count can reveal a necessary hidden direction

For multiplication of a linear form and a quadratic form, five input coefficients produce four output coefficients. The derivative supplied by the syllabus must therefore lose at least one direction.

## Reactivate symmetric-form dimensions

Let $V$ be a two-dimensional vector space over a field $k$, and choose a dual basis $T,S$ of $V^\vee$. The binary forms of degree $d$ form $\operatorname{Sym}^dV^\vee$, with basis $T^d,T^{d-1}S,\ldots,S^d$ and dimension $d+1$. Direct sums add dimensions. Rank–nullity applies once the displayed formula is recognized as a linear map in the dotted variables.

## Type the supplied map before counting

Fix nonzero binary forms $L\in\operatorname{Sym}^1V^\vee$ and $Q\in\operatorname{Sym}^2V^\vee$. The syllabus supplies

$$dM_{(L,Q)}:\operatorname{Sym}^1V^\vee\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^2V^\vee\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^3V^\vee,$$

$$dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q.$$

This week treats that formula as a given linear map. Week 16 will derive derivative and Jacobian language.

content.title: Count the typed dimensions
content.introMarkdown: Compute the source and target dimensions and deduce the strongest unconditional lower bound on the kernel dimension.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether you wrote rank $=4$ or only rank $\le4$.

The codomain dimension bounds rank but does not prove every cubic is reached.

Use rank $\le4$ in rank–nullity and conclude only nullity $\ge1$.

## The relative-scaling direction is visibly lost

Substituting $(\dot L,\dot Q)=(L,-Q)$ gives

$$dM_{(L,Q)}(L,-Q)=LQ-LQ=0.$$

Thus relative rescaling supplies a concrete kernel direction. This proves existence, not uniqueness, of the lost direction.

content.title: Verify the infinitesimal scaling direction
content.introMarkdown: Verify directly that $(2L,-2Q)$ lies in the kernel of $dM_{(L,Q)}$ and explain why this does not determine the whole kernel.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your conclusion says “is contained in” or “equals.”

One nonzero kernel vector proves a lower bound, not an upper bound.

Keep the direct calculation, then weaken the conclusion to line containment.

## Complete worked model

Fix $(a,b)=(2,3)$ and define $D_{(2,3)}:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ by $D_{(2,3)}(u,v)=3u+2v$.

Analyze the kernel as an elementary analogue of the multiplication formula.

### Strategy

Solve one homogeneous equation and compare its solution dimension with rank–nullity.

### Hypotheses

The map is nonzero because $D_{(2,3)}(1,0)=3$.

### Intermediate claims

The kernel equation $3u+2v=0$ gives $(u,v)=s(2,-3)$. The map has rank one because its codomain is one-dimensional and the map is nonzero.

### Justification

Rank–nullity then gives nullity $2-1=1$, confirming that the displayed line is the whole kernel.

### Conclusion

An exact kernel conclusion requires both a kernel witness and a matching upper bound from rank.

content.title: Identify the missing argument in the polynomial case
content.introMarkdown: Explain what analogous fact would be needed to conclude that the polynomial multiplication differential has a one-dimensional kernel.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Ask which inequality must become equality in the five-to-four dimension count.

Exact kernel dimension cannot be inferred from source and target sizes alone.

State rank $=4$ and translate it into surjectivity onto cubic forms.

## Preview boundary: linear algebra now, geometry later

The notation $dM$ anticipates the total derivative, and its kernel will later describe directions tangent to a fiber. Those interpretations are previews only.

Today we have proved a statement about one supplied linear map. We have not defined a Jacobian, proved differentiability, constructed an affine variety, or identified a Zariski tangent space.

content.title: Classify the justified claims
content.introMarkdown: Identify the valid conclusion available today and the additional theories that the proposed conclusion would require.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Underline the first geometric word that has not yet been defined in this week.

A correct linear dimension count cannot silently supply geometric hypotheses.

Retain only the kernel lower bound and list the later definitions and theorem needed for smoothness.

## Transfer: make the strongest justified prediction

A good dimension heuristic states both its evidence and its uncertainty. It can guide the next proof without masquerading as that proof.

content.title: Write the dimension argument with an honest boundary
content.introMarkdown: Write a complete argument for the kernel lower bound, exhibit the scaling direction, and formulate the one-dimensional-kernel statement explicitly as a conjectural generic expectation.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether any sentence turns the rank upper bound into equality without proof.

The week deliberately stops before the exact kernel theorem.

Replace the equality claim by a lower bound, retain the scaling witness, and state rank $4$ as the missing condition.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-12, source lines 677 to 684.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Exact locator:** Unit I, Sessions 6 and 9: column space, nullspace, basis, and dimension in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Use rank, nullity, and the four-subspaces framework to audit the supplied multiplication differential without importing later geometry.
Tomorrow’s synthesis will reconnect this calculation to earlier inverse-image, system-solving, and matrix viewpoints.
Day 4 is complete when you can justify nullity at least one, exhibit the scaling direction, and explain exactly why the kernel has not yet been proved one-dimensional.

activities.title: Count the typed dimensions
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the displayed type of $dM_{(L,Q)}$ for binary forms.

Compute the source and target dimensions and deduce the strongest unconditional lower bound on the kernel dimension.

Do not assume surjectivity.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The source has dimension $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^1+dim\operatorname{Sym}^2=2+3=5$, while the target has dimension $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^3=4$. Hence rank is at most $4$, and rank–nullity gives $\dim\ker dM_{(L,Q)}=5-\operatorname{rank}dM_{(L,Q)}\ge1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The dimensions and lower bound are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument does not replace the rank bound with an unproved surjectivity claim.

activities.title: Verify the infinitesimal scaling direction
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $L=T+2S$ and $Q=T^2-TS+3S^2$.

Verify directly that $(2L,-2Q)$ lies in the kernel of $dM_{(L,Q)}$ and explain why this does not determine the whole kernel.

Use bilinearity of multiplication and separate membership from equality of subspaces.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel calculation and its limited scope are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes a witnessed subspace from a complete kernel description.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $dM_{(L,Q)}(2L,-2Q)=2LQ+L(-2Q)=0$, so the pair is a kernel vector. It spans the same scaling direction as $(L,-Q)$. The calculation proves only that this line is contained in the kernel; other independent kernel vectors are not excluded.

activities.title: Identify the missing argument in the polynomial case
activities.promptMarkdown:
In the scalar model, nonzeroness forced full rank because the target dimension was one.

Explain what analogous fact would be needed to conclude that the polynomial multiplication differential has a one-dimensional kernel.

State the required rank and an equivalent image statement.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: One would need to prove that $\operatorname{rank}dM_{(L,Q)}=4$, equivalently that the map is surjective onto the four-dimensional cubic-form space. Only then would rank–nullity give nullity $5-4=1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The missing rank or surjectivity statement is correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response links exact nullity to the precise unproved upper bound.

activities.title: Classify the justified claims
activities.promptMarkdown:
A solution concludes from the five-to-four dimension count that the later factorization space is a smooth threefold.

Identify the valid conclusion available today and the additional theories that the proposed conclusion would require.

Separate kernel dimension, differentiability, defining equations, and smoothness.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Today the dimension count proves only $\dim\ker dM_{(L,Q)}\ge1$ and the scaling calculation gives one kernel direction. A smooth-threefold conclusion would require a defined geometric space, its equations, differentiability or algebraic tangent theory, the relevant rank condition, and a theorem connecting that condition to smoothness.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The valid and deferred claims are separated correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response names the missing bridges rather than treating dimension counting as a smoothness proof.

activities.title: Write the dimension argument with an honest boundary
activities.promptMarkdown:
For nonzero $L\in\operatorname{Sym}^1V^\vee$ and $Q\in\operatorname{Sym}^2V^\vee$, use the supplied formula for $dM_{(L,Q)}$.

Write a complete argument for the kernel lower bound, exhibit the scaling direction, and formulate the one-dimensional-kernel statement explicitly as a conjectural generic expectation.

Your final sentence must name the additional rank statement needed for proof.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The dimension count, kernel witness, and conditional expectation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response marks the precise boundary between theorem, evidence, and conjectural generic behavior.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The source has dimension $5$ and the target dimension $4$, so rank–nullity gives nullity at least $1$. The nonzero pair $(L,-Q)$ lies in the kernel because $LQ-LQ=0$. Thus the relative-scaling line is contained in the kernel. It is reasonable to expect generically that this is the entire kernel, but proving that expectation requires rank $4$, equivalently surjectivity of $dM_{(L,Q)}$; it does not follow from the dimension count alone.

lessons.title: Rank–nullity synthesis and scheduled retrieval
lessons.summary: Integrate inverse-image, system, matrix, quotient, and rank–nullity viewpoints while distinguishing proved conclusions from dimension heuristics.
objectives: Integrate inverse-image, system, matrix, quotient, and rank–nullity viewpoints while distinguishing proved conclusions from dimension heuristics.

content.markdown:
## One theorem, several established viewpoints

The week closes by retrieving three earlier ideas at their scheduled intervals and then using them inside one structural analysis. Review is labelled because these are old objects in a more independent setting.

## Prepare the synthesis

Recall that a kernel is the inverse image of zero, a homogeneous system describes a nullspace, and a matrix represents a linear map only relative to bases. Rank–nullity must agree with all three descriptions.

## Scheduled 8-week review: inverse images

Week 4 Day 3 established image and inverse-image notation. Retrieve it now without notes and connect it to kernels.

content.title: Recover a kernel as an inverse image
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\ker T=T^{-1}(\{0_W\})$ and explain why this inverse image is a subspace.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write the three equivalent membership statements for an arbitrary $v$.

The kernel notation is a special case of the inverse-image concept, not a separate set operation.

Prove the set equality elementwise, then apply linearity to the resulting set.

## Scheduled 3-week review: free variables

Week 9 Day 3 interpreted a homogeneous system through pivots and free variables. Recover the same information now as rank and nullity.

content.title: Translate a row reduction into rank–nullity
content.introMarkdown: State the rank, nullity, and dimension of the solution space, and justify the identification of that solution space.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Count columns, not rows, when determining the number of source variables.

Rank–nullity splits the source dimension into pivot and free directions.

Use five source coordinates, three pivot columns, and two free columns.

## Scheduled 1-week review: matrices of maps

Week 11 Day 1 built matrices from basis images. Retrieve that construction and use its columns to determine the image.

content.title: Read rank and nullity from basis images
content.introMarkdown: Construct the matrix, then find a kernel basis, image basis, rank, and nullity.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write the column relation with coefficients in source-coordinate order.

A relation among image columns becomes a vector annihilated by the map.

Use column one plus column two minus column three, then identify the independent image columns.

## Synthesis principle: kernels grow under composition

For composable linear maps $V\xrightarrow{A}W\xrightarrow{B}Z$, every vector killed by $A$ is also killed by $B\circ A$. Thus $\ker A\subseteq\ker(B\circ A)$.

The inclusion may be strict because $B$ can kill nonzero vectors already reached by $A$. This observation connects exactness, quotient information, and rank loss.

content.title: Prove the composition inclusion
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\ker A\subseteq\ker(B\circ A)$ and state a condition equivalent to equality.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

After proving the inclusion, inspect vectors that lie simultaneously in $\operatorname{im}A$ and $\ker B$.

Strict growth of the kernel occurs exactly through those intermediate vectors.

Translate a vector in $\ker(B\circ A)$ through its image under $A$, then state when that image must be zero.

## Complete worked model

Let $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ be $A(x,y,z)=(x+y,y+z)$ and $B:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $B(u,v)=u-v$. Write $F=B\circ A$.

Determine the exact kernel and image of $F$, construct $\mathbb R^3/\ker F\cong\operatorname{im}F$, compare $\ker F$ with $\ker A$, and distinguish an exact nullity calculation from a dimension-only lower bound.

### Strategy

Compute the composite formula, solve both kernel systems, prove that $F$ reaches its target, and only then pass from cosets to the image. Finish by asking which conclusions would survive if surjectivity had not been proved.

### Hypotheses

$F(x,y,z)=x-z$.

### Intermediate claims

$\ker F=\{(x,y,x)\}=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,0)\}$, while $\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,1)\}$. Since $F(1,0,0)=1$, $\operatorname{im}F=\mathbb R$. The formula $\overline F((x,y,z)+\ker F)=x-z$ therefore defines a candidate map $\mathbb R^3/\ker F\to\mathbb R$.

### Justification

The candidate is well-defined because two representatives of one coset differ by a vector on which $x-z$ is zero. It is injective because $\overline F([v])=0$ implies $v\in\ker F$, and it is surjective because $F$ is surjective. Thus $\overline F$ is an isomorphism. Rank–nullity now gives the exact value $\dim\ker F=3-1=2$. Without the explicit surjectivity calculation, the one-dimensional codomain would give only $\operatorname{rank}F\le1$ and hence $\dim\ker F\ge2$.

### Conclusion

The computation proves both $\mathbb R^3/\ker F\cong\operatorname{im}F=\mathbb R$ and $\ker A\subsetneq\ker F$. It also shows exactly why a proved image statement yields an exact nullity, whereas a codomain count alone yields only a lower bound.

content.title: Analyze a new composite
content.introMarkdown: Compute $R\circ C$, determine its kernel and rank, and prove $\ker C\subseteq\ker(R\circ C)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Expand $x-2y+z$ after substituting the three outputs of $C$.

The simplified functional controls both rank and kernel.

Recompute the four coefficients, then prove the kernel inclusion from $C(v)=0$.

## Final transfer: theorem, calculation, and scope

The final task combines a kernel calculation, an image proof, a quotient interpretation, and a bounded dimension argument. Each conclusion must be attached to the evidence that actually proves it.

content.title: Complete the Week 12 proof
content.introMarkdown: Determine kernel and image, prove the induced quotient isomorphism, verify rank–nullity, and compare the strength of this exact result with the Week 12 statement about $dM_{(L,Q)}$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether you explicitly proved that both target basis vectors lie in the image of $H$.

That surjectivity proof is the decisive difference between the exact and heuristic dimension conclusions.

Use $1$ and $t$, finish the quotient and dimension arguments, then contrast rank $=2$ with rank $\le4$.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-12, source lines 677 to 684.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Exact locator:** Unit I, Sessions 6–10: column space, nullspace, independence, basis, dimension, and the four fundamental subspaces in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Use the four fundamental subspaces as a final cross-check on the week’s kernel, image, quotient, and rank–nullity arguments.
Week 13 turns from the dimensions of linear maps to the determinant as an alternating multilinear measure of volume and invertibility.

Week 12 is complete when you can prove rank–nullity, identify a quotient with an image, verify elementary exactness, and keep the multiplication-differential kernel claim within the evidence actually established.

activities.title: Recover a kernel as an inverse image
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $T:V\to W$ be linear and let $\{0_W\}\subseteq W$.

Prove $\ker T=T^{-1}(\{0_W\})$ and explain why this inverse image is a subspace.

Use set membership in both directions, then linearity.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The set equality and subspace proof are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response retrieves inverse-image membership and transfers it to a linear setting.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $v\in V$, $v\in\ker T$ exactly when $T(v)=0_W$, which is exactly when $T(v)\in\{0_W\}$, hence when $v\in T^{-1}(\{0_W\})$. The set is a subspace because $0$ maps to $0$ and linear combinations of vectors mapped to zero also map to zero.

activities.title: Translate a row reduction into rank–nullity
activities.promptMarkdown:
A homogeneous system in five variables has reduced matrix with pivots in columns $1,3,4$.

State the rank, nullity, and dimension of the solution space, and justify the identification of that solution space.

Connect the homogeneous solution set to the kernel of the represented map.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: There are three pivots, so rank is $3$. There are two free variables, so the homogeneous solution space has dimension $2$. It is the kernel of the matrix map $\mathbb R^5\to\mathbb R^m$, hence its dimension is the nullity. Rank–nullity reads $5=3+2$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The pivot, free-variable, rank, and nullity counts agree.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The solution space is correctly identified as a kernel.

activities.title: Read rank and nullity from basis images
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfy $T(e_1)=(1,0,1)$, $T(e_2)=(0,1,1)$, and $T(e_3)=(1,1,2)$.

Construct the matrix, then find a kernel basis, image basis, rank, and nullity.

Notice the relation among the image columns before row reducing.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The matrix has the three displayed vectors as columns, and the third column is the sum of the first two. Thus $e_1+e_2-e_3$ spans the kernel. The first two columns are independent and span the image, so rank $=2$, nullity $=1$, and $3=2+1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The matrix and all subspace data are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The column relation is translated into a source kernel vector.

activities.title: Prove the composition inclusion
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:V\to W$ and $B:W\to Z$ be linear maps.

Prove $\ker A\subseteq\ker(B\circ A)$ and state a condition equivalent to equality.

Prove the inclusion elementwise. For equality, describe what $B$ must do on $\operatorname{im}A$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The inclusion and equality criterion are both correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The equality criterion identifies precisely which additional image directions the second map could kill.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $v\in\ker A$, then $A(v)=0$, so $(B\circ A)(v)=B(0)=0$; hence $v\in\ker(B\circ A)$. Equality holds exactly when $\ker B\cap\operatorname{im}A=\{0\}$, equivalently when the restriction of $B$ to $\operatorname{im}A$ is injective.

activities.title: Analyze a new composite
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $C:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C(a,b,c,d)=(a+b,b+c,c+d)$ and $R:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be $R(x,y,z)=x-2y+z$.

Compute $R\circ C$, determine its kernel and rank, and prove $\ker C\subseteq\ker(R\circ C)$.

Use the composite formula and a general composition argument for the inclusion.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The composite, kernel, rank, and inclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The general kernel inclusion is proved from composition rather than inferred from the example alone.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $(R\circ C)(a,b,c,d)=a-b-c+d$. This nonzero functional has rank one and kernel $\{a-b-c+d=0\}$, a three-dimensional subspace. If $v\in\ker C$, then $(R\circ C)(v)=R(0)=0$, so $\ker C\subseteq\ker(R\circ C)$.

activities.title: Complete the Week 12 proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Define $H:\mathbb R[t]_{\le3}\to\mathbb R^2$ by $H(p)=(p(0),p'(0))$.

Determine kernel and image, prove the induced quotient isomorphism, verify rank–nullity, and compare the strength of this exact result with the Week 12 statement about $dM_{(L,Q)}$.

End by naming why exact nullity is available for $H$ but not yet for the supplied multiplication differential.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All exact data for $H$ and the comparison with $dM$ are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response identifies proven surjectivity as the evidence that upgrades a lower bound to exact nullity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $H(a+bt+ct^2+dt^3)=(a,b)$, so $\ker H=\operatorname{span}\{t^2,t^3\}$ and $H$ is surjective because $H(1)=(1,0)$ and $H(t)=(0,1)$. Thus rank $=2$, nullity $=2$, and $4=2+2$. The map $p+\ker H\mapsto H(p)$ is a well-defined isomorphism onto $\mathbb R^2$. Exact nullity is available because surjectivity has been proved; for $dM_{(L,Q)}$, Week 12 has only rank $\le4$ and therefore only nullity $\ge1$.

lessons.title: Alternating multilinearity determines the determinant
lessons.summary: Derive the zero-column, equal-column, swap, scaling, and triangular determinant laws from alternating multilinearity and normalization.
objectives: Derive the zero-column, equal-column, swap, scaling, and triangular determinant laws from alternating multilinearity and normalization.

content.markdown:
## A determinant is a structured measurement, not a memorized expansion

Over $\mathbb R$, the determinant measures oriented volume. Over any field $k$, its algebraic laws follow from three principles: linearity in each column, sign reversal when two columns are exchanged, and the normalization $\det I_n=1$.

Beginning from these principles makes later product and block formulas reconstructible instead of mysterious.

## Reactivate proof and basis language

A multilinear map is linear in one argument while the others are held fixed. An alternating map vanishes when two arguments agree. Exchanging two columns changes the algebraic sign. Over $\mathbb R$, that sign change reverses orientation.

## The defining properties

For column vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in k^n$, the determinant

$$\det(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$$

is multilinear, alternating, and normalized by $\det(e_1,\ldots,e_n)=1$.

If one column is zero, linearity gives a zero determinant. If two columns are equal, alternation gives zero. These are not separate axioms.

content.title: Derive the zero-column law
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $D(v_1,\ldots,0,\ldots,v_n)=0$ without using a determinant expansion.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Use linearity in exactly the column that equals zero.

The derivation exposes which determinant axiom is doing the work.

Replace zero by $0+0$, expand once, and subtract.

## Alternation implies the swap rule

Suppose adjacent columns $u,v$ are replaced by $u+v,u+v$. Alternation makes the determinant zero. Expanding in both columns leaves the two mixed terms because the equal-column terms vanish.

Therefore $\det(\ldots,u,v,\ldots)+\det(\ldots,v,u,\ldots)=0$. A single swap changes the sign.

content.title: Prove the swap rule
content.introMarkdown: Derive $D(\ldots,v,u,\ldots)=-D(\ldots,u,v,\ldots)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write all four terms before cancelling anything.

The two equal-column terms vanish for a different reason from the mixed terms.

Mark the alternating terms as zero, then isolate the two remaining determinants.

## Complete worked model

Let $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&r&s\\0&b&t\\0&0&c\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

Derive $\det A=abc$ using multilinearity and alternation.

### Strategy

Write each column as a diagonal basis component plus earlier basis components, then expand.

### Hypotheses

The columns are $ae_1$, $re_1+be_2$, and $se_1+te_2+ce_3$.

### Intermediate claims

Every expanded term except $\det(ae_1,be_2,ce_3)$ repeats a basis vector or contains a zero coefficient.

### Justification

Alternation kills the repeated-basis terms, while multilinearity extracts $abc$.

### Conclusion

$\det A=abc\det(e_1,e_2,e_3)=abc$.

content.title: Diagnose the triangular proof
content.introMarkdown: Identify the unique term that survives a column-based multilinear expansion and explain why all other terms vanish.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

List which standard basis row each selected term contributes.

Alternation eliminates a term only after a repeated row is visible.

Keep the diagonal choices and show that every off-diagonal choice forces repetition.

## Boundary: multilinearity without alternation is not a determinant

The function $F(v_1,v_2)=v_{11}v_{22}$ is bilinear, but it need not vanish when $v_1=v_2$. Multilinearity alone therefore does not encode oriented area.

Normalization also matters: a scalar multiple $c\det$ is alternating and multilinear but sends the identity basis to $c$.

content.title: Audit an impostor determinant
content.introMarkdown: Verify bilinearity and give one equal-column input showing that $F$ is not alternating.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Test the function on two identical nonzero vectors.

Alternation, not bilinearity alone, detects collapsed oriented area.

Use $(1,1)$ twice and compare the nonzero value with the alternating requirement.

## Transfer: derive before calculating

A determinant argument should name the defining property that justifies each transformation. Row replacement, row scaling, and row exchange have different effects because they use different combinations of multilinearity and alternation.

content.title: Derive the row-operation laws
content.introMarkdown: Prove the determinant effect of scaling one row by $c$, swapping two rows, and replacing row $i$ by row $i+c$ row $j$ for $i\ne j$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Separate the three operations before writing their effects.

A row swap and a row replacement cannot share the same determinant rule.

Use scalar extraction, the swap identity, and an equal-row vanishing term in that order.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-13, source lines 685 to 694.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Exact locator:** Unit II, Session 18: properties of determinants — multilinearity, row operations, and normalization in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Compare the axiomatic derivations with the determinant properties used in elimination.
Tomorrow we will use uniqueness of the normalized alternating multilinear form to prove the product formula.
Day 1 is complete when zero, swap, scaling, replacement, and triangular laws can all be reconstructed from multilinearity, alternation, and normalization.

activities.title: Derive the zero-column law
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $D:(k^n)^n\to k$ be multilinear.

Prove that $D(v_1,\ldots,0,\ldots,v_n)=0$ without using a determinant expansion.

Use the identity $0=0+0$ in the zero column and subtract the resulting equality.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The zero-column conclusion follows from multilinearity.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof derives the property instead of importing an expansion formula.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Holding all other columns fixed, linearity in the chosen column gives $D(\ldots,0,\ldots)=D(\ldots,0+0,\ldots)=D(\ldots,0,\ldots)+D(\ldots,0,\ldots)$. Subtracting one copy yields $D(\ldots,0,\ldots)=0$.

activities.title: Prove the swap rule
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $D$ be alternating and multilinear, with adjacent arguments $u$ and $v$.

Derive $D(\ldots,v,u,\ldots)=-D(\ldots,u,v,\ldots)$.

Expand $D(\ldots,u+v,u+v,\ldots)=0$ into four terms and identify the two that vanish.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The sign-change identity is derived correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses both multilinearity and alternation at explicit steps.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Alternation gives $0=D(\ldots,u+v,u+v,\ldots)$. Multilinearity expands this as $D(\ldots,u,u,\ldots)+D(\ldots,u,v,\ldots)+D(\ldots,v,u,\ldots)+D(\ldots,v,v,\ldots)$. The first and last terms vanish, so the mixed terms sum to zero, proving the sign rule.

activities.title: Diagnose the triangular proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}p&0&0\\u&q&0\\v&w&r\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

Identify the unique term that survives a column-based multilinear expansion and explain why all other terms vanish.

Do not expand by minors.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The columns are $p e_1+u e_2+v e_3$, $q e_2+w e_3$, and $r e_3$. The only choice with three distinct standard basis vectors is $p e_1,q e_2,r e_3$, contributing $pqr$. Choosing $u e_2$ repeats $e_2$ if the second column contributes $q e_2$; choosing $v e_3$ or $w e_3$ repeats $e_3$. Every other term therefore vanishes by alternation, so $\det B=pqr$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The surviving term and product are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response transfers the triangular argument to a new column pattern without invoking minors.

activities.title: Audit an impostor determinant
activities.promptMarkdown:
Define $F((x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2))=x_1y_2$.

Verify bilinearity and give one equal-column input showing that $F$ is not alternating.

Then state which determinant axiom fails.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Each variable appears linearly when the other is fixed, so $F$ is bilinear. But $F((1,1),(1,1))=1\ne0$, even though the two columns agree. Thus alternation fails, so $F$ is not the determinant.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Bilinearity and the counterexample are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The failed defining axiom is identified precisely.

activities.title: Derive the row-operation laws
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and view its determinant as an alternating multilinear function of the rows.

Prove the determinant effect of scaling one row by $c$, swapping two rows, and replacing row $i$ by row $i+c$ row $j$ for $i\ne j$.

Derive all three laws from the axioms and explain why the replacement term vanishes.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three row-operation laws are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each law is tied to the exact defining property that proves it.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Linearity extracts $c$ when one row is scaled. The swap rule derived from alternation changes the sign. For row replacement, multilinearity gives the original determinant plus $c$ times a determinant in which rows $i$ and $j$ are equal; alternation makes the second term zero. Hence row replacement preserves the determinant.

lessons.title: The determinant product formula
lessons.summary: Prove $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ from alternating multilinearity and use it to characterize invertibility.
objectives: Prove $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ from alternating multilinearity and use it to characterize invertibility.

content.markdown:
## Composition should multiply volume factors

Over $\mathbb R$, if $B$ changes an oriented unit box by a factor $\det B$ and $A$ then acts by $\det A$, their composite should scale by the product. The proof below establishes the algebraic identity over any field.

## Reactivate maps, bases, and the determinant axioms

Matrix multiplication represents composition. The columns of $AB$ are $A b_1,\ldots,A b_n$ when $b_i$ are the columns of $B$. Yesterday established the determinant axioms; today we prove the uniqueness statement needed for composition.

## Permutation sign, the determinant formula, and uniqueness

For a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)$ be the number of pairs $i<j$ with $\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$. Define $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}$. Each adjacent swap changes the inversion parity and therefore changes this sign.

Now write each column as $v_j=\sum_i v_{ij}e_i$ and expand an alternating multilinear form $D(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$. Every term with a repeated basis vector vanishes. The surviving index tuples are precisely the permutations $\sigma$, and reordering their basis vectors by adjacent swaps gives

$$D(e_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,e_{\sigma(n)})=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)D(e_1,\ldots,e_n).$$

Consequently

$$D(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=D(e_1,\ldots,e_n)\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{j=1}^n v_{\sigma(j),j}.$$

For the normalized form, the sum is the determinant permutation formula. Every alternating multilinear form is therefore its value on the standard basis times the determinant, so the normalized form is unique.

For fixed $A$, define $F_A(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=\det(Av_1,\ldots,Av_n)$. This is alternating and multilinear in the $v_i$.

Its value on the standard basis is $F_A(e_1,\ldots,e_n)=\det A$. Therefore uniqueness of alternating multilinear forms gives

$$F_A(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=\det A\,\det(v_1,\ldots,v_n).$$

content.title: Verify the auxiliary form
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $F_A$ is multilinear and alternating.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Apply $A$ to the linear combination before expanding the determinant.

The auxiliary form inherits multilinearity through two separate linear steps.

Write one argument calculation and then check what equal inputs become after applying $A$.

## Apply the lemma to the columns of $B$

If $B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ by columns, then $AB=(Ab_1,\ldots,Ab_n)$. Hence

$$\det(AB)=F_A(b_1,\ldots,b_n)=\det A\det B.$$

The proof never assumes either matrix invertible.

content.title: Write the complete product proof
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ using the auxiliary form and its normalization value.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your auxiliary form has been compared with the normalized determinant.

Alternating multilinearity alone determines the form only up to a scalar.

Evaluate on the standard basis to identify that scalar as $\det A$.

## Complete worked model

Suppose $A$ is invertible with inverse $A^{-1}$.

Derive the determinant of the inverse and the nonzero determinant criterion in this direction.

### Strategy

Apply the product formula to $AA^{-1}=I$.

### Hypotheses

$\det(AA^{-1})=\det A\det A^{-1}$ and $\det I=1$.

### Intermediate claims

$1=\det A\det A^{-1}$, so neither factor is zero.

### Justification

A product equal to one consists of units in the field.

### Conclusion

$\det A\ne0$ and $\det A^{-1}=(\det A)^{-1}$.

content.title: Diagnose the converse
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $A$ is injective by ruling out a nonzero kernel vector.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Turn the hypothetical kernel vector into the first column of an invertible basis matrix.

That construction produces a zero determinant product while keeping the change-of-basis factor nonzero.

Form $P$, examine the first column of $AP$, and apply the product formula.

## Boundary: rectangular matrices have no determinant of this kind

The normalized alternating $n$-linear construction compares $n$ source directions with an $n$-dimensional target. A rectangular matrix can have rank and minors, but it has no single determinant satisfying the square-matrix product theorem.

content.title: Reject a rectangular determinant claim
content.introMarkdown: Explain why the expression $\det R\det S$ is undefined in the present theory although $RS$ is a square matrix.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write the dimensions beside each matrix before applying determinant notation.

The determinant is defined here only for an endomorphism of an equal-dimensional space.

Keep $\det(RS)$ and replace the two rectangular determinant symbols by rank or minor language.

## Transfer: composition, powers, and inverse criteria

The product formula converts structural questions about repeated composition into scalar identities. The final task combines powers, inverses, and a parameter boundary.

content.title: Analyze a parameterized composition
content.introMarkdown: Determine exactly when $A_t$ is invertible, compute $\det(A_t^m)$ for $m\ge1$, and give $\det(A_t^{-1})$ when it exists.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Factor $t^2-1$ before stating the invertible parameter set.

The singular boundary controls whether the inverse determinant is meaningful.

Find the two excluded parameters, then apply the product theorem to powers and the identity product.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-13, source lines 685 to 694.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

**Exact locator:** Unit II, Sessions 18–19: determinant properties, formulas, and the product rule in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Fall 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Reconstruct the product formula and compare its proof with the composition interpretation.
Tomorrow we will turn the determinant into oriented volume and derive block-triangular formulas.
Day 2 is complete when the product formula, inverse determinant, and nonzero determinant criterion can all be proved rather than quoted.

activities.title: Verify the auxiliary form
activities.promptMarkdown:
Fix a linear map $A:k^n\to k^n$ and define $F_A$ as above.

Prove that $F_A$ is multilinear and alternating.

Use linearity of $A$ before applying the corresponding determinant property.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both structural properties are proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response composes linearity of $A$ with the determinant axioms.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In one argument, $A(av+bw)=aAv+bAw$, and determinant multilinearity then gives the same linear combination of $F_A$ values. If two inputs agree, their images under $A$ agree, so the determinant has two equal columns and vanishes. Thus $F_A$ is multilinear and alternating.

activities.title: Write the complete product proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A,B\in M_n(k)$, with no invertibility assumption.

Prove $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ using the auxiliary form and its normalization value.

Name the columns of $B$ and make the uniqueness step explicit.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The product identity is proved without circularity.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The normalization and column-composition steps are both explicit.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For fixed $A$, $F_A(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=\det(Av_1,\ldots,Av_n)$ is alternating and multilinear, and $F_A(e_1,\ldots,e_n)=\det A$. Uniqueness therefore gives $F_A=(\det A)\det$. If $b_i$ are the columns of $B$, then the columns of $AB$ are $Ab_i$, so $\det(AB)=F_A(b_1,\ldots,b_n)=\det A\det B$.

activities.title: Diagnose the converse
activities.promptMarkdown:
Assume $\det A\ne0$ for a linear map $A:k^n\to k^n$.

Prove that $A$ is injective by ruling out a nonzero kernel vector.

Extend a hypothetical nonzero kernel vector to a basis and use the determinant of its image columns.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The converse invertibility argument is correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses a basis extension and the product formula without assuming the conclusion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $0\ne v\in\ker A$, extend $v=v_1$ to a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$. The matrix $P$ with these basis columns is invertible, so $\det P\ne0$. But the first column of $AP$ is $Av=0$, hence $\det(AP)=0$. The product formula gives $0=\det A\det P$, contradicting both factors being nonzero. Thus $A$ is injective and, in equal finite dimensions, invertible.

activities.title: Reject a rectangular determinant claim
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $R$ be $2\times3$ and $S$ be $3\times2$.

Explain why the expression $\det R\det S$ is undefined in the present theory although $RS$ is a square matrix.

State what determinant is defined and what data could replace the missing rectangular determinants.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $R$ and $S$ are not square, so neither has the determinant defined this week. The $2\times2$ matrix $RS$ does have a determinant. Rank or maximal minors can describe the rectangular maps, but they do not turn the undefined product $\det R\det S$ into a valid formula.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The typing distinction is correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response does not extend the product theorem to undefined factors.

activities.title: Analyze a parameterized composition
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A_t=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t&1\\1&t\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

Determine exactly when $A_t$ is invertible, compute $\det(A_t^m)$ for $m\ge1$, and give $\det(A_t^{-1})$ when it exists.

Derive every formula from the product theorem and the two-by-two determinant.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The parameter boundary and determinant formulas are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The product theorem supports the power and inverse conclusions.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\det A_t=t^2-1$, so $A_t$ is invertible exactly when $t\ne\pm1$. Repeated use of the product formula gives $\det(A_t^m)=(t^2-1)^m$. When $t\ne\pm1$, $1=\det(A_tA_t^{-1})=(t^2-1)\det(A_t^{-1})$, so $\det(A_t^{-1})=(t^2-1)^{-1}$.

lessons.title: Oriented volume, orientation, and block-triangular matrices
lessons.summary: Interpret determinant sign and magnitude geometrically and prove the block-triangular determinant formula.
objectives: Interpret determinant sign and magnitude geometrically and prove the block-triangular determinant formula.

content.markdown:
## Magnitude and sign carry different geometric information

The absolute value of a determinant is a volume-scaling factor. Its sign records whether orientation is preserved or reversed. Block-triangular matrices expose the same information without expanding a large determinant.

## Reactivate bases and the product theorem

An ordered basis determines an orientation. Yesterday proved the determinant product formula, and Day 1 proved the triangular product of diagonal entries.

## Oriented parallelepipeds

For columns $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $|\det(v_1,\ldots,v_n)|$ is the Euclidean volume of their parallelepiped. A positive determinant agrees with the standard orientation; a negative determinant reverses it.

The volume is zero exactly when the columns are linearly dependent.

content.title: Separate area from orientation
content.introMarkdown: Compute the oriented area, ordinary area, and orientation of $(u,v)$, then compare with $(v,u)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Keep the signed determinant separate from its absolute value.

A negative determinant does not mean negative physical area.

Compute the signed value first, then take its absolute value only for ordinary area.

## Linear dependence and zero volume

If the columns are dependent, one is a linear combination of the others. Multilinearity expands the determinant into terms with repeated columns, all zero.

Conversely, $\det A=0$ implies $A$ is not invertible, so its columns cannot form a basis and are dependent.

content.title: Prove the dependent-column direction
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\det(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=0$ directly from multilinearity and alternation.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

After expansion, point to the two positions occupied by the same vector.

Dependence alone does not finish the proof until alternation is applied term by term.

Expand the last column and annotate the repeated $v_i$ in every summand.

## Complete worked model

Let $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with square blocks $A\in M_p(k)$ and $D\in M_q(k)$.

Prove $\det M=\det A\det D$.

### Strategy

Use the permutation formula and classify exactly which permutation terms can survive the zero lower-left block.

### Hypotheses

A nonzero determinant term must assign each of the final $q$ rows to one of the final $q$ columns. Assigning one of those rows to a first-block column would select an entry from the zero block.

### Intermediate claims

Because a permutation is bijective, the final $q$ rows use all final $q$ columns, while the first $p$ rows use all first $p$ columns. Every surviving term therefore splits into one permutation term from $A$ and one from $D$.

### Justification

The sign of the combined block-preserving permutation is the product of the two within-block signs. Summing all surviving terms therefore factors as $\det A\det D$. The same permutation formula proves $\det X^T=\det X$: replace each permutation by its inverse, which has the same sign, and reorder the scalar factors.

### Conclusion

$\det\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\det A\det D$.

content.title: Prove the lower block-triangular formula
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\det N=\det A\det D$ without expanding scalar minors.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Transpose the full block matrix, including the off-diagonal block.

The upper-triangular theorem applies only after the zero block is in the lower-left position.

Write $N^T$, apply the upper formula, and use $\det A^T=\det A$.

## Boundary: the diagonal blocks must be square

In a two-by-two block display, the visual shape does not guarantee that $A$ and $D$ are square. The formula $\det A\det D$ is typed only when both determinants exist and the full matrix is square with compatible block sizes.

content.title: Type-check a block formula
content.introMarkdown: Explain why the formula $\det M=\det A\det D$ cannot be invoked from the block picture.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write the row and column counts of both diagonal blocks.

A block determinant formula cannot contain undefined determinants.

Reject the formula for this partition and require a square $p\times p$ leading block.

## Transfer: use block structure before scalar expansion

Block triangularity can turn a large determinant into two smaller ones. The method is useful only when the zero block and square diagonal blocks are stated explicitly.

content.title: Compute a five-dimensional block determinant
content.introMarkdown: Compute $\det M$ and explain why the answer is independent of $B$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compute the two square diagonal blocks before inspecting $B$.

The block-triangular theorem makes the off-diagonal block irrelevant.

Find $5$ and $-5$, multiply them, and cite the zero lower-left block.

**Reading purpose:** Connect determinant sign and magnitude to orientation and use block structure before scalar expansion.
Tomorrow we will factor a general two-by-two block matrix and derive the Schur-complement determinant formula under an explicit invertibility hypothesis.
Day 3 is complete when determinant magnitude, sign, dependence, and block-triangular products form one coherent geometric and algebraic picture.

activities.title: Separate area from orientation
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $u=(2,1)$ and $v=(-1,3)$ in $\mathbb R^2$.

Compute the oriented area, ordinary area, and orientation of $(u,v)$, then compare with $(v,u)$.

Use determinant sign and magnitude separately.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\det(u,v)=2\cdot3-(-1)\cdot1=7$. Thus the oriented area is $7$, the ordinary area is $7$, and $(u,v)$ has positive orientation. Swapping gives determinant $-7$: the ordinary area is unchanged but orientation reverses.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both determinant values and interpretations are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Magnitude and sign are assigned to area and orientation respectively.

activities.title: Prove the dependent-column direction
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $v_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_iv_i$.

Prove $\det(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=0$ directly from multilinearity and alternation.

Expand only the final column and identify the repeated column in each term.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The dependent-column determinant is proved zero.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each term is eliminated by a named repeated column.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Multilinearity in the final column gives $\det(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_i\det(v_1,\ldots,v_{n-1},v_i)$. In the $i$th term, $v_i$ already appears among the first $n-1$ columns, so alternation makes that term zero. Hence the sum is zero.

activities.title: Prove the lower block-triangular formula
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $N=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&0\\C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with square $A$ and $D$.

Prove $\det N=\det A\det D$ without expanding scalar minors.

Use transpose or a typed block factorization and state why it preserves the determinant.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The lower block formula is proved correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument transfers through transpose while preserving block types.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $N^T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A^T&C^T\\0&D^T\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is upper block triangular, the proved formula gives $\det N^T=\det A^T\det D^T$. Because determinant is unchanged by transpose, $\det N=\det A\det D$.

activities.title: Type-check a block formula
activities.promptMarkdown:
A $5\times5$ matrix is partitioned with $A$ of size $2\times3$ in the upper-left corner.

Explain why the formula $\det M=\det A\det D$ cannot be invoked from the block picture.

Identify the undefined expression and the incompatible complementary block sizes.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $A$ is rectangular, so $\det A$ is undefined. The complementary diagonal block would have size $3\times2$, also rectangular. Therefore this partition is not a block-triangular decomposition with square diagonal blocks, even though the full matrix is square.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The block-size defect is identified correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response checks types before applying a visual pattern.

activities.title: Compute a five-dimensional block determinant
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ where $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $D=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&2&0\\0&-1&4\\0&0&5\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; $B$ is any $2\times3$ matrix.

Compute $\det M$ and explain why the answer is independent of $B$.

Use the proved block formula and derive each smaller determinant.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The two block determinants and final product are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The independence from $B$ follows from the proved block theorem.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\det A=6-1=5$. The triangular matrix $D$ has determinant $1\cdot(-1)\cdot5=-5$. Therefore $\det M=\det A\det D=-25$. The upper-right block does not enter the block-triangular product because elimination or multilinearity removes its contribution while the lower-left block is zero.

lessons.title: The Schur-complement determinant formula
lessons.summary: Derive the typed Schur-complement determinant formula for a two-by-two block matrix with an invertible leading block.
objectives: Derive the typed Schur-complement determinant formula for a two-by-two block matrix with an invertible leading block.

content.markdown:
## Eliminate a block without expanding the whole determinant

The Schur complement is block Gaussian elimination written as a formula. It replaces one large determinant by determinants of a pivot block and a corrected remaining block.

## Reactivate typed composition and block triangularity

Let $A$ be $p\times p$, $B$ be $p\times q$, $C$ be $q\times p$, and $D$ be $q\times q$. Then $CA^{-1}B$ is $q\times q$ only when $A$ is invertible.

## The factorization

For $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with invertible $A$, define the Schur complement $S=D-CA^{-1}B$.

Then

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}I_p&0\\CA^{-1}&I_q\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&S\end{pmatrix}.$$

The first factor has determinant one and the second is block upper triangular. Therefore $\det M=\det A\det S$.

content.title: Verify the block factorization
content.introMarkdown: Multiply the two block factors and recover all four blocks of $M$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compute the lower-left block before simplifying the lower-right block.

The order $CA^{-1}$ is forced by the block types.

Write the four block products in a two-by-two grid and substitute the definition of $S$ last.

## Determinants of the two factors

The lower block-unitriangular factor has diagonal blocks $I_p$ and $I_q$, so its determinant is one. The second factor has determinant $\det A\det S$.

Combining this with the product theorem gives

$$\det\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}=\det A\det(D-CA^{-1}B).$$

content.title: Prove the Schur-complement formula
content.introMarkdown: Derive the determinant formula from the verified factorization.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Do not jump from the factorization to the final formula without evaluating each factor.

The proof depends on both the product theorem and block triangularity.

Write $\det M=\det L\det U$, compute the two determinants, then substitute $S$.

## Complete worked model

Let $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\3&5\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, viewed as one-by-one blocks with $A=(2)$.

Compute the determinant through the Schur complement.

### Strategy

Use $S=5-3(2^{-1})1$ and multiply by $\det A$.

### Hypotheses

$A=(2)$ is invertible over $\mathbb R$.

### Intermediate claims

$S=5-3/2=7/2$.

### Justification

$\det M=2\cdot(7/2)=7$, agreeing with $2\cdot5-3\cdot1$.

### Conclusion

The block formula specializes to the ordinary two-by-two scalar determinant.

content.title: Apply a matrix-valued Schur complement
content.introMarkdown: Compute the determinant of $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ using the Schur complement.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Multiply the $1\times2$ row by the $2\times1$ column in that order.

Reversing the order would produce a $2\times2$ matrix and the wrong Schur complement.

Compute $CB$ as a scalar, subtract it from $4$, and multiply by $\det I_2$.

## Boundary: the chosen pivot block must be invertible

If $A$ is singular, $A^{-1}$ and therefore $D-CA^{-1}B$ are undefined. The full matrix may still be invertible, so singularity of the chosen block is not singularity of the whole matrix.

One may pivot differently or use a formula based on invertible $D$, but the present theorem cannot be applied unchanged.

content.title: Reject an undefined Schur complement
content.introMarkdown: Explain why the $A$-Schur formula is unavailable even though $M$ is invertible.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether $A^{-1}$ exists before forming the complement.

A correct final determinant cannot rescue an undefined intermediate formula.

State the actual determinant, reject the chosen pivot, and name the missing invertibility hypothesis.

## Transfer and preview boundary

Block determinant factorizations will later simplify Jacobian determinants. That is a destination only: Week 16 first defines total derivatives and Jacobian matrices.

Today’s theorem is entirely linear algebra. It does not assert differentiability or any local inverse.

content.title: Derive and audit a parameterized block formula
content.introMarkdown: Compute the block determinant for all $s,t$, verify the result by block reasoning, and state why no Jacobian conclusion follows.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Multiply $A^{-1}$ by $B$ before applying $C$.

The typed order makes the complement scalar and reveals its independence from $t$.

Compute the three factors in order, obtain $s$, and end with the explicit Week 16 boundary.

## Course reference

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Fall 2011.

Tomorrow’s retrieval and synthesis will connect determinant reasoning to logic, basis coordinates, and quotient dimensions.
Day 4 is complete when the Schur complement is typed, factored, proved, applied, and withheld whenever the chosen pivot block is singular.

activities.title: Verify the block factorization
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the typed blocks $A,B,C,D$ and $S=D-CA^{-1}B$.

Multiply the two block factors and recover all four blocks of $M$.

Show the lower-right calculation explicitly.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Block multiplication gives upper-left $A$, upper-right $B$, lower-left $CA^{-1}A=C$, and lower-right $CA^{-1}B+S=CA^{-1}B+D-CA^{-1}B=D$. Thus the product equals $M$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All four block products are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The cancellation in the lower-right block uses the exact definition of $S$.

activities.title: Prove the Schur-complement formula
activities.promptMarkdown:
Assume exactly that $A\in M_p(k)$ is invertible and the remaining blocks have the compatible sizes.

Derive the determinant formula from the verified factorization.

Name the product theorem and both block-triangular determinant evaluations.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The formula follows from the factorization correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Every determinant step cites an already proved theorem.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The factorization writes $M=LU$ with $L=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&0\\CA^{-1}&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $U=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\0&S\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The product theorem gives $\det M=\det L\det U$. Block triangularity gives $\det L=1$ and $\det U=\det A\det S$. Substituting $S=D-CA^{-1}B$ proves the formula.

activities.title: Apply a matrix-valued Schur complement
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=I_2$, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $C=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, and $D=(4)$.

Compute the determinant of $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ using the Schur complement.

Check the dimensions of $CB$ before evaluating the scalar complement.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $CA^{-1}B=CB=3\cdot1+(-1)\cdot2=1$, so $S=D-CA^{-1}B=(3)$. Since $\det A=1$, the block determinant is $1\cdot3=3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The typed block product and determinant are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response preserves the row-column order in $CA^{-1}B$.

activities.title: Reject an undefined Schur complement
activities.promptMarkdown:
Take $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with scalar leading block $A=(0)$.

Explain why the $A$-Schur formula is unavailable even though $M$ is invertible.

Compute $\det M$ and identify the undefined operation.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\det M=-1$, so $M$ is invertible. However, $A=(0)$ has no inverse, so $D-CA^{-1}B$ is undefined. The theorem’s leading-block hypothesis fails even though the whole matrix is nonsingular.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The matrix and hypothesis audit are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes invertibility of a block from invertibility of the full matrix.

activities.title: Derive and audit a parameterized block formula
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $C=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, and $D=(s)$.

Compute the block determinant for all $s,t$, verify the result by block reasoning, and state why no Jacobian conclusion follows.

Find $A^{-1}$, calculate $CA^{-1}B$, and keep the preview boundary explicit.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The inverse, complement, and determinant are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response preserves the linear-algebra scope and rejects a premature Jacobian inference.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $A^{-1}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-t\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, so $A^{-1}B=(1,0)^T$ and $CA^{-1}B=0$. Thus $S=(s)$ and $\det M=\det A\det S=s$. This is a determinant identity for a parameterized family of matrices. Without a defined differentiable map and proof that this matrix is its derivative, it yields no Jacobian or local-invertibility conclusion.
