Day 1 established that these exponent pairs also classify symmetric tensor classes.

## Ordered-index bases

If $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ is a basis of $V$, then

$$e_{i_1}\cdots e_{i_d}\qquad(i_1\le\cdots\le i_d)$$

form a basis of $\operatorname{Sym}^dV$. For $n=2$, the basis is $e_1^{d-i}e_2^i$ for $0\le i\le d$.

content.title: List the ordered-index classes
content.introMarkdown: List every ordered-index basis monomial exactly once.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Sort the three factors and group by how many $x$ factors occur.

A systematic ordering prevents both duplicates and omissions.

List exponent triples $(a,b,c)$ with $a+b+c=3$, then translate each triple into a monomial.

## Complete worked model

Let $V$ have basis $(x,y)$. Compute $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^4V$.

Produce a basis and justify both the list and the dimension.

### Strategy

Classify quotient classes by the number of $y$ factors.

### Hypotheses

Every degree-four tensor word has $i$ copies of $y$ for a unique $i\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$.

### Intermediate claims

Its class is $x^{4-i}y^i$, giving $x^4,x^3y,x^2y^2,xy^3,y^4$.

### Justification

The quotient gives spanning. Their polynomial realization gives linear independence by coefficient uniqueness.

### Conclusion

The five monomials form a basis, so $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^4V=5$.

content.title: Adapt the dimension proof
content.introMarkdown: Give a basis and prove its size, rather than only citing a formula.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Parameterize the classes by $i=0,\ldots,5$.

The parameter gives both an exhaustive list and the dimension count.

Write $x^{5-i}y^i$, explain why every tensor-word class has this form, then invoke monomial independence.

## The general count

For an $n$-dimensional space, basis monomials correspond to exponent vectors $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_i\ge0$ and $a_1+\cdots+a_n=d$. Stars and bars counts these vectors:

$$\dim\operatorname{Sym}^dV=\binom{n+d-1}{d}.$$

For $n=2$, this becomes $d+1$.

content.title: Derive a three-variable dimension
content.introMarkdown: Derive $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^4V$ from exponent triples and evaluate the binomial coefficient.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write the exponent equation before the binomial coefficient.

The formula is meaningful only after its counted objects have been identified.

Describe the nonnegative solutions to $a_1+a_2+a_3=4$, then apply stars and bars.

## Exact degree is not bounded degree

The space $k[T,S]_d$ contains homogeneous forms of exactly degree $d$. The space of polynomials of degree at most $d$ contains all degrees from zero through $d$ and therefore has dimension

$$1+2+\cdots+(d+1)=\frac{(d+1)(d+2)}2.$$

Confusing these two spaces changes both the basis and the dimension.

content.title: Separate two polynomial spaces
content.introMarkdown: Give a basis and dimension for each space, and identify where $1+T+S^2$ belongs.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Inspect every monomial degree before choosing the ambient space.

Symmetric powers correspond to one homogeneous graded piece, not the full truncated polynomial ring.

List degree zero, one, and two monomials separately, then compare with the degree-two-only list.

## Verify the syllabus dimensions from the theorem

For a two-dimensional space, the formula gives $\binom d d+\binom d{d-1}$ in disguise: there is one monomial for every possible exponent of $S$, from zero through $d$.

content.title: Prove the dimensions 2, 3, and 4
content.introMarkdown: Construct the three bases and prove that their dimensions are respectively $2,3,4$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write the degree-$d$ monomial pattern before specializing.

The syllabus asks for verification, not memorized dimensions.

Use $T^{d-i}S^i$, justify spanning and independence, then substitute $d=1,2,3$.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-15, source lines 704 to 712.

**Resource version:** Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics 129, 2004 electronic edition.

**Exact locator:** Appendix B §B.2, pp. 472–473: exterior and symmetric powers, quotient construction, and ordered-index basis in Fulton & Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course, Springer GTM 129.

**Reading purpose:** Use the ordered-index basis statement to connect the quotient definition with concrete monomial bases and dimension counts.
Day 3 uses these graded pieces as the source and target of polynomial multiplication.
Day 2 is complete when you can derive the dimension from exponent vectors and distinguish homogeneous degree $d$ from degree at most $d$.

activities.title: List the ordered-index classes
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V$ have basis $(x,y,z)$. Consider $\operatorname{Sym}^3V$.

List every ordered-index basis monomial exactly once.

Organize the list by the exponent of $x$ so that omissions are detectable.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The ten monomials are $x^3,x^2y,x^2z,xy^2,xyz,xz^2,y^3,y^2z,yz^2,z^3$. Each corresponds to a nondecreasing length-three index sequence, and every such sequence appears once.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All ten ordered-index monomials appear exactly once.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The organization demonstrates completeness rather than presenting an unverified list.

activities.title: Adapt the dimension proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V$ have basis $(x,y)$ and consider $\operatorname{Sym}^5V$.

Give a basis and prove its size, rather than only citing a formula.

Use the number of $y$ factors as the classification parameter.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The degree-five basis and dimension are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response proves both spanning and independence through a unique exponent count.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every length-five word has $i$ copies of $y$ for a unique $0\le i\le5$, and its quotient class is $x^{5-i}y^i$. Thus $x^5,x^4y,x^3y^2,x^2y^3,xy^4,y^5$ span. Their polynomial images are distinct monomials and hence independent. They form a six-element basis, so the dimension is six.

activities.title: Derive a three-variable dimension
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $\dim V=3$ and $d=4$.

Derive $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^4V$ from exponent triples and evaluate the binomial coefficient.

Explain what the stars and bars count is counting in this vector-space problem.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The exponent count and dimension are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The combinatorial objects are explicitly matched to symmetric monomials.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A basis monomial is $e_1^{a_1}e_2^{a_2}e_3^{a_3}$ with nonnegative exponents summing to four. Stars and bars counts these triples as $\binom{4+3-1}{3-1}=\binom62=15$. Hence $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^4V=15$.

activities.title: Separate two polynomial spaces
activities.promptMarkdown:
Compare homogeneous binary quadratics with binary polynomials of degree at most two.

Give a basis and dimension for each space, and identify where $1+T+S^2$ belongs.

Do not use the same symbol for the two spaces.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The homogeneous degree-two space has basis $T^2,TS,S^2$ and dimension three; it realizes $\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^\vee)$. The degree-at-most-two space has basis $1,T,S,T^2,TS,S^2$ and dimension six. The polynomial $1+T+S^2$ belongs only to the latter because its monomials have three different total degrees.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both bases, dimensions, and the example classification are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The distinction is tied to exact total degree rather than informal polynomial size.

activities.title: Prove the dimensions 2, 3, and 4
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V$ be two-dimensional with basis $(T,S)$ and consider degrees $1,2,3$.

Construct the three bases and prove that their dimensions are respectively $2,3,4$.

Make the general $d+1$ mechanism visible instead of reporting three unexplained counts.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three bases and dimensions are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer derives the counts from the unique exponent classification and proves basis status.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In degree $d$, every symmetric class is $T^{d-i}S^i$ for a unique $i\in\{0,\ldots,d\}$, and these monomials are independent. For $d=1$ the basis is $(T,S)$; for $d=2$, $(T^2,TS,S^2)$; for $d=3$, $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$. The lists have $2,3,4$ elements respectively. The same classification proves the general dimension $d+1$.

lessons.title: Multiplication in the symmetric algebra
lessons.summary: Construct and analyze the bilinear multiplication map from degree one and degree two binary forms to degree three binary forms.
objectives: Construct and analyze the bilinear multiplication map from degree one and degree two binary forms to degree three binary forms.

content.markdown:
## Symmetric powers fit together as a graded algebra

The spaces $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V^\vee)$ are not isolated. Multiplying a degree-$a$ form by a degree-$b$ form produces a degree-$(a+b)$ form. This graded multiplication is the algebraic operation used later to factor binary forms.

## Reactivate bilinearity and degree addition

Polynomial multiplication distributes over addition and respects scalar multiplication in each factor. Total degrees add under multiplication. Days 1 and 2 established the symmetric-power interpretation and monomial bases.

## The graded multiplication map

For all $a,b\ge0$, multiplication defines

$$\mu_{a,b}:\operatorname{Sym}^a(V^\vee)\times\operatorname{Sym}^b(V^\vee)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{a+b}(V^\vee),\qquad(F,G)\longmapsto FG.$$

It is bilinear, not generally injective as a map of pairs, and it is not linear on the Cartesian product. The syllabus case is $\mu_{1,2}$.

content.title: Prove multiplication is bilinear
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\mu_{1,2}$ is linear in each variable and that its values have the stated degree.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Do not stop after proving linearity in the first input.

Bilinearity requires two independent families of identities.

Write addition and scalar compatibility first in $L$, then in $Q$, and finish with the degree calculation.

## Complete worked model

Multiply $L=T-2S$ and $Q=3T^2+TS+S^2$.

Compute the cubic, then recover each coefficient as a short convolution.

### Strategy

Distribute $T$ and $-2S$ separately and align equal cubic monomials.

### Hypotheses

$TQ=3T^3+T^2S+TS^2$ and $-2SQ=-6T^2S-2TS^2-2S^3$.

### Intermediate claims

Combining like terms gives $3T^3-5T^2S-TS^2-2S^3$.

### Justification

Every term has degree three, and the coefficients are $(1)(3)$, $(1)(1)+(-2)(3)$, $(1)(1)+(-2)(1)$, and $(-2)(1)$.

### Conclusion

$\mu_{1,2}(L,Q)=3T^3-5T^2S-TS^2-2S^3$.

content.title: Compute a new product by convolution
content.introMarkdown: Compute $LQ$ and explain the source of the $T^2S$ and $TS^2$ coefficients.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Keep the $2TQ$ and $SQ$ rows separate until like terms are aligned.

Each middle coefficient receives two contributions.

Write the two partial products, align the cubic basis, and add column by column.

## The complete basis table

With bases $(T,S)$, $(T^2,TS,S^2)$, and $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$, the six basis products are

$$T\cdot T^2=T^3,\ T\cdot TS=T^2S,\ T\cdot S^2=TS^2,$$

$$S\cdot T^2=T^2S,\ S\cdot TS=TS^2,\ S\cdot S^2=S^3.$$

This table determines the bilinear map completely.

content.title: Derive the coordinate formula
content.introMarkdown: Derive the four output coefficients of $LQ$ from the basis table.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Expand the six scalar multiples corresponding to the six basis products.

The two middle coordinates each combine two basis contributions.

Use the table in order, collect coefficients of $T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3$, then write the coordinate vector.

## Surjectivity is not factorization by every chosen pair

Every nonzero complex binary cubic has a linear factor, so over $\mathbb C$ the map $\mu_{1,2}$ reaches every cubic. Over $\mathbb R$, this remains true for odd-degree binary forms after dehomogenizing, but such a field-dependent factorization theorem is separate from the elementary basis table.

More basically, bilinearity alone does not prove surjectivity, uniqueness, or injectivity. For example $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ has the same product as $(L,Q)$ when $\lambda\ne0$.

content.title: Separate what the basis table proves
content.introMarkdown: Refute both claims and state exactly what the table does prove.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Test the pair after reciprocal rescaling.

A visible family of equal products immediately rules out uniqueness and pairwise injectivity.

Compute $(\lambda L)(\lambda^{-1}Q)$, then limit the table’s conclusion to basis values and target degree.

## From basis values to the whole map

A bilinear map is determined by its values on all ordered pairs of basis vectors. The six products therefore provide a complete coordinate description of $\mu_{1,2}$, not merely six examples.

content.title: Construct the full multiplication map
content.introMarkdown: Construct $\mu_{1,2}$ from all basis products, prove bilinearity, derive its coordinate formula, and state one property that the calculation does not by itself establish.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Type the source and target before expanding coefficients.

The graded degrees explain why multiplication has this codomain and prevent an untyped calculation.

Write the map, verify the two linearity variables, give all six basis products, collect coefficients, and finish with the scaling boundary.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-15, source lines 704 to 712.

**Resource version:** Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics 129, 2004 electronic edition.

**Exact locator:** Appendix B §B.2, pp. 472–475: symmetric powers and the graded symmetric algebra in Fulton & Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course, Springer GTM 129.

**Reading purpose:** Use the symmetric-algebra discussion to place the degree-one times degree-two calculation inside the general graded multiplication.
Day 4 studies how linear changes of variables induce maps on every symmetric power.
Day 3 is complete when you can construct $\mu_{1,2}$ from its basis table, derive the coefficient formula, and avoid inferring injectivity or unique factorization from bilinearity.

activities.title: Prove multiplication is bilinear
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider $\mu_{1,2}:\operatorname{Sym}^1(V^\vee)\times\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^\vee)\to\operatorname{Sym}^3(V^\vee)$.

Prove that $\mu_{1,2}$ is linear in each variable and that its values have the stated degree.

Write both distributive identities and both scalar identities.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Separate linearity and target degree are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof checks both variables rather than citing distributivity vaguely.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $L_1,L_2$ linear and $Q$ quadratic, $(L_1+L_2)Q=L_1Q+L_2Q$ and $(cL_1)Q=c(L_1Q)$. Likewise, $L(Q_1+Q_2)=LQ_1+LQ_2$ and $L(cQ_1)=c(LQ_1)$. Each product has total degree $1+2=3$, so it lies in $\operatorname{Sym}^3(V^\vee)$. Thus $\mu_{1,2}$ is bilinear with the stated target.

activities.title: Compute a new product by convolution
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $L=2T+S$ and $Q=T^2-3TS+4S^2$.

Compute $LQ$ and explain the source of the $T^2S$ and $TS^2$ coefficients.

Align terms by the ordered cubic basis.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $2TQ=2T^3-6T^2S+8TS^2$ and $SQ=T^2S-3TS^2+4S^3$. Therefore $LQ=2T^3-5T^2S+5TS^2+4S^3$. The middle coefficients are $2(-3)+1(1)=-5$ and $2(4)+1(-3)=5$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The cubic product and middle coefficients are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response traces each middle coefficient to both contributing products.

activities.title: Derive the coordinate formula
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

Derive the four output coefficients of $LQ$ from the basis table.

State the coordinate vector in the cubic monomial basis.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All four coefficient formulas are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The formula is derived from bilinearity and the complete basis table.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Using bilinearity and the six basis products, $LQ=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3$. Thus the coordinate vector in $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$ is $(ac,ad+bc,ae+bd,be)$.

activities.title: Separate what the basis table proves
activities.promptMarkdown:
A student says: “The six basis products prove that $\mu_{1,2}$ is injective and every cubic has a unique factorization $LQ$.”

Refute both claims and state exactly what the table does prove.

Use the scaling symmetry for one refutation.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The table proves the values of a bilinear map on basis pairs, so it determines the map and shows that products land in the cubic space. It does not prove injectivity: for any nonzero $\lambda$, $(L,Q)$ and $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ have the same product. It also does not prove existence or uniqueness of factorization for every cubic; those are separate field-dependent claims.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both unsupported conclusions are correctly rejected.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes determination of the bilinear map from global properties of its fibers and image.

activities.title: Construct the full multiplication map
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the standard bases of $\operatorname{Sym}^1(V^\vee)$, $\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^\vee)$, and $\operatorname{Sym}^3(V^\vee)$ for two-dimensional $V$.

Construct $\mu_{1,2}$ from all basis products, prove bilinearity, derive its coordinate formula, and state one property that the calculation does not by itself establish.

Give a complete argument in the order: typed spaces, basis table, bilinearity, coordinate formula, scope boundary.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The full map, basis table, and coordinate law are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof establishes bilinearity and includes an explicit logical boundary.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The map is $\mu_{1,2}(L,Q)=LQ$ from the stated degree-one and degree-two spaces to degree three. Polynomial distributivity and scalar compatibility prove bilinearity. On the basis pairs, $T(T^2)=T^3$, $T(TS)=T^2S$, $T(S^2)=TS^2$, $S(T^2)=T^2S$, $S(TS)=TS^2$, and $S(S^2)=S^3$. Hence $(aT+bS)(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3$. This construction alone does not prove unique factorization or injectivity; reciprocal rescaling preserves the product.

lessons.title: Induced maps and changes of variables
lessons.summary: Construct the map induced on a symmetric power by a linear map and compute its action on binary forms under a change of variables.
objectives: Construct the map induced on a symmetric power by a linear map and compute its action on binary forms under a change of variables.

content.markdown:
## A linear map acts on every degree

Once a linear change of coordinates is known on $V$ or $V^\vee$, it acts on products by applying the map to every factor. This turns a small matrix into a structured action on a much larger polynomial space.

## Reactivate composition and dual pullback

Week 14 defined the dual map by precomposition. Here we use an ordinary linear map $A:W\to V$ and its dual $A^\vee:V^\vee\to W^\vee$. Day 1 established symmetric products; Day 3 established their multiplication.

## Functoriality of symmetric powers

A linear map $A:V\to W$ induces

$$\operatorname{Sym}^d(A):\operatorname{Sym}^dV\to\operatorname{Sym}^dW,$$

$$v_1\cdots v_d\longmapsto A(v_1)\cdots A(v_d).$$

This is well defined because permuting the input factors only permutes the output factors. It respects identities and composition: $\operatorname{Sym}^d(B\circ A)=\operatorname{Sym}^d(B)\circ\operatorname{Sym}^d(A)$.

content.title: Prove the induced map is well defined
content.introMarkdown: Prove that the rule descends from $V^{\otimes2}$ to $\operatorname{Sym}^2V$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compare the images of $u\otimes v$ and $v\otimes u$.

A rule on representatives defines a quotient map only when equivalent representatives have equal images.

Write the generating difference, map both terms, and use commutativity in the target symmetric square.

## Complete worked model

Let $A$ act on the basis $(T,S)$ by $A(T)=T+S$ and $A(S)=S$. Compute $\operatorname{Sym}^2(A)$.

Find the images of the quadratic basis and the resulting matrix.

### Strategy

Apply $A$ to every factor, expand, then read coordinate columns.

### Hypotheses

$A(T)^2=(T+S)^2$, $A(T)A(S)=(T+S)S$, and $A(S)^2=S^2$.

### Intermediate claims

The images are $T^2+2TS+S^2$, $TS+S^2$, and $S^2$.

### Justification

In the basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$, these are the columns $(1,2,1)^T$, $(0,1,1)^T$, and $(0,0,1)^T$.

### Conclusion

The induced matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\1&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

content.title: Compute an induced cubic map
content.introMarkdown: Compute $\operatorname{Sym}^3(B)$ on the cubic monomial basis and give its matrix.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Count separately how many $T$ and $S$ factors occur in each monomial.

Each factor contributes its own scalar to the induced map.

For $T^{3-i}S^i$, multiply $2^{3-i}$ by $(-1)^i$, then place the result on the diagonal.

## Pulling back binary forms

If $A:W\to V$, then $A^\vee:V^\vee\to W^\vee$ sends a linear form to its composition with $A$. Applying $\operatorname{Sym}^d$ gives the substitution action on degree-$d$ forms:

$$F\longmapsto F\circ A.$$

The direction matters: points move by $A$, while functions pull back by composition.

content.title: Compute a cubic pullback
content.introMarkdown: Compute $F\circ A$ and identify the symmetric-power map responsible for the substitution.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Start with $(F\circ A)(t,s)=F(t+s,s)$.

Writing the composition first prevents reversing the action on functions.

Substitute the two coordinate functions, expand, then name $\operatorname{Sym}^3(A^\vee)$.

## Characteristic and symmetrization

The symmetric power is always defined as a quotient. In characteristic zero, one can also average a tensor over all $d!$ permutations and identify symmetric tensors with an invariant subspace. That averaging requires division by $d!$.

Therefore the quotient definition remains safe in every characteristic, while the averaging projection must not be used when the field characteristic divides $d!$.

content.title: Diagnose an invalid averaging argument
content.introMarkdown: Explain why this formula is unavailable and state the valid construction that remains.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the scalar $2$ is invertible in the field.

Averaging is an optional characteristic-dependent tool, whereas the quotient is the definition.

Reject $1/2$, then write the permutation-relation quotient without division.

## Functoriality is a proof tool

Once well-definedness is established, identities and composition can be checked on pure symmetric products. This gives a compact proof that coordinate substitutions compose exactly as the underlying linear maps do.

content.title: Prove and compute functoriality
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\operatorname{Sym}^2(B\circ A)=\operatorname{Sym}^2(B)\circ\operatorname{Sym}^2(A)$ and compute both sides on $T^2$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Evaluate both composite maps on a general pure product $uv$.

Pure products expose the definition and span the symmetric square.

Prove equality on $uv$, invoke spanning, then compute $(2T+S)^2$.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-15, source lines 704 to 712.

**Resource version:** Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics 129, 2004 electronic edition.

**Exact locator:** Appendix B §B.1, pp. 471–472, and §B.2, pp. 472–475: functorial tensor constructions and symmetric powers in Fulton & Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course, Springer GTM 129.

**Reading purpose:** Read the functoriality statements with the quotient construction to justify induced maps and coordinate substitutions.
Day 5 retrieves the scheduled proof tools and synthesizes bases, multiplication, and induced maps in one independent argument.
Day 4 is complete when you can prove an induced symmetric-power map is well defined, compute it on a basis, and keep point maps separate from pullbacks of forms.

activities.title: Prove the induced map is well defined
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:V\to W$ be linear and define a proposed map by $uv\mapsto A(u)A(v)$.

Prove that the rule descends from $V^{\otimes2}$ to $\operatorname{Sym}^2V$.

Check the exact generating relation of the quotient.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The quotient relation is correctly preserved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Well-definedness is proved against the generating permutation relation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The symmetric-square quotient identifies $u\otimes v$ with $v\otimes u$. Their proposed images are $A(u)A(v)$ and $A(v)A(u)$, which are equal in $\operatorname{Sym}^2W$. Therefore the generating relations lie in the kernel of the tensor-level map, so the rule descends to a well-defined linear map on the quotient.

activities.title: Compute an induced cubic map
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $B(T)=2T$ and $B(S)=-S$.

Compute $\operatorname{Sym}^3(B)$ on the cubic monomial basis and give its matrix.

Apply $B$ to each factor before simplifying.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $B(T^3)=8T^3$, $B(T^2S)=-4T^2S$, $B(TS^2)=2TS^2$, and $B(S^3)=-S^3$. Hence the matrix in $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(8,-4,2,-1)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All cubic images and the diagonal matrix are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each scalar is raised according to its factor multiplicity.

activities.title: Compute a cubic pullback
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:W\to V$ be given in domain coordinates $(t,s)$ by $A(t,s)=(t+s,s)$. Let $(T,S)$ be the target coordinate functionals and let $F(T,S)=T^2S$.

Compute $F\circ A$ and identify the symmetric-power map responsible for the substitution.

Keep the direction $A:W\to V$ and $A^\vee:V^\vee\to W^\vee$ explicit.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $(F\circ A)(t,s)=(t+s)^2s=t^2s+2ts^2+s^3$. The linear pullback satisfies $A^\vee(T)=t+s$ and $A^\vee(S)=s$ as functionals on $W$; applying $\operatorname{Sym}^3(A^\vee)$ sends the target form $T^2S$ to the domain form $(t+s)^2s$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The cubic substitution and responsible induced map are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response tracks the contravariant function pullback separately from the point map.

activities.title: Diagnose an invalid averaging argument
activities.promptMarkdown:
Over a field of characteristic $2$, a student defines the symmetric-square projection by $t\mapsto\tfrac12(t+\tau t)$.

Explain why this formula is unavailable and state the valid construction that remains.

Identify the exact scalar that cannot be inverted.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In characteristic two, $2=0$ and has no multiplicative inverse, so the coefficient $1/2$ is undefined. The symmetric square is still validly defined as the quotient of $V^{\otimes2}$ by the span of $u\otimes v-v\otimes u$. The failure concerns the averaging projection, not the quotient construction.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The characteristic obstruction and valid quotient construction are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes a failed representation of the construction from failure of the construction itself.

activities.title: Prove and compute functoriality
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A(T)=T+S$, $A(S)=S$ and $B(T)=2T$, $B(S)=S$.

Prove $\operatorname{Sym}^2(B\circ A)=\operatorname{Sym}^2(B)\circ\operatorname{Sym}^2(A)$ and compute both sides on $T^2$.

First prove the general pure-product identity, then specialize.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The functorial identity and concrete image are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Equality is proved on a spanning family before the coordinate verification.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For every $uv\in\operatorname{Sym}^2V$, $\operatorname{Sym}^2(B\circ A)(uv)=B(A(u))B(A(v))$, which equals $\operatorname{Sym}^2(B)(A(u)A(v))$. Pure products span, so the maps are equal. Here $(B\circ A)(T)=2T+S$, so the left side sends $T^2$ to $(2T+S)^2=4T^2+4TS+S^2$. On the right, $\operatorname{Sym}^2(A)(T^2)=(T+S)^2$, and applying $B$ to every factor gives the same result.

lessons.title: Synthesis: bases, products, and transformations
lessons.summary: Retrieve the scheduled proof structures and synthesize the quotient definition, monomial bases, graded multiplication, and induced maps on symmetric powers.
objectives: Retrieve the scheduled proof structures and synthesize the quotient definition, monomial bases, graded multiplication, and induced maps on symmetric powers.

content.markdown:
## The week forms one reusable construction

A quotient removes factor order, a monomial basis makes the quotient computable, graded multiplication links degrees, and functoriality transports the construction through linear maps.

The final lesson begins with three scheduled retrievals, then uses those tools in new symmetric-power arguments.

## Closed-book retrieval first

Attempt the first three questions without notes. They deliberately review Weeks 7, 12, and 14 in new contexts. The remaining questions return to Week 15 and culminate in one proof that combines all four parts of the construction.

## Scheduled 8-week review: disprove before repairing

Week 7 distinguished a counterexample from a repaired theorem. Retrieve that discipline on a claim about homogeneous degree.

content.title: Retrieve counterexample and repair
content.introMarkdown: Disprove the claim and state a correct replacement with the missing hypothesis.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Choose two homogeneous forms whose degrees differ.

A universal claim is disproved by one valid counterexample, but a useful repair must identify the missing hypothesis.

Use $T$ and $S^2$, then require equal degree and inspect the degrees of all surviving terms.

## Scheduled 3-week review: kernel, image, and rank-nullity

Week 12 linked a linear map’s kernel and image to dimension. Retrieve the theorem on a symmetric-square map.

content.title: Retrieve rank-nullity on a symmetric square
content.introMarkdown: Compute its kernel and image in the basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$ and verify rank-nullity.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compute the three basis images before describing subspaces.

The images expose both the image generator and the kernel generators.

Map $T^2,TS,S^2$, then read off bases and check that rank plus nullity equals three.

## Scheduled 1-week review: dual pullback

Week 14 showed that functions move contravariantly. Retrieve the definition before extending it to symmetric powers.

content.title: Retrieve a dual pullback
content.introMarkdown: Compute $A^\vee(T)$ and $A^\vee(S)$ from the definition.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write $A^\vee(T)=T\circ A$ before substituting coordinates.

The definition fixes the contravariant direction and prevents transposing the wrong map.

Compose each target coordinate with $A$ and simplify the resulting linear form.

## Synthesis setup

Let $V^\vee=\langle T,S\rangle$. The ordered monomial bases identify $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V^\vee)$ with binary forms. Multiplication links degrees, and any $A^\vee$ acts on a product by

$$\operatorname{Sym}^{a+b}(A^\vee)(FG)=\operatorname{Sym}^a(A^\vee)(F)\operatorname{Sym}^b(A^\vee)(G).$$

This compatibility follows by applying $A^\vee$ to every factor.

content.title: Prove multiplication commutes with pullback
content.introMarkdown: Prove $(FG)\circ A=(F\circ A)(G\circ A)$ and express it as compatibility of symmetric-power maps with $\mu_{1,2}$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Evaluate the two forms on the same arbitrary input $w$.

Pointwise evaluation gives the shortest complete proof and fixes every source and target.

Expand both evaluations, identify the common scalar product, then rewrite the result using $\mu_{1,2}$.

## Complete worked model

Let $L=T+S$, $Q=T^2+S^2$, and let $A^\vee(T)=T-S$, $A^\vee(S)=S$.

Transform the product $LQ$ in two ways and prove the answers agree.

### Strategy

First multiply and substitute. Then transform each factor and multiply.

### Hypotheses

$LQ=T^3+T^2S+TS^2+S^3$; the transformed factors are $T$ and $(T-S)^2+S^2$.

### Intermediate claims

The factorwise route gives $T(T^2-2TS+2S^2)=T^3-2T^2S+2TS^2$.

### Justification

Direct substitution into the expanded cubic gives the same polynomial after collecting terms.

### Conclusion

The agreement is a concrete instance of compatibility between graded multiplication and the induced symmetric-power map.

content.title: Transfer the two-route verification
content.introMarkdown: Compute the transformed cubic directly and factorwise, then show the two results coincide.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Keep the direct and factorwise calculations on separate lines.

Two distinguishable routes provide a genuine check rather than the same expansion written twice.

Expand $LQ$ before substitution, then restart from the two factors, transform them, multiply, and compare coefficients.

## Three distinctions to preserve

The symmetric quotient is not the full tensor power. Homogeneous degree $d$ is not degree at most $d$. A coordinate substitution on forms is a pullback and therefore reverses the direction of the point map.

A complete solution names these boundaries exactly where they matter.

content.title: Audit a compressed argument
content.introMarkdown: Correct each assertion with the smallest precise replacement.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Correct the tensor-power equality before addressing coordinates.

The first conflation removes the quotient that defines the subject.

Write one sentence each for quotient, exact homogeneous degree, and pullback direction.

## Final proof architecture

A complete Week 15 proof should move in a controlled order: define the quotient, construct the ordered monomial bases, verify the required low-degree dimensions, build the multiplication table, and then prove compatibility with an induced change of variables.

content.title: Synthesize the Week 15 construction
content.introMarkdown: Prove the binary-form realization of $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V^\vee)$, verify dimensions $2,3,4$ for $d=1,2,3$, construct $\mu_{1,2}$ on the monomial bases, and prove that pullback by $A$ commutes with this multiplication.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Begin with the quotient and its ordered monomial classes; do not begin with an unexplained dimension formula.

The basis, dimensions, multiplication, and induced action all depend on that construction.

Build the proof in five paragraphs: quotient, basis, low degrees, multiplication table, pullback compatibility; finish with the dimension-eight versus dimension-four boundary.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-15, source lines 704 to 712.

**Resource version:** Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics 129, 2004 electronic edition.

**Exact locator:** Appendix B §§B.1–B.2, pp. 471–475: tensor products, symmetric powers, bases, and multiplication in Fulton & Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course, Springer GTM 129.

**Reading purpose:** Use the complete appendix sequence to consolidate the week’s construction and check every source, target, and quotient relation.
Week 16 will differentiate polynomial maps; the multiplication map studied here becomes a concrete source of Jacobian computations.
Week 15 is complete when you can reconstruct the symmetric-power quotient, derive its binary-form basis, build the graded product, and prove that linear changes of variables act compatibly.

activities.title: Retrieve counterexample and repair
activities.promptMarkdown:
Claim: for all homogeneous binary forms $F$ and $G$, the sum $F+G$ is homogeneous.

Disprove the claim and state a correct replacement with the missing hypothesis.

Use nonzero forms of different degrees, then prove the corrected statement.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The counterexample and repaired statement are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The missing same-degree hypothesis is identified and used in a proof.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Take $F=T$ and $G=S^2$. Both are homogeneous, but $F+G=T+S^2$ has terms of degrees one and two, so it is not homogeneous. A correct statement is: if $F$ and $G$ are homogeneous of the same degree $d$, then $F+G$ is either zero or homogeneous of degree $d$. Every surviving monomial in the sum still has degree $d$.

activities.title: Retrieve rank-nullity on a symmetric square
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:k^2\to k^2$ satisfy $A(T)=T$ and $A(S)=0$. Consider $\operatorname{Sym}^2(A)$.

Compute its kernel and image in the basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$ and verify rank-nullity.

Name bases for both subspaces.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel, image, rank, nullity, and dimension check are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The theorem is verified from explicit basis images.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The induced map sends $T^2\mapsto T^2$, $TS\mapsto0$, and $S^2\mapsto0$. Its image is $\langle T^2\rangle$, so its rank is one. Its kernel is $\langle TS,S^2\rangle$, so its nullity is two. Since the domain has dimension three, $1+2=3$ verifies rank-nullity.

activities.title: Retrieve a dual pullback
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:W\to V$ be $A(t,s)=(t+s,t-s)$ in domain coordinates $(t,s)$. Let $(T,S)$ be the target coordinate functionals.

Compute $A^\vee(T)$ and $A^\vee(S)$ from the definition.

Evaluate each composite on a general $(t,s)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both pulled-back coordinate functionals are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The computation begins from precomposition and keeps the direction of the map explicit.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: By definition $A^\vee(\ell)=\ell\circ A$. Hence $(A^\vee T)(t,s)=T(t+s,t-s)=t+s$, so $A^\vee(T)=t+s$ as a functional on $W$. Similarly $(A^\vee S)(t,s)=t-s$, so $A^\vee(S)=t-s$.

activities.title: Prove multiplication commutes with pullback
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:W\to V$, $F\in\operatorname{Sym}^1(V^\vee)$, and $G\in\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^\vee)$.

Prove $(FG)\circ A=(F\circ A)(G\circ A)$ and express it as compatibility of symmetric-power maps with $\mu_{1,2}$.

Evaluate both sides at an arbitrary $w\in W$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The pointwise identity and typed symmetric-power identity are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Equality is proved by evaluation and then translated into the graded-map language.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For every $w\in W$, $((FG)\circ A)(w)=(FG)(A(w))=F(A(w))G(A(w))=((F\circ A)(G\circ A))(w)$. Therefore the forms are equal. Equivalently, $\operatorname{Sym}^3(A^\vee)(\mu_{1,2}(F,G))=\mu_{1,2}(\operatorname{Sym}^1(A^\vee)F,\operatorname{Sym}^2(A^\vee)G)$.

activities.title: Transfer the two-route verification
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $L=2T-S$, $Q=T^2+TS$, and $B^\vee(T)=T+S$, $B^\vee(S)=S$.

Compute the transformed cubic directly and factorwise, then show the two results coincide.

Display both routes separately before comparing.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First $LQ=2T^3+T^2S-TS^2$. Direct substitution gives $2(T+S)^3+(T+S)^2S-(T+S)S^2=2T^3+7T^2S+7TS^2+2S^3$. Factorwise, $B^\vee(L)=2(T+S)-S=2T+S$ and $B^\vee(Q)=(T+S)^2+(T+S)S=T^2+3TS+2S^2$. Their product is again $2T^3+7T^2S+7TS^2+2S^3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both transformed cubics agree and are correctly computed.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The two independent routes verify the compatibility identity in a concrete case.

activities.title: Audit a compressed argument
activities.promptMarkdown:
A proposed solution says: “$V^{\otimes d}=\operatorname{Sym}^dV$, every polynomial of degree at most $d$ lies in that space, and $A$ sends a form forward by $F\mapsto F\circ A^{-1}$.”

Correct each assertion with the smallest precise replacement.

Do not replace the paragraph with a vague warning; state three corrected claims.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First, $\operatorname{Sym}^dV$ is a quotient of $V^{\otimes d}$, generally of smaller dimension. Second, under a dual-basis identification it corresponds to homogeneous forms of exactly degree $d$, not all forms of degree at most $d$. Third, a map $A:W\to V$ pulls a form on $V$ back to $W$ by $F\mapsto F\circ A$; the formula with $A^{-1}$ describes a different convention and requires invertibility.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three conflations are corrected precisely.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each repair names the relevant construction, degree, or map direction and its hypotheses.

activities.title: Synthesize the Week 15 construction
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V$ be two-dimensional with dual basis $(T,S)$, and let $A:W\to V$ be linear.

Prove the binary-form realization of $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V^\vee)$, verify dimensions $2,3,4$ for $d=1,2,3$, construct $\mu_{1,2}$ on the monomial bases, and prove that pullback by $A$ commutes with this multiplication.

Include one explicit boundary statement distinguishing the quotient from the full tensor power.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Every required construction, dimension, product, and compatibility claim is correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof connects the stages in order and preserves the tensor-quotient and pullback boundaries.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The symmetric power is the quotient of $(V^\vee)^{\otimes d}$ by permutation relations. With dual basis $(T,S)$, each tensor-word class reduces to exactly one monomial $T^{d-i}S^i$ for $0\le i\le d$, and every element has a unique linear-combination expression in these monomial classes. An element such as $T^d+S^d$ is therefore not generally one monomial. Polynomial coefficient uniqueness proves that the monomial classes are independent, so they form a basis and identify the space with homogeneous degree-$d$ binary forms. For $d=1,2,3$ the bases have respectively $2,3,4$ elements. Multiplication $\mu_{1,2}(L,Q)=LQ$ is bilinear, and its basis products are $T(T^2)=T^3$, $T(TS)=S(T^2)=T^2S$, $T(S^2)=S(TS)=TS^2$, and $S(S^2)=S^3$. For $w\in W$, $((LQ)\circ A)(w)=L(Aw)Q(Aw)=((L\circ A)(Q\circ A))(w)$, proving compatibility with the induced pullbacks. The full tensor power is generally larger: when $d=3$, it has dimension eight, while the symmetric quotient has dimension four.

lessons.title: The derivative is a linear approximation
lessons.summary: Derive the Jacobian columns from the definition of differentiability and distinguish the total derivative from partial and directional derivatives.
objectives: Derive the Jacobian columns from the definition of differentiability and distinguish the total derivative from partial and directional derivatives.

content.markdown:
## Why begin with an error term?

In one variable, a derivative is more than a collection of slopes: it is the linear map that predicts the whole first-order change. The same idea survives in several variables, but the linear map is now represented by a matrix.

Starting from that approximation prevents a common mistake. A table of existing partial derivatives is not, by itself, a proof that a function is differentiable.

## Reactivate maps, norms, and matrices

A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ has a matrix once bases are fixed. The Euclidean norm measures the size of the input increment $h$, and matrix multiplication computes $Ah$.

Week 11 separated a linear map from its matrix. Week 13 related a square matrix to its determinant. Week 15 supplied polynomial maps that we will differentiate later.

## Differentiability at a point

Let $F:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ and let $a$ be an interior point of $U$. We say that $F$ is differentiable at $a$ when there is a linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ such that

$$F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h),\qquad \frac{\|r(h)\|}{\|h\|}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0).$$

The quotient says that the error is small compared with every first-order displacement. The linear map is unique and is denoted $DF_a$.

content.title: Read a remainder estimate
content.introMarkdown: Prove from the displayed inequality that $A$ satisfies the differentiability remainder condition.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compare the remainder with $\|h\|$, not with the constant $1$.

Differentiability controls the error relative to the size of the displacement.

Write the quotient inequality for nonzero $h$ and take its limit.

## Complete worked model

Let $F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $F(x,y)=(x^2+xy,\,y^2)$ and fix $a=(a_1,a_2)$.

Derive $DF_a$ directly by expanding $F(a+h)$ and prove that the remainder is $o(\|h\|)$.

### Strategy

Expand both coordinates, collect every term linear in $h=(u,v)$ into one map, and bound the remaining quadratic terms.

### Hypotheses

Use $|u|,|v|\le\|h\|$ and the triangle inequality.

### Intermediate claims

Expansion gives the linear part $((2a_1+a_2)u+a_1v,\,2a_2v)$ and remainder $(u^2+uv,\,v^2)$.

### Justification

The remainder norm is at most a fixed multiple of $\|h\|^2$, because each of $|u|^2$, $|uv|$, and $|v|^2$ is bounded by $\|h\|^2$.

### Conclusion

$DF_a(u,v)=((2a_1+a_2)u+a_1v,2a_2v)$, represented in standard coordinates by $\begin{pmatrix}2a_1+a_2&a_1\\0&2a_2\end{pmatrix}$.

content.title: Derive a derivative without quoting partials
content.introMarkdown: Display the linear map, the remainder, and a bound proving that the remainder divided by $\|(u,v)\|$ tends to zero.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Separate terms linear in $(u,v)$ from terms containing two increments.

Only the linear part can be the derivative; the rest must satisfy the small-error condition.

Expand both components, box the linear terms, and bound the remaining pair by a constant times $\|(u,v)\|^2$.

## Partial derivatives are columns of the derivative

Assume $F$ is differentiable at $a$. Put $h=te_j$, where $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate vector. Dividing

$$F(a+te_j)-F(a)=tDF_a(e_j)+r(te_j)$$

by $t$ and taking $t\to0$ gives $\partial_jF(a)=DF_a(e_j)$. Thus the $j$th Jacobian column is forced by the total derivative; it is not an independent definition of differentiability.

content.title: Recover every Jacobian column
content.introMarkdown: Prove carefully that the coordinate partial derivative $\partial_jF(a)$ exists and equals $Ae_j$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Replace $t$ by $|t|$ inside the norm comparison.

The derivative limit approaches from both signs, so the norm estimate must be sign-safe.

Set $h=te_j$, divide the vector equation, then estimate the norm of the remainder quotient.

## Existing directional derivatives need not assemble into a derivative

For a differentiable map, every directional derivative satisfies $D_vF(a)=DF_a(v)$ and therefore depends linearly on $v$. The converse fails: all directional derivatives can exist while no single linear map gives a uniform first-order approximation.

The function $f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ away from the origin, with $f(0,0)=0$, is a standard warning. Its directional derivatives exist, but their dependence on the direction is not linear.

content.title: Detect nonlinearity in the direction
content.introMarkdown: Compute $D_{(p,q)}f(0,0)$ and use its dependence on $(p,q)$ to prove that $f$ is not differentiable at the origin.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Test the direction map on $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and their sum.

One derivative must assign directional rates through a single linear map.

Compute the three values and compare the value at the sum with the sum of the values.

## A complete derivative argument

For a polynomial map, expansion provides a reliable proof pattern: identify the constant value, collect the homogeneous degree-one increment, and prove that all terms of increment degree at least two form an $o(\|h\|)$ remainder.

content.title: Prove differentiability from first principles
content.introMarkdown: At an arbitrary $(a,b)$, derive $DH_{(a,b)}$ from the differentiability definition and give its $3\times2$ Jacobian matrix.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first increment term whose degree was classified incorrectly.

A single misplaced quadratic term changes either the proposed derivative or the required error estimate.

Re-expand one coordinate at a time, group by total degree in $(u,v)$, and bound the degree-two-or-higher group.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.024, Chapter C notes, Spring 2011.

activities.title: Read a remainder estimate
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h)$ and $\|r(h)\|\le 3\|h\|^2$ whenever $\|h\|<1$.

Prove from the displayed inequality that $A$ satisfies the differentiability remainder condition.

Divide by $\|h\|$ for $h\ne0$ and state the limit explicitly.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $0<\|h\|<1$, $0\le\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\le3\|h\|$. The right-hand side tends to $0$ as $h\to0$, so the squeeze theorem gives $\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$. Thus the error is $o(\|h\|)$ and $A$ is the derivative.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The little-o condition follows correctly from the quadratic bound.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response divides by the input scale and completes the limiting argument.

activities.title: Derive a derivative without quoting partials
activities.promptMarkdown:
For $G(x,y)=(x^2-y,\,xy)$, derive $DG_{(a,b)}$ from the remainder definition.

Display the linear map, the remainder, and a bound proving that the remainder divided by $\|(u,v)\|$ tends to zero.

Use the worked expansion as an architecture, but compute this new target completely.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The derivative, remainder, bound, and coordinate matrix are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument is derived from the definition instead of assuming differentiability from formal partials.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $G(a+u,b+v)-G(a,b)=(2au-v,\,bu+av)+(u^2,uv)$. Hence $DG_{(a,b)}(u,v)=(2au-v,bu+av)$. Since $\|(u^2,uv)\|\le\sqrt2\|(u,v)\|^2$, its quotient by $\|(u,v)\|$ tends to zero. The Jacobian matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2a&-1\\b&a\end{pmatrix}$.

activities.title: Recover every Jacobian column
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ be differentiable at $a$ with derivative $A$.

Prove carefully that the coordinate partial derivative $\partial_jF(a)$ exists and equals $Ae_j$.

Track the sign of $t$ when dividing the norm estimate.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The coordinate derivative is correctly identified with the corresponding derivative column.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses the remainder estimate on a coordinate line and handles absolute values correctly.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Write $F(a+te_j)-F(a)=tAe_j+r(te_j)$. For $t\ne0$, division by $t$ gives $[F(a+te_j)-F(a)]/t=Ae_j+r(te_j)/t$. Moreover $\|r(te_j)/t\|=\|r(te_j)\|/\|te_j\|\to0$, because $\|e_j\|=1$. Therefore the difference quotient converges to $Ae_j$.

activities.title: Detect nonlinearity in the direction
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f(0,0)=0$ and $f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ otherwise.

Compute $D_{(p,q)}f(0,0)$ and use its dependence on $(p,q)$ to prove that $f$ is not differentiable at the origin.

A total derivative would have to be a linear functional of the direction.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The directional derivative formula and the explicit failure of linearity are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer invokes a necessary consequence of total differentiability rather than merely asserting discontinuity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $(p,q)\ne(0,0)$, $f(tp,tq)/t=p^3/(p^2+q^2)$, so $D_{(p,q)}f(0,0)=p^3/(p^2+q^2)$. This direction map is not additive: it takes $(1,0)$ to $1$, $(0,1)$ to $0$, but $(1,1)$ to $1/2$. If $f$ were differentiable, these values would equal one linear map applied to the directions, which is impossible.

activities.title: Prove differentiability from first principles
activities.promptMarkdown:
Define $H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3$ by $H(x,y)=(x^2y,\,x-y^2,\,xy)$.

At an arbitrary $(a,b)$, derive $DH_{(a,b)}$ from the differentiability definition and give its $3\times2$ Jacobian matrix.

Your proof must show a norm bound for the complete remainder, not only list partial derivatives.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three linear components, the remainder, its bound, and the matrix are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion follows from the definition and preserves the distinction between the linear map and its coordinate matrix.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $h=(u,v)$, the linear increment is $(2ab\,u+a^2v,\,u-2bv,\,bu+av)$. The remainder is $(bu^2+2auv+u^2v,\,-v^2,\,uv)$. For $\|h\|\le1$, its norm is at most $C_{a,b}\|h\|^2$ for a constant depending only on $(a,b)$, so the remainder quotient tends to zero. Hence $DH_{(a,b)}(u,v)$ is the displayed linear increment and its matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2ab&a^2\\1&-2b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}$.

lessons.title: Triangular maps and structured Jacobians
lessons.summary: Compute Jacobians of triangular maps, derive their determinant, and state exactly what the pointwise calculation does and does not prove.
objectives: Compute Jacobians of triangular maps, derive their determinant, and state exactly what the pointwise calculation does and does not prove.

content.markdown:
## Why triangular form matters

A triangular polynomial map makes dependence visible: the first output uses the first input, the second may use the first two, and so on. Its Jacobian inherits zeros above the diagonal, so its determinant is the product of diagonal derivatives.

The structure accelerates calculation, but it does not license an automatic global inverse claim.

## Reactivate the derivative and triangular determinants

Day 1 defined $DF_a$ as a linear approximation and identified its coordinate columns with partial derivatives. Week 13 proved that the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

## The dependency pattern

A lower triangular map has the form $F_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=F_i(x_1,\ldots,x_i)$. Therefore $\partial F_i/\partial x_j=0$ whenever $j>i$, and $JF$ is lower triangular.

Its determinant is $\prod_i \partial F_i/\partial x_i$. This conclusion comes from matrix structure after differentiability is known.

content.title: Read zeros from variable dependence
content.introMarkdown: Compute $JF(x,y,z)$ and decide whether the map is lower triangular in the stated variable order.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the derivative of the second output with respect to $z$.

One nonzero entry above the diagonal destroys lower triangularity.

Write the full dependency table and then compare row and column indices.

## Complete worked model

$T(x,y,z)=(x,\,y+x^2,\,z+xy)$.

Compute the Jacobian, determinant, and inverse by back-substitution.

### Strategy

Differentiate row by row, use triangularity for the determinant, then recover inputs in the same order as the outputs reveal them.

### Hypotheses

The standard coordinates are fixed, and polynomial maps are differentiable.

### Intermediate claims

$JT=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2x&1&0\\y&x&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det JT=1$. From $(X,Y,Z)=T(x,y,z)$, first $x=X$, then $y=Y-X^2$, then $z=Z-X(Y-X^2)$.

### Justification

A triangular determinant is the diagonal product. Each back-substitution uses only values already recovered.

### Conclusion

This particular unitriangular polynomial map has an explicit global polynomial inverse; that conclusion comes from the construction, not from the determinant alone.

content.title: Compute and invert a new triangular map
content.introMarkdown: Compute $JS$, its determinant, and the explicit inverse map.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Recover $x$ before substituting into the equation for $y$.

Triangular inversion is an ordered argument; later coordinates depend on earlier ones.

Rename the outputs $(X,Y,Z)$ and solve the three equations from top to bottom.

## A parameterized triangular family

For $F(x,y)=(f(x),g(x,y))$,

$$JF(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}f'(x)&0\\ \partial_xg(x,y)&\partial_yg(x,y)\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det JF=f'(x)\partial_yg(x,y).$$

The formula isolates two possible local degeneracies. It does not say that nonzero diagonal derivatives make $F$ globally one-to-one.

content.title: Analyze a triangular family
content.introMarkdown: Compute the Jacobian determinant and describe exactly where it vanishes.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Decide whether $e^x+3y^2$ can ever be zero.

A product equation should not create a nonexistent branch of the zero set.

Prove the second factor is positive, then solve $3x^2-c=0$ by cases on $c$.

## Nonzero Jacobian is local information

For a continuously differentiable square map, an invertible derivative at one point gives a local inverse near that point by the inverse function theorem, introduced next week.

It does not by itself give a global inverse. Even in one variable, a map on a disconnected domain can have nonzero derivative everywhere and still take the same value on different components.

content.title: Refute a premature global conclusion
content.introMarkdown: Show that $f'(x)$ never vanishes on $U$ but $f$ is not injective.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Choose one positive input and its negative inside the two components.

A global injectivity claim is disproved by one collision, even when all derivatives are nonzero.

Verify domain membership, compute both images, and state why the derivative test does not exclude the collision.

## Structured computation with a proof boundary

A polished triangular-map solution has four parts: the dependency pattern, the full Jacobian, its determinant, and a separately justified conclusion about the original map. The determinant can support a local claim; global claims require additional reasoning such as explicit back-substitution.

content.title: Complete a triangular-map analysis
content.introMarkdown: Compute $JF$, its determinant, and prove by explicit recursion that $F$ has a global polynomial inverse.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first recovered coordinate that still contains an unrecovered input.

A recursive inverse formula must depend only on output data and already recovered coordinates.

Solve the four output equations in order and then substitute the earlier formulas into each later one.

activities.title: Read zeros from variable dependence
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(x,y,z)=(x^2,\,y+xz,\,z+y^2+x)$.

Compute $JF(x,y,z)$ and decide whether the map is lower triangular in the stated variable order.

Inspect each output's actual dependencies before naming the matrix shape.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JF=\begin{pmatrix}2x&0&0\\z&1&x\\1&2y&1\end{pmatrix}$. The entry $\partial F_2/\partial z=x$ lies above the diagonal, so the map is not lower triangular in the order $(x,y,z)$, despite several zeros.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Every entry and the matrix-shape conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response tests the defining zero pattern rather than judging by appearance.

activities.title: Compute and invert a new triangular map
activities.promptMarkdown:
$S(x,y,z)=(2x,\,3y+x^2,\,-z+xy)$.

Compute $JS$, its determinant, and the explicit inverse map.

Solve successively for $x$, then $y$, then $z$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JS=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\2x&3&0\\y&x&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\det JS=2\cdot3\cdot(-1)=-6$. If $(X,Y,Z)=S(x,y,z)$, then $x=X/2$, $y=(Y-X^2/4)/3$, and $z=xy-Z=X(Y-X^2/4)/6-Z$. These formulas define the inverse on all of $\mathbb R^3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The matrix, determinant, and all inverse coordinates are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The global conclusion is justified by two-sided back-substitution.

activities.title: Analyze a triangular family
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F_c(x,y)=(x^3-cx,\,e^x y+y^3)$, where $c\in\mathbb R$.

Compute the Jacobian determinant and describe exactly where it vanishes.

Solve the product equation by treating each factor separately.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The determinant and its parameter-dependent zero set are complete.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The positivity of the second factor is used to eliminate spurious cases.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JF_c=\begin{pmatrix}3x^2-c&0\\e^xy&e^x+3y^2\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det JF_c=(3x^2-c)(e^x+3y^2)$. The second factor is always positive. Hence the determinant vanishes exactly when $3x^2=c$: at no real point if $c<0$, at $x=0$ if $c=0$, and on the two vertical lines $x=\pm\sqrt{c/3}$ if $c>0$.

activities.title: Refute a premature global conclusion
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $U=(-2,-1)\cup(1,2)$ and define $f:U\to\mathbb R$ by $f(x)=x^2$.

Show that $f'(x)$ never vanishes on $U$ but $f$ is not injective.

Give an explicit pair of distinct points with the same image.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The derivative condition and the explicit collision are both correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response states the precise logical gap between local derivative data and a global map property.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $f'(x)=2x$, which is nonzero because $0\notin U$. Nevertheless $3/2$ and $-3/2$ both belong to $U$ and have image $9/4$. Thus pointwise invertibility of the derivative does not imply global injectivity.

activities.title: Complete a triangular-map analysis
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(x_1,\,x_2+x_1^2,\,2x_3+x_1x_2,\,-x_4+x_2x_3)$.

Compute $JF$, its determinant, and prove by explicit recursion that $F$ has a global polynomial inverse.

Use named output coordinates and write every recovery formula.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The full matrix, determinant, recursive formulas, and inverse conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The global inverse is established by construction rather than inferred from a constant determinant.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JF=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\2x_1&1&0&0\\x_2&x_1&2&0\\0&x_3&x_2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det JF=-2$. For output $(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)$, recover $x_1=X_1$, $x_2=X_2-X_1^2$, $x_3=(X_3-x_1x_2)/2$, and $x_4=x_2x_3-X_4$. Each expression is polynomial in the outputs, and substitution into the defining equations proves both composite identities.

lessons.title: Proving the matrix chain rule
lessons.summary: Prove the multivariable chain rule from remainder estimates and use source and target dimensions to determine the matrix order.
objectives: Prove the multivariable chain rule from remainder estimates and use source and target dimensions to determine the matrix order.

content.markdown:
## Why the order must be proved

For $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ and $G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$, the derivative of $G\circ F$ must send an $n$-dimensional increment to a $p$-dimensional one. This already predicts the order $DG_{F(a)}DF_a$.

The proof must also show that the composed error remains negligible after the inner map distorts the increment.

## Reactivate linear approximation

Write $F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h)$ and $G(b+k)=G(b)+Bk+s(k)$ with $b=F(a)$. The little-o statements are $\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$ and $\|s(k)\|/\|k\|\to0$.

## Substitute the inner approximation

Set $k=F(a+h)-F(a)=Ah+r(h)$. Then

$$G(F(a+h))=G(F(a))+B(Ah+r(h))+s(Ah+r(h)).$$

The candidate derivative is $BA$. The remaining terms are $Br(h)$ and $s(Ah+r(h))$; both must be divided by $\|h\|$ and controlled.

content.title: Identify the composed remainder
content.introMarkdown: Substitute exactly and separate the linear term in $h$ from the complete remainder.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check what vector is substituted for the outer increment $k$.

The outer error estimate applies to $F(a+h)-F(a)$, not directly to $h$.

Name $k=Ah+r(h)$ first, then expand and place every non-linear term in one bracket.

## The bounded-ratio bridge

Since $r(h)=o(\|h\|)$, the ratio $\|r(h)\|/\|h\|$ is bounded near zero. Therefore

$$\frac{\|Ah+r(h)\|}{\|h\|}\le \|A\|+\frac{\|r(h)\|}{\|h\|}$$

is bounded. This bridge lets us convert $s(k)=o(\|k\|)$ into $s(k)=o(\|h\|)$ for the special increment $k=Ah+r(h)$.

content.title: Prove the bridge estimate
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\|k(h)\|/\|h\|$ is bounded near $h=0$, and explain what happens when $k(h)=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Bound $\|Ah\|$ by $\|A\|\|h\|$ before dividing.

The chain-rule proof needs a uniform comparison between the inner and original increments.

Apply the triangle inequality, divide by $\|h\|$, and state a separate sentence for $k(h)=0$.

## Complete worked model

$F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at $a$, and $G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ is differentiable at $F(a)$.

Prove that $G\circ F$ is differentiable at $a$ with derivative $DG_{F(a)}\circ DF_a$.

### Strategy

Expand both maps, isolate the candidate composition, and split the outer remainder quotient into a product of two controlled ratios.

### Hypotheses

Let $A=DF_a$, $B=DG_{F(a)}$, $r(h)=o(\|h\|)$, and $s(k)=o(\|k\|)$.

### Intermediate claims

The remainder is $R(h)=Br(h)+s(Ah+r(h))$. The first term satisfies $\|Br(h)\|/\|h\|\le\|B\|\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$. For $k(h)=Ah+r(h)$, $k(h)\to0$ and $\|k(h)\|/\|h\|$ is bounded.

### Justification

When $k(h)\ne0$, $\|s(k(h))\|/\|h\|=[\|s(k(h))\|/\|k(h)\|][\|k(h)\|/\|h\|]$, whose first factor tends to zero and second is bounded. At $k(h)=0$, the numerator is zero.

### Conclusion

$R(h)=o(\|h\|)$, so $D(G\circ F)_a=B\circ A$. In standard bases, $J(G\circ F)(a)=JG(F(a))JF(a)$.

content.title: Reconstruct the proof with named estimates
content.introMarkdown: Give the complete estimate for both remainder terms and conclude with the typed derivative and matrix formulas.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first remainder quotient whose limit was asserted without a bound.

The chain rule is a theorem about uniform first-order error, not just formal substitution.

Insert the operator-norm estimate for $Br(h)$ or the two-factor estimate for $s(k(h))$, whichever is missing first.

## Matrix order is fixed by types

If $JF(a)$ is $m\times n$ and $JG(F(a))$ is $p\times m$, only $JG(F(a))JF(a)$ has the required size $p\times n$. Reversing the order may be undefined; when both matrices are square, it may be defined but still wrong.

content.title: Use dimensions to reject the wrong order
content.introMarkdown: Compute the derivative matrix of $G\circ F$ and explain why the reverse product is ill-typed.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Place the matrix that acts last on the left.

Matrix multiplication records composition order and must preserve the map's domain and codomain.

Label the dimensions $2\to3\to1$, then translate that arrow chain into matrix sizes.

## From theorem to concrete composition

After the proof, a calculation should still show where each matrix is evaluated. The outer Jacobian is evaluated at $F(a)$, while the inner Jacobian is evaluated at $a$.

content.title: Apply and justify the chain rule
content.introMarkdown: Compute $D(G\circ F)_{(1,2)}$ in two ways—by multiplying Jacobians and by differentiating the expanded composition—and reconcile the results.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether $JG$ was evaluated at $(1,2)$ or at the required point $F(1,2)$.

The outer derivative depends on where the inner map lands.

Compute $F(1,2)$ first, rebuild the two matrices, and compare with the derivative of the expanded composition.

Day 3 is complete when you can prove the chain rule from small-error estimates and determine every matrix order and evaluation point from types.

activities.title: Identify the composed remainder
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h)$ and $G(b+k)=G(b)+Bk+s(k)$, with $b=F(a)$.

Substitute exactly and separate the linear term in $h$ from the complete remainder.

Do not replace the argument of $s$ by $h$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Taking $k=Ah+r(h)$ gives $G(F(a+h))=G(F(a))+BAh+[Br(h)+s(Ah+r(h))]$. Thus $BA$ is the candidate derivative and the bracketed expression is the composed remainder.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The candidate linear term and both remainder contributions are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The outer remainder is evaluated at the actual inner increment.

activities.title: Prove the bridge estimate
activities.promptMarkdown:
Assume $r(h)=o(\|h\|)$ and put $k(h)=Ah+r(h)$.

Prove that $\|k(h)\|/\|h\|$ is bounded near $h=0$, and explain what happens when $k(h)=0$.

Use the operator norm of $A$ and avoid division by $\|k(h)\|$ at a zero value.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The operator-norm estimate and zero-increment case are handled correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof establishes the exact bounded factor needed for the outer little-o term.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For nonzero $h$, $\|k(h)\|/\|h\|\le\|A\|+\|r(h)\|/\|h\|$. The second term tends to zero, so the sum is bounded near zero. If $k(h)=0$, then $s(k(h))=s(0)=0$ for a remainder normalized at zero, so no quotient by $\|k(h)\|$ is needed at that value.

activities.title: Reconstruct the proof with named estimates
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the theorem just modelled, but write the proof with your own notation for the two remainders.

Give the complete estimate for both remainder terms and conclude with the typed derivative and matrix formulas.

Your proof must include the bounded-ratio bridge, not the unsupported phrase “little-o terms compose.”

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both remainder estimates and both typed conclusions are complete.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument exposes the bounded factor that makes the outer little-o substitution valid.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Write $F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h)$ and $G(F(a)+k)=G(F(a))+Bk+s(k)$. Substitution yields linear term $BAh$ and remainder $Br(h)+s(Ah+r(h))$. The first quotient tends to zero by the operator norm of $B$. Set $k(h)=Ah+r(h)$. Then $k(h)\to0$ and $\|k(h)\|/\|h\|\le\|A\|+\|r(h)\|/\|h\|$ is bounded. Factoring the outer remainder quotient proves it tends to zero. Hence $D(G\circ F)_a=B\circ A$ and $J(G\circ F)(a)=JG(F(a))JF(a)$.

activities.title: Use dimensions to reject the wrong order
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3$ and $G:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$. At the relevant points, $JF=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $JG=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&3\end{pmatrix}$.

Compute the derivative matrix of $G\circ F$ and explain why the reverse product is ill-typed.

Write both matrix sizes before multiplying.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JG$ has size $1\times3$ and $JF$ has size $3\times2$, so $JGJF=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\end{pmatrix}$ has size $1\times2$, appropriate for a map $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$. The reverse expression would multiply a $3\times2$ matrix by a $1\times3$ matrix; the inner dimensions $2$ and $1$ do not match.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The correct matrix product, entries, and dimensions are all correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The order is justified by the source-intermediate-target types.

activities.title: Apply and justify the chain rule
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(x,y)=(x+y,xy)$ and $G(u,v)=(u^2+v,\,uv)$.

Compute $D(G\circ F)_{(1,2)}$ in two ways—by multiplying Jacobians and by differentiating the expanded composition—and reconcile the results.

Show the evaluation point for $JG$ and the order of multiplication.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both derivative calculations produce the same correct matrix.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The solution evaluates the outer derivative at the inner image and explains why the agreement is meaningful.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $F(1,2)=(3,2)$, $JF(1,2)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, and $JG(3,2)=\begin{pmatrix}6&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Their product is $\begin{pmatrix}8&7\\8&5\end{pmatrix}$. Directly, $G\circ F=((x+y)^2+xy,\,(x+y)xy)$; differentiating at $(1,2)$ gives the same matrix. Agreement checks both the evaluation point and multiplication order.

lessons.title: Determinant chain rule and differential viewpoint
lessons.summary: Derive the determinant chain rule for square maps, interpret derivatives as maps between coordinate tangent copies, and preserve the boundary with later algebraic tangent-space theory.
objectives: Derive the determinant chain rule for square maps, interpret derivatives as maps between coordinate tangent copies, and preserve the boundary with later algebraic tangent-space theory.

content.markdown:
## From composition to volume scaling

For maps between equal-dimensional Euclidean spaces, the determinant of the derivative records infinitesimal signed volume scaling. The chain rule composes the linear maps; determinant multiplicativity then multiplies the scaling factors.

This interpretation is powerful, but it remains pointwise. It does not turn a local determinant identity into a global theorem.

## Reactivate two theorems

Day 3 proved $D(G\circ F)_a=DG_{F(a)}DF_a$. Week 13 proved $\det(BA)=\det(B)\det(A)$ for square matrices of the same size.

## The determinant chain rule

Let $F,G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be differentiable at the required points. Taking determinants in the matrix chain rule gives

$$\det J(G\circ F)(a)=\det JG(F(a))\,\det JF(a).$$

No new calculus proof is hidden here: the result is precisely the chain rule followed by determinant multiplicativity.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether every derivative matrix in your determinant expression is square.

Determinant multiplicativity applies to compatible square matrices.

Write the matrix chain rule first, annotate sizes, and only then apply determinants.

## Complete worked model

$F(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ and $G(x,y)=(x+y,x-y)$.

Compute the determinant of $G\circ F$ by the chain rule and verify it directly.

### Strategy

Find both Jacobian determinants, evaluate the outer one at $F(r,\theta)$, multiply, then differentiate the explicit composition.

### Hypotheses

Both maps are differentiable on $\mathbb R^2$.

### Intermediate claims

$\det JF(r,\theta)=r$ and $\det JG(x,y)=-2$. Hence the rule predicts $\det J(G\circ F)(r,\theta)=-2r$.

### Justification

$G\circ F=(r(\cos\theta+\sin\theta),r(\cos\theta-\sin\theta))$, whose direct Jacobian determinant simplifies to $-2r$.

### Conclusion

The factors are evaluated at their proper points and the direct calculation confirms the product.

content.introMarkdown: Use the determinant chain rule to compute $\det J(G\circ F)(x,y)$ and verify the result by direct differentiation.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Replace $u$ and $v$ in the outer determinant by the two components of $F(x,y)$.

The determinant chain rule inherits the same evaluation point as the matrix chain rule.

Compute the two determinant functions separately, substitute $F(x,y)$ into the outer one, then multiply.

## Differential notation as typed linear algebra

At a point $a\in\mathbb R^n$, we may write the derivative as $dF_a:T_a\mathbb R^n\to T_{F(a)}\mathbb R^m$. For Euclidean spaces, these tangent spaces are canonical copies of $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^m$ that remember their base points.

Then the chain rule is $d(G\circ F)_a=dG_{F(a)}\circ dF_a$. This is a coordinate-free restatement of the theorem, not a new calculation.

content.introMarkdown: Write the domains and codomains of $dF_a$, $dG_{F(a)}$, and $d(G\circ F)_a$, then write the typed composition.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the target of $dF_a$ equals the source of the outer differential.

Typed notation makes an incorrect composition order visibly impossible.

Draw the arrows from $a$ to $F(a)$ to $G(F(a))$, then attach the corresponding tangent copies.

## Preview boundary: not yet the Zariski tangent space

Today $T_a\mathbb R^n$ means the ordinary tangent copy used in multivariable calculus. Later, an affine algebraic set will be defined by polynomial equations, and its Zariski tangent space will be cut out by their differentials.

We are only previewing that destination. We have not yet defined affine varieties, coordinate rings, or proved that the kernel of a Jacobian gives the correct algebraic tangent space.

A complete argument should state the two square maps, apply the matrix chain rule at the correct point, use determinant multiplicativity, and interpret only the resulting pointwise scaling. Any global conclusion needs a separate theorem.
