lessons.title: Derivative of polynomial multiplication
lessons.summary: Retrieve prerequisite proof objects, derive the derivative of polynomial multiplication, and integrate the definition, matrix chain rule, and determinant scope.
objectives: Retrieve prerequisite proof objects, derive the derivative of polynomial multiplication, and integrate the definition, matrix chain rule, and determinant scope.

content.markdown:
## Why multiplication is the right synthesis

Week 15 made polynomial multiplication a bilinear map. Bilinearity makes its first-order change visible by expansion: two linear terms appear, followed by one product of increments.

That last product is quadratic in the joint increment, so it is exactly the remainder that the total-derivative definition knows how to control.

## Three scheduled retrievals

The synthesis needs a typed proof boundary from Week 8, determinant multiplicativity from Week 13, and the symmetric-power multiplication map from Week 15. Each review below retrieves the exact earlier object before it is used in the new derivative argument.

For this real multivariable-calculus chapter, set $V_d=\mathbb R[T,S]_d$. Thus the dimensions $2,3,4$ and the displayed $4\times5$ matrix are real dimensions and a real matrix. The same coefficient formula also extends complex-linearly, but that is not the scalar setting used in today's derivative proof.

## Deliberate review: function data after eight weeks

A derivative belongs to a declared map. Before differentiating multiplication, identify its source product space and target space; otherwise even the size of the derivative is undetermined.

### Use the feedback before continuing

A derivative acts on a pair of increments, so its source is the direct-product vector space.

Write the three monomial bases, count them, and place target dimension by source dimension.

## Deliberate review: determinant scope after three weeks

Determinants belong to square endomorphism matrices. Multiplicativity supports the determinant chain rule only when source and target dimensions agree at each stage.

A rectangular linear map may have rank properties, but it does not have a determinant.

## Deliberate review: polynomial multiplication after one week

For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, multiplication sends the five input coefficients to four cubic coefficients.

content.title: Reconstruct the coefficient map
content.introMarkdown: Expand $LQ$ and write $M(a,b,c,d,e)$ in the cubic monomial basis $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Match each product term to its cubic monomial before combining coefficients.

The derivative calculation will depend on the exact coordinate formula.

Write the six pairwise products, group the two middle pairs, and order by descending power of $T$.

## Complete worked model

Let $B:E\times F\to G$ be a continuous bilinear map between finite-dimensional normed vector spaces.

Derive the total derivative of $B$ at $(x,y)$ directly from the remainder definition.

### Strategy

Expand $B(x+h,y+k)$ using bilinearity, collect the two terms linear in the joint increment, and bound the final mixed term.

### Hypotheses

Finite-dimensional continuity gives $\|B(h,k)\|\le C\|h\|\|k\|$ for some $C$.

### Intermediate claims

$B(x+h,y+k)-B(x,y)=B(h,y)+B(x,k)+B(h,k)$. The candidate derivative is $(h,k)\mapsto B(h,y)+B(x,k)$.

### Justification

With the product norm $\|(h,k)\|=(\|h\|^2+\|k\|^2)^{1/2}$, $\|B(h,k)\|\le C\|h\|\|k\|\le(C/2)\|(h,k)\|^2$, so the remainder quotient tends to zero.

### Conclusion

$DB_{(x,y)}(h,k)=B(h,y)+B(x,k)$. Both summands are needed because both inputs vary.

content.title: Transfer the product rule to matrices
content.introMarkdown: Derive $DB_{(A,C)}(H,K)$ and identify the remainder using a submultiplicative matrix norm.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your proposed derivative includes variation in both matrix factors.

The derivative is linear in the joint increment and must record both first-order changes.

Expand all four products, keep the two single-increment terms, and bound the double-increment term.

## The derivative of polynomial multiplication

Apply the bilinear rule to $M(L,Q)=LQ$. At $(L,Q)$ and increment $(\dot L,\dot Q)$,

$$DM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot L\,Q+L\,\dot Q,$$

because $(L+\dot L)(Q+\dot Q)-LQ$ has the additional remainder $\dot L\dot Q$, quadratic in the joint coefficient increment.

content.introMarkdown: Compute $JM(a,b,c,d,e)$ and verify that its action on $(\dot a,\dot b,\dot c,\dot d,\dot e)$ matches $\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compare the first mismatching row with the corresponding cubic coefficient.

The matrix must represent the same linear map as the product-rule formula.

Differentiate one output coefficient at a time, then multiply your matrix by a symbolic increment vector.

## Kernel behavior at degenerate factors

The formula changes character at $(L,Q)=(0,0)$: the derivative is the zero map although $M$ itself is not constant. At a point with one zero factor, only variation in the other factor contributes at first order.

This is not a contradiction. Derivatives describe first-order behavior at one base point; the omitted product of increments is second order.

content.title: Analyze three base points
content.introMarkdown: Describe the derivative at $(0,0)$, at $(L,0)$ with $L\ne0$, and at $(0,Q)$ with $Q\ne0$; give each kernel.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Substitute the base-point factors into the derivative formula before solving for the kernel.

Different base points eliminate different first-order terms.

Handle the three cases separately and use no-zero-divisors only after simplifying the derivative.

## Week synthesis

The week's ideas now form one chain: differentiability is a uniform linear approximation; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian; composition multiplies derivative maps in typed order; determinants multiply only for square derivative matrices; and bilinear multiplication differentiates by retaining its two first-order terms.

content.introMarkdown: Prove the derivative formula from the total-derivative definition, derive its $4\times5$ matrix, verify one directional derivative, and explain why neither a determinant nor global invertibility follows.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first place where a second-order product was treated as part of the linear map or left unbounded.

The product rule follows only after the mixed increment is proved negligible at first order.

Re-expand the product, isolate the two single-increment terms, bound the double-increment term, and then rebuild the coordinate matrix and scope statement.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-16, source lines 713 to 722.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02SC, Fall 2010.

**Exact locator:** Unit 2, Part B, Sessions 32, 34, and 38: total differentials, chain rules with several variables, and directional derivatives in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010.

**Reading purpose:** Use the three sessions to consolidate total differentials and directional checks, then compare their scalar examples with the bilinear polynomial multiplication proof.

Week 17 adds the inverse and implicit function theorems. Their hypotheses will use the derivatives constructed here, while their conclusions must remain local unless additional global reasoning is supplied.

Week 16 is complete when you can prove a derivative from its remainder, compute structured Jacobians, prove both chain rules, and differentiate polynomial multiplication with exact dimensional and global-scope boundaries.

activities.promptMarkdown:
$M:\mathbb R[T,S]_1\times\mathbb R[T,S]_2\to\mathbb R[T,S]_3$ sends $(L,Q)$ to $LQ$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Expansion gives $M(L+\dot L,Q+\dot Q)-M(L,Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q+\dot L\dot Q$. The first two terms define a linear map in $(\dot L,\dot Q)$. In finite-dimensional coefficient norms, $\|\dot L\dot Q\|\le C\|\dot L\|\|\dot Q\|\le(C/2)\|(\dot L,\dot Q)\|^2$, so the quotient by the joint increment norm tends to zero. Hence $DM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$. In the ordered coefficient bases its matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}c&0&a&0&0\\d&c&b&a&0\\e&d&0&b&a\\0&e&0&0&b\end{pmatrix}$. Along direction $(R,S)$ the directional derivative is $RQ+LS$, as the total derivative predicts. The matrix is rectangular, so it has no determinant; moreover dimension and factorization collisions prevent any conclusion that $M$ is globally invertible.

lessons.title: What the inverse function theorem actually says
lessons.summary: State the inverse function theorem with every hypothesis, derive the derivative of the local inverse, and distinguish its neighborhood conclusion from a global inverse claim.
objectives: State the inverse function theorem with every hypothesis, derive the derivative of the local inverse, and distinguish its neighborhood conclusion from a global inverse claim.

content.markdown:
## A theorem with a deliberately local conclusion

An invertible derivative says that a map has an invertible first-order model at one point. The inverse function theorem upgrades that approximation to a genuine inverse only after restricting both source and target to suitable neighborhoods.

The neighborhoods are part of the conclusion. Removing them changes the theorem into a false global statement.

## Reactivate the derivative and matrix inverse

Week 16 proved that a derivative is a linear map and that derivatives compose. Week 13 established the determinant test for an invertible square matrix. Recall also that injectivity is a property of a declared map on its whole domain, not of its formula near one point.

## Precise inverse function theorem

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuously differentiable, and let $a\in U$. If $Df_a$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $W$ of $f(a)$ such that

$$f|_V:V\longrightarrow W$$

is bijective. Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is continuously differentiable. The theorem asserts existence of some suitable $V$ and $W$; it does not say that $f$ is injective on all of $U$ or surjective onto all of $\mathbb R^n$.

content.title: Separate hypotheses from conclusions
content.introMarkdown: Rewrite the statement with the missing domain, regularity, neighborhoods, restriction, and inverse codomain.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing typed set or regularity hypothesis.

Without open neighborhoods and a restricted map, the theorem statement is false.

Write the source open set, the $C^1$ hypothesis, the point, and then name $V$, $W$, $f|_V$, and $g$.

## Derivative of the local inverse

On $V$, the identity $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_V$ holds. Differentiating at $a$ and using the chain rule gives

$$Dg_{f(a)}Df_a=I,$$

so $Dg_{f(a)}=(Df_a)^{-1}$. The formula follows after the local inverse exists; the formula alone does not construct that inverse.

content.title: Derive the inverse derivative with types
content.introMarkdown: Prove the formula for $Dg_{f(a)}$ and state the source and target of each derivative.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the outer derivative is evaluated at $f(a)$.

The inverse begins at the image point, so its derivative must be evaluated there.

Write the tangent-space arrows, differentiate $g\circ f$, and solve the resulting matrix equation.

## Complete worked model

$F(x,y)=(x+y,\,y+x^2)$ at $a=(0,0)$.

Verify the theorem, construct the branch of the inverse near the origin, and identify why another algebraic branch does not belong to the same local inverse.

### Strategy

Compute $DF_0$, apply the theorem, then solve the output equations and choose the branch passing through the base point.

### Hypotheses

$F$ is polynomial and therefore $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Its derivative at the origin is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant one.

### Intermediate claims

For output $(u,v)$, $y=u-x$ and $x$ satisfies $x^2-x+(u-v)=0$. The root near $x=0$ is $x=(1-\sqrt{1-4(u-v)})/2$, and then $y=u-x$.

### Justification

At $(u,v)=(0,0)$ the minus branch gives $x=0$, whereas the plus branch gives $x=1$. Restricting to a sufficiently small neighborhood keeps the square root defined and isolates the branch through the chosen point.

### Conclusion

The theorem supplies neighborhoods on which the minus branch is the unique $C^1$ inverse. It makes no claim that the quadratic equation has only one solution globally.

content.title: Apply the theorem to a related map

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the base image or one entry of the derivative before taking its inverse.

Every later conclusion depends on applying the theorem at the correct source and target points.

Compute $H(0,0)$, then $DH_{(0,0)}$, then its determinant and inverse, and only then state $V$ and $W$.

## Invertible everywhere still need not mean globally injective

Consider $P(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)$. Its Jacobian determinant is $e^{2x}>0$ at every point, so the theorem gives a local inverse around every point.

But $P(x,y+2\pi)=P(x,y)$. The map wraps the plane around the punctured plane infinitely many times, so it has no global inverse on $\mathbb R^2$.

## The application checklist

A complete inverse-function argument names an open source, verifies $C^1$ regularity, evaluates a square derivative at the chosen point, proves it invertible, and states restricted neighborhoods. Only then may it differentiate the inverse.

lessons.title: The cube map: locally invertible, globally three-to-one
lessons.summary: Analyze the cube map on the punctured complex plane through its real Jacobian, local inverse neighborhoods, and exact global fibers.
objectives: Analyze the cube map on the punctured complex plane through its real Jacobian, local inverse neighborhoods, and exact global fibers.

content.markdown:
## One map, two different scales

The map $z\mapsto z^3$ is the smallest model for the course's later three-sheeted constructions. Near any nonzero input, one cube-root branch can be selected. Across the whole punctured plane, three inputs differ by cube roots of unity and share one output.

## Reactivate complex multiplication as a real map

Write $z=x+iy$ and identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$. Then a complex polynomial becomes a real polynomial map, so Day 1's real inverse function theorem applies after we compute its $2\times2$ Jacobian.

## Real Jacobian of the complex cube

For $f(z)=z^3$,

$$f(x,y)=(x^3-3xy^2,\,3x^2y-y^3).$$

Its real Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}3x^2-3y^2&-6xy\\6xy&3x^2-3y^2\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $9(x^2+y^2)^2=9|z|^4$. It is invertible exactly when $z\ne0$.

content.title: Derive the cube-map determinant
content.introMarkdown: Compute the full real Jacobian, simplify its determinant, and identify its singular set.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sign in the off-diagonal derivative of the real part.

One sign error changes the determinant from a positive square to an incorrect locus.

Differentiate each component row-wise, compute $ad-bc$, and complete the square in $x^2$ and $y^2$.

## Complete worked model

Study $f(z)=z^3$ at the base point $z_0=1$.

Prove the existence of one local cube-root branch through $1$ and compute its derivative.

### Strategy

Apply the real inverse function theorem at $(1,0)$ and translate the inverse derivative back into complex multiplication.

### Hypotheses

The cube map is polynomial, hence $C^1$, and its real derivative determinant at $1$ is $9$.

### Intermediate claims

There are neighborhoods $V$ of $1$ and $W$ of $1$ such that $z\mapsto z^3$ restricts to a $C^1$ bijection $V\to W$.

### Justification

The complex derivative is multiplication by $3z_0^2=3$, so the derivative of the selected local inverse branch at $1$ is multiplication by $1/3$.

### Conclusion

Exactly one cube root lying in $V$ is selected for each $w\in W$. The other two global cube roots lie outside the chosen source neighborhood.

content.title: Move the local branch to another base point
content.introMarkdown: Prove that a local inverse branch through $i$ exists near $-i$ and compute its complex derivative at $-i$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Evaluate $3z_0^2$ before inverting it.

Different preimages of the same value support different local branches.

Compute $i^3$, verify nonzero determinant, state $V$ and $W$, then invert multiplication by $-3$.

## Global fibers and cube roots of unity

Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Then $1,\omega,\omega^2$ are distinct and each has cube $1$. More generally, if $z^3=w\ne0$, then the complete fiber is

$$\{z,\omega z,\omega^2z\}.$$

Indeed, any second root $u$ satisfies $(u/z)^3=1$. This is a global algebraic statement, not a contradiction to local injectivity.

content.title: Classify a nonzero fiber
content.introMarkdown: List the three roots and prove there are no others.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

After listing roots, justify why a fourth root cannot occur.

A global fiber classification needs both existence and completeness.

Divide an arbitrary root by $-2$ and solve the resulting cube-root-of-unity equation.

## The origin is a genuine branch point

At $z=0$, the derivative of $z^3$ is the zero map, so the inverse function theorem does not apply. More strongly, no inverse branch through $0$ can be differentiable with finite derivative: along positive reals it would behave like $w^{1/3}$.

content.title: Explain the failure at zero
content.introMarkdown: Show that such a $g$ cannot be differentiable at zero with a finite real derivative.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Use the magnitude of a cube root rather than choosing an arbitrary argument branch.

The magnitude obstruction applies to every possible local selection.

Set $w=t>0$, use $|g(t)|=t^{1/3}$, divide by $t$, and take the limit.

## Complete two-scale analysis

The final argument must use different evidence at different scales: derivative invertibility for a neighborhood result, roots of unity for the global fiber, and a singular derivative plus growth estimate at the excluded origin.

content.title: Analyze the cube map locally and globally
content.introMarkdown: Prove local invertibility at every domain point, classify every global fiber, and explain precisely what changes if zero is added to source and target.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first claim supported by evidence from the wrong scale.

A local derivative theorem cannot classify a global fiber, and a global collision does not negate local invertibility.

Write three separate paragraphs: nonzero local theorem, nonzero global fiber, and the origin boundary.

## Course reference

**Resource version:** Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, 1965 edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 2, Theorem 2-11 and proof, pp. 35–40: local one-to-one restriction and continuously differentiable inverse in Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, W. A. Benjamin, 1965 edition.

**Reading purpose:** Use the theorem statement to check exactly which parts of the cube-map analysis come from calculus and which require the roots-of-unity argument.
Day 3 turns local inversion into the implicit function theorem, which solves selected variables as functions of the remaining ones near a regular solution.
Day 2 is complete when you can prove local cube-root branches, classify the three-point global fibers, and isolate the singular origin.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: One root is $-2$. The three roots are $-2$, $-2\omega$, and $-2\omega^2$, and they are distinct. If $u^3=-8$, then $(u/(-2))^3=1$, so $u/(-2)$ is one of $1,\omega,\omega^2$. Hence the list is complete.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For positive real $t$ in the target neighborhood, any cube root has magnitude $t^{1/3}$. Thus $|g(t)-g(0)|/|t-0|=t^{1/3}/t=t^{-2/3}\to\infty$. A differentiable map at zero would have bounded difference quotients near zero, so no differentiable inverse branch through the origin exists.

activities.title: Analyze the cube map locally and globally
activities.promptMarkdown:
$f:\mathbb C^\times\to\mathbb C^\times$ is $f(z)=z^3$.

Prove local invertibility at every domain point, classify every global fiber, and explain precisely what changes if zero is added to source and target.

Use the real Jacobian for the theorem and roots of unity for the fiber.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The pointwise determinant, local conclusion, complete fibers, and origin obstruction are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof assigns the inverse theorem, algebraic classification, and difference quotient to their proper claims.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, $\det Df_z=9|z|^4$, which is positive for every $z\in\mathbb C^\times$. The real inverse function theorem therefore gives a $C^1$ local inverse near each nonzero point. If $z^3=w\ne0$, then all preimages are $z,\omega z,\omega^2z$, and any preimage has this form because its quotient by $z$ is a cube root of unity. Thus the map is globally three-to-one, not globally injective. If zero is included, the derivative at zero is singular and any cube-root selection through zero has difference quotients of magnitude $t^{-2/3}$ along positive reals, so no differentiable local inverse exists there.

lessons.title: Solving equations locally with the implicit function theorem
lessons.summary: State and derive the implicit function theorem for a selected variable block, solve two equations locally, and distinguish a local graph from a global solution formula.
objectives: State and derive the implicit function theorem for a selected variable block, solve two equations locally, and distinguish a local graph from a global solution formula.

content.markdown:
## Equations can define functions without displaying them

A system $F(x,y)=0$ may not provide a formula for $y$. If the derivative with respect to the variables $y$ is invertible at one known solution, the implicit function theorem proves that nearby solutions form the graph of a unique function $y=g(x)$.

## Reactivate block matrices and the inverse theorem

Partition the variables as $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $y\in\mathbb R^m$. Week 16 supplies the blocks $D_xF$ and $D_yF$; Day 1 supplies local inversion for a square map.

## Precise implicit function theorem

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, let $(a,b)\in U$, and suppose $F(a,b)=0$. If the square block $D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $a$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ of $b$, with $A\times B\subseteq U$, and a unique $C^1$ map $g:A\to B$ such that

$$F(x,y)=0\text{ for }(x,y)\in A\times B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=g(x).$$

The equivalence is local inside $A\times B$. It does not classify solutions elsewhere.

content.title: Type the solved-variable block
content.introMarkdown: State the required point equation and derivative-block condition, then give the typed local solution map.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your derivative block differentiates with respect to the two solved variables.

Invertibility of the wrong block does not justify solving the intended variables.

Partition the five inputs into three free and two solved coordinates, then write $D_yF$ and $g:A\to B$.

## Complete worked model

Assume the hypotheses of the implicit function theorem for $F(x,y)$.

Derive the local solution graph from the inverse function theorem using an augmented map.

### Strategy

Define $\Phi(x,y)=(x,F(x,y))$, prove its derivative is invertible, invert it locally, and read the zero-level slice.

### Hypotheses

$D\Phi(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\D_xF(a,b)&D_yF(a,b)\end{pmatrix}$ is block lower triangular.

### Intermediate claims

Its determinant is $\det D_yF(a,b)\ne0$, so $\Phi$ has a local inverse. Because the first component of $\Phi$ is $x$, that inverse has the form $\Phi^{-1}(x,z)=(x,h(x,z))$.

### Justification

Set $g(x)=h(x,0)$. Then $\Phi(x,g(x))=(x,0)$, hence $F(x,g(x))=0$. Conversely, local injectivity of $\Phi$ forces every nearby solution of $F(x,y)=0$ to have $y=g(x)$.

### Conclusion

The implicit theorem is a structured inverse theorem. Differentiating $F(x,g(x))=0$ gives $Dg(a)=-D_yF(a,b)^{-1}D_xF(a,b)$.

content.title: Reconstruct the augmented-map proof
content.introMarkdown: Prove the derivative block is invertible, construct $g$, establish both directions of the local equivalence, and derive $Dg(a)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first step where the local inverse of $\Phi$ was used without preserving its neighborhoods.

The zero-slice argument proves uniqueness only where the augmented map is one-to-one.

State the local inverse first, define $h$ and $g$, prove both implications, then differentiate the identity.

## Complete worked model

$F(x,y,u,v)=(x+y+u^2-1,\,x-y+v-1)$ at $(1,0,0,0)$.

Solve $(x,y)$ locally as functions of $(u,v)$ and verify the derivative formula.

### Strategy

Use the $(x,y)$ block for the theorem, then solve the linear equations explicitly as a check.

### Hypotheses

$F(1,0,0,0)=0$ and $D_{(x,y)}F=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-2$.

### Intermediate claims

The equations give $x=(2-u^2-v)/2$ and $y=(v-u^2)/2$.

### Justification

These formulas are $C^1$ and pass through $(x,y)=(1,0)$ at $(u,v)=(0,0)$. Their derivative at zero agrees with $-D_{(x,y)}F^{-1}D_{(u,v)}F$.

### Conclusion

The solution set near the base point is a graph over the two free coordinates $(u,v)$.

content.title: Solve a related two-equation system
content.introMarkdown: Verify the base point, decide whether $(x,y)$ can be solved as functions of $(u,v)$, and compute the derivative of that local solution map.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the value of $e^y$ and its derivative at $y=1$.

The selected block and its inverse depend on the correct base point.

Evaluate the equations, build the $(x,y)$ block, invert it, and multiply by the free-variable block.

## A singular chosen block does not end every analysis

For $F(x,y)=y^2-x$ at $(0,0)$, $\partial F/\partial y=0$, so the theorem does not solve $y$ as a $C^1$ function of $x$ there. But $\partial F/\partial x=-1$, so the same equation solves $x=y^2$ as a function of $y$.

Failure of one selected block means that one theorem application is unavailable. It does not say the solution set has no local description.

content.title: Change the solved variable
content.introMarkdown: Prove that no differentiable function $y=g(x)$ can describe the whole nearby zero set through the origin, then show how the theorem solves $x$ as a function of $y$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether one $x>0$ has one or two nearby $y$ values.

A graph over $x$ can contain only one output for each input.

Exhibit the two branches, then exchange the roles of $x$ and $y$ and inspect $F_x$.

## Independent implicit-function proof

The final solution must name the free and solved variables, verify the base equation, compute the correct square block, state local existence and uniqueness, and derive the solution derivative. An explicit formula is optional unless the equations yield one.

content.introMarkdown: Determine whether $(x,y)$ can be solved uniquely as a $C^1$ function of $(u,v)$ near the point, and compute the derivative of that solution map.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first mismatch between your chosen free variables and the derivative block you inverted.

The theorem solves only the variables belonging to the invertible block.

Declare $(u,v)$ free and $(x,y)$ solved, then recompute the point equation, block inverse, neighborhoods, and derivative.

## Course reference

**Resource version:** Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, 1965 edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 2, Theorem 2-12, pp. 41–42: implicit function theorem, base-point condition, invertible solved-variable block, and unique local solution in Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, W. A. Benjamin, 1965 edition.

**Reading purpose:** Use the scalar theorem and examples to check the base-point, nonzero-block, branch, and local-uniqueness clauses before returning to systems.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $D\Phi(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\D_xF&D_yF\end{pmatrix}$ has nonzero determinant because $D_yF(a,b)$ is invertible. The inverse function theorem gives a local inverse $(x,z)\mapsto(x,h(x,z))$. Set $g(x)=h(x,0)$. Then $F(x,g(x))=0$. If a nearby $(x,y)$ also satisfies $F(x,y)=0$, then $\Phi(x,y)=(x,0)=\Phi(x,g(x))$, and local injectivity gives $y=g(x)$. Differentiating the identity gives $D_xF+D_yF\,Dg=0$, hence $Dg=-D_yF^{-1}D_xF$ at $(a,b)$.

content.markdown:
## The course's central equations enter the analysis

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb C^5$ be cut out by

$$f_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1=0,\qquad f_2=ad+bc-1=0.$$

Two independent complex equations should leave three complex coordinates free. Today makes that count local and exact at one regular point.

## Scalar-setting boundary

We identify $\mathbb C^5$ with $\mathbb R^{10}$ and the two complex equations with four real equations. An invertible complex $2\times2$ coordinate block becomes an invertible real $4\times4$ block. The real implicit theorem then gives six real free coordinates, grouped naturally as three complex coordinates. Holomorphic dependence is not claimed until Week 18.

## Verify the regular point and gradients

Take $p=(0,1,1,0,0)$. Both equations vanish there. Their complex coordinate gradients are

$$\nabla f_1=(2ae-bd,\,-ad+2cb,\,b^2,\,-ab,\,a^2),$$

$$\nabla f_2=(d,c,b,a,0).$$

At $p$ these become $(0,2,1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,1,0,0)$, which are linearly independent.

### Use the feedback before continuing

The selected minor and the dimension conclusion depend on these two entries.

Differentiate term by term, substitute $p$, then solve the two-coordinate linear relation.

## Choose the variables that the equations solve

Use $(a,d,e)$ as free coordinates and $(b,c)$ as solved coordinates. The selected complex derivative block is

$$D_{(b,c)}(f_1,f_2)(p)=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},$$

with determinant one. Its realification is invertible, so the real implicit function theorem solves $(b,c)$ uniquely near $(1,1)$ as a $C^1$ function of $(a,d,e)$ near $(0,0,0)$.

## Complete worked model

$G_1=b+c+a-2$ and $G_2=b-c+d$ at $(a,b,c,d,e)=(0,1,1,0,0)$.

Construct the local solution graph over $(a,d,e)$ and reconcile complex and real dimensions.

### Strategy

Check the selected $(b,c)$ block, solve the linear system explicitly, and view the same formulas on real and imaginary parts.

### Hypotheses

$D_{(b,c)}G=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-2$.

### Intermediate claims

The equations give $b=1-(a+d)/2$ and $c=1-(a-d)/2$, while $e$ remains free.

### Justification

The formulas are complex-linear in the three free complex coordinates. Their realification is a graph from $\mathbb R^6$ to $\mathbb R^4$.

### Conclusion

The zero set has three free complex coordinate slots and real dimension six near the point. In this linear model, holomorphic dependence is explicit; the nonlinear central example currently uses only the real $C^1$ conclusion.

Invert the $2\times2$ block carefully, solve for $b,c$, and verify both equations before counting free variables.

## Local dimension is not a global coordinate system

The implicit theorem supplies one graph near $p$. Another point may require solving a different pair of coordinates, and a single global formula for $(b,c)$ need not exist.

Nor does independent gradient data prove that $X$ is globally isomorphic to affine three-space. That much stronger statement belongs to the later algebraic and geometric parts of the course.

The final proof follows a fixed sequence: verify the point, compute both gradients, choose and invert a coordinate minor, invoke the realified implicit theorem, count free coordinates, and state the holomorphic and global boundaries.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Both equations vanish at $p$. Their gradients are $(0,2,1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,1,0,0)$, and the $(b,c)$ minor is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant one. Local-versus-global logic, translated solution sets, pullbacks, and the matrix chain rule each control a different step in local inversion. The scheduled reviews retrieve those objects before the final proof asks you to coordinate them.

$F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ is $F(x,y,z)=(x+y+z,\,x-y+z^2)$ at the origin.

Verify the point, invert the $(x,y)$ block, invoke the implicit theorem, and compare with the explicit formulas.

$D_{(x,y)}F(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-2$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The inverse function theorem says that a $C^1$ map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ with invertible derivative at a point restricts to a $C^1$ bijection between neighborhoods of that point and its image; it does not assert global injectivity. For $F$, define $\Phi(x,y)=(x,F(x,y))$. Its derivative is block lower triangular with invertible diagonal blocks $I$ and $D_yF(a,b)$, so $\Phi$ has a local inverse. Taking the zero slice gives neighborhoods $A,B$ and a unique $C^1$ map $g:A\to B$ such that nearby zeros are exactly $(x,g(x))$. Differentiating yields $Dg(a)=-D_yF(a,b)^{-1}D_xF(a,b)$. For the cube map, the real Jacobian determinant is $9|z|^4>0$ on $\mathbb C^\times$, so local inverses exist everywhere, but $1^3=\omega^3=1$ with $1\ne\omega$. content.markdown:
## The regularity upgrade

Week 17 produced local inverses that were only known to be real $C^1$. A holomorphic map carries extra structure: its real derivative is complex-linear. When that derivative is invertible, the local inverse preserves the same complex structure.

The conclusion is still local. Holomorphic regularity strengthens the inverse inside the chosen neighborhoods; it does not enlarge those neighborhoods to the whole domain.

## Reactivate the real theorem

Identify $\mathbb C^n$ with $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Week 17 says that an invertible real derivative gives a $C^1$ inverse between neighborhoods. We now track the additional fact that the derivatives are complex-linear.

## Holomorphic maps and their derivatives

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open. A map $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ is holomorphic when it is complex differentiable in a neighborhood of every point. Equivalently for the maps used here, $F$ is real $C^1$ and every real derivative $DF_z:\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb R^{2m}$ is complex-linear.

In one variable, writing $F=u+iv$, complex linearity is exactly the Cauchy-Riemann system $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$.

content.introMarkdown: Compute the real Jacobian, verify the Cauchy-Riemann equations, and identify the complex derivative.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sign of the derivative of $x^2-y^2$ with respect to $y$.

The sign is what makes the real matrix represent complex multiplication.

Differentiate $u$ and $v$ separately, verify both Cauchy-Riemann equations, then compare with multiplication by $2x+2iy$.

## Complex inverse function theorem

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If the complex-linear map $DF_a$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ of $F(a)$ such that

$$F|_V:V\longrightarrow W$$

is bijective and its inverse $G:W\to V$ is holomorphic. Moreover, $DG_{F(a)}=(DF_a)^{-1}$.

## Complete worked model

Explain why the real inverse supplied for a holomorphic $F$ is holomorphic.

Derive the complex theorem from the real theorem and complex-linearity of derivatives.

### Strategy

Realify $F$, apply Week 17, then inspect the derivative of the inverse at every point of the target neighborhood.

### Hypotheses

An invertible complex-linear map is invertible as a real map, and its real inverse is again complex-linear.

### Intermediate claims

The real theorem gives a $C^1$ inverse $G$. At $w=F(z)$, the chain rule gives $DG_w=(DF_z)^{-1}$.

### Justification

Because $DF_z$ is complex-linear and invertible on a smaller neighborhood, $DG_w$ is complex-linear. A real $C^1$ map with complex-linear derivative at every point is holomorphic.

### Conclusion

The inverse is holomorphic on $W$. The argument upgrades regularity but preserves the same local neighborhoods.

For $F(z)=z^2$ at $0$, the complex derivative is zero. The theorem does not apply, and no holomorphic inverse branch through zero exists: a hypothetical $G(w)^2=w$ would give $2G(0)G'(0)=1$, hence $0=1$.

lessons.title: Simple roots move holomorphically with the coefficients
lessons.summary: Use the holomorphic implicit function theorem to construct and differentiate the unique local branch of a simple polynomial root under coefficient perturbations.
objectives: Use the holomorphic implicit function theorem to construct and differentiate the unique local branch of a simple polynomial root under coefficient perturbations.

content.markdown:
## A root becomes a function

A polynomial equation $P(c,z)=0$ couples a coefficient vector $c$ to a root $z$. At a simple root, the derivative with respect to $z$ is nonzero, so the equation solves for one nearby root as a holomorphic function of all nearby coefficients.

## Reactivate simplicity

For a one-variable polynomial $p$, a root $\zeta$ is simple exactly when $p(\zeta)=0$ and $p'(\zeta)\ne0$. Day 1 supplies the local-inverse mechanism; today we apply its implicit-function form.

## Coefficients as complex parameters

For monic degree $d$, write

$$P(c,z)=z^d+c_{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots+c_1z+c_0,$$

with $c\in\mathbb C^d$. If $P(c^*,\zeta^*)=0$ and $\partial_zP(c^*,\zeta^*)=p_{c^*}'(\zeta^*)\ne0$, the holomorphic implicit theorem gives neighborhoods $A$ of $c^*$ and $B$ of $\zeta^*$ and a unique holomorphic $\zeta:A\to B$ whose graph is exactly the nearby zero set inside $A\times B$.

Here is the mechanism. Define $H(c,z)=(c,P(c,z))$. Its derivative is block triangular:

$$DH_{(c^*,\zeta^*)}=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\D_cP&\partial_zP\end{pmatrix}.$$

The lower-right scalar is nonzero, so $DH_{(c^*,\zeta^*)}$ is invertible. The complex inverse function theorem makes $H$ locally biholomorphic. In the inverse, setting the second output coordinate equal to $0$ produces the root graph $z=\zeta(c)$.

content.title: Type the simple-root theorem
content.introMarkdown: State the derivative condition and the exact local holomorphic graph conclusion.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the derivative is taken with respect to the root variable.

The theorem solves only the variable whose derivative block is invertible.

Write the base equation, $\partial_zP\ne0$, then name $A$, $B$, and the graph equivalence inside their product.

## Differentiate the root branch

From $P(c,\zeta(c))=0$, differentiation in a coefficient increment $\delta c$ gives

$$D_cP(c^*,\zeta^*)[\delta c]+p_{c^*}'(\zeta^*)D\zeta(c^*)[\delta c]=0.$$

Therefore

$$D\zeta(c^*)[\delta c]=-\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\delta c_j(\zeta^*)^j}{p_{c^*}'(\zeta^*)}.$$

content.markdown:

That coefficient is the simple-root derivative that must be inverted.

Differentiate all three terms, substitute $a=-2,b=0,\zeta=0$, and solve the resulting scalar equation.

## Complete worked model

$P(s,z)=z^2-s$ at $(s,z)=(1,1)$.

Construct the root branch through $1$, differentiate it, and explain why the root near $-1$ does not violate uniqueness.

### Strategy

Check $P_z$, invoke the holomorphic implicit theorem, then differentiate $\zeta(s)^2=s$.

### Hypotheses

$P(1,1)=0$ and $P_z(1,1)=2\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

There are neighborhoods $A$ of $1$ and $B$ of $1$ containing a unique holomorphic root branch $\zeta:A\to B$.

### Justification

Differentiation gives $2\zeta(s)\zeta'(s)=1$, so $\zeta'(1)=1/2$.

### Conclusion

The second square root lies near $-1$, outside $B$. Local uniqueness means one root in the selected root neighborhood, not one root of the polynomial globally.

## Local uniqueness does not merge all roots

If the base polynomial has several distinct simple roots, each root has its own disjoint root neighborhood and its own holomorphic branch. The theorem follows one selected root; it does not choose an ordering of every root over an arbitrary large coefficient domain.

lessons.summary: Use Taylor factorization to diagnose repeated roots, show that the simple-root theorem's hypothesis fails there, and determine separately whether branches exist or are unique.
objectives: Use Taylor factorization to diagnose repeated roots, show that the simple-root theorem's hypothesis fails there, and determine separately whether branches exist or are unique.

content.markdown:
## Where one branch stops being distinguished

At a repeated root, the derivative with respect to the root variable vanishes. Nearby roots may split, collide, or require fractional-power behavior. The simple-root theorem no longer singles out one root branch.

## Reactivate the algebraic criterion

Week 3 proved that $\zeta$ is repeated exactly when $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$. Day 2 used the complementary condition $p'(\zeta)\ne0$ as the invertible derivative block.

## Order of a zero

If a holomorphic function is not identically zero near $\zeta$, then

$$f(z)=(z-\zeta)^m q(z),\qquad q(\zeta)\ne0,$$

for a unique integer $m\ge0$ and a function $q$ that is holomorphic near $\zeta$. If $m=0$, then $\zeta$ is not a zero. Among zeros, $m=1$ means simple and $m\ge2$ means repeated. Differentiation shows that a zero is simple exactly when $f'(\zeta)\ne0$.

content.title: Read multiplicity from the first nonzero term
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $f'(\zeta)\ne0$ if and only if $m=1$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the exponent of the first term after differentiation.

That exponent determines whether evaluation at the root leaves a nonzero term.

Differentiate by the product rule and evaluate separately for $m=1$ and $m\ge2$.

## Complete worked model

$P(t,z)=z^2-t$ at $(0,0)$.

Prove that no holomorphic root branch through the repeated root exists on a full neighborhood of $t=0$.

### Strategy

Assume a holomorphic branch and differentiate its defining identity.

### Hypotheses

$P(0,0)=0$ but $P_z(0,0)=0$, so the simple-root theorem is unavailable.

### Intermediate claims

A hypothetical branch $g$ would satisfy $g(0)=0$ and $g(t)^2=t$.

### Justification

Differentiating at zero gives $2g(0)g'(0)=1$, hence $0=1$.

### Conclusion

No holomorphic branch through zero exists. This is a direct contradiction, stronger than saying only that the theorem does not apply.

content.introMarkdown: Derive the contradiction and explain why it proves more than $P_z(0,0)=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your conclusion follows only from the zero derivative or from the differentiated identity.

Failure of a sufficient condition is not itself an impossibility proof.

State the failed hypothesis first, then assume the branch, differentiate, substitute zero, and derive the contradiction.

## Repeated does not mean branchless

For $P(t,z)=z^2-t^2$, the root at $(0,0)$ is repeated in $z$, yet two holomorphic branches meet there: $z=t$ and $z=-t$. The defect is lack of a unique branch selected by the repeated root, not a universal ban on holomorphic parameterizations.

content.introMarkdown: Exhibit both holomorphic branches and prove that no unique root branch in one neighborhood can contain the whole nearby zero set.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the two displayed branches are distinct for nonzero $t$.

The uniqueness failure requires two nearby outputs for the same parameter.

Factor the polynomial, write both graphs, compare them for $t\ne0$, and state the union-of-graphs conclusion.

## Preview: four different global words

A **local biholomorphism** has a holomorphic inverse near each source point. A **covering map** evenly covers each target neighborhood by disjoint sheets. A continuous map is **proper** when inverse images of compact sets are compact. A **global bijection** is one-to-one and onto on the declared whole spaces.

These words are not synonyms. For example, $z\mapsto z^n$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ is locally biholomorphic and has $n$ sheets, but for $n>1$ it is not globally injective. Covering maps and properness receive their full theory later; this week uses the vocabulary only to prevent premature identifications.

## Classify only what the evidence proves

Derivative evidence proves local biholomorphic behavior. An explicit collision disproves global injectivity. Fiber calculations count preimages. Compact-preimage and evenly-covered-neighborhood claims need additional global arguments.

A rigorous diagnosis states the multiplicity, computes the root derivative block, identifies what theorem is unavailable, and then separately proves whether branches exist and whether they are unique.

For every small nonzero $t$, they give two distinct roots in any fixed root neighborhood of zero. Thus the full nearby zero set is the union of two graphs, not the graph of one unique function.

activities.title: Match evidence to local and global claims
activities.promptMarkdown:

Globally $e^{z+2\pi i}=e^z$, and $p_n(1)=p_n(e^{2\pi i/n})=1$ for $n>1$, so neither map is globally injective. These facts alone do not prove compact-preimage or evenly-covered-neighborhood statements.

activities.title: Explain exactly what repeated roots destroy
activities.promptMarkdown:

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For both families, $P_i(0,0)=0$ and $(P_i)_z(0,0)=0$, so the simple-root implicit theorem does not apply. For $P_1$, a branch $g^2=t$ would give $2g(0)g'(0)=1$, impossible, so no holomorphic branch through zero exists. For $P_2=(z-t)(z+t)$, the two holomorphic branches $z=t$ and $z=-t$ meet at zero, so branches exist but are not unique for the full nearby zero set. Thus a repeated root removes the simple-root theorem's unique selected branch; further analysis decides the actual branch behavior.

lessons.title: Why constant Jacobian does not visibly give global injectivity
lessons.summary: Write a complete, carefully bounded explanation of why a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant proves local biholomorphic behavior but does not by itself display a global inverse in several variables.
objectives: Write a complete, carefully bounded explanation of why a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant proves local biholomorphic behavior but does not by itself display a global inverse in several variables.

content.markdown:
## A local theorem inside a global problem

For a polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, the condition $\det JF\equiv c\ne0$ makes every derivative invertible. The complex inverse theorem therefore works at every point. The unresolved step is to coordinate all those local inverses into one inverse on the whole target.

## Claim boundary

This page explains the logical gap; it does not announce a counterexample to the polynomial Jacobian conjecture. A nonpolynomial map may illustrate the local-to-global failure, while a polynomial shear may illustrate that a separate explicit inverse can close the gap in a special case.

## What constant determinant proves immediately

If $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ is polynomial and $\det JF(x)=c\ne0$ for every $x$, then $DF_x$ is invertible at every point. Hence every $x$ has a neighborhood $V_x$ on which $F$ is biholomorphic onto an open neighborhood of $F(x)$.

The neighborhood $V_x$ may depend on $x$. The theorem does not compare $V_x$ with $V_y$ for distant points, and it does not rule out $F(x)=F(y)$ when $x\ne y$.

content.title: State the exact pointwise conclusion
content.introMarkdown: State exactly what the complex inverse theorem gives at every point and what it does not compare.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your inverse neighborhood depends on the source point.

A family of local inverses is not yet one globally compatible inverse.

Begin 'for each $x$ there exist $V_x,W_x$,' then list the distant-point and global-inverse questions left open.

## Complete worked model

$S(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $T(u,v)=(u,v+u^2)$, and $F=T\circ S$.

Prove $\det JF\equiv1$ and prove global bijectivity using a separate explicit inverse.

### Strategy

Use determinant multiplicativity for the local condition, then reverse the two shears for the global inverse.

### Hypotheses

$JS=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $JT=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2u&1\end{pmatrix}$ both have determinant one.

### Intermediate claims

$F(x,y)=(x+y^2,\,y+(x+y^2)^2)$. For output $(u,v)$, first apply $T^{-1}(u,v)=(u,v-u^2)$ and then $S^{-1}(r,s)=(r-s^2,s)$.

### Justification

Thus $F^{-1}(u,v)=(u-(v-u^2)^2,\,v-u^2)$, and direct composition in both orders gives the identity.

### Conclusion

Constant determinant proves local invertibility; the displayed polynomial inverse separately proves global bijectivity for this map.

content.title: Verify the global inverse rather than guessing
content.introMarkdown: Compute the determinant, propose a polynomial inverse, and verify both compositions.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether you verified the inverse in both composition orders.

One composition alone may establish only a left or right inverse.

Compute $JG$, define $H$, evaluate $H\circ G$ and $G\circ H$, then label the evidence roles.

## Why one variable is different

If a polynomial $p:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ satisfies $p'(z)=c\ne0$ for every $z$, then the polynomial $p'(z)-c$ is identically zero. Comparing coefficients gives $p(z)=cz+d$, which is globally bijective.

In several variables, $\det JF\equiv c$ does not make the whole matrix $JF$ constant. Its entries may vary and cancel inside the determinant, as the shear examples show.

content.title: Prove the one-variable conclusion
content.introMarkdown: Prove $p(z)=cz+a_0$ and write its global inverse.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check which coefficients of $p'$ must vanish when it is constant.

The affine conclusion comes from coefficient identities, not from local inversion alone.

Differentiate the polynomial, compare every power of $z$, reconstruct $p$, and solve for $z$.

## A logic illustration that is not a polynomial counterexample

The exponential map $e^z:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C^\times$ has nonzero derivative everywhere and is locally biholomorphic, but $e^{z+2\pi i}=e^z$. It cleanly shows why pointwise local inverses do not imply global injectivity.

It does **not** disprove the polynomial constant-Jacobian statement: $e^z$ is not polynomial, and its derivative is not constant. The example diagnoses the logical gap only.

content.title: Audit the exponential example
content.introMarkdown: State what the example proves about local-to-global reasoning and why it is not a counterexample to the polynomial constant-Jacobian problem.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the exponential satisfies both 'polynomial' and 'constant determinant.'

An example outside the hypothesis class cannot settle the polynomial problem.

State the local theorem and collision, then explicitly test polynomiality and constancy of the derivative.

## Structure for the two-page explanation

A strong explanation has five moves: state the polynomial condition; derive the all-points local conclusion; expose the quantifier gap; contrast one variable with several variables; and classify examples by whether they prove a special case, illustrate the logic, or fall outside the hypothesis class.

That is the exact unsupported step the exercise is designed to expose.

Rebuild the answer in five paragraphs following the displayed structure and label what each example does and does not prove.

content.markdown:
## Four earlier objects support one continuation theorem

The factor theorem identifies simplicity, polynomial bases define coefficient directions, symmetric-power dimensions count parameters, and the implicit derivative formula computes the root response. Friday retrieves each object before the final synthesis.

## Retrieval rule

Each deliberate review repeats one exact earlier object after 16, 8, 3, or 1 weeks. The new context is holomorphic root continuation, not another copy of the earlier exercise.

## Deliberate review: Week 2 after sixteen weeks

If $p(z)=(z-\zeta)q(z)$, then $p'(\zeta)=q(\zeta)$. A simple root is exactly a factor whose complementary quotient does not vanish at the root.

## Deliberate review: Week 10 after eight weeks

A binary degree-$d$ form has unique monomial coordinates. After choosing an affine chart, those same coefficients become the parameter directions in the root-branch differential.

## Deliberate review: Week 15 after three weeks

A binary degree-$d$ form has $d+1$ coefficient directions. The root equation adds one complex root variable and one complex scalar equation; at a simple root the equation solves that variable locally.

## Deliberate review: Week 17 after one week

For $P(c,\zeta(c))=0$, the solved-variable block is the scalar $P_z$. The general matrix formula becomes the coefficient-to-root response formula.

## Complete worked model

$P(a,b,z)=z^3+az+b$ at $(-1,0,1)$.

Coordinate the simple-root check, holomorphic graph, parameter derivative, and local uniqueness boundary.

### Strategy

Evaluate $P$ and $P_z$, invoke the holomorphic implicit theorem, then specialize the block derivative formula.

### Hypotheses

$P(-1,0,1)=0$ and $P_z(-1,0,1)=2\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

A unique branch through $1$ exists in a selected root neighborhood, and its differential is $D\zeta(\delta a,\delta b)=-(\delta a+\delta b)/2$.

### Justification

The numerator is the coefficient perturbation $\delta a\,z+\delta b$ evaluated at $z=1$; the denominator is the simple-root derivative $2$.

### Conclusion

The branch is holomorphic and unique inside its root neighborhood. No ordering or continuation of the other roots over a large parameter domain follows.

## The recurring boundary

Nonzero derivative selects a local branch; repeated roots require separate branch analysis. Constant nonzero determinant gives local inverses everywhere; global injectivity still requires a global argument. Neither boundary can be crossed by changing an adjective.

The term outcome is analytic local invertibility: recognize a simple root as an invertible solved-variable block, construct its holomorphic branch, diagnose repeated-root failure, and refuse to turn local inverses into a global bijection without additional evidence.

lessons.title: Group laws and the six permutations of three roots
lessons.summary: Verify a group from its axioms, calculate in the permutation group of three objects, and distinguish root-label symmetry from a Galois-group claim.
objectives: Verify a group from its axioms, calculate in the permutation group of three objects, and distinguish root-label symmetry from a Galois-group claim.

content.markdown:
## From individual formulas to symmetry

Earlier weeks studied maps one at a time. A group records a whole family of reversible transformations together with a rule for composing them. The axioms make repeated transformations calculable.

For a cubic with three distinct roots, any relabelling of the three root positions is a permutation. Those six relabellings form the symmetric group $S_3$. This is a statement about labels; identifying a Galois group requires additional field-theoretic information that is not supplied this week.

## Reactivate composition and roots

A function has a domain and codomain, and composition is performed right to left. A generic cubic in this lesson means only a cubic with three distinct roots $r_1,r_2,r_3$ in a chosen splitting field. Distinctness lets the labels be permuted without collapsing two root positions.

## The four pieces of a group

A group is a set $G$ with a binary operation $(g,h)\mapsto gh$ satisfying four requirements:

1. **Closure:** $gh\in G$ for all $g,h\in G$.
2. **Associativity:** $(gh)k=g(hk)$.
3. **Identity:** some $e\in G$ satisfies $eg=ge=g$.
4. **Inverses:** every $g\in G$ has $g^{-1}\in G$ with $gg^{-1}=g^{-1}g=e$.

Closure is part of the data: an operation that leaves the proposed set does not define a group on that set.

content.title: Test a proposed group
content.introMarkdown: Verify closure, associativity, the identity, and inverses, naming the element used in each check.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first group axiom that your response has not checked on the stated set.

A familiar operation can fail to make a particular subset into a group.

Write the four axioms as separate lines and supply the relevant complex number on each line.

## Permutations form a group

For a set $X$, a permutation is a bijection $X\to X$. The set $S_X$ of all permutations of $X$ is a group under composition. Closure follows because a composite of bijections is bijective; associativity is the associativity of function composition; the identity map is the identity element; and the inverse bijection is the group inverse.

For $X=\{1,2,3\}$, write $S_3$. We use cycle notation: $(12)$ swaps $1$ and $2$, while $(123)$ sends $1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto1$.

## Complete worked model

A polynomial $p(T)=(T-r_1)(T-r_2)(T-r_3)$ has three distinct roots in a chosen splitting field.

Identify the full relabelling symmetry of the ordered root list and explain what is, and is not, being claimed.

### Strategy

List permutations by cycle type, check that each only changes labels, and separate this combinatorial symmetry from field automorphisms.

### Hypotheses

The three root positions are distinct. A relabelling sends $(r_1,r_2,r_3)$ to $(r_{\sigma^{-1}(1)},r_{\sigma^{-1}(2)},r_{\sigma^{-1}(3)})$.

### Intermediate claims

There is one identity, three transpositions $(12),(13),(23)$, and two three-cycles $(123),(132)$, hence six relabellings. The unordered product remains $p(T)$.

### Justification

Multiplication of the three linear factors is commutative, so permuting their order does not change the polynomial. Composition of relabellings matches multiplication in $S_3$.

### Conclusion

The root labels have an $S_3$ relabelling symmetry. This does not prove that every relabelling is induced by an automorphism of the splitting field, so it does not by itself compute the Galois group of $p$.

content.title: Transfer the root-label symmetry
content.introMarkdown: Describe what $(13)$ does to the ordered triple and show that the expanded polynomial is unchanged.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Identify whether your argument uses only commutativity of factors or also constructs a field automorphism.

Those are different mathematical claims even when both involve permutations of roots.

Write the permuted ordered triple, rewrite the factor product, then state exactly which structure has acted.

## A family of transformations is not automatically a group

To claim a symmetry group, the transformations must include the identity, be closed under composition, and contain inverses. For example, the two maps $x\mapsto x+1$ and $x\mapsto x-1$ do not by themselves form a group: composing $x\mapsto x+1$ with itself gives $x\mapsto x+2$, which is missing.

content.title: Diagnose a failed transformation family
content.introMarkdown: Name the first group requirement visibly absent and give a concrete calculation.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compose one listed transformation with itself.

Closure must hold for every pair of elements in the proposed group.

Calculate $t_1\circ t_1$ and enlarge the index set until every integer sum is represented.

## Day 1 synthesis

A group is not merely a set of visually similar operations. Its composition law, identity, and inverses must stay inside the set. For three distinct root labels, the six bijections form $S_3$, and the group law is composition.

content.title: Prove the root relabelling symmetry

The exercise asks both for a genuine group and for an exact interpretation of its symmetry.

Verify the four group requirements first, identify the six elements, and finish with separate combinatorial and field-theoretic sentences.

lessons.title: Subgroups, cyclic groups, generators, and orders
lessons.summary: Use the subgroup test, compute cyclic subgroups and element orders, and classify the subgroups generated by permutations in $S_3$.
objectives: Use the subgroup test, compute cyclic subgroups and element orders, and classify the subgroups generated by permutations in $S_3$.

content.markdown:
## Symmetry often comes in layers

A large symmetry group contains smaller families that remain groups under the same operation. A subgroup isolates one coherent kind of symmetry: rotations inside all rigid motions, even permutations inside all permutations, or powers of one transformation inside a larger group.

## Retrieve yesterday's group law

Recall the identity, inverse, and composition convention in $S_3$. Today every proposed subgroup uses that same operation; it does not receive a new multiplication law.

## The subgroup test

Let $G$ be a group and let $H\subseteq G$ be nonempty. Then $H$ is a subgroup if and only if

$$xy^{-1}\in H\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in H.$$

This one-step test contains closure and inverses. Taking $x=y$ gives $e=xx^{-1}\in H$. Taking $x=e$ gives $y^{-1}\in H$. Applying the test to $x$ and $y^{-1}$ then gives $xy\in H$. Associativity is inherited from $G$.

content.title: Apply the subgroup test once
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $2\mathbb Z$ is a subgroup using the additive form of the one-step subgroup test.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether your formula uses the inverse operation for addition.

In additive notation, multiplication becomes addition and inversion becomes negation.

Write $x=2m$, $y=2n$, and calculate $x-y$.

## Complete worked model

For $g\in G$, define $\langle g\rangle=\{g^n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$.

Prove that $\langle g\rangle$ is a subgroup and is contained in every subgroup containing $g$.

### Strategy

Use exponent laws for the subgroup test, then use closure and inverses in an arbitrary subgroup containing $g$.

### Hypotheses

$G$ is a group, so integer powers are defined by positive products, $g^0=e$, and negative powers of $g^{-1}$.

### Intermediate claims

For $g^m,g^n\in\langle g\rangle$, one has $g^m(g^n)^{-1}=g^{m-n}\in\langle g\rangle$. If $K\le G$ and $g\in K$, closure and inverses give $g^n\in K$ for every integer $n$.

### Justification

The one-step subgroup test proves the first claim. The second follows by induction for positive powers and by inversion for negative powers.

### Conclusion

$\langle g\rangle$ is the smallest subgroup of $G$ containing $g$; it is the cyclic subgroup generated by $g$.

content.title: Compute a generated subgroup
content.introMarkdown: List $\langle g\rangle$ and find the least positive integer $n$ with $g^n=e$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Compute the image of $1,2,3$ under the next power before naming the cycle.

The order is the first positive return to the identity, not the number of symbols written in cycle notation.

Calculate $g^0,g^1,g^2,g^3$ in order and remove repetitions.

## Cyclic groups and element order

A group is cyclic if $G=\langle g\rangle$ for some $g$. The order of an element $g$ is the size of $\langle g\rangle$; when finite, it is also the least positive $n$ such that $g^n=e$.

The group $S_3$ is not cyclic. Its elements have orders $1$, $2$, or $3$, so no single element generates all six permutations.

content.title: Classify orders in $S_3$
content.introMarkdown: Find the order of each cycle type and use the result to prove that $S_3$ is not cyclic.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the least positive exponent for one representative of each cycle type.

A finite cyclic group must contain an element whose order equals the group order.

Compute powers of $(12)$ and $(123)$, then compare their orders with $|S_3|$.

## A subset can fail in one product

The set of transpositions $\{(12),(13),(23)\}$ is not a subgroup of $S_3$. It omits the identity, and multiplying two distinct transpositions produces a three-cycle. A subgroup test needs only one counterexample to fail.

content.title: Find the decisive subgroup failure
content.introMarkdown: Determine whether $H$ is a subgroup and justify the answer with one exact product.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Multiply two different transpositions and check whether the result is listed.

Containing the identity and every inverse is not sufficient without closure.

Use $(12)$ and $(23)$, compute right to left, and compare with $H$.

## Day 2 synthesis

The subgroup test turns four group requirements into one calculation inside an already known group. Generated subgroups then organize the powers of a single symmetry and make element order visible.

content.title: Classify the cyclic subgroups of $S_3$
content.introMarkdown: List every distinct cyclic subgroup of $S_3$ and prove that your list is complete.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the two three-cycles generate different sets or the same set.

Different generators can generate one cyclic subgroup.

Compute the powers of one representative of each cycle type, deduplicate the resulting sets, and finish with the cycle-type exhaustion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The set $2\mathbb Z$ is nonempty because $0=2\cdot0$ belongs to it. If $x=2m$ and $y=2n$, then the additive version of $xy^{-1}$ is $x-y=2(m-n)\in2\mathbb Z$. The subgroup test therefore proves that $2\mathbb Z\le\mathbb Z$.

$g=(123)\in S_3$.

activities.title: Classify orders in $S_3$
activities.promptMarkdown:
The elements of $S_3$ are $e$, three transpositions, and two three-cycles.

Find the order of each cycle type and use the result to prove that $S_3$ is not cyclic.

Do not infer noncyclicity merely from noncommutativity; use the computed orders.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The identity has order $1$. Every transposition squares to $e$, so each has order $2$. Every three-cycle has cube $e$ and is not the identity before the third power, so each has order $3$. A generator of a six-element cyclic group would have order $6$, but $S_3$ has no such element. Therefore $S_3$ is not cyclic.

rubric.description: The three element orders and the noncyclicity conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.promptMarkdown:
$H=\{e,(12),(13),(23)\}\subset S_3$.

Determine whether $H$ is a subgroup and justify the answer with one exact product.

A size argument is not enough; calculate inside $S_3$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The set is not a subgroup. For example, $(12)(23)=(123)$, and $(123)\notin H$. Thus $H$ is not closed under the group operation.

activities.title: Classify the cyclic subgroups of $S_3$
activities.promptMarkdown:
Generate a subgroup from each possible cycle type in $S_3$.

List every distinct cyclic subgroup of $S_3$ and prove that your list is complete.

Treat identity, transpositions, and three-cycles separately, noting when two generators produce the same subgroup.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All distinct cyclic subgroups are listed without duplication or omission.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Completeness follows from the exhaustive classification of elements by cycle type.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The identity generates $\{e\}$. Each transposition generates a distinct subgroup of order $2$: $\{e,(12)\}$, $\{e,(13)\}$, and $\{e,(23)\}$. Either three-cycle generates the same order-$3$ subgroup $\{e,(123),(132)\}$. Every element of $S_3$ has one of these three cycle types, so every cyclic subgroup appears on the list. There are five distinct cyclic subgroups.

lessons.title: Group actions and product-preserving rescaling
lessons.summary: Verify the two action axioms, convert an action into permutations, and prove that relative rescaling acts on factor pairs while preserving their product.
objectives: Verify the two action axioms, convert an action into permutations, and prove that relative rescaling acts on factor pairs while preserving their product.

content.markdown:
## A group becomes useful when it moves something

A group action says how every group element transforms every point of a set, compatibly with multiplication in the group. The action may reveal information that the group alone does not: fixed points, orbits, and quantities unchanged by every transformation.

## Retrieve the two structures

Yesterday supplied a group $G$ and its multiplication. Today we also specify a set $X$. The symbol $g\cdot x$ is an action, not necessarily multiplication of two elements of the same set.

## The two action axioms

A left action of a group $G$ on a set $X$ is a rule $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$ such that

$$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. For each $g$, the map $T_g(x)=g\cdot x$ is automatically a bijection with inverse $T_{g^{-1}}$. Thus an action is equivalently a homomorphism $G\to S_X$.

content.title: Verify a translation action
content.introMarkdown: Verify both action axioms with the correct additive group law.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Identify the identity element of the acting group before applying the action.

The notation $e$ changes with the group law; for $(\mathbb Z,+)$ it is $0$.

Check $0\cdot x$, then compare $(m+n)\cdot x$ with $m\cdot(n\cdot x)$.

## Every action gives permutations

Fix $g\in G$. From the action law, $T_g\circ T_{g^{-1}}=T_e=\operatorname{id}_X$ and similarly in the other order. Hence $T_g$ is a permutation of $X$. Moreover $T_{gh}=T_g\circ T_h$, so $g\mapsto T_g$ preserves the group operation.

content.title: Derive the permutation representation
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $T_g$ is bijective and that $T_{gh}=T_g\circ T_h$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proposed inverse transformation is attached to $g^{-1}$.

The action law converts multiplication in $G$ into composition of transformations.

Compute both composites with $T_{g^{-1}}$, then compare $T_{gh}(x)$ with $(T_g\circ T_h)(x)$.

## Complete worked model

Let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be spaces of nonzero linear and quadratic forms. For $\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times$, define $\lambda\cdot(L,Q)=(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

Prove that this is an action of $\mathbb C^\times$ on $V_1\times V_2$ and that multiplication $M(L,Q)=LQ$ is invariant.

### Strategy

Check the identity and compatibility before checking invariance; these are logically separate obligations.

### Hypotheses

$\lambda$ is nonzero, so $\lambda^{-1}$ exists. Scalar multiplication keeps a linear form linear, a quadratic form quadratic, and nonzero factors nonzero.

### Intermediate claims

$1\cdot(L,Q)=(L,Q)$. For $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb C^\times$, $(\lambda\mu)\cdot(L,Q)=((\lambda\mu)L,(\lambda\mu)^{-1}Q)=\lambda\cdot(\mu\cdot(L,Q))$.

### Justification

The inverse scalar satisfies $(\lambda\mu)^{-1}=\lambda^{-1}\mu^{-1}$ because complex multiplication is commutative. Finally, $M(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)=(\lambda L)(\lambda^{-1}Q)=LQ$.

### Conclusion

Relative rescaling is a group action, and every orbit lies inside one fiber of the product map $M$. The calculation does not yet prove that an entire fiber is one orbit.

content.title: Adapt the weight calculation
content.introMarkdown: Verify the action axioms and prove that $xy$ is invariant.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether every displayed negative power is defined on the proposed acting set.

An invariant calculation cannot repair an action that is not well defined.

State $\lambda,\mu\ne0$, verify the two action laws, then multiply the transformed coordinates.

## Invariance is weaker than orbit classification

If a function $I:X\to Y$ satisfies $I(g\cdot x)=I(x)$ for all $g,x$, then $I$ is constant on each orbit. The converse need not hold: two points can have the same invariant value without belonging to the same orbit. Proving that fibers equal orbits needs an additional argument.

content.title: Separate a fiber from an orbit
content.introMarkdown: Show that $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ have the same product but are not in the same orbit.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Write the general point $\lambda\cdot(1,0)$ before comparing it with $(0,1)$.

One invariant may forget more information than the action does.

Parametrize the first orbit, compare coordinate-zero patterns, and only then state the conclusion.

## Day 3 synthesis

An action requires identity and composition compatibility. An invariant is a separate object whose value remains fixed along the action. Relative rescaling has both properties: it is an action on factor pairs and it preserves multiplication.

content.title: Prove the factor-rescaling symmetry completely
content.introMarkdown: Prove well-definedness, both action axioms, and invariance of $M(L,Q)=LQ$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing obligation among well-definedness, identity, compatibility, invariance, and scope.

Each obligation proves a different part of the symmetry claim.

Use five short paragraphs in that order and write the final implication as orbit contained in fiber.
