activities.title: Verify a translation action
activities.promptMarkdown:
$(\mathbb Z,+)$ acts on $\mathbb R$ by $n\cdot x=x+n$.

Verify both action axioms with the correct additive group law.

Also write the inverse of the transformation attached to $n$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both action laws and the inverse transformation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The calculation uses addition in the acting group and composition on the transformed set.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The identity of $(\mathbb Z,+)$ is $0$, and $0\cdot x=x+0=x$. For $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, $(m+n)\cdot x=x+m+n$, while $m\cdot(n\cdot x)=m\cdot(x+n)=x+n+m=x+m+n$. Thus the compatibility law holds. The transformation $x\mapsto x+n$ has inverse $x\mapsto x-n$, attached to $-n$.

activities.title: Derive the permutation representation
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $G$ act on a set $X$ and define $T_g:X\to X$ by $T_g(x)=g\cdot x$.

Prove that $T_g$ is bijective and that $T_{gh}=T_g\circ T_h$.

Name the inverse map explicitly.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The inverse and operation-preserving identity are proved pointwise.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Both conclusions are derived from the two action axioms without an extra assumption.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For every $x$, $(T_g\circ T_{g^{-1}})(x)=g\cdot(g^{-1}\cdot x)=(gg^{-1})\cdot x=e\cdot x=x$, and the reverse composite is also the identity. Thus $T_g^{-1}=T_{g^{-1}}$. Also $T_{gh}(x)=(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)=(T_g\circ T_h)(x)$ for every $x$, so the two maps are equal.

activities.title: Adapt the weight calculation
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb R^\times$ acts on $\mathbb R^2$ by $\lambda\cdot(x,y)=(\lambda^2x,\lambda^{-2}y)$.

Verify the action axioms and prove that $xy$ is invariant.

State why $\lambda=0$ must be excluded.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The identity, compatibility, invariance, and nonzero-scalar condition are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response separates well-definedness, the action law, and preservation of the function.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $\lambda=1$, $1\cdot(x,y)=(x,y)$. For nonzero $\lambda,\mu$, $(\lambda\mu)\cdot(x,y)=((\lambda\mu)^2x,(\lambda\mu)^{-2}y)=\lambda\cdot(\mu^2x,\mu^{-2}y)=\lambda\cdot(\mu\cdot(x,y))$. The product becomes $(\lambda^2x)(\lambda^{-2}y)=xy$. The scalar $0$ is excluded because $0^{-2}$ is undefined and because $0$ has no multiplicative inverse.

activities.title: Separate a fiber from an orbit
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb R^\times$ acts on $\mathbb R^2$ by $\lambda\cdot(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-1}y)$.

Show that $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ have the same product but are not in the same orbit.

Use one coordinate that cannot become zero under multiplication by a nonzero scalar.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Both points have product $0$. Every point in the orbit of $(1,0)$ has the form $(\lambda,0)$ with $\lambda\ne0$, so its first coordinate is nonzero and its second coordinate is zero. The point $(0,1)$ has the opposite pattern and cannot lie in that orbit. Thus equal invariant values do not force equal orbits.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The common invariant value and distinct-orbit proof are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response identifies a coordinate property preserved along the relevant orbit.

activities.title: Prove the factor-rescaling symmetry completely
activities.promptMarkdown:
For nonzero binary forms $L$ of degree $1$ and $Q$ of degree $2$, let $\lambda\cdot(L,Q)=(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times$.

Prove well-definedness, both action axioms, and invariance of $M(L,Q)=LQ$.

Finish by stating the strongest orbit-fiber conclusion justified by the calculation.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Well-definedness, the two action laws, invariance, and the orbit-fiber boundary are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof keeps the action verification separate from the invariant calculation and avoids the converse.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $\lambda\ne0$, both scalars are defined and preserve the degrees and nonzeroness of $L,Q$. The identity acts by $1\cdot(L,Q)=(L,Q)$. For $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb C^\times$, $(\lambda\mu)\cdot(L,Q)=((\lambda\mu)L,(\lambda\mu)^{-1}Q)=\lambda\cdot(\mu L,\mu^{-1}Q)$. Hence this is an action. Moreover $M(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)=(\lambda L)(\lambda^{-1}Q)=LQ$. Therefore each rescaling orbit is contained in one product fiber. The calculation alone does not prove that every product fiber is a single orbit.

lessons.title: Stabilizers and fixed-point calculations
lessons.summary: Define the stabilizer of a point, prove it is a subgroup, and compute stabilizers in permutation, translation, and rescaling actions.
objectives: Define the stabilizer of a point, prove it is a subgroup, and compute stabilizers in permutation, translation, and rescaling actions.

content.markdown:
## Measure the symmetry that remains

An action moves points, but some group elements may leave a selected point unchanged. The stabilizer records exactly those residual symmetries. It depends on both the action and the point.

## Retrieve the action law

Use $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$. The subgroup test from Day 2 will turn the fixed-point condition into a proof that stabilizers are subgroups.

## Stabilizer of a point

If $G$ acts on $X$ and $x\in X$, the stabilizer of $x$ is

$$G_x=\operatorname{Stab}_G(x)=\{g\in G:g\cdot x=x\}.$$

The subscript matters. The same action can have points with different stabilizers, and a different action of the same group can change every stabilizer.

content.title: Compute a root-label stabilizer
content.introMarkdown: List every element of $\operatorname{Stab}_{S_3}(1)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Evaluate each candidate permutation at the point $1$.

A stabilizer is determined by the chosen point, not by whether a permutation looks simple.

Partition $S_3$ into permutations that send $1$ to $1$, $2$, or $3$.

## Complete worked model

Let a group $G$ act on a set $X$ and fix $x\in X$.

Prove that $G_x$ is a subgroup of $G$.

### Strategy

Use the one-step subgroup test with two elements known to fix $x$.

### Hypotheses

The identity fixes $x$, so $G_x$ is nonempty. Let $g,h\in G_x$, meaning $g\cdot x=x$ and $h\cdot x=x$.

### Intermediate claims

From $h\cdot x=x$, apply $h^{-1}$ to obtain $h^{-1}\cdot x=x$. Then $(gh^{-1})\cdot x=g\cdot(h^{-1}\cdot x)=g\cdot x=x$.

### Justification

Both equalities use the action compatibility law. Hence $gh^{-1}\in G_x$.

### Conclusion

The one-step subgroup test gives $G_x\le G$.

content.title: Reconstruct the stabilizer proof
content.introMarkdown: Prove $G_y\le G$ using the subgroup test.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first point where the proof needs to know that $h^{-1}$ also fixes $y$.

The subgroup test uses $gh^{-1}$, not just $gh$.

Apply $h^{-1}$ to $h\cdot y=y$, then substitute that result into $(gh^{-1})\cdot y$.

## Free actions and exceptional points

An action is free when every stabilizer is trivial. The translation action of $(\mathbb Z,+)$ on $\mathbb R$ is free: $x+n=x$ forces $n=0$. Relative rescaling on all of $\mathbb C^2$ is not free because every scalar fixes $(0,0)$.

content.title: Compute three rescaling stabilizers
content.introMarkdown: Compute the stabilizers of $(1,1)$, $(1,0)$, and $(0,0)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a coordinate equation may be cancelled when that coordinate equals zero.

Zero coordinates can enlarge a stabilizer dramatically.

Write both coordinate equations separately for each point and solve them without cancelling zero.

## Stabilizers of root data

Under the $S_3$-action on one selected root label, two permutations fix that label. Under the induced action on an ordered triple of three distinct roots, only the identity fixes the entire ordered triple. The object being stabilized therefore matters as much as the acting group.

content.title: Compare two stabilizers
content.introMarkdown: Compare the stabilizer of $1$ with the stabilizer of $(a,b,c)$ when $a,b,c$ are distinct.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

State exactly what a permutation must fix in each action.

The phrase 'the stabilizer in $S_3$' is incomplete until the point and action are named.

List the freedom left after fixing one position, then check every position of the ordered triple.

## Day 4 synthesis

A stabilizer is a subgroup because fixed-point conditions survive identity, inverses, and products. Calculating it means solving $g\cdot x=x$ with care at exceptional points.

content.title: Analyze stabilizers across three actions
content.introMarkdown: Prove the general stabilizer-subgroup theorem, then compute one nontrivial, one trivial, and one whole-group stabilizer from these actions.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first stabilizer claim that lacks either an action, a point, or a solved fixed-point equation.

Stabilizers are not properties of the group alone.

Prove the general subgroup statement first, then solve each named action equation on a separate line.

activities.title: Compute a root-label stabilizer
activities.promptMarkdown:
$S_3$ acts on $\{1,2,3\}$ by permutation.

List every element of $\operatorname{Stab}_{S_3}(1)$.

Explain why no other permutation belongs to the stabilizer.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A permutation fixing $1$ may either fix both $2$ and $3$ or swap them. Therefore $\operatorname{Stab}_{S_3}(1)=\{e,(23)\}$. Every remaining element sends $1$ to $2$ or $3$, so no other element fixes the selected point.

activities.title: Reconstruct the stabilizer proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
For an arbitrary action $G\curvearrowright X$ and point $y\in X$, let $G_y=\{g:g\cdot y=y\}$.

Prove $G_y\le G$ using the subgroup test.

Show explicitly why $h^{-1}$ fixes $y$ when $h$ does.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Nonemptiness and closure under $gh^{-1}$ are proved correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The identity fixes $y$, so $G_y$ is nonempty. If $g,h\in G_y$, then $h\cdot y=y$. Acting by $h^{-1}$ gives $y=h^{-1}\cdot(h\cdot y)=h^{-1}\cdot y$. Hence $(gh^{-1})\cdot y=g\cdot(h^{-1}\cdot y)=g\cdot y=y$, so $gh^{-1}\in G_y$. The subgroup test proves $G_y\le G$.

activities.title: Compute three rescaling stabilizers
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb C^\times$ acts on $\mathbb C^2$ by $\lambda\cdot(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-1}y)$.

Compute the stabilizers of $(1,1)$, $(1,0)$, and $(0,0)$.

Solve the fixed-point equations rather than guessing from the invariant $xy$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $(1,1)$, the equations $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda^{-1}=1$ give stabilizer $\{1\}$. For $(1,0)$, the first coordinate again forces $\lambda=1$, while the second equation is automatic, so the stabilizer is $\{1\}$. Every $\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times$ fixes $(0,0)$, so its stabilizer is the whole group.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three fixed-point equations and stabilizers are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response treats zero coordinates as exceptional rather than cancelling them.

activities.title: Compare two stabilizers
activities.promptMarkdown:
$S_3$ acts on $\{1,2,3\}$ and also on ordered triples of pairwise distinct entries by permuting positions.

Compare the stabilizer of $1$ with the stabilizer of $(a,b,c)$ when $a,b,c$ are distinct.

Explain the difference using the exact fixed-point conditions.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The stabilizer of $1$ is $\{e,(23)\}$ because fixing the first label still permits swapping the other two. If a permutation fixes the ordered triple $(a,b,c)$ with distinct entries, it must leave every position unchanged, so its stabilizer is $\{e\}$. The second object records all three positions and therefore has less residual symmetry.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both stabilizers and their dependence on the acted-on object are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response derives the difference from the two fixed-point equations.

activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the $S_3$ action on three labels, the $\mathbb Z$ translation action on $\mathbb R$, and the $\mathbb C^\times$ relative-rescaling action on factor pairs.

Prove the general stabilizer-subgroup theorem, then compute one nontrivial, one trivial, and one whole-group stabilizer from these actions.

Name the action and point before each calculation.

rubric.description: The subgroup theorem and the three requested stabilizer types are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For any action, the identity fixes $x$. If $g,h$ fix $x$, then $h^{-1}$ fixes $x$ and $(gh^{-1})\cdot x=x$, so the subgroup test gives $G_x\le G$. For $S_3\curvearrowright\{1,2,3\}$, $G_1=\{e,(23)\}$ is nontrivial. For translations, the stabilizer of any $x$ is $\{0\}$ because $x+n=x$ implies $n=0$. For relative rescaling, the stabilizer of a pair of nonzero forms is $\{1\}$, while the zero pair, if included in the acted-on space, is fixed by all of $\mathbb C^\times$. These calculations depend on the named point and domain.

lessons.title: Cubic symmetries and factor-pair synthesis
lessons.summary: Coordinate root permutations, stabilizers, and factor rescaling in one precise account of cubic symmetry while retrieving the prerequisite polynomial structures.
objectives: Coordinate root permutations, stabilizers, and factor rescaling in one precise account of cubic symmetry while retrieving the prerequisite polynomial structures.

content.markdown:
## Two symmetries, two kinds of information

Choosing one root of a cubic gives a linear factor and a complementary quadratic factor. Permuting which root is marked changes that factorization. Relative rescaling changes the representative of one fixed factorization. Both preserve the cubic, but they are not the same action.

## Retrieval before synthesis

The four review checkpoints below are deliberate repetitions at scheduled intervals. Each appears in a new role: roots identify factor choices, matrices represent multiplication, derivatives linearize multiplication, and holomorphic continuation tracks a selected simple root.

## Deliberate review: Week 3 roots

Without notes, state the derivative criterion for a repeated root and explain why a cubic with three distinct roots has three genuinely different choices of marked root.

content.title: Retrieve the distinct-root criterion
content.introMarkdown: State the repeated-root criterion and the hypothesis that makes the three marked-root choices distinct.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether both equations in the repeated-root criterion are present.

Distinct root positions are what make the ordered-triple permutation action faithful.

State $p(r)=p'(r)=0$, negate it in the root case, and count the distinct marked choices.

## Deliberate review: Week 11 multiplication map

Retrieve how multiplication by a fixed linear form becomes a matrix. Today the same product map is viewed through a symmetry of its input pair.

content.title: Retrieve the multiplication matrix
content.introMarkdown: Write the matrix of $Q\mapsto LQ$ in the ordered bases $(T^2,TS,S^2)$ and $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the output basis coordinate of the first missing monomial.

Each column must represent one complete product in the declared order.

Multiply $L$ by the three input basis vectors one at a time and stack their coordinate columns.

## Deliberate review: Week 16 derivative

Retrieve the first-order product expansion. Then place the tangent vector generated by relative rescaling into the derivative.

content.title: Differentiate the rescaling orbit
content.introMarkdown: Retrieve $dM_{(L,Q)}$ and show that $\gamma'(0)$ lies in its kernel.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the derivative of $e^{-t}$ at $t=0$.

The opposite sign is exactly what makes the product derivative cancel.

Expand the product to first order, differentiate both exponential factors, and substitute the tangent pair.

## Deliberate review: Week 18 root branch

Retrieve the simple-root implicit-function theorem. The local branch tracks one marked root; it does not globally order all roots around every loop.

content.title: Retrieve simple-root continuation
content.introMarkdown: State the local branch conclusion and its derivative, then explain why it does not remove the global root-label symmetry.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first omitted neighborhood or nonzero derivative hypothesis.

A local selected branch is weaker than a global ordering of every root.

State the base point and neighborhoods, give the derivative formula, and finish with the local-versus-global distinction.

## Complete worked model

$C=(T-u)(T-v)(T-w)$ has three distinct roots, with the marked factorization $L=T-u$ and $Q=(T-v)(T-w)$.

Distinguish a permutation that changes the marked root from relative rescaling of the fixed factor pair.

### Strategy

Write the factor pair produced by each operation, multiply it back to $C$, and compare the zero of the new linear factor.

### Hypotheses

The roots are distinct, and the rescaling scalar $\lambda$ is nonzero.

### Intermediate claims

Swapping the labels $u$ and $v$ gives $(T-v,(T-u)(T-w))$, whose linear factor vanishes at $v$. Rescaling gives $(\lambda(T-u),\lambda^{-1}(T-v)(T-w))$, whose linear factor still vanishes at $u$.

### Justification

Both products equal $C$: the first only reorders its three factors, while the second cancels the opposite scalars.

### Conclusion

The permutation changes the discrete marking. Relative rescaling preserves that marking and changes only its representative. Product preservation alone does not identify the two actions.

content.title: Distinguish the two cubic symmetries
content.introMarkdown: Describe what $(ab)\in S_3$ changes and what $\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times$ changes.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the zero set of the linear factor changes under the proposed operation.

The marked root separates the discrete permutation from continuous rescaling.

Write the new factor pair under each operation, multiply it, and compare the zero of its linear factor.

## Three boundaries to preserve

The $S_3$ label action does not automatically equal a Galois group. Product invariance proves that each rescaling orbit lies in a product fiber, not that the fiber is one orbit. A stabilizer calculation always belongs to a named action and a named point.

content.title: Repair three symmetry overclaims
content.introMarkdown: Replace each clause by the strongest statement established this week.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first implication whose converse or arithmetic interpretation was assumed without proof.

Symmetry language is precise only when the acting group, object, and direction of implication are explicit.

Rewrite the clauses as label action, orbit contained in fiber, and point-dependent fixed-element subgroup.

## Final Week 19 proof

The week has built one chain: verify a group, let it act, solve the fixed-point equation for stabilizers, and identify invariants. The cubic application uses two actions on related but different data, so a complete proof must keep them separate.

content.title: Complete the cubic-symmetry synthesis
content.introMarkdown: Give one coherent proof describing the root-label action, the stabilizer of one marked label, and the relative-rescaling action on its factor pair.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first place where the acting group, acted-on object, or direction of implication is not explicit.

The same preserved cubic can arise from different symmetry mechanisms.

Write four paragraphs: $S_3$ action, marked-label stabilizer, rescaling action and invariant, then the two evidence boundaries.

activities.title: Retrieve the distinct-root criterion
activities.promptMarkdown:
A cubic $p$ splits as $(T-r_1)(T-r_2)(T-r_3)$.

State the repeated-root criterion and the hypothesis that makes the three marked-root choices distinct.

Connect the criterion to the $S_3$ action without recomputing the whole week.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A root $r$ is repeated exactly when $p(r)=p'(r)=0$. If the cubic has three distinct roots, then $p'(r_i)\ne0$ for each $i$ and the three choices of marked root are different. Permuting those three positions therefore gives the full six-element label action.

rubric.description: The repeated-root criterion and distinct-root consequence are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.title: Retrieve the multiplication matrix
activities.promptMarkdown:
$L=aT+bS$ and $Q=xT^2+yTS+zS^2$.

Write the matrix of $Q\mapsto LQ$ in the ordered bases $(T^2,TS,S^2)$ and $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$.

Justify each column by multiplying $L$ by one basis vector.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The products are $L(T^2)=aT^3+bT^2S$, $L(TS)=aT^2S+bTS^2$, and $L(S^2)=aTS^2+bS^3$. Thus the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}a&0&0\\b&a&0\\0&b&a\\0&0&b\end{pmatrix}$. Its columns are precisely the coordinate vectors of those three products.

rubric.description: The matrix and all basis-column products are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The matrix is derived from the linear map rather than recalled without types.

activities.title: Differentiate the rescaling orbit
activities.promptMarkdown:
$M(L,Q)=LQ$ and $\gamma(t)=(e^tL,e^{-t}Q)$.

Retrieve $dM_{(L,Q)}$ and show that $\gamma'(0)$ lies in its kernel.

Derive both formulas rather than quoting only the conclusion.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Expanding $(L+\varepsilon\dot L)(Q+\varepsilon\dot Q)$ gives $LQ+\varepsilon(\dot LQ+L\dot Q)+O(\varepsilon^2)$, so $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$. Since $\gamma'(0)=(L,-Q)$, one gets $dM_{(L,Q)}(L,-Q)=LQ-LQ=0$. The action supplies a tangent direction that multiplication forgets.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The differential, orbit tangent, and kernel calculation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The kernel direction is derived from the action curve and the product rule.

activities.title: Retrieve simple-root continuation
activities.promptMarkdown:
$P(c^*,\zeta^*)=0$ and $P_z(c^*,\zeta^*)\ne0$.

State the local branch conclusion and its derivative, then explain why it does not remove the global root-label symmetry.

Keep the neighborhoods and the selected root visible.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The holomorphic implicit theorem gives neighborhoods $A$ of $c^*$ and $B$ of $\zeta^*$ and a unique holomorphic branch $\zeta:A\to B$ with $P(c,\zeta(c))=0$ and $D\zeta=-P_z^{-1}D_cP$. The branch tracks the one root selected near $\zeta^*$ inside $B$. It neither labels all roots globally nor proves that continuation around large loops returns every label unchanged.

rubric.description: The local branch, derivative, neighborhoods, and global boundary are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response connects local root selection to, but does not confuse it with, global label permutations.

activities.title: Distinguish the two cubic symmetries
activities.promptMarkdown:
$C=(T-a)(T-b)(T-c)$ with $a,b,c$ distinct, and the marked factorization $L=T-a$, $Q=(T-b)(T-c)$.

Describe what $(ab)\in S_3$ changes and what $\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times$ changes.

For each operation, state why the product remains $C$ and whether the marked root changes.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The transposition exchanging the labels $a$ and $b$ replaces the marked factor by $T-b$ and the complementary factor by $(T-a)(T-c)$; their product is still $C$, but the marked root changes. Relative rescaling replaces $(L,Q)$ by $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$; the scalars cancel in the product and the zero of $L$ remains $a$. Thus the first changes the discrete marking and the second changes only its representative.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both transformations, product checks, and effects on the marked root are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes the objects acted on rather than merging two product-preserving calculations.

activities.title: Repair three symmetry overclaims
activities.promptMarkdown:
A draft says: “The cubic has Galois group $S_3$; equal products mean equal rescaling orbits; and the stabilizer is always trivial.”

Replace each clause by the strongest statement established this week.

Name the missing evidence needed for every stronger conclusion.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The three distinct root labels carry an $S_3$ relabelling action, but determining the Galois group needs information about field automorphisms. Relative rescaling preserves the product, so each orbit lies in a product fiber; the reverse inclusion needs a separate factor-comparison argument. Stabilizers depend on the action and point: they can be trivial, nontrivial, or the whole group, as the fixed-point equations show.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three repaired claims and missing-evidence statements are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response replaces universal assertions with the exact implications proved.

activities.title: Complete the cubic-symmetry synthesis
activities.promptMarkdown:
$C=(T-r_1)(T-r_2)(T-r_3)$ has three distinct roots, and choosing $r_i$ gives $C=L_iQ_i$.

Give one coherent proof describing the root-label action, the stabilizer of one marked label, and the relative-rescaling action on its factor pair.

Verify both products and finish with the exact Galois-group and orbit-fiber boundaries.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The two actions, stabilizer, product calculations, and scope boundaries are all correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The synthesis keeps discrete marking, continuous rescaling, and stronger unproved conclusions logically separate.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: All bijections of the three root positions form $S_3$ under composition and preserve $C$ because they only reorder its linear factors. The stabilizer of the first marked label consists of the identity and the transposition of the other two labels, so it has two elements. Choosing $r_1$ gives $L_1=T-r_1$ and $Q_1=(T-r_2)(T-r_3)$. The rule $\lambda\cdot(L_1,Q_1)=(\lambda L_1,\lambda^{-1}Q_1)$ is an action of $\mathbb C^\times$: the identity and composition laws follow from scalar multiplication, and $(\lambda L_1)(\lambda^{-1}Q_1)=C$. Root permutation changes the discrete marked root, while rescaling keeps that root and changes only the representative. The label action alone does not determine the Galois group, and product invariance proves only that each rescaling orbit lies inside a product fiber.

lessons.title: Homomorphisms, kernels, and images
lessons.summary: Verify a group homomorphism, calculate its kernel and image, and prove the basic structural facts that follow from the homomorphism law.
objectives: Verify a group homomorphism, calculate its kernel and image, and prove the basic structural facts that follow from the homomorphism law.

content.markdown:
## Maps that preserve a group law

A group homomorphism does more than send elements from one set to another. It preserves multiplication, so it transports identity elements, inverses, equations, and subgroups in a controlled way.

The kernel records what the map forgets. The image records what it reaches. Those two objects will drive the quotient construction and the first isomorphism theorem later this week.

## Reactivate typed functions and group laws

Write the source and target before calculating. If the source operation is written additively and the target operation multiplicatively, the homomorphism law is $\phi(x+y)=\phi(x)\phi(y)$, not $\phi(x+y)=\phi(x)+\phi(y)$.

## Definition and first consequences

A homomorphism $\phi:G\to H$ satisfies $\phi(xy)=\phi(x)\phi(y)$ for every $x,y\in G$.

Putting $x=y=e_G$ gives $\phi(e_G)=\phi(e_G)^2$, hence $\phi(e_G)=e_H$. Applying $\phi$ to $xx^{-1}=e_G$ then gives $\phi(x^{-1})=\phi(x)^{-1}$.

content.title: Verify a doubling homomorphism
content.introMarkdown: Verify the homomorphism law and determine $\ker d$ and $\operatorname{im}d$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the first equality that fails to use the source operation.

A formula is not a group homomorphism until it preserves the declared operation.

Write $d(m+n)$, calculate it, then solve $d(n)=0$ and describe every reached integer.

## Kernel and image

The kernel and image are $\ker\phi=\{g\in G:\phi(g)=e_H\}$ and $\operatorname{im}\phi=\{\phi(g):g\in G\}$.

Both are subgroups of their ambient groups. For the image, $e_H=\phi(e_G)$ is reached, and if $a=\phi(x)$ and $b=\phi(y)$ are reached, then $ab^{-1}=\phi(x)\phi(y)^{-1}=\phi(xy^{-1})$ is reached. The one-step subgroup test therefore gives $\operatorname{im}\phi\le H$.

Moreover, $\phi$ is injective exactly when $\ker\phi=\{e_G\}$, while it is surjective exactly when $\operatorname{im}\phi=H$.

content.title: Calculate what reduction forgets
content.introMarkdown: Calculate the kernel and image and explain what information the map forgets.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the kernel equation uses the target identity class.

The kernel is an inverse image of the identity, not the set mapped to the integer zero by notation alone.

Solve $[n]_6=[0]_6$, then choose a representative for an arbitrary target class.

## Complete worked model

$\det:GL_2(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R^\times$ sends an invertible matrix to its determinant.

Prove that determinant is a homomorphism, identify its kernel, and prove that it is onto.

### Strategy

Use multiplicativity for the homomorphism law, solve the identity equation for the kernel, and construct a diagonal preimage of an arbitrary nonzero scalar.

### Hypotheses

Both matrices are invertible, so their determinants lie in $\mathbb R^\times$.

### Intermediate claims

$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$; the identity of $\mathbb R^\times$ is $1$; and $\det\operatorname{diag}(t,1)=t$ for $t\ne0$.

### Justification

Multiplicativity proves the group law. Thus the kernel is exactly $SL_2(\mathbb R)=\{A:\det A=1\}$. For any $t\in\mathbb R^\times$, the invertible diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(t,1)$ maps to $t$.

### Conclusion

Determinant is a surjective group homomorphism with kernel $SL_2(\mathbb R)$.

## Prove that kernels are subgroups

A calculation should expose why the kernel is closed. If $x,y\in\ker\phi$, then $\phi(xy^{-1})=\phi(x)\phi(y)^{-1}=e_He_H^{-1}=e_H$. The one-step subgroup test gives $xy^{-1}\in\ker\phi$.

content.title: Reconstruct the kernel proof
content.introMarkdown: Prove $\ker\phi\le G$ using the one-step subgroup test.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first missing use of the homomorphism law or subgroup test.

The kernel subgroup theorem is the foundation for quotienting by forgotten information.

Show $e_G$ belongs, take two kernel elements, and calculate $\phi(xy^{-1})$ one equality at a time.

## A plausible formula can fail

The function $s:\mathbb R^\times\to\mathbb R^\times$, $s(x)=x^2$, is not a counterexample: it is a homomorphism because the group is abelian. By contrast, the squaring map on a nonabelian group need not preserve multiplication, since $(xy)^2$ need not equal $x^2y^2$.

content.title: Diagnose squaring in a nonabelian group
content.introMarkdown: Decide whether $q$ is a homomorphism by one explicit pair.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the same pair was used on both sides of the homomorphism equation.

A formula that respects powers elementwise need not respect multiplication between different elements.

Choose two noncommuting transpositions, compute $q(\sigma\tau)$, and compare it with $q(\sigma)q(\tau)$.

## Day 1 synthesis

A homomorphism is controlled by one equation, but that equation forces identities and inverses to behave correctly. Its kernel and image then reveal injectivity, surjectivity, and the information lost.

The theorem chain is only useful when each structural conclusion is justified.

activities.title: Verify a doubling homomorphism
activities.promptMarkdown:
$d:(\mathbb Z,+)\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is defined by $d(n)=2n$.

Verify the homomorphism law and determine $\ker d$ and $\operatorname{im}d$.

State injectivity and surjectivity only after the kernel and image calculations.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $d(m+n)=2m+2n=d(m)+d(n)$, so $d$ is a homomorphism. Its kernel is $\{0\}$ and its image is $2\mathbb Z$. Therefore it is injective but not surjective onto $\mathbb Z$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The law, kernel, image, and two map properties are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Injectivity and surjectivity are derived from typed calculations.

activities.title: Calculate what reduction forgets
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\rho:(\mathbb Z,+)\to(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z,+)$ sends $n$ to $[n]_6$.

Calculate the kernel and image and explain what information the map forgets.

Use coset notation and justify surjectivity.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\rho(n)=[0]_6$ exactly when $6\mid n$, so $\ker\rho=6\mathbb Z$. Every residue class is $\rho(r)$ for an integer representative $r$, so $\operatorname{im}\rho=\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$. The map forgets the choice of integer inside one congruence class.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel, image, and interpretation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer solves the identity equation and proves reachability.

activities.title: Reconstruct the kernel proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\phi:G\to H$ is a group homomorphism.

Prove $\ker\phi\le G$ using the one-step subgroup test.

Include nonemptiness and type every identity element.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The nonempty and closure-under-$xy^{-1}$ steps are complete.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each equality follows from the homomorphism law or a typed identity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $\phi(e_G)=e_H$, the kernel is nonempty. If $x,y\in\ker\phi$, then $\phi(xy^{-1})=\phi(x)\phi(y^{-1})=\phi(x)\phi(y)^{-1}=e_He_H^{-1}=e_H$. Hence $xy^{-1}\in\ker\phi$, so the subgroup test gives $\ker\phi\le G$.

activities.title: Diagnose squaring in a nonabelian group
activities.promptMarkdown:
$q:S_3\to S_3$ is defined by $q(\sigma)=\sigma^2$.

Decide whether $q$ is a homomorphism by one explicit pair.

Use right-to-left composition and show both sides of the law.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Take $\sigma=(12)$ and $\tau=(23)$. Then $q(\sigma)=q(\tau)=e$, so $q(\sigma)q(\tau)=e$. But $\sigma\tau=(123)$, hence $q(\sigma\tau)=(132)\ne e$. Therefore $q$ is not a homomorphism.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The counterexample and both sides of the law are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: One failed universal instance is used to refute the homomorphism claim.

activities.title: Analyze determinant as a group map
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\det:GL_n(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R^\times$ with $n\ge1$.

Prove the homomorphism law, identify kernel and image, and state injectivity and surjectivity.

Give a counterexample to injectivity when $n\ge2$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The complete analysis and dimension boundary are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Every map property is supported by a calculation or construction.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Multiplicativity gives $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$. The kernel is $SL_n(\mathbb R)$. Every $t\ne0$ is the determinant of $\operatorname{diag}(t,1,\ldots,1)$, so the image is $\mathbb R^\times$ and the map is surjective. For $n=1$, determinant is the identity map $\mathbb R^\times\to\mathbb R^\times$, so it is injective. For $n\ge2$, $I_n$ and $\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2,1,\ldots,1)$ are distinct kernel elements, so the map is not injective.

lessons.title: Normal subgroups and quotient groups
lessons.summary: Prove normality, construct a quotient group from cosets, and explain exactly why normality makes the quotient operation independent of representatives.
objectives: Prove normality, construct a quotient group from cosets, and explain exactly why normality makes the quotient operation independent of representatives.

content.markdown:
## Turn forgotten differences into equality

Elements in the same kernel coset have the same image under a homomorphism. A quotient group makes that identification into a new group, but multiplication of cosets works only when the subgroup is normal.

## Reactivate cosets

For $N\le G$, the left coset $gN$ is $\{gn:n\in N\}$. Two cosets are equal exactly when their representatives differ by an element of $N$. The quotient construction asks whether $gN\cdot hN=(gh)N$ is independent of the chosen representatives.

## Normality

A subgroup $N\le G$ is normal, written $N\trianglelefteq G$, when $gNg^{-1}=N$ for every $g\in G$. Equivalently, $gN=Ng$ for every $g$.

Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal. In a nonabelian group, normality is extra structure, not automatic.

A subgroup of index two is normal. Indeed, its left cosets are $N$ and the complement $G\setminus N$; its right cosets are the same two sets. Hence $gN=Ng$ for every $g$.

content.title: Test normality in $S_3$
content.introMarkdown: Show that conjugation by a transposition preserves $A_3$ and conclude normality.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the conjugating element was allowed to range over all of $S_3$.

Normality concerns the position of a subgroup inside its ambient group.

Calculate one conjugate for each claim and explain why the normal case covers every conjugating element.

## Complete worked model

$\phi:G\to H$ is a group homomorphism and $K=\ker\phi$.

Prove $K\trianglelefteq G$ directly from conjugation.

### Strategy

Take an arbitrary $g\in G$ and $k\in K$, then apply $\phi$ to $gkg^{-1}$.

### Hypotheses

$\phi(k)=e_H$ because $k\in K$.

### Intermediate claims

$\phi(gkg^{-1})=\phi(g)\phi(k)\phi(g)^{-1}=e_H$.

### Justification

The homomorphism and inverse laws give the displayed equality. Thus $gkg^{-1}\in K$, so $gKg^{-1}\subseteq K$. Replacing $g$ by $g^{-1}$ gives the reverse inclusion.

### Conclusion

$gKg^{-1}=K$ for every $g$, hence $K\trianglelefteq G$.

## Cosets become quotient elements

If $N\trianglelefteq G$, define $G/N=\{gN:g\in G\}$ and $(gN)(hN)=(gh)N$. The identity is $N=eN$ and $(gN)^{-1}=g^{-1}N$.

The quotient map $\pi:G\to G/N$, $\pi(g)=gN$, is a surjective homomorphism with kernel $N$.

content.title: Calculate in a quotient
content.introMarkdown: List the elements of $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ and calculate $[3]+[2]$ and $-[3]$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether equality is being asserted for integers or for cosets.

A quotient changes the equality relation.

Write brackets around every quotient element, calculate with representatives, and reduce modulo four.

## Why the product is well defined

Suppose $gN=g'N$ and $hN=h'N$. Write $g'=gn_1$ and $h'=hn_2$. Then $g'h'=gn_1hn_2=gh(h^{-1}n_1h)n_2$. Normality puts $h^{-1}n_1h$ back in $N$, so $g'h'N=ghN$.

This is the decisive step: the result depends only on the cosets, not on the representatives.

content.title: Reconstruct well-definedness
content.introMarkdown: Prove $(g'h')N=(gh)N$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the point where an element of $N$ must cross the representative $h$.

Without that step, quotient multiplication may depend on the spelling of a coset.

Insert $hh^{-1}$, isolate $h^{-1}n_1h$, invoke normality, and finish by the coset equality criterion.

## Orbit sets are not automatically quotient groups

A quotient group $G/N$ requires a normal subgroup and inherits multiplication. An orbit set $X/G$ records which points of a $G$-set lie in the same orbit. Unless $X$ carries compatible additional structure, $X/G$ is only a set of equivalence classes.

content.title: Separate two kinds of quotient
content.introMarkdown: State what equivalence relation each construction uses and what operation is justified.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a multiplication has been claimed without an operation on $X$.

Quotient group, orbit space, and slice play different roles later in the course.

Name the representatives, equivalence relation, and justified output structure for each slash.

## Day 2 synthesis

Normality is exactly what lets subgroup elements move across representatives. Kernels are normal, and quotient maps recover every normal subgroup as the information deliberately forgotten.

content.title: Construct $S_3/A_3$
content.introMarkdown: Prove normality, list the quotient elements, calculate the quotient law, and identify the resulting group.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing justification between index, normality, cosets, and the cyclic law.

A named quotient is not understood until its elements and operation are explicit.

Prove index-two normality, list the two cosets, square the nonidentity coset, then connect it to sign.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-20, source lines 755 to 763.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.701 Algebra I, Fall 2010.

**Exact locator:** Problem Set 2, p. 1, Problems 1–4: cyclic subgroups, conjugation, equivalence relations, and coset partitions in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.701 Algebra I, Fall 2010.

**Reading purpose:** Use Problems 1–4 to connect subgroup structure, conjugation, equivalence relations, and cosets before formal quotient proofs.
Day 3 proves that every homomorphism factors through its kernel quotient and identifies that quotient with the image.
Day 2 is complete when you can prove normality and show, line by line, why quotient multiplication is well defined.

activities.title: Test normality in $S_3$
activities.promptMarkdown:
$A_3=\{e,(123),(132)\}\le S_3$.

Show that conjugation by a transposition preserves $A_3$ and conclude normality.

Also show that $\langle(12)\rangle$ is not normal by one conjugate.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The subgroup $A_3$ has index two in $S_3$. Its left cosets are $A_3$ and the set of odd permutations; its right cosets are the same two sets, so $gA_3=A_3g$ for every $g$ and $A_3\trianglelefteq S_3$. Directly, conjugation fixes $e$ and permutes the two three-cycles; for example $(12)(123)(12)=(132)$. But $(23)(12)(23)=(13)\notin\langle(12)\rangle$, so $\langle(12)\rangle$ is not normal.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both the normal and nonnormal conclusions have valid witnesses.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Conjugation is checked inside the correct ambient group.

activities.title: Calculate in a quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
$4\mathbb Z\trianglelefteq(\mathbb Z,+)$.

List the elements of $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ and calculate $[3]+[2]$ and $-[3]$.

Identify the kernel of the quotient map.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The quotient has $[0],[1],[2],[3]$. We have $[3]+[2]=[5]=[1]$ and $-[3]=[-3]=[1]$. The quotient map $n\mapsto[n]$ has kernel $4\mathbb Z$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The cosets, operations, and kernel are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Representative calculations are reduced only after the quotient operation is applied.

activities.title: Reconstruct well-definedness
activities.promptMarkdown:
$N\trianglelefteq G$, $g'=gn_1$, and $h'=hn_2$ with $n_1,n_2\in N$.

Prove $(g'h')N=(gh)N$.

Name the exact expression to which normality is applied.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The representative calculation and normality step are complete.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof identifies the precise obstruction removed by normality.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $g'h'=gn_1hn_2=gh(h^{-1}n_1h)n_2$. Since $N$ is normal, $h^{-1}n_1h\in N$, so $(h^{-1}n_1h)n_2\in N$. Therefore $g'h'$ and $gh$ differ by right multiplication by an element of $N$, and $(g'h')N=(gh)N$.

activities.title: Separate two kinds of quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
$G/N$ is a quotient group and $X/G$ is the orbit set of a $G$-action.

State what equivalence relation each construction uses and what operation is justified.

Explain why the notation slash does not make the two objects identical.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In $G/N$, two group elements are equivalent when they lie in the same $N$-coset, and normality makes coset multiplication well defined. In $X/G$, two points are equivalent when one is obtained from the other by the action. This always defines a set of orbits, but it supplies no group law on that set by itself.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both equivalence relations and the structure boundary are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer distinguishes inherited structure from shared notation.

activities.title: Construct $S_3/A_3$
activities.promptMarkdown:
$A_3\le S_3$.

Prove normality, list the quotient elements, calculate the quotient law, and identify the resulting group.

Relate the quotient map to permutation parity.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Normality, cosets, law, isomorphism type, and parity are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The quotient is constructed before it is identified with a familiar group.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $A_3$ has index two, hence is normal. The quotient has two cosets: $A_3$ and $(12)A_3$, the even and odd permutations. The odd coset squared is $A_3$, so the quotient is cyclic of order two. The sign homomorphism sends even permutations to $1$ and odd permutations to $-1$; its kernel is $A_3$, so parity is exactly the information retained by the quotient.

lessons.title: The first isomorphism theorem
lessons.summary: Construct and prove the canonical isomorphism $G/\ker\phi\cong\operatorname{im}\phi$, including well-definedness, injectivity, and surjectivity.
objectives: Construct and prove the canonical isomorphism $G/\ker\phi\cong\operatorname{im}\phi$, including well-definedness, injectivity, and surjectivity.

content.markdown:
## The kernel is the complete ambiguity

If $\phi(g)=\phi(g')$, then $g^{-1}g'\in\ker\phi$. Thus the kernel does not merely contain some lost information: its cosets are exactly the fibers of the map over the image.

## Reactivate yesterday’s quotient map

Let $K=\ker\phi$. Because $K\trianglelefteq G$, the quotient $G/K$ exists. The candidate map is forced: send the coset $gK$ to $\phi(g)$. The proof must show that this does not depend on the representative.

## Statement of the theorem

For a group homomorphism $\phi:G\to H$, the first isomorphism theorem states $G/\ker\phi\cong\operatorname{im}\phi$ by $g\ker\phi\mapsto\phi(g)$.

The codomain is the image, not automatically all of $H$. Only a surjective $\phi$ gives $G/\ker\phi\cong H$.

content.title: Write the induced map with types
content.introMarkdown: Write the induced map, its domain, its codomain, and the formula on a coset.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the codomain is $H$ or the part of $H$ actually reached.

A proof cannot establish an isomorphism to elements the map never reaches.

Write $G/K\to\operatorname{im}\phi$, give the coset formula, and state the representative-independence test.

## Complete worked model

$\phi:G\to H$ is a group homomorphism and $K=\ker\phi$.

Prove $\bar\phi:G/K\to\operatorname{im}\phi$, $gK\mapsto\phi(g)$, is an isomorphism.

### Strategy

Check the four obligations in order: well-defined function, homomorphism, injectivity, and surjectivity.

### Hypotheses

$K$ is normal because it is a kernel, so $G/K$ is a group.

### Intermediate claims

If $gK=g'K$, then $g'^{-1}g\in K$ and $\phi(g)=\phi(g')$. Also $\bar\phi((gK)(hK))=\bar\phi(ghK)=\phi(g)\phi(h)$.

### Justification

For injectivity, $\bar\phi(gK)=e_H$ implies $g\in K$, hence $gK=K$. For surjectivity onto the image, every $y\in\operatorname{im}\phi$ equals $\phi(g)=\bar\phi(gK)$ for some $g$.

### Conclusion

$\bar\phi$ is a well-defined bijective homomorphism, so $G/K\cong\operatorname{im}\phi$.

## Well-definedness is a fiber calculation

The equality $gK=g'K$ means $g'^{-1}g\in K$. Applying $\phi$ yields $\phi(g')^{-1}\phi(g)=e_H$, hence $\phi(g)=\phi(g')$.

Conversely, equal images imply $g'^{-1}g\in K$, so the kernel cosets are precisely the nonempty fibers.

content.title: Prove representative independence
content.introMarkdown: Derive $\phi(g)=\phi(g')$ without skipping the coset criterion.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first direction where equal cosets or equal images was used without translation.

Well-definedness and the fiber description are the logical center of the theorem.

Translate coset equality into membership in $K$, apply $\phi$, and reverse the argument.

## Injectivity and surjectivity use different evidence

Injectivity of $\bar\phi$ follows because only the identity coset maps to $e_H$. Surjectivity follows from choosing the codomain to be $\operatorname{im}\phi$.

Do not merge these arguments: one uses the kernel, the other uses the definition of image.

content.title: Separate the bijection proof
content.introMarkdown: Prove injectivity and surjectivity in two labelled paragraphs.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the surjectivity paragraph chose an arbitrary element of the stated codomain.

The image codomain makes one half immediate but does not replace the proof.

Use the trivial-kernel criterion for injectivity and the definition of image for surjectivity.

## Do not cancel the kernel too early

The theorem does not say $G\cong\operatorname{im}\phi$. It says that $G$ becomes isomorphic to the image after all elements in the same kernel coset are identified.

content.title: Repair a false theorem statement
content.introMarkdown: Explain why $\mathbb Z\not\cong\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ and state the correct isomorphism.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the source group was quotiented by the full kernel.

The theorem measures lost information; omitting the quotient destroys its meaning.

Compare a group invariant, calculate the kernel, and write the quotient-to-image isomorphism.

## Day 3 synthesis

A complete first-isomorphism proof is short only after its four obligations are visible. The induced formula is forced, but well-definedness is not optional.

content.title: Apply the theorem to the sign map
content.introMarkdown: Prove the first-isomorphism conclusion for this map from the homomorphism law through the induced isomorphism.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing link among homomorphism, kernel, well-definedness, and bijectivity.

This is the week’s central proof and the model for later quotient arguments.

Use five paragraphs: sign law, kernel and image, induced formula, well-defined homomorphism, then bijection.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-20, source lines 755 to 763.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare RES.18-011, Fall 2021.

**Reading purpose:** Compare the theorem proof with today’s four-obligation structure, paying special attention to the induced map and its kernel.

Day 3 is complete when you can construct the induced map and prove well-definedness, homomorphism, injectivity, and surjectivity in the correct order.

activities.title: Write the induced map with types
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\phi:G\to H$ and $K=\ker\phi$.

Write the induced map, its domain, its codomain, and the formula on a coset.

State the one question that must be settled before the formula defines a function.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Define $\bar\phi:G/K\to\operatorname{im}\phi$ by $\bar\phi(gK)=\phi(g)$. Before using it, one must prove well-definedness: if $gK=g'K$, then $\phi(g)=\phi(g')$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The map is typed and the well-definedness obligation is exact.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes a candidate formula from an established function.

activities.title: Prove representative independence
activities.promptMarkdown:
$gK=g'K$ where $K=\ker\phi$.

Derive $\phi(g)=\phi(g')$ without skipping the coset criterion.

Then prove the converse and interpret the result as a fiber statement.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both directions and the fiber interpretation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof passes through the exact coset equality criterion.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: From $gK=g'K$ we get $g'^{-1}g\in K$, so $e_H=\phi(g'^{-1}g)=\phi(g')^{-1}\phi(g)$ and therefore $\phi(g)=\phi(g')$. Conversely, if the images are equal, the same equation gives $\phi(g'^{-1}g)=e_H$, so $g'^{-1}g\in K$ and $gK=g'K$. Thus each nonempty fiber is one kernel coset.

activities.title: Separate the bijection proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\bar\phi:G/K\to\operatorname{im}\phi$ is the induced homomorphism.

Prove injectivity and surjectivity in two labelled paragraphs.

Name the definition used in each paragraph.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both halves of bijectivity are complete and correctly sourced.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response does not use surjectivity of the original map onto all of $H$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: **Injective.** If $\bar\phi(gK)=e_H$, then $\phi(g)=e_H$, so $g\in K$ and $gK=K$. Thus the kernel of $\bar\phi$ is trivial. **Surjective.** If $y\in\operatorname{im}\phi$, then by definition $y=\phi(g)$ for some $g\in G$, hence $y=\bar\phi(gK)$.

activities.title: Repair a false theorem statement
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\rho:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ is reduction modulo six.

Explain why $\mathbb Z\not\cong\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ and state the correct isomorphism.

Identify exactly which elements must be identified.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\mathbb Z$ is infinite and torsion-free, whereas $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ is finite and every element has finite order, so they are not isomorphic. The kernel is $6\mathbb Z$, and the correct theorem gives $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\cong\operatorname{im}\rho=\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$. Integers differing by a multiple of six are identified.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The counterinvariant, kernel, and corrected theorem are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The repair explains the role of quotienting rather than replacing one symbol.

activities.title: Apply the theorem to the sign map
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\operatorname{sgn}:S_3\to\{1,-1\}$ sends even permutations to $1$ and odd permutations to $-1$.

Prove the first-isomorphism conclusion for this map from the homomorphism law through the induced isomorphism.

Construct the map $S_3/A_3\to\{1,-1\}$ and prove every obligation.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The law, kernel, image, induced map, and four proof obligations are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The theorem is instantiated without skipping representative independence.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Parity is multiplicative, so sign is a homomorphism. Its kernel is $A_3$ and its image is $\{1,-1\}$. Define $\overline{\operatorname{sgn}}(\sigma A_3)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$. If two cosets agree, their representatives differ by an even permutation, so they have the same sign; hence the map is well defined. It preserves products. Its kernel is the identity coset $A_3$, so it is injective, and both signs occur, so it is surjective. Therefore $S_3/A_3\cong\{1,-1\}$.

lessons.title: Orbits, stabilizers, equivariant maps, and slices
lessons.summary: Prove orbit-stabilizer, verify equivariance, and distinguish an orbit space from a slice that selects representatives only on a stated locus.
objectives: Prove orbit-stabilizer, verify equivariance, and distinguish an orbit space from a slice that selects representatives only on a stated locus.

content.markdown:
## Quotient an action without confusing the constructions

An orbit gathers all points reachable from one another. A stabilizer records the transformations that do not move a point. Orbit-stabilizer relates these objects through a quotient of the acting group.

A slice is different: it is a chosen subset intended to meet orbits in controlled representatives. Existence and uniqueness must be proved on the locus where the slice is claimed.

## Reactivate the action law

For a left action, $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$. The orbit is $G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$ and the stabilizer is $G_x=\{g:g\cdot x=x\}$.

## Orbit-stabilizer as a quotient bijection

The map $\theta:G/G_x\to G\cdot x$ defined by $gG_x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is well defined and bijective.

For finite $G$, counting gives $|G\cdot x|=[G:G_x]=|G|/|G_x|$. The theorem is a statement about sets unless additional structure is proved.

content.title: Count the orbit of one root label
content.introMarkdown: Compute the orbit and stabilizer of $1$ and verify the counting formula.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether each listed permutation actually fixes the chosen point.

Orbit size depends on the chosen point through its stabilizer.

List images of $1$, solve $\sigma(1)=1$, and substitute the two cardinalities.

## Complete worked model

$G$ acts on $X$ and $x\in X$.

Prove $G/G_x\to G\cdot x$, $gG_x\mapsto g\cdot x$, is a bijection.

### Strategy

Prove representative independence, surjectivity, and injectivity in that order.

### Hypotheses

$G_x$ is a subgroup by the stabilizer theorem from Week 19.

### Intermediate claims

If $gG_x=hG_x$, then $h^{-1}g\in G_x$, so $g\cdot x=h\cdot x$. Every orbit point is $g\cdot x$ for some $g$.

### Justification

If $g\cdot x=h\cdot x$, applying $h^{-1}$ gives $(h^{-1}g)\cdot x=x$, so $h^{-1}g\in G_x$ and $gG_x=hG_x$.

### Conclusion

The map is well defined, onto, and one-to-one; hence $G/G_x\cong G\cdot x$ as sets.

## Equivariant maps respect actions

If $G$ acts on $X$ and $Y$, a map $F:X\to Y$ is equivariant when $F(g\cdot x)=g\cdot F(x)$ for every $g,x$.

Equivariance sends each orbit in $X$ into one orbit in $Y$. It also gives $G_x\subseteq G_{F(x)}$: anything fixing $x$ must fix its image.

content.title: Verify equivariance and compare stabilizers
content.introMarkdown: Prove equivariance and verify $G_x\subseteq G_{F(x)}$ for $x=0$ and $x\ne0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check which action is used on the codomain.

The same group can act differently on source and target.

Write both action laws, evaluate each stabilizer, and compare the two sets.

## Orbit space versus slice

The orbit space $X/G$ is the set of all orbits. A slice $S\subseteq X$ is a chosen set of representatives with a claimed intersection property.

To say that $S$ parametrizes an orbit locus, prove existence: every relevant orbit meets $S$. Then prove uniqueness: it meets $S$ once. A convenient equation alone proves neither.

content.title: Audit a proposed slice
content.introMarkdown: Prove exactly which orbits meet the unit circle and whether the intersection is unique.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proposed normalizing scalar belongs to the acting group and is unique.

Changing the acting group can change a genuine slice into a multiple intersection.

Solve the norm equation for $\lambda$, impose the group condition, then repeat after allowing negative scalars.

## Normalization on a restricted locus

Let $k$ be a field. Write $\mathbb G_m=k^\times$ and $\mathbb A^2=k^2$. Let $\mathbb G_m$ act on pairs by $\lambda\cdot(a,b)=(\lambda a,\lambda^{-1}b)$. The product $ab$ is invariant.

On the locus $a\ne0$, every orbit has a unique representative $(1,ab)$, obtained with $\lambda=a^{-1}$. Orbits with $a=0$ never meet the slice $a=1$.

content.title: Prove the normalization claim
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $a=1$ is a unique slice on $a\ne0$ and state what fails on $a=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first place where division by $a$ occurs without the nonzero hypothesis.

A normalization is only a theorem on the locus where its defining equation can be solved uniquely.

Verify the invariant, solve $\lambda a=1$, prove uniqueness, then analyze $a=0$ separately.

## Day 4 synthesis

Orbit-stabilizer identifies an orbit with cosets of its stabilizer. Equivariance respects orbits. A slice is additional chosen geometry and must earn both existence and uniqueness.

### Use the feedback before continuing

This pattern is the foundation for later normalization arguments.

Use separate paragraphs for freeness, invariance, existence, uniqueness, and the excluded locus.

activities.title: Count the orbit of one root label
activities.promptMarkdown:
$S_3$ acts on $\{1,2,3\}$ by permutation.

Compute the orbit and stabilizer of $1$ and verify the counting formula.

List the stabilizer elements explicitly.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The orbit of $1$ is $\{1,2,3\}$. Its stabilizer is $\{e,(23)\}$, of order two. Hence $|S_3\cdot1|=6/2=3$, agreeing with the direct orbit calculation.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Orbit, stabilizer, and count are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The direct and quotient counts are explicitly reconciled.

activities.title: Verify equivariance and compare stabilizers
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\{\pm1\}$ acts on $\mathbb R$ by multiplication and on $[0,\infty)$ trivially. Let $F(x)=x^2$.

Prove equivariance and verify $G_x\subseteq G_{F(x)}$ for $x=0$ and $x\ne0$.

State why equality of stabilizers need not hold.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Equivariance and both stabilizer comparisons are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The strict-inclusion example explains what the map forgets.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $F(\varepsilon x)=(\varepsilon x)^2=x^2=\varepsilon\cdot F(x)$ because the target action is trivial, so $F$ is equivariant. For $x\ne0$, $G_x=\{1\}$ while $G_{F(x)}=\{\pm1\}$. For $x=0$, both stabilizers are $\{\pm1\}$. Thus inclusion always holds, but equality can fail because the map can forget symmetry-breaking information.

activities.title: Audit a proposed slice
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb R_{>0}$ acts on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ by $\lambda\cdot(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda y)$; propose the unit circle as a slice.

Prove exactly which orbits meet the unit circle and whether the intersection is unique.

Contrast the answer with allowing all nonzero real scalars.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $(x,y)\ne0$, the unique positive scalar sending it to the unit circle is $\lambda=1/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Thus each positive-scaling orbit meets the circle once. If all nonzero real scalars act, both a unit vector and its negative lie in the same orbit, so the full unit circle meets each orbit twice; one would need an additional sign convention for uniqueness.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The scalar, existence, uniqueness, and changed-group boundary are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The slice claim is tied to the acting group and locus.

activities.title: Prove the normalization claim
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb G_m$ acts on $\mathbb A^2$ by $\lambda\cdot(a,b)=(\lambda a,\lambda^{-1}b)$.

Prove that $a=1$ is a unique slice on $a\ne0$ and state what fails on $a=0$.

Include the invariant and solve for the scalar.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Invariant, scalar, uniqueness, and exceptional locus are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof solves the orbit-intersection equation instead of assuming normalization.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The product is invariant because $(\lambda a)(\lambda^{-1}b)=ab$. If $a\ne0$, the equation $\lambda a=1$ has the unique solution $\lambda=a^{-1}$, producing $(1,ab)$. If $a=0$, then every rescaled first coordinate remains zero, so that orbit cannot meet $a=1$. Thus the slice claim is valid exactly on the locus $a\ne0$.

activities.title: Coordinate orbit, stabilizer, and slice
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb G_m$ acts on $U=\{(a,b):a\ne0\}$ by $\lambda\cdot(a,b)=(\lambda a,\lambda^{-1}b)$, and $P(a,b)=ab$.

Prove that the action is free, $P$ is invariant, and each orbit has one representative $(1,c)$.

Explain which implications are proved and why this does not yet describe the excluded locus $a=0$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Freeness, invariance, slice proof, and locus boundary are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion is exactly matched to the solved equations.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $\lambda\cdot(a,b)=(a,b)$ with $a\ne0$, then $\lambda a=a$, so $\lambda=1$; the action is free. The product satisfies $P(\lambda a,\lambda^{-1}b)=ab$. Choosing $\lambda=a^{-1}$ sends $(a,b)$ to $(1,ab)$, and the equation $\lambda a=1$ makes this scalar unique. Hence each orbit in $U$ meets the slice $a=1$ once, and $P$ labels it by $c=ab$. This proof concerns only $U$; when $a=0$, no orbit reaches the slice.

lessons.title: Relative scaling, normalization, and synthesis
lessons.summary: Identify the relative-scaling subgroup of $\mathbb G_m^2$, prove its action preserves multiplication, and justify normalization as a slice only on its valid locus.
objectives: Identify the relative-scaling subgroup of $\mathbb G_m^2$, prove its action preserves multiplication, and justify normalization as a slice only on its valid locus.

content.markdown:
## One product, many representatives

A nonzero linear form $L$ and a nonzero quadratic form $Q$ can be rescaled oppositely without changing $LQ$. The symmetry is a subgroup of the two independent scaling parameters, and normalization chooses one representative only where its chosen coefficient is invertible.

## Scheduled retrieval before the final proof

The next four checkpoints deliberately retrieve product sets, a quotient direction, a local-versus-global boundary, and the action law. Each old idea now supports one step of the relative-scaling proof.

## Deliberate review: Week 4 product sets

Retrieve what an ordered pair in a Cartesian product means, then type the two scaling parameters separately.

content.title: Type the two-scaling group
content.introMarkdown: State its elements, multiplication, identity, and inverses.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether multiplication or inversion was applied coordinatewise.

The relative-scaling subgroup is defined by a relation between two initially independent coordinates.

Write a generic ordered pair, multiply two pairs, then solve each inverse coordinate separately.

## Deliberate review: Week 12 kernel direction

Retrieve the derivative of multiplication and the direction $(L,-Q)$ that it forgets.

content.title: Recover the infinitesimal symmetry
content.introMarkdown: Compute $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)$ and evaluate it on $(L,-Q)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the sign of the second component.

Equal-direction scaling changes the product; opposite scaling preserves it.

Expand to first order, substitute $(L,-Q)$, and compare with derivatives of $e^t$ and $e^{-t}$.

## Deliberate review: Week 17 local and global claims

Retrieve why local solvability does not classify every global fiber, then transfer that caution to normalization.

content.title: Retrieve the evidence boundary
content.introMarkdown: State the local inverse conclusion and the separate global fiber fact.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first sentence that removes a neighborhood or nonzero-locus restriction.

Local choice and global classification require different evidence.

State the local neighborhoods, count the global fiber separately, then name the normalization locus.

## Deliberate review: Week 19 action law

Retrieve the action verification and product invariant before identifying the subgroup inside $\mathbb G_m^2$.

content.title: Retrieve the rescaling action
content.introMarkdown: Verify the identity and composition laws and show that multiplication is invariant.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the inverse in the second coordinate and the direction of the orbit-fiber inclusion.

The final quotient argument depends on a genuine action and an honestly stated invariant.

Calculate identity, nested action, and product separately, then state only orbit-contained-in-fiber.

## Complete worked model

$\mathbb G_m^2$ acts on nonzero factor pairs by $(\lambda,\mu)\cdot(L,Q)=(\lambda L,\mu Q)$.

Identify the subgroup preserving $LQ$ and prove a coefficient normalization gives one representative on its valid locus.

### Strategy

Express product preservation as a kernel equation, parametrize that kernel, then solve the normalization equation and prove uniqueness.

### Hypotheses

$L,Q$ are nonzero and the selected coefficient $a(L)$ is nonzero on the locus under discussion.

### Intermediate claims

The product changes by $\lambda\mu$, so the preserving subgroup is $H=\{(\lambda,\mu):\lambda\mu=1\}=\ker m$, where $m(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda\mu$. The map $\lambda\mapsto(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})$ is an isomorphism $\mathbb G_m\to H$.

### Justification

Choosing $\lambda=a(L)^{-1}$ makes the selected coefficient of $\lambda L$ equal to one. The equation $\lambda a(L)=1$ has only that solution. If $a(L)=0$, rescaling leaves it zero, so this slice is unreachable.

### Conclusion

Relative scaling is the kernel subgroup $H\cong\mathbb G_m$, and the coefficient-one condition is a unique slice only on $a(L)\ne0$.

## Identify the relative-scaling subgroup

Let $m:\mathbb G_m^2\to\mathbb G_m$ be $m(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda\mu$. It is a homomorphism, and $H=\ker m$ is normal.

Solving $\lambda\mu=1$ gives $H=\{(\lambda,\lambda^{-1}):\lambda\in\mathbb G_m\}$. Thus the familiar one-parameter action is not an informal convention; it is the kernel of total scaling.

content.title: Prove the subgroup identification
content.introMarkdown: Prove $m$ is a homomorphism and identify $\ker m$ with $\mathbb G_m$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the coordinatewise multiplication before rearranging scalar factors.

The subgroup identification connects homomorphisms, kernels, and the geometric symmetry.

Verify $m(xx')=m(x)m(x')$, solve $\lambda\mu=1$, and check both composites of the proposed isomorphism.

## Preview weights without using the future theorem

Under relative scaling, a coordinate that multiplies by $\lambda^k$ is said to have weight $k$. This language will be taught systematically in Week 53.

Resultants will later supply important semi-invariants, but resultants are first taught in Week 27. This week uses only the directly verified invariant $LQ$ and does not assess either future concept.

content.title: Classify proved and previewed claims
content.introMarkdown: State what is proved now and what remains only previewed.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a later theorem was used to justify today’s invariant.

Previewing a connection must not create a hidden prerequisite.

List direct calculations first, then label weights and resultants with their future teaching weeks.

## Week 20 synthesis

The week’s algebra now forms one chain: a homomorphism exposes a normal kernel; quotienting removes exactly that kernel; orbit-stabilizer quotients the acting group by a point stabilizer; and a slice selects representatives only after existence and uniqueness are proved.

content.title: Prove the complete relative-scaling quotient
content.introMarkdown: Identify the product-preserving subgroup, prove its action, and prove $a(L)=1$ is a unique slice on $a(L)\ne0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing link among total scaling, kernel, action law, normalization equation, and evidence boundary.

The synthesis must distinguish a canonical quotient from a chosen representative and an invariant from a fiber classification.

Use five paragraphs: homomorphism and kernel, first isomorphism theorem, action and invariant, slice existence and uniqueness, then excluded-locus and orbit-fiber boundaries.
