**Resource version:** Michael Artin, Algebra, second edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 2 §§2.5–2.10 and Chapter 6 §§6.7–6.11: homomorphisms, cosets, quotient groups, group operations, counting, and permutation representations in Michael Artin, Algebra, second edition.

**Reading purpose:** Consolidate the homomorphism–quotient–action chain and compare the abstract group-operation language with the relative-scaling subgroup.
Week 21 moves from groups to rings, fields, units, zero divisors, domains, and ring homomorphisms.
Week 20 is complete when you can prove the first isomorphism theorem, distinguish an orbit space from a slice, and justify relative-scaling normalization with its exact locus and logical boundaries.

activities.title: Type the two-scaling group
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb G_m^2=\mathbb G_m\times\mathbb G_m$.

State its elements, multiplication, identity, and inverses.

Keep the two coordinates ordered.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: An element is an ordered pair $(\lambda,\mu)$ of nonzero scalars. Multiplication is coordinatewise: $(\lambda,\mu)(\lambda',\mu')=(\lambda\lambda',\mu\mu')$. The identity is $(1,1)$ and the inverse is $(\lambda^{-1},\mu^{-1})$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All product-group data are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The ordered coordinates remain separately typed.

activities.title: Recover the infinitesimal symmetry
activities.promptMarkdown:
$M(L,Q)=LQ$.

Compute $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)$ and evaluate it on $(L,-Q)$.

Explain how the signs anticipate opposite rescaling.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$. Hence $dM_{(L,Q)}(L,-Q)=LQ-LQ=0$. The opposite signs are the first-order form of multiplying $L$ by $\lambda$ and $Q$ by $\lambda^{-1}$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The differential, kernel calculation, and interpretation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The global symmetry is connected to its actual tangent direction.

activities.title: Retrieve the evidence boundary
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(z)=z^3$ near a nonzero base point.

State the local inverse conclusion and the separate global fiber fact.

Connect the distinction to a slice claimed only where one coefficient is nonzero.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: At $z_0\ne0$, the derivative is nonzero, so $F$ has an inverse on suitable neighborhoods of $z_0$ and $z_0^3$. Globally, a nonzero value has three complex cube roots, so the map is not globally injective. Likewise, solving a normalization uniquely where a coefficient is nonzero does not prove that the same slice meets orbits on the excluded zero locus.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The local theorem, global fiber, and normalization analogy are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response preserves the scope of each conclusion.

activities.title: Retrieve the rescaling action
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\lambda\cdot(L,Q)=(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

Verify the identity and composition laws and show that multiplication is invariant.

Do not claim that every product fiber is one orbit.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both action axioms, invariance, and the one-way boundary are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The retrieved statement is neither weakened nor overextended.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $1\cdot(L,Q)=(L,Q)$. Also $\lambda\cdot(\mu\cdot(L,Q))=(\lambda\mu L,(\lambda\mu)^{-1}Q)=(\lambda\mu)\cdot(L,Q)$. Finally $(\lambda L)(\lambda^{-1}Q)=LQ$, so each orbit lies in one multiplication fiber. The calculation alone does not prove the reverse inclusion.

activities.title: Prove the subgroup identification
activities.promptMarkdown:
$m:\mathbb G_m^2\to\mathbb G_m$, $m(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda\mu$.

Prove $m$ is a homomorphism and identify $\ker m$ with $\mathbb G_m$.

Give the isomorphism and its inverse.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The law, kernel, parametrization, isomorphism, and inverse are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The subgroup is derived as a kernel rather than guessed from notation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because scalar multiplication is commutative, $m((\lambda,\mu)(\lambda',\mu'))=\lambda\lambda'\mu\mu'=(\lambda\mu)(\lambda'\mu')$. Thus $m$ is a homomorphism. Its kernel is $H=\{(\lambda,\mu):\lambda\mu=1\}=\{(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})\}$. The map $i:\mathbb G_m\to H$, $i(\lambda)=(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})$, is a homomorphism with inverse the first projection.

activities.title: Classify proved and previewed claims
activities.promptMarkdown:
$L\mapsto\lambda L$ and $Q\mapsto\lambda^{-1}Q$.

State what is proved now and what remains only previewed.

Include the later week for each preview.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Now proved: the rule is a group action, $L$ scales with exponent $1$, $Q$ with exponent $-1$, and $LQ$ is invariant. Preview only: the systematic torus-weight formalism taught in Week 53 and resultant semi-invariants first taught in Week 27. Neither preview is needed for the present action or slice proofs.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Current results and both future concepts are correctly separated.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: No future terminology is used as present mastery evidence.

activities.title: Prove the complete relative-scaling quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb G_m^2$ acts on pairs $(L,Q)$ by independent scaling, and $a(L)$ is a selected linear coefficient.

Identify the product-preserving subgroup, prove its action, and prove $a(L)=1$ is a unique slice on $a(L)\ne0$.

Connect the subgroup to the first isomorphism theorem and state every excluded-locus and orbit-fiber boundary.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel quotient, action, invariant, slice proof, and boundaries are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Every conclusion is tied to its equation and valid locus.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The total-scaling homomorphism $m(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda\mu$ is surjective because $m(t,1)=t$, and its kernel is $H=\{(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})\}\cong\mathbb G_m$. By the first isomorphism theorem, $\mathbb G_m^2/H\cong\mathbb G_m$. The subgroup acts by $(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})\cdot(L,Q)=(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$; the identity and composition laws follow coordinatewise, and the product is invariant. If $a(L)\ne0$, the unique scalar making the selected coefficient equal to one is $\lambda=a(L)^{-1}$, so each orbit on this locus meets the slice once. If $a(L)=0$, rescaling cannot reach the slice. Product invariance proves that each orbit lies in a product fiber; equality with a whole fiber would require an additional factorization argument not supplied here.

lessons.title: Rings, subrings, and structure-preserving maps
lessons.summary: Verify the ring and subring axioms in concrete examples and test whether a typed function is a unital ring homomorphism.
objectives: Verify the ring and subring axioms in concrete examples and test whether a typed function is a unital ring homomorphism.

content.markdown:
## Two operations, one coherent structure

Linear algebra uses addition and scalar multiplication. Ring theory instead studies addition and multiplication inside the same set. The interaction law is distributivity, and it is strong enough to organize integers, residue classes, polynomials, functions, and coordinate rings in one language.

This course uses commutative rings with an identity element $1$, and a ring homomorphism is required to send $1$ to $1$. Stating that convention now prevents later ambiguity.

## Reactivate proof by axioms

To verify a structure, do not appeal to familiarity. Name the ambient set, the two operations, and the exact axioms inherited from a known ring. For a map, write its source and target before checking any equation.

## The commutative ring axioms

A commutative ring $A$ has an abelian addition law, an associative and commutative multiplication law with identity $1_A$, and distributivity: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$.

The additive identity is denoted $0_A$. From distributivity, $a0_A=a(0_A+0_A)=a0_A+a0_A$, so cancellation in the additive group gives $a0_A=0_A$.

content.title: Verify a product ring
content.introMarkdown: Identify $0$ and $1$, and explain why distributivity holds.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proposed multiplicative identity preserves both coordinates.

A ring identity must act as an identity on every element, not only on one factor.

Multiply a general pair by the candidate on both coordinates, then write one distributive expansion.

## Subrings inherit operations

A subset $B\subseteq A$ is a unital subring when it contains $1_A$ and is closed under subtraction and multiplication. These checks make $B$ a ring under the operations already defined in $A$.

The requirement $1_A\in B$ is part of our convention. Thus $2\mathbb Z$ is closed under subtraction and multiplication but is not a unital subring of $\mathbb Z$.

content.title: Test a polynomial subset
content.introMarkdown: Prove that it is a unital subring under the inherited operations.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing subring condition.

Closure under addition alone does not control products.

Check $1$, then a general coefficient of $f-g$, then a general coefficient of $fg$.

## Unital ring homomorphisms

A unital ring homomorphism $\varphi:A\to B$ satisfies $\varphi(a+b)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)$, $\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, and $\varphi(1_A)=1_B$.

Additive preservation then forces $\varphi(0_A)=0_B$ and $\varphi(-a)=-\varphi(a)$. These are consequences, not extra axioms.

content.title: Verify polynomial evaluation
content.introMarkdown: Verify all three unital ring-homomorphism conditions.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first omitted preservation law.

Preserving one operation does not make a function a ring homomorphism.

Write three separate lines for sums, products, and the constant polynomial $1$.

## Complete worked model

$D:\mathbb R[x]\to\mathbb R[x]$ sends $f$ to its formal derivative $f'$.

Decide rigorously whether $D$ is a unital ring homomorphism.

### Strategy

Check the homomorphism laws separately and stop at the first failed law.

### Hypotheses

The source and target use ordinary polynomial addition and multiplication.

### Intermediate claims

$D(f+g)=D(f)+D(g)$, but $D(fg)=f'g+fg'$ is generally not $D(f)D(g)$; moreover $D(1)=0$.

### Justification

Taking $f=g=x$ gives $D(x^2)=2x$ while $D(x)D(x)=1$. The identity condition also fails because $0\ne1$ in $\mathbb R[x]$.

### Conclusion

Differentiation is additive and satisfies the Leibniz rule, but it is not a unital ring homomorphism.

## Derive the forced additive identities

If $\varphi:A\to B$ preserves addition, then $\varphi(0_A)=\varphi(0_A)+\varphi(0_A)$, so additive cancellation in $B$ gives $\varphi(0_A)=0_B$. Applying $\varphi$ to $a+(-a)=0_A$ then gives $\varphi(-a)=-\varphi(a)$.

content.title: Derive zero and negative preservation
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\varphi(0_A)=0_B$ and $\varphi(-a)=-\varphi(a)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the target zero was assumed before it was derived.

Consequences of a definition must not be silently promoted to hypotheses.

Start from $0_A+0_A=0_A$, cancel in $B$, then apply the result to $a+(-a)$.

## Type-check a proposed homomorphism

A formula may fail before any algebra begins. The map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $n\mapsto2n$, preserves addition but sends $1$ to $2$ and does not preserve products.

The fastest reliable test is therefore typed: verify the declared codomain, then $1$, then a generic product and sum.

content.title: Classify three proposed maps
content.introMarkdown: Determine exactly which are unital ring homomorphisms.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether one accepted map was tested only for addition.

A ring map must preserve the entire two-operation structure and the identity.

For each map, check $1$, a generic sum, and a generic product; give a numerical counterexample when a law fails.

## Course reference

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare RES.18-012, Spring 2022.

**Exact locator:** Lecture 8 §§8.1–8.3, pp. 41–44: ring axioms, fields, homomorphisms, and subrings in MIT 18.702 Algebra II Student Notes, Spring 2022.

**Reading purpose:** Compare the formal ring, subring, and homomorphism definitions with the concrete verifications on this page.
Day 2 uses the multiplication law to separate units, zero divisors, integral domains, and fields.
Day 1 is complete when you can verify a ring or subring from axioms and can accept or reject a typed unital ring homomorphism with explicit equations.

activities.title: Verify a product ring
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z$ has coordinatewise addition and multiplication.

Identify $0$ and $1$, and explain why distributivity holds.

Also determine whether $(1,0)$ is a multiplicative identity.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The additive identity is $(0,0)$ and the multiplicative identity is $(1,1)$. Coordinatewise integer distributivity gives $(a,b)((c,d)+(e,f))=(ac+ae,bd+bf)=(a,b)(c,d)+(a,b)(e,f)$. The element $(1,0)$ is not an identity because $(1,0)(a,b)=(a,0)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The two identities and distributive calculation are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response checks the declared coordinatewise operations.

activities.title: Test a polynomial subset
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\mathbb R[x]$ is viewed as a subset of $\mathbb C[x]$.

Prove that it is a unital subring under the inherited operations.

Use the subtraction–multiplication test and mention the common identity.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Identity, subtraction closure, and multiplication closure are proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Coefficient closure is tied to the ambient operations.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The polynomial $1$ has real coefficients. If $f,g\in\mathbb R[x]$, then every coefficient of $f-g$ and of $fg$ is obtained from real coefficients by real addition, subtraction, and multiplication. Hence $f-g,fg\in\mathbb R[x]$, so $\mathbb R[x]$ is a unital subring of $\mathbb C[x]$.

activities.title: Verify polynomial evaluation
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\operatorname{ev}_2:\mathbb R[x]\to\mathbb R$ sends $f$ to $f(2)$.

Verify all three unital ring-homomorphism conditions.

Do not replace the multiplication calculation with the phrase “evaluation is compatible.”

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Addition, multiplication, and identity preservation are all verified.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each equation is evaluated on arbitrary source elements.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $f,g\in\mathbb R[x]$, $(f+g)(2)=f(2)+g(2)$ and $(fg)(2)=f(2)g(2)$. Also $\operatorname{ev}_2(1)=1$. Therefore $\operatorname{ev}_2$ is a unital ring homomorphism.

activities.title: Derive zero and negative preservation
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\varphi:A\to B$ preserves addition between rings.

Prove that $\varphi(0_A)=0_B$ and $\varphi(-a)=-\varphi(a)$.

Use additive cancellation and do not assume either conclusion as an axiom.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both forced identities are derived correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses only addition preservation and additive-group laws.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $0_A+0_A=0_A$, preservation gives $\varphi(0_A)+\varphi(0_A)=\varphi(0_A)$. Cancelling $\varphi(0_A)$ in the additive group of $B$ yields $\varphi(0_A)=0_B$. Then $0_B=\varphi(0_A)=\varphi(a-a)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(-a)$, so $\varphi(-a)$ is the additive inverse of $\varphi(a)$.

activities.title: Classify three proposed maps
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider complex conjugation $\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, inclusion $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb Q$, and doubling $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$.

Determine exactly which are unital ring homomorphisms.

For every rejection, exhibit the earliest failed law with explicit elements.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three maps are correctly classified with valid witnesses.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The first failed axiom is identified rather than asserted.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Conjugation preserves sums, products, and $1$, so it is a unital ring homomorphism. Inclusion preserves the same operations and identity, so it is also one. Doubling sends $1$ to $2$, already violating the identity law; it also sends $mn$ to $2mn$ while the product of the images is $4mn$.

lessons.title: Units, zero divisors, domains, and fields
lessons.summary: Classify elements as units or zero divisors and use the domain and field axioms to justify cancellation.
objectives: Classify elements as units or zero divisors and use the domain and field axioms to justify cancellation.

content.markdown:
## What can multiplication lose?

In a field, every nonzero element can be divided out. In a general ring, a nonzero factor may annihilate another nonzero factor. The vocabulary of units, zero divisors, domains, and fields records exactly which familiar algebraic moves remain legal.

## Reactivate products and cancellation

Integer and polynomial multiplication have no zero divisors. Modular arithmetic may behave differently. Never cancel a factor until you have proved it is a unit or proved that the ambient ring is an integral domain and the factor is nonzero.

## Units and zero divisors

An element $u\in A$ is a unit when some $v\in A$ satisfies $uv=1$. A nonzero element $a$ is a zero divisor when $ab=0$ for some nonzero $b$.

A zero divisor cannot be a unit: if $ab=0$ and $a^{-1}$ existed, then $b=a^{-1}ab=0$, contradicting the witness $b\ne0$.

content.title: Classify elements modulo eight
content.introMarkdown: Classify $[2]$, $[3]$, and $[4]$ as units, zero divisors, or neither.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a claimed zero-divisor witness is itself zero.

The equation $a\cdot0=0$ would make every element a zero divisor and therefore proves nothing.

Multiply the displayed residue classes and label both the inverse equation and the nonzero annihilator equation.

## Integral domains and cancellation

An integral domain is a nonzero commutative ring with no zero divisors. If $ac=bc$ and $c\ne0$, then $(a-b)c=0$; the absence of zero divisors forces $a-b=0$, hence $a=b$.

This proof shows both the power and the boundary of cancellation: it needs a nonzero factor and a domain.

content.title: Diagnose failed cancellation
content.introMarkdown: Explain why cancelling $[2]$ is invalid and identify the zero-divisor witness.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find where the argument divides by an element with no inverse.

Illegal cancellation can turn a true modular equality into a false conclusion.

Move the terms to one side, factor, and test whether the cancelled factor is a unit or a zero divisor.

## Complete worked model

Let $K$ be a field and suppose $ab=0$ in $K$.

Prove that $a=0$ or $b=0$.

### Strategy

Split on whether the first factor is zero; in the nonzero case, use its field inverse.

### Hypotheses

Every nonzero element of $K$ has a multiplicative inverse.

### Intermediate claims

If $a=0$ the conclusion is immediate. If $a\ne0$, then $a^{-1}$ exists.

### Justification

Multiplying $ab=0$ by $a^{-1}$ gives $b=a^{-1}ab=a^{-1}0=0$.

### Conclusion

A field has no zero divisors and is therefore an integral domain.

## Fields and the direction of implication

A field is a nonzero commutative ring in which every nonzero element is a unit. Every field is a domain, but a domain need not be a field.

The integers form a domain, yet $2$ has no integer inverse. The implication fails because absence of zero divisors is weaker than existence of inverses.

content.title: Separate domains from fields
content.introMarkdown: Prove that it is an integral domain but not a field.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether “not every element is invertible” has a named nonzero witness.

A counterexample to an implication needs an object satisfying the premise and failing the conclusion.

Prove the zero-product property, then solve the inverse equation for $2$ and show it has no integer solution.

## A nonzero nonunit need not be a zero divisor

The three labels unit, zero divisor, and nonzero nonunit are not interchangeable. In $\mathbb Z$, the element $2$ is a nonzero nonunit but not a zero divisor.

In a finite commutative ring, every non-zero-divisor is a unit: multiplication by that element is injective on a finite set, hence surjective, so it reaches $1$.

content.title: Prove the finite-ring dichotomy
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $a$ is a unit.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first step that uses finiteness without naming it.

The statement is false for infinite rings such as $\mathbb Z$.

Prove $m_a$ injective, invoke the finite-set theorem, then take a preimage of $1$.

## Synthesize the multiplicative hierarchy

The reliable implication chain is: field $\Rightarrow$ integral domain $\Rightarrow$ cancellation by nonzero factors. Neither converse holds without extra hypotheses.

content.title: Classify two residue rings
content.introMarkdown: Determine which is a field or domain and classify every nonzero class in each as a unit or zero divisor.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the first residue class whose classification lacks an inverse or annihilator.

A complete classification cannot rest on unverified pattern recognition.

Use Bézout for the prime modulus; for modulus $12$, list the coprime classes and provide a nonzero annihilator for each remaining class.

activities.title: Classify elements modulo eight
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z$.

Classify $[2]$, $[3]$, and $[4]$ as units, zero divisors, or neither.

Give an inverse for each unit and a nonzero annihilator for each zero divisor.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $[3]$ is a unit because $[3][3]=[1]$. The classes $[2]$ and $[4]$ are zero divisors: $[2][4]=[0]$, with both factors nonzero. Thus neither $[2]$ nor $[4]$ is a unit.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Each classification has a valid inverse or annihilator witness.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The witnesses are nonzero where the definition requires it.

activities.title: Diagnose failed cancellation
activities.promptMarkdown:
In $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$, $[2][1]=[2][4]$.

Explain why cancelling $[2]$ is invalid and identify the zero-divisor witness.

Rewrite the equality as one zero product.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Subtracting gives $[2]([1]-[4])=[2][3]=[0]$. Both $[2]$ and $[3]$ are nonzero, so $[2]$ is a zero divisor and the ring is not a domain. The domain cancellation theorem therefore does not apply.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The zero product and nonzero witnesses are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The failed hypothesis is explicitly connected to cancellation.

activities.title: Separate domains from fields
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider the ring $\mathbb Z$.

Prove that it is an integral domain but not a field.

Prove both claims; do not cite them as familiar facts.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both the domain property and a nonunit witness are established.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response proves each side of the strict implication.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $ab=0$ for integers, the ordinary order or prime factorization law gives $a=0$ or $b=0$, so $\mathbb Z$ has no zero divisors. It is nonzero and commutative, hence a domain. It is not a field because the equation $2n=1$ has no integer solution, so $2$ is a nonzero nonunit.

activities.title: Prove the finite-ring dichotomy
activities.promptMarkdown:
$A$ is a finite commutative ring and $a\in A$ is not a zero divisor.

Prove that $a$ is a unit.

Use the function $m_a(x)=ax$ and explain both injectivity and surjectivity.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The multiplication map proof correctly produces an inverse.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Finiteness is used exactly to pass from injectivity to surjectivity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $m_a(x)=m_a(y)$, then $a(x-y)=0$. Since $a$ is not a zero divisor, $x-y=0$, so $m_a$ is injective. An injective self-map of the finite set $A$ is surjective, so some $b$ satisfies $m_a(b)=ab=1$. Thus $a$ is a unit.

activities.title: Classify two residue rings
activities.promptMarkdown:
Compare $\mathbb Z/7\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$.

Determine which is a field or domain and classify every nonzero class in each as a unit or zero divisor.

Give a general inverse argument modulo $7$ and explicit witnesses modulo $12$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both rings and all nonzero classes are correctly classified.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The field proof and zero-divisor witnesses justify every label.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every nonzero class $[a]$ modulo $7$ has $\gcd(a,7)=1$, so Bézout gives integers $u,v$ with $ua+7v=1$ and $[u][a]=[1]$. Hence $\mathbb Z/7\mathbb Z$ is a field and domain. Modulo $12$, the units are $[1],[5],[7],[11]$. The other nonzero classes are zero divisors: $[2][6]=0$, $[3][4]=0$, $[4][3]=0$, $[6][2]=0$, $[8][3]=0$, $[9][4]=0$, and $[10][6]=0$. Thus $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ is neither a domain nor a field.

lessons.title: Units in polynomial and Laurent-polynomial rings
lessons.summary: Prove that the units of $\mathbb C[x]$ are the nonzero constants and that the units of $\mathbb C[x,x^{-1}]$ are the monomials $cx^n$.
objectives: Prove that the units of $\mathbb C[x]$ are the nonzero constants and that the units of $\mathbb C[x,x^{-1}]$ are the monomials $cx^n$.

content.markdown:
## Invertibility is visible in exponents

A polynomial inverse would have to make every nonconstant term disappear. Degree prevents that in $\mathbb C[x]$. Laurent polynomials allow negative exponents, so powers of $x$ become invertible, but the width of the exponent support still prevents sums of several monomials from being units.

## Reactivate leading and trailing exponents

For nonzero polynomials, $\deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g$. For a nonzero Laurent polynomial, record both its smallest and largest occurring exponents; both endpoints add under multiplication because the endpoint coefficients multiply and cannot vanish over $\mathbb C$.

## Degree detects polynomial units

If nonzero polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb C[x]$ satisfy $fg=1$, then $0=\deg1=\deg f+\deg g$. Both degrees are nonnegative, so both are zero.

Conversely, every nonzero constant $c$ has inverse $c^{-1}$. Therefore $\mathbb C[x]^\times=\mathbb C^\times$.

content.title: Use degree to reject an inverse
content.introMarkdown: Prove that no polynomial $g$ satisfies $(x+1)g=1$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether degree was assigned to the zero polynomial.

The degree-addition theorem applies only to nonzero factors.

Exclude $g=0$, then compare the degree of the proposed product with the degree of $1$.

## Complete worked model

Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$.

Prove the biconditional: $f$ is a unit exactly when $f=1$ or $f=-1$.

### Strategy

Prove necessity from the degree of an inverse product, then prove sufficiency by constructing the inverse.

### Hypotheses

If $f$ is a unit, there is $g\in\mathbb Z[x]$ with $fg=1$; neither factor is zero.

### Intermediate claims

$\deg f+\deg g=0$, so $\deg f=\deg g=0$.

### Justification

Degrees are nonnegative integers and add for products of nonzero polynomials. Thus $f$ and $g$ are integer constants whose product is $1$, so each is $1$ or $-1$. Conversely, both $1$ and $-1$ are their own inverses.

### Conclusion

The unit group of $\mathbb Z[x]$ is $\{1,-1\}$.

## Write both directions of a classification proof

A unit classification is an “if and only if” statement. The degree argument proves only that every unit must be constant. The explicit inverse proves that every nonzero constant really is a unit.

content.title: Classify units over the reals
content.introMarkdown: Prove that its units are exactly the nonzero real constants.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first direction of the biconditional that is only asserted.

An obstruction does not by itself construct every allowed inverse.

Separate the proof into “unit implies” and “nonzero constant implies,” ending the second with an explicit inverse.

## Laurent polynomials and support endpoints

A Laurent polynomial is a finite sum $f=\sum_{k=m}^n a_kx^k$ with integer exponents and nonzero endpoint coefficients $a_m,a_n$. Define $\operatorname{minexp}(f)=m$ and $\operatorname{maxexp}(f)=n$.

For nonzero Laurent polynomials, both endpoints add under multiplication: $\operatorname{minexp}(fg)=\operatorname{minexp}(f)+\operatorname{minexp}(g)$ and similarly for $\operatorname{maxexp}$. Hence the width $w(f)=\operatorname{maxexp}(f)-\operatorname{minexp}(f)$ is nonnegative and satisfies $w(fg)=w(f)+w(g)$.

content.title: Track Laurent endpoints
content.introMarkdown: Find the smallest and largest exponents of $fg$ without expanding every term.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether an extreme exponent could be produced in more than one way.

The width proof depends on endpoint coefficients surviving multiplication.

Add the two minimum exponents and multiply their coefficients; repeat for the maxima.

## Complete worked model

Let $f\in\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$ be nonzero.

Prove that $f$ is a unit exactly when $f=\pm t^n$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$.

### Strategy

Use additive support width for necessity, then construct the inverse of a monomial.

### Hypotheses

If $fg=1$, then $f,g$ are nonzero Laurent polynomials and the support endpoint laws apply.

### Intermediate claims

$0=w(1)=w(fg)=w(f)+w(g)$. Since both widths are nonnegative, $w(f)=0$, so the smallest and largest exponent of $f$ coincide.

### Justification

A Laurent polynomial of width zero has one term, so $f=ct^n$ and its inverse has the form $dt^{-n}$. The coefficient equation $cd=1$ in $\mathbb Z$ forces $c=d=1$ or $c=d=-1$. Conversely, $\pm t^n$ has inverse $\pm t^{-n}$.

### Conclusion

$\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]^\times=\{\pm t^n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$.

## Test candidate Laurent units

Over $\mathbb C$, the conclusion is $\mathbb C[x,x^{-1}]^\times=\{cx^n:c\in\mathbb C^\times,\ n\in\mathbb Z\}$. A monomial may have any integer exponent because $x^{-1}$ is present. A sum of two or more distinct powers has positive support width and therefore cannot be a unit.

content.title: Classify four Laurent elements
content.introMarkdown: For every unit give its inverse; for every nonunit give its positive width.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a factored expression was mistaken for one monomial.

Multiplication by a power of $x$ shifts support but does not collapse its width.

Expand only enough to list distinct exponents, then use the classification theorem.

## Prove the two unit classifications independently

The polynomial proof uses nonnegative degree. The Laurent proof cannot: negative exponents permit degree cancellation. Its replacement is the pair of support endpoints, or equivalently their width.

content.title: Prove both unit theorems
content.introMarkdown: Determine the complete unit group of each ring and prove both directions of both classifications.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first classification direction or support-endpoint claim left unjustified.

The syllabus asks for complete unit groups, not a list of plausible examples.

Write two biconditional proofs: degree plus scalar inverse, then support width plus monomial inverse.

activities.title: Use degree to reject an inverse
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider $x+1\in\mathbb C[x]$.

Prove that no polynomial $g$ satisfies $(x+1)g=1$.

Use degree and separately exclude the zero polynomial.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The zero polynomial cannot be an inverse. If $g\ne0$, then $\deg((x+1)g)=1+\deg g\ge1$, whereas $\deg1=0$. Hence $(x+1)g$ cannot equal $1$, so $x+1$ is not a unit.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The degree contradiction and zero case are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses the multiplicative degree law under its nonzero hypotheses.

activities.title: Classify units over the reals
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $\mathbb R[t]$.

Prove that its units are exactly the nonzero real constants.

Label the necessity and sufficiency directions.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both directions and the nonzero condition are proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Necessity and sufficiency use different evidence.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Necessity: if $fg=1$ with $f,g\in\mathbb R[t]$, both are nonzero and $0=\deg1=\deg f+\deg g$, so $\deg f=0$ and $f$ is constant. It is nonzero because it has an inverse. Sufficiency: if $f=c\in\mathbb R^\times$, then $c^{-1}\in\mathbb R[t]$ and $cc^{-1}=1$.

activities.title: Track Laurent endpoints
activities.promptMarkdown:
$f=2x^{-3}+x^2$ and $g=3x^{-1}-4x^5$.

Find the smallest and largest exponents of $fg$ without expanding every term.

Name the endpoint coefficients to rule out cancellation.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The smallest exponent is $-3+(-1)=-4$, with coefficient $2\cdot3=6\ne0$. The largest is $2+5=7$, with coefficient $1\cdot(-4)=-4\ne0$. Thus $\operatorname{minexp}(fg)=-4$, $\operatorname{maxexp}(fg)=7$, and $w(fg)=11=w(f)+w(g)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both support endpoints, coefficients, and width are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The unique endpoint terms justify absence of cancellation.

activities.title: Classify four Laurent elements
activities.promptMarkdown:
Classify $3x^{-4}$, $x+x^{-1}$, $-2$, and $x^2(1+x)$ in $\mathbb C[x,x^{-1}]$.

For every unit give its inverse; for every nonunit give its positive width.

Simplify supports before calculating widths.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $3x^{-4}$ is a unit with inverse $\frac13x^4$, and $-2$ is a unit with inverse $-\frac12$. The support of $x+x^{-1}$ has width $1-(-1)=2$, so it is not a unit. The element $x^2(1+x)=x^2+x^3$ has width $1$, so it is not a unit.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All four classifications, inverses, and widths are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each classification applies the proved criterion.

activities.title: Prove both unit theorems
activities.promptMarkdown:
Compare $\mathbb C[x]$ and $\mathbb C[x,x^{-1}]$.

Determine the complete unit group of each ring and prove both directions of both classifications.

Explain why ordinary degree proves the first theorem but support width is needed for the second.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both necessity and sufficiency proofs are complete and use valid invariants.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response explains why the proof tool changes between the two rings.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $fg=1$ in $\mathbb C[x]$, then $0=\deg f+\deg g$, so both factors are nonzero constants; every nonzero constant has its scalar inverse. Thus $\mathbb C[x]^\times=\mathbb C^\times$. In the Laurent ring, let $w$ be largest minus smallest occurring exponent. Endpoint coefficients do not cancel, so $w(fg)=w(f)+w(g)$. If $fg=1$, both widths are zero; therefore $f=cx^n$ and $g=dx^m$. Conversely $cx^n$ has inverse $c^{-1}x^{-n}$. Hence the Laurent units are exactly $cx^n$. Ordinary degree alone is unsuitable there because negative exponents allow top exponents to sum to zero without either factor being constant.

lessons.title: Polynomial fractions and kernel ideals
lessons.summary: Distinguish polynomial from rational functions and prove that the kernel of a unital ring homomorphism is an ideal.
objectives: Distinguish polynomial from rational functions and prove that the kernel of a unital ring homomorphism is an ideal.

content.markdown:
## Division enlarges the ring

The polynomial $x$ is not invertible in $\mathbb C[x]$, but it becomes invertible after passing to rational functions. This enlargement keeps polynomial arithmetic while allowing quotients by every nonzero polynomial.

At the same time, a ring homomorphism may identify many source elements. Its kernel is not merely a subring: it absorbs multiplication by every element of the ambient ring. That stronger closure property is the definition of an ideal.

## Reactivate fractions and kernels

A field of fractions can be formed only from an integral domain. Equality of fractions is proved by cross-multiplication, and a kernel is always defined relative to a typed map and the zero of its target.

## From polynomials to rational functions

The field $\mathbb C(x)$ consists of fractions $f/g$ with $f,g\in\mathbb C[x]$ and $g\ne0$, where $f/g=f'/g'$ exactly when $fg'=f'g$.

The map $f\mapsto f/1$ embeds $\mathbb C[x]$ into $\mathbb C(x)$. It is injective because $f/1=0/1$ implies $f=0$.

content.title: Test equality of rational functions
content.introMarkdown: Prove equality in the fraction field and state the pointwise-domain distinction.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether pointwise formulas were confused with fraction-field elements.

A removable hole in one expression does not change the algebraic rational function it represents.

Prove the polynomial cross-product identity, then discuss evaluation domains in a separate sentence.

## Polynomial and rational functions are different rings

Every polynomial determines a rational function, but not every rational function is polynomial. For example, $1/x$ cannot equal a polynomial $p$: equality would give $xp=1$, contradicting the unit classification in $\mathbb C[x]$.

Thus $\mathbb C[x]\subsetneq\mathbb C(x)$. The first ring is a domain but not a field; the second is its field of fractions.

content.title: Prove the inclusion is proper
content.introMarkdown: Prove that it is not the image of a polynomial under $p\mapsto p/1$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first step that assumes a rational expression is automatically polynomial.

The field of fractions is genuinely larger than its source domain.

Assume a polynomial representative exists, cross-multiply, and identify the resulting forbidden unit.

## Ideals absorb ambient multiplication

An ideal $I\subseteq A$ is an additive subgroup such that $ra\in I$ for every $r\in A$ and $a\in I$. The multiplier comes from all of $A$, not merely from $I$.

Every ideal is a subring under nonunital conventions, but a unital subring need not be an ideal. For instance, $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q$ is a unital subring but not an ideal because $(1/2)\cdot1\notin\mathbb Z$.

content.title: Prove a principal set is an ideal
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $I$ is an ideal.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the multiplier was restricted to the candidate ideal.

Ideal absorption is stronger than closure under internal multiplication.

Name arbitrary $r\in\mathbb R[x]$ and rewrite its product with a general ideal element as another multiple of the generator.

## Complete worked model

Let $\pi:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ send $n$ to $[n]_6$.

Compute $\ker\pi$ and prove directly that it is an ideal of $\mathbb Z$.

### Strategy

Solve the kernel congruence, then verify zero, subtraction, and absorption by an arbitrary integer.

### Hypotheses

$\pi(n)=[0]_6$ exactly when $6$ divides $n$.

### Intermediate claims

$\ker\pi=6\mathbb Z$. It contains zero; differences of multiples of six remain multiples of six; and an arbitrary integer times a multiple of six remains a multiple of six.

### Justification

If $x=6m$ and $y=6n$, then $x-y=6(m-n)$. For $r\in\mathbb Z$, $rx=6(rm)$. These calculations verify the ideal axioms in the source ring.

### Conclusion

$\ker\pi=6\mathbb Z$ is an ideal of $\mathbb Z$.

## Compute a concrete kernel

For evaluation $\operatorname{ev}_a:\mathbb C[x]\to\mathbb C$, the factor theorem gives $\ker(\operatorname{ev}_a)=(x-a)$. This is both a calculation and an example of the general kernel-ideal theorem.

content.title: Compute the kernel of evaluation at one
content.introMarkdown: Prove that its kernel is the ideal $(x-1)$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the missing direction in the set equality.

Showing that every kernel element is divisible does not alone show every multiple evaluates to zero.

Prove kernel-to-ideal using the factor theorem, then substitute $x=1$ in a general multiple.

## Preview quotient rings without using them

Week 22 will form the quotient ring $A/I$, where elements differing by an ideal element become equal. Today we use only the motivating fact that a homomorphism sends every element of its kernel to zero.

No quotient-ring construction or congruence calculation is assessed here. The present proof obligation is solely the ideal property of the kernel.

content.title: Prove the kernel-ideal theorem independently
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $\ker\psi$ is an ideal of $A$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first ideal axiom that is asserted without applying $\psi$.

The kernel theorem is foundational for quotient rings and later coordinate-ring arguments.

Write three paragraphs: zero, subtraction, and multiplication by arbitrary $r\in A$; compute the image in each.

activities.title: Test equality of rational functions
activities.promptMarkdown:
Compare $(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ and $x+1$ as elements of $\mathbb C(x)$.

Prove equality in the fraction field and state the pointwise-domain distinction.

Do not cancel before naming the nonzero denominator polynomial.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $x-1$ is a nonzero polynomial and $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$, cross-multiplication gives $(x^2-1)\cdot1=(x+1)(x-1)$, so the two fractions are equal in $\mathbb C(x)$. As pointwise expressions, the first displayed quotient is undefined at $x=1$ while the polynomial $x+1$ is defined there; the fraction-field equality concerns rational functions represented algebraically.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The algebraic equality and pointwise-domain distinction are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Cross-multiplication is used with a nonzero denominator.

activities.title: Prove the inclusion is proper
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider $1/(x^2+1)\in\mathbb C(x)$.

Prove that it is not the image of a polynomial under $p\mapsto p/1$.

Reduce the claim to a statement about units in $\mathbb C[x]$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The proper-inclusion proof correctly invokes the unit theorem.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Fraction equality is converted into an impossible polynomial inverse.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $p/1=1/(x^2+1)$, cross-multiplication gives $(x^2+1)p=1$. This would make the nonconstant polynomial $x^2+1$ a unit of $\mathbb C[x]$, contradicting the theorem that only nonzero constants are units. Hence the rational function is not polynomial.

activities.title: Prove a principal set is an ideal
activities.promptMarkdown:
$I=(x^2+1)=\{(x^2+1)q:q\in\mathbb R[x]\}\subseteq\mathbb R[x]$.

Prove that $I$ is an ideal.

Check zero, subtraction, and multiplication by an arbitrary polynomial.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All ideal axioms are proved with an arbitrary ambient multiplier.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each closure statement exhibits the required factorization.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The zero polynomial is $(x^2+1)0$, so it lies in $I$. If $(x^2+1)q$ and $(x^2+1)s$ lie in $I$, their difference is $(x^2+1)(q-s)\in I$. If $r\in\mathbb R[x]$, then $r(x^2+1)q=(x^2+1)(rq)\in I$. Hence $I$ is an ideal.

activities.title: Compute the kernel of evaluation at one
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\operatorname{ev}_1:\mathbb C[x]\to\mathbb C$ sends $f$ to $f(1)$.

Prove that its kernel is the ideal $(x-1)$.

Prove both set inclusions and name the factor theorem.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both inclusions and the factor-theorem step are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The kernel equation is translated into divisibility and back.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $f\in\ker(\operatorname{ev}_1)$, then $f(1)=0$, so the factor theorem gives $f=(x-1)q$ and $f\in(x-1)$. Conversely, if $f=(x-1)q$, then $f(1)=0$, so $f$ lies in the kernel. Thus $\ker(\operatorname{ev}_1)=(x-1)$.

activities.title: Prove the kernel-ideal theorem independently
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\psi:A\to B$ is a unital homomorphism of commutative rings.

Prove that $\ker\psi$ is an ideal of $A$.

Use the ideal definition directly and state why each displayed image is zero. Mention quotient rings only as next week’s motivation.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Zero, subtraction closure, and ambient absorption are all proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Every ideal obligation follows from a named homomorphism law.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $\psi(0_A)=0_B$, the kernel contains zero. If $x,y\in\ker\psi$, then $\psi(x-y)=\psi(x)-\psi(y)=0_B-0_B=0_B$, so $x-y$ is in the kernel. If $r\in A$ and $x\in\ker\psi$, then $\psi(rx)=\psi(r)\psi(x)=\psi(r)0_B=0_B$, so $rx$ is in the kernel. Thus the kernel is an additive subgroup and absorbs multiplication by every element of $A$, hence is an ideal. Week 22 will use ideals to define quotient rings, but that construction is not needed in this proof.

lessons.title: Retrieval and ring-theory synthesis
lessons.summary: Integrate proof logic, determinants, local–global boundaries, quotients, and ring structure in one rigorous classification argument.
objectives: Integrate proof logic, determinants, local–global boundaries, quotients, and ring structure in one rigorous classification argument.

content.markdown:
## Build one connected algebraic argument

The week’s definitions become useful only when they control proof moves: quantifiers specify ideal absorption, determinants supply multiplicative homomorphisms, local theorems impose scope boundaries, and quotient reasoning explains what a kernel forgets.

## Retrieve before synthesizing

Each review below is deliberate and labelled. Reconstruct the earlier result from memory, correct it from feedback, and only then use it in the final ring-theory proof.

## Deliberate review: Week 5 quantifier discipline

Retrieve how universal variables are introduced before proving a closure statement.

content.title: Quantify the ideal axiom
content.introMarkdown: Write the absorption axiom with explicit quantifiers and negate it correctly.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether a universal quantifier became universal after negation.

The logical form separates a subring from an ideal.

Write both variables with their domains, then change each universal quantifier to existential and negate membership.

## Deliberate review: Week 13 determinant structure

Retrieve the determinant product law and its connection with invertibility. For $n\ge2$, $M_n(\mathbb C)$ is noncommutative, so it lies outside this week’s standing commutative-ring convention. Determinant is multiplicative but not additive, hence it is not a ring homomorphism.

content.title: Retrieve matrix units
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $A$ is a unit of the matrix ring exactly when $\det A\ne0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first direction of the biconditional that lacks a justification.

Unit classification in a matrix ring is a direct bridge from linear algebra to ring theory.

Start from an inverse for necessity; use the adjugate or invertibility theorem for sufficiency.

## Deliberate review: Week 18 local–global boundary

Retrieve why a local theorem cannot silently become a global statement.

content.title: Retrieve the scope boundary
content.introMarkdown: State the local inverse conclusion at $1$ and the separate global fiber fact.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first sentence that removes the neighborhood restriction or denies the global three-point fibers.

Scope errors recur when local analytic evidence is transferred to algebraic charts.

State the local neighborhoods, count the global fiber separately, then name the excluded algebraic locus.

## Deliberate review: Week 20 kernels and quotients

Retrieve the group theorem without importing next week’s quotient-ring construction.

content.title: Retrieve what a kernel forgets
content.introMarkdown: State the first isomorphism theorem and the four obligations for its induced map.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the induced formula depends on a chosen representative.

Week 22 will require the analogous well-definedness discipline for quotient rings.

Write the induced formula, prove well-definedness, then verify homomorphism, injectivity, and surjectivity.

## Connect the week’s classification tools

A ring question should now trigger a sequence: identify the ambient ring and convention; test units with an inverse equation; test zero divisors with a nonzero annihilator; use degree or support width only under their hypotheses; and use the homomorphism laws to control a kernel.

content.title: Analyze evaluation at zero
content.introMarkdown: Prove it is a surjective ring homomorphism, compute its kernel, and determine which source units map to target units.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first conclusion not tied to a preservation, preimage, divisibility, or unit argument.

Synthesis requires choosing the right proof tool for each structural claim.

Use four paragraphs: homomorphism laws, constant preimages, zero constant term, and nonzero constant units.

## Complete worked model

$\operatorname{ev}_{-1}:\mathbb C[x]\to\mathbb C$ sends $f$ to $f(-1)$.

Verify the ring map, compute its kernel, and track its effect on polynomial units.

### Strategy

Check the three homomorphism laws, use the factor theorem for the kernel, and apply the polynomial-unit classification.

### Hypotheses

Evaluation is taken at the fixed scalar $-1$, and $\mathbb C[x]$ uses its ordinary unital ring structure.

### Intermediate claims

Evaluation preserves sums, products, and $1$; its kernel is $(x+1)$; every source unit is a nonzero constant.

### Justification

Substitution commutes with addition and multiplication. The factor theorem gives $f(-1)=0$ exactly when $x+1$ divides $f$. A nonzero constant evaluates to the same nonzero scalar.

### Conclusion

The map is a surjective unital ring homomorphism with kernel $(x+1)$, and it sends every source unit to a target unit.

## Diagnose a plausible but false chain

The statement “a nonzero element is either a unit or a zero divisor” is false in infinite rings. The integer $2$ is the standard counterexample.

The corrected statement holds in finite commutative rings, where multiplication by a non-zero-divisor is an injective self-map of a finite set and therefore surjective.

content.title: Apply the repaired dichotomy
content.introMarkdown: Correct both errors using the infinite-ring counterexample and the finite-ring theorem.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check the first classification lacking an inverse, annihilator, or coefficient argument.

The theorem’s hypothesis must control exactly where the dichotomy is used.

Use coefficients for $xg=0$, then display $2\cdot8\equiv1$ and $6\cdot5\equiv0\pmod{15}$.

## Week 21 synthesis

Rings organize two compatible operations. Their multiplicative behavior ranges from zero-divisor-rich rings to domains and fields. Polynomial degree and Laurent support classify units, fraction fields legalize division, and kernel ideals record what a ring homomorphism sends to zero.

content.title: Write the complete Week 21 argument
content.introMarkdown: Classify the units in the first two rings, prove the second inclusion into rational functions, and prove $\ker(\operatorname{ev}_1)=(x-1)$ is an ideal.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first missing converse, unjustified embedding, or ideal obligation.

The capstone is the learner’s durable proof model for the algebraic-geometry weeks that follow.

Organize the response into four labelled parts: polynomial units, Laurent units, embeddings, and evaluation kernel; close with the Week 22 boundary.

## Course reference

**Resource version:** J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, version 4.01.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 1, p. 3: commutative rings, integral domains, and subrings in J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, version 4.01.

**Reading purpose:** Consolidate the week’s ring, domain, and subring vocabulary in the syllabus-named commutative-algebra reference.
Week 22 turns the kernel-ideal motivation into the construction and universal behavior of quotient rings.
Week 21 is complete when you can classify the two requested unit groups, distinguish polynomials from rational functions, and prove the kernel-ideal theorem from first principles.

activities.title: Quantify the ideal axiom
activities.promptMarkdown:
$I$ is a subset of a ring $A$.

Write the absorption axiom with explicit quantifiers and negate it correctly.

Distinguish the ambient-ring variable from the ideal variable.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Absorption is $\forall r\in A\,\forall x\in I,\ rx\in I$. Its negation is $\exists r\in A\,\exists x\in I$ such that $rx\notin I$. The multiplier $r$ ranges over all of $A$, not merely over $I$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The statement and negation have the correct domains and quantifiers.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The ambient multiplier is explicitly distinguished.

activities.title: Retrieve matrix units
activities.promptMarkdown:
$A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$.

Prove that $A$ is a unit of the matrix ring exactly when $\det A\ne0$.

Use determinant multiplicativity in the necessary direction and a standard inverse theorem in the sufficient direction.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both directions of the determinant unit criterion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Multiplicativity and the inverse construction have distinct roles.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $n\ge2$, $M_n(\mathbb C)$ is a noncommutative ring. Determinant is multiplicative, but it is not additive and therefore is not a ring homomorphism. If $AB=I$, then $1=\det I=\det A\det B$, so $\det A\ne0$. Conversely, if $\det A\ne0$, the adjugate formula gives $A^{-1}=(\det A)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(A)$, so $A$ is a unit. Thus matrix-ring units are exactly the invertible matrices.

activities.title: Retrieve the scope boundary
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(z)=z^3$ is studied near $z_0=1$ and on all of $\mathbb C$.

State the local inverse conclusion at $1$ and the separate global fiber fact.

Explain why neither statement can replace the other, then connect that scope discipline to chartwise algebraic formulas.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $F'(1)=3\ne0$, the holomorphic inverse-function theorem gives neighborhoods of $1$ and $1$ on which $F$ is bijective with a holomorphic inverse. Globally, every nonzero complex value has three cube roots, so $F$ is not injective on $\mathbb C$. The neighborhood theorem and the global fiber count have different scopes. Likewise, a formula proved on one algebraic chart does not automatically extend across the excluded locus.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The derivative, local conclusion, global fiber count, and chart analogy are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response preserves the scope of both analytic statements.

activities.title: Retrieve what a kernel forgets
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\phi:G\to H$ is a group homomorphism.

State the first isomorphism theorem and the four obligations for its induced map.

Keep the codomain equal to the image and explain why well-definedness uses the kernel.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The theorem, codomain, and four obligations are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Kernel membership is used exactly for representative independence.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The induced map $\bar\phi:G/\ker\phi\to\operatorname{im}\phi$ is $\bar\phi(g\ker\phi)=\phi(g)$. If two cosets agree, their representatives differ by a kernel element, so their images agree; hence the map is well defined. It is a homomorphism by the product law, injective because its kernel is the identity coset, and surjective by the definition of $\operatorname{im}\phi$. Thus $G/\ker\phi\cong\operatorname{im}\phi$.

activities.title: Analyze evaluation at zero
activities.promptMarkdown:
$\operatorname{ev}_0:\mathbb C[x]\to\mathbb C$ sends $f$ to $f(0)$.

Prove it is a surjective ring homomorphism, compute its kernel, and determine which source units map to target units.

Use the factor theorem or coefficient form for the kernel and the polynomial unit classification for the final clause.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All map, kernel, surjectivity, and unit claims are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each conclusion invokes its appropriate theorem.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Evaluation preserves sums, products, and $1$, so it is a unital ring homomorphism. Every $c\in\mathbb C$ is the image of the constant polynomial $c$, so it is surjective. Its kernel is the polynomials with zero constant term, exactly $(x)$. The source units are nonzero constants, and each maps to the same nonzero scalar, hence to a target unit.

activities.title: Apply the repaired dichotomy
activities.promptMarkdown:
A draft calls $x\in\mathbb Z[x]$ a zero divisor because it is not a unit, then claims that $[2]$ and $[6]$ behave the same way in $\mathbb Z/15\mathbb Z$.

Correct both errors using the infinite-ring counterexample and the finite-ring theorem.

Prove the status of $x$, give an inverse for $[2]$, and give a nonzero annihilator for $[6]$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The polynomial $x$ is not a unit in $\mathbb Z[x]$ by degree, but it is not a zero divisor because $xg=0$ forces every coefficient of $g$ to be zero. Modulo $15$, $[2]$ is a unit because $[2][8]=[1]$. The class $[6]$ is a zero divisor because $[6][5]=[0]$ and both classes are nonzero. The finite-ring dichotomy applies to the two residue classes but not to the infinite ring $\mathbb Z[x]$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The polynomial and both residue classes are correctly classified with witnesses.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The finite hypothesis is applied only to the finite quotient ring.

activities.title: Write the complete Week 21 argument
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use $\mathbb C[x]\subset\mathbb C[x,x^{-1}]\subset\mathbb C(x)$ and evaluation $\operatorname{ev}_1:\mathbb C[x]\to\mathbb C$.

Classify the units in the first two rings, prove the second inclusion into rational functions, and prove $\ker(\operatorname{ev}_1)=(x-1)$ is an ideal.

Include every converse, state where degree is replaced by support width, and keep quotient rings labelled as Week 22 material.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All classifications, inclusions, kernel calculations, and scope boundaries are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each major conclusion is supported by its exact invariant or homomorphism law.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In $\mathbb C[x]$, if $fg=1$, degree additivity gives $0=\deg f+\deg g$, so $f$ and $g$ are nonzero constants; conversely every nonzero constant has its scalar inverse. In $\mathbb C[x,x^{-1}]$, support width is additive, so a factor of $1$ has width zero and is $cx^n$; conversely $(cx^n)^{-1}=c^{-1}x^{-n}$. Every Laurent polynomial is a rational function because $\sum_{k=m}^na_kx^k=x^m p(x)$ can be written with a power of $x$ in the denominator when $m<0$; the embedding is injective because the source is a domain. Evaluation at $1$ preserves sums, products, and $1$. Its kernel consists exactly of polynomials divisible by $x-1$ by the factor theorem, so it is $(x-1)$. Independently, the general kernel proof shows it contains zero, is closed under subtraction, and absorbs multiplication by every source polynomial. Quotient-ring construction is motivated by this kernel but begins in Week 22.

lessons.title: From ideals to quotient rings
lessons.summary: Construct a quotient ring from an ideal, prove that its operations are well defined, and calculate congruence classes.
objectives: Construct a quotient ring from an ideal, prove that its operations are well defined, and calculate congruence classes.

content.markdown:
## Make a relation into an equality

A quotient ring records equations as algebraic rules. If an ideal contains $xy-1$, then the quotient treats the classes of $xy$ and $1$ as equal. The construction is useful only after we prove that adding or multiplying representatives gives an answer independent of the representatives chosen.

Today begins with the ideal axioms, builds the equivalence relation $a\sim b$ when $a-b\in I$, and ends with computations that use the resulting congruence honestly.

## Reactivate the kernel proof

Week 21 proved that a homomorphism kernel contains zero, is closed under subtraction, and absorbs multiplication by every element of the source ring. Those are exactly the ideal properties needed below.

## Ideals are the subsets that can be collapsed to zero

Let $A$ be a commutative ring with identity. A subset $I\subseteq A$ is an ideal when $0\in I$, when $u-v\in I$ for all $u,v\in I$, and when $au\in I$ for every $a\in A$ and $u\in I$.

The multiplier comes from the whole ring. An additive subgroup that is closed only under multiplication by its own elements may be a subring without being an ideal.

content.title: Test an ideal in the integers
content.introMarkdown: Prove directly from the three ideal obligations that $2\mathbb Z$ is an ideal.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the multiplier was allowed to range over all of $\mathbb Z$.

Absorption is the property that later makes quotient multiplication well defined.

Write the three obligations separately and use a fresh arbitrary multiplier in the last one.

## Generated ideals package all allowed multiples

For $s_1,\ldots,s_m\in A$, the generated ideal is $(s_1,\ldots,s_m)=\{a_1s_1+\cdots+a_ms_m:a_i\in A\}$. It is the smallest ideal containing every generator.

Membership requires an explicit combination or another valid ideal-membership argument. Sharing a zero set is not by itself a proof of membership in the displayed ideal.

content.title: Write an ideal certificate
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $x^2+4x+6\in I$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first generator whose coefficient is missing or belongs to the wrong ring.

Later reductions in a quotient ring depend on exact membership certificates.

Expand the proposed combination and verify both its value and coefficient domains.

## Cosets and congruence modulo an ideal

Define $a\sim b$ when $a-b\in I$. The ideal axioms make this an equivalence relation. The class of $a$ is the coset $a+I$, written $[a]$ when the ideal is fixed.

The quotient set $A/I$ becomes a ring by $[a]+[b]=[a+b]$ and $[a][b]=[ab]$. Equality $[a]=[b]$ means exactly that $a-b\in I$.

content.title: Recognize equal residue classes
content.introMarkdown: Decide whether $[17]=[5]$ and whether $[8]=[1]$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the difference, rather than the original numbers, was tested.

Congruence is equality in the quotient, not informal numerical similarity.

Subtract the representatives and test exact membership in $6\mathbb Z$.

## Complete worked model

Let $I$ be an ideal of a commutative ring $A$ with $a-a'\in I$ and $b-b'\in I$.

Prove that $ab-a'b'\in I$, so $[a][b]=[a'][b']$.

### Strategy

Insert the mixed term $a'b$ and use ideal absorption twice.

### Hypotheses

Write $a-a'=u\in I$ and $b-b'=v\in I$.

### Intermediate claims

$ab-a'b'=b(a-a')+a'(b-b')=bu+a'v$.

### Justification

Because $I$ absorbs multiplication by every element of $A$, both $bu$ and $a'v$ lie in $I$. Closure under addition follows from the subtraction condition, so their sum lies in $I$.

### Conclusion

The product class depends only on $[a]$ and $[b]$. The same argument with $(a+b)-(a'+b')$ proves addition is well defined.

## Transfer the representative argument

A well-definedness proof starts with two choices of representatives for each input. It ends by proving that the two proposed outputs lie in the same equivalence class.

content.title: Prove addition is well defined
content.introMarkdown: Prove $[a+b]=[a'+b']$ in $A/I$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether the proof compared the two outputs rather than merely restating the input congruences.

Without representative independence, the proposed quotient operation is not a function.

Subtract the two output representatives, regroup the difference, and place it in $I$.

## Compute by replacing a relation

In $\mathbb C[x]/(x^2-1)$, the relation $[x^2]=[1]$ lets us reduce powers. This is equality of classes; the ambient polynomials $x^2$ and $1$ remain different.

content.title: Construct and use a polynomial quotient
content.introMarkdown: Prove $[x^5+2x^2-3]=[x-1]$ and explain why this is not an ambient polynomial identity.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first unsupported replacement or incorrect factorization.

Every later quotient-ring calculation needs a checkable certificate.

Subtract the proposed representatives, factor the result by the defining relation, then state the scope of the equality.

Day 1 is complete when you can produce ideal-membership certificates, compare quotient classes, and prove both quotient operations are well defined.

activities.title: Test an ideal in the integers
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider $2\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb Z$.

Prove directly from the three ideal obligations that $2\mathbb Z$ is an ideal.

Check zero, subtraction, and absorption by an arbitrary integer.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three ideal obligations are verified.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The absorption step quantifies over every ambient integer.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: We have $0=2\cdot0\in2\mathbb Z$. If $2m,2n\in2\mathbb Z$, then $2m-2n=2(m-n)\in2\mathbb Z$. If $r\in\mathbb Z$ and $2m\in2\mathbb Z$, then $r(2m)=2(rm)\in2\mathbb Z$. Hence $2\mathbb Z$ is an ideal.

activities.title: Write an ideal certificate
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $\mathbb Z[x]$ with $I=(2,x)$.

Prove that $x^2+4x+6\in I$.

Display the polynomial as an $A$-linear combination of the two generators.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $x^2+4x+6=(x+4)x+3\cdot2$. Both coefficients lie in $\mathbb Z[x]$, so this is an explicit membership certificate and $x^2+4x+6\in(2,x)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The displayed combination expands to the target.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The coefficients belong to the ambient polynomial ring.

activities.title: Recognize equal residue classes
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$.

Decide whether $[17]=[5]$ and whether $[8]=[1]$.

Use divisibility of the difference by $6$ in each case.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $17-5=12\in6\mathbb Z$, we have $[17]=[5]$. Since $8-1=7\notin6\mathbb Z$, we have $[8]\ne[1]$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both class comparisons are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each conclusion is tied to membership of the difference in the ideal.

activities.title: Prove addition is well defined
activities.promptMarkdown:
Assume $a-a'\in I$ and $b-b'\in I$.

Prove $[a+b]=[a'+b']$ in $A/I$.

Compute the difference of the proposed representatives and cite the exact ideal closure property.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The representative difference is in the ideal.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof invokes closure under addition at the decisive step.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $(a+b)-(a'+b')=(a-a')+(b-b')$. Both summands lie in $I$, and an ideal is closed under addition, so the difference lies in $I$. Therefore $[a+b]=[a'+b']$.

activities.title: Construct and use a polynomial quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $B=\mathbb C[x]/(x^2-1)$.

Prove $[x^5+2x^2-3]=[x-1]$ and explain why this is not an ambient polynomial identity.

Give an ideal-membership certificate for the difference.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The factorization and quotient conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer distinguishes quotient equality from ambient equality.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The difference is $(x^5+2x^2-3)-(x-1)=x^5-x+2x^2-2=(x^2-1)(x^3+x+2)$. Hence the difference lies in $(x^2-1)$, so the classes are equal. The two ambient polynomials are not identical because their difference is a nonzero multiple of $x^2-1$.

lessons.title: Prime ideals, maximal ideals, and quotient tests
lessons.summary: Classify proper ideals as prime or maximal by analyzing zero divisors and inverses in their quotient rings.
objectives: Classify proper ideals as prime or maximal by analyzing zero divisors and inverses in their quotient rings.

content.markdown:
## Read an ideal through what survives after quotienting

A prime ideal forbids a product from entering the ideal unless one factor already lies there. A maximal ideal cannot be enlarged without becoming the whole ring. Quotients translate these order-theoretic definitions into familiar ring properties.

## Reactivate domains and fields

Week 21 proved that a field has no nonzero zero divisors. It also distinguished a domain, where nonzero products stay nonzero, from a field, where every nonzero element is invertible.

## Prime ideals correspond to quotient domains

A proper ideal $P\subsetneq A$ is prime when $ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$. This is equivalent to $A/P$ being an integral domain.

Indeed, $[a][b]=[0]$ means $ab\in P$. Primality says one factor class is zero, which is exactly the absence of nonzero zero divisors.

content.title: Detect a nonprime ideal
content.introMarkdown: Prove it is not prime in two matching ways.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check that both factors are genuinely outside the ideal.

A zero product is evidence against primality only when both factor classes are nonzero.

Verify factor nonmembership before passing to the quotient classes.

## Maximal ideals correspond to quotient fields

A proper ideal $M$ is maximal when the only ideals containing it are $M$ and $A$. This is equivalent to $A/M$ being a field.

To prove the equivalence, use the correspondence between ideals of $A/M$ and ideals $J$ with $M\subseteq J\subseteq A$. Maximality says the quotient has only the zero ideal and the whole ring as ideals. A nonzero commutative ring has exactly those two ideals precisely when every nonzero element is invertible, so it is a field.

Every maximal ideal is prime because every field is a domain. The converse can fail: a quotient may be a domain without being a field.

content.title: Separate prime from maximal
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $(0)$ is prime but not maximal.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether domain and field were treated as the same property.

Prime and maximal ideals encode different strengths of quotient structure.

State the quotient, test zero divisors, then test inverses separately.

## Complete worked model

Let $k$ be a field and consider $(x-2)\subseteq k[x]$.

Prove that $(x-2)$ is maximal and therefore prime.

### Strategy

Construct a quotient map directly from evaluation at $2$ and prove that it is a bijective ring homomorphism.

### Hypotheses

Define $\Theta:k[x]/(x-2)\to k$ by $\Theta([f])=f(2)$.

### Intermediate claims

The map $\Theta$ is well defined, preserves the ring operations, is surjective, and is injective.

### Justification

If $[f]=[g]$, then $f-g$ is divisible by $x-2$, so $f(2)=g(2)$. Evaluation preserves sums, products, and $1$. Every scalar is the image of its constant class. If $\Theta([f])=0$, then $f(2)=0$, so the factor theorem gives $f\in(x-2)$ and $[f]=[0]$. Thus $\Theta$ is bijective.

### Conclusion

The ideal $(x-2)$ is maximal and prime.

## Classify a nilpotent quotient

A nonzero nilpotent element is automatically a zero divisor. Thus a quotient relation such as $[x]^2=0$ often gives the fastest proof that an ideal is not prime.

content.title: Use a nilpotent class
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $I$ is not prime.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Check whether nonzeroness of $[x]$ was actually proved.

A nilpotent witness fails if its class was already zero.

Prove $x\notin(x^2)$ before computing the square of its class.

## Generated ideals in two variables

The quotient by $(x,y)$ sets both variables equal to zero. Evaluation at the origin turns that observation into an isomorphism with the coefficient field.

content.title: Prove the origin ideal is maximal
content.introMarkdown: Prove $M$ is maximal.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Naming a plausible kernel is not enough; both inclusions must be justified.

Divide successively by $x-1$ and $y+2$, then prove the induced evaluation map is bijective.

## Independent quotient classification

Use the quotient criterion that matches the requested conclusion. A maximality proof needs a field quotient; a primality proof needs only a domain quotient.
