**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare RES.18-012, Spring 2022.

**Exact locator:** Lecture 19 §§19.3–19.4 and Lecture 20 §§20.1–20.3, pp. 89–92: free-module maps, generators, relations, and quotient presentations in MIT 18.702 Algebra II Student Notes, Spring 2022.

**Reading purpose:** Consolidate the distinctions between a generating family, a basis, a relation module, and a quotient presentation.
Week 25 will invert the element $a$. The weight bookkeeping established here will make the resulting Laurent terms and solved equations auditable.
Week 24 is complete when the exact equations, quotient grading, and scaling interpretation can be reconstructed without confusing weight with ordinary degree.

activities.title: Repair four false statements
activities.promptMarkdown:
Audit: (i) every cyclic module is free; (ii) every additive subgroup is a submodule; (iii) $a^2e-1$ is not homogeneous; (iv) weight-zero monomials have ordinary degree zero.

Refute or qualify every statement with an exact reason or counterexample.

Use a different definition or example for each repair.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: (i) False: $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is cyclic as a $\mathbb Z$-module but not free because it has torsion. (ii) False: a subgroup must also be closed under every scalar; for example $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q$ is an additive subgroup but not a $\mathbb Q$-submodule. (iii) It is homogeneous of weight zero because both terms have weight zero, though not ordinarily homogeneous because their ordinary degrees are three and zero. (iv) False: $ad$ and $a^2e$ have weight zero but ordinary degrees two and three.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All four statements are repaired with valid evidence.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each correction identifies the exact definition that was confused.

activities.title: Audit the small-ring model
activities.promptMarkdown:
In the same ring, add the homogeneous relation $x^2y^2-1$.

Explain why the ideal $(xy-1,x^2y^2-1)$ is homogeneous and why the second generator is redundant.

Prove both claims by weights and an explicit ideal identity.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Homogeneity and redundancy are both proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response uses weights for structure and an ideal identity for equality.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Both $xy-1$ and $x^2y^2-1$ have weight zero, so the ideal they generate is homogeneous. Moreover $x^2y^2-1=(xy-1)(xy+1)$, so the second generator lies in $(xy-1)$. The reverse containment is immediate because $xy-1$ is one of the two generators. Hence $(xy-1,x^2y^2-1)=(xy-1)$.

activities.title: Prove the component maps are inverse
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\bigoplus_mA_m$. Let $\Phi(a)$ be the finite family of homogeneous components of $a$, and let $\Psi((a_m))=\sum_ma_m$.

Prove that $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are mutual inverses.

Write and justify both compositions.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both compositions and the role of directness are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The prior inverse-proof template is transferred to a new graded object.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $a\in A$, uniqueness of its homogeneous decomposition shows that the components of $\sum_ma_m=a$ are exactly the original components, so $\Psi(\Phi(a))=a$. Conversely, for a finite-support family $(a_m)$ with $a_m\in A_m$, the homogeneous components of its sum are exactly the $a_m$, again by directness. Hence $\Phi(\Psi((a_m)))=(a_m)$. Both compositions are identities, so the maps are mutual inverses.

activities.title: Compute the algebraic differential of multiplication
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $M:A_r\times A_s\to A_{r+s}$ be multiplication. Take $x,\dot x\in A_r$ and $y,\dot y\in A_s$.

Derive the algebraic differential $dM_{(x,y)}(\dot x,\dot y)=\dot xy+x\dot y$ and verify its weight.

Expand with a formal parameter $\varepsilon$ satisfying $\varepsilon^2=0$; do not invoke an unspecified limit or topology.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The derivative and the graded target are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The first-order coefficient is computed algebraically, while the weight statement uses the grading law.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In the dual-number extension with $\varepsilon^2=0$, $(x+\varepsilon\dot x)(y+\varepsilon\dot y)=xy+\varepsilon(\dot xy+x\dot y)$. The coefficient of $\varepsilon$ is therefore the algebraic differential $dM_{(x,y)}(\dot x,\dot y)=\dot xy+x\dot y$. Both products have weight $r+s$, because $\dot x,x\in A_r$ and $\dot y,y\in A_s$. Thus the differential lands in $A_{r+s}$.

activities.title: Locate the domain hypothesis in a module proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $R$ be a domain and $M=R^n$. Suppose $0\ne r\in R$ and $rx=0$ in $M$.

Prove $x=0$ and show why the claim can fail over a non-domain.

Use coordinates, then give one explicit counterexample over $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Coordinate cancellation and the counterexample are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The hypothesis is tied to the exact inference it supports.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Write $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. The equality $rx=0$ gives $rx_i=0$ for every $i$. Since $R$ is a domain and $r\ne0$, each $x_i=0$, so $x=0$. Over $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$, take $r=[2]$ and the nonzero vector $x=([3],0,\ldots,0)$; then $rx=0$. Thus the domain hypothesis is essential.

activities.title: Separate weight from divisibility
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $p,q,r$ be homogeneous elements of the UFD $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]$, with $\gcd(p,q)=1$ and $p\mid qr$.

Prove $p\mid r$ and explain why homogeneity alone does not prove it.

Use irreducible multiplicities and then state the role of the grading.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The divisibility proof and the boundary of grading information are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response assigns distinct logical roles to factorization and weight.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Factor $p$ into irreducibles. Coprimality says that none of its irreducible factors occurs in $q$. Since the full multiplicity of every factor of $p$ occurs in $qr$, it must occur in $r$. Hence $p\mid r$. Homogeneity only records weights and shows that weights add under products; it does not control common irreducible factors. The divisibility conclusion therefore comes from the UFD and coprimality hypotheses, not from the grading.

activities.title: Write the Week 24 synthesis proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work with $A=\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]$, the Week 24 weights, and the relations $F$ and $G$.

Give a coherent proof connecting modules, the grading, homogeneous relations, the quotient, and rescaling invariance.

Write five short labelled paragraphs, one for each logical step, and end with the ordinary-degree contrast.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All five structural steps and the exact degree contrast are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument progresses from definitions to proofs and keeps later geometry outside the claim.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Modules: each $A_m$ is a complex vector space and therefore a $\mathbb C$-module; the whole ring is also a module over itself. Grading: $A_m$ is spanned by monomials $a^ib^jc^kd^\ell e^q$ with $i-\ell-2q=m$. Monomial uniqueness gives $A=\bigoplus_mA_m$, and exponent addition gives $A_rA_s\subseteq A_{r+s}$. Relations: every term of $F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $G=ad+bc-1$ has weight zero. Quotient: since $F$ and $G$ are homogeneous, $(F,G)$ is a homogeneous ideal, so the images of the $A_m$ grade $A/(F,G)$. Rescaling: substituting $(\lambda a,b,c,\lambda^{-1}d,\lambda^{-2}e)$ multiplies a weight-$m$ monomial by $\lambda^m$; hence $F$ and $G$ are invariant. This weight differs from ordinary degree: $a^2e$ and $ad$ both have weight zero but ordinary degrees three and two, while $e^2$ has degree two and weight minus four.

lessons.title: Localization as a universal ring construction
lessons.summary: Construct a localization, calculate with its fractions, and use its universal property without silently assuming that the source ring is a domain.
objectives: Construct a localization, calculate with its fractions, and use its universal property without silently assuming that the source ring is a domain.

content.markdown:
## Permit one chosen division, and no more

A fraction field inverts every nonzero element of a domain. Localization is more selective: choose a multiplicative set $S\subseteq A$, and require every element of $S$ to become a unit. Other elements may become units as a consequence; the construction imposes no extra relations beyond those forced by this requirement. For one element $f$, the standard choice is $S=\{1,f,f^2,\ldots\}$, and the resulting ring is written $A_f$.

This construction is algebraic, not merely symbolic. Fractions are identified by a precise equivalence relation, and every homomorphism that already makes the chosen denominators invertible factors uniquely through the localization.

## Reactivate rings, quotients, and legal cancellation

Week 21 separated domains from rings with zero divisors. Week 22 established universal properties for quotient rings. Week 23 made polynomial divisibility precise. Those distinctions remain active: in a general ring, equality of fractions may require an extra power of the denominator because ordinary cross-cancellation can fail.

## Fractions over a general ring

Let $S$ be a multiplicative subset of a commutative ring $A$. A symbol $x/s$ uses $x\in A$ and $s\in S$. Define

$$\frac{x}{s}=\frac{y}{t}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u(tx-sy)=0\text{ for some }u\in S.$$

If $A$ is a domain and $0\notin S$, this reduces to $tx=sy$. The extra factor $u$ is essential when zero divisors are present.

content.title: Test equality of fractions with zero divisors
content.introMarkdown: Decide whether the two fractions are equal by applying the definition exactly.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first place where equality is decided from the cross-difference alone or from only one multiplier.

In a ring with zero divisors, a later denominator power may annihilate a nonzero cross-difference.

List all elements of the stated multiplicative set and test the defining annihilation condition.

## Arithmetic and the canonical map

Addition and multiplication use the familiar formulas

$$\frac{x}{s}+\frac{y}{t}=\frac{tx+sy}{st},\qquad \frac{x}{s}\frac{y}{t}=\frac{xy}{st}.$$

The canonical homomorphism $\iota:A\to S^{-1}A$ sends $x$ to $x/1$. It need not be injective: $x/1=0/1$ exactly when some $u\in S$ annihilates $x$.

content.title: Compute a localization kernel
content.introMarkdown: Determine the kernel of $A\to A_f$ and identify the resulting ring.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first assertion that the canonical map is injective merely because it is called canonical.

Localization can erase elements supported where the inverted function vanishes.

Compute $f^n(m,n)$ first, then build both directions of the proposed isomorphism.

## Complete worked model

Let $f\in A$, let $B$ be a ring, and let $\varphi:A\to B$ be a homomorphism such that $\varphi(f)$ is a unit.

Construct the unique homomorphism $\widetilde\varphi:A_f\to B$ extending $\varphi$.

### Strategy

The image of a fraction is forced by the requirement that $f/1$ become invertible; prove that the forced formula is well-defined.

### Hypotheses

Elements of $A_f$ have the form $x/f^n$, and equality permits annihilation by a further power of $f$.

### Intermediate claims

Define $\widetilde\varphi(x/f^n)=\varphi(x)\varphi(f)^{-n}$. If $x/f^n=y/f^m$, then $f^N(f^mx-f^ny)=0$ for some $N$.

### Justification

Applying $\varphi$ and multiplying by the inverse of $\varphi(f)^{N+m+n}$ gives $\varphi(x)\varphi(f)^{-n}=\varphi(y)\varphi(f)^{-m}$. The fraction formulas then prove that $\widetilde\varphi$ is a homomorphism.

### Conclusion

The extension exists. It is unique because any extension must send $x/f^n$ to $\varphi(x)\varphi(f)^{-n}$.

content.title: Transfer the universal-property proof
content.introMarkdown: Determine whether $\varphi$ extends to $A_f$ and, if it does, compute the image of $(x+2)/(2x)^3$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first extension claim made without proving that the chosen denominator maps to a unit.

The universal property applies precisely to maps that already allow the requested division.

Evaluate $f$ under the original map, prove its image is invertible, and only then evaluate the fraction.

## Principal localization as adjoining an inverse

The universal property gives a concrete presentation

$$A_f\cong A[u]/(fu-1).$$

The class of $u$ is the inverse of $f$. Conversely, the canonical image of $f$ is a unit in $A_f$, so the quotient presentation and the fraction construction factor uniquely through one another.

content.title: Prove an inverse-adjoining presentation
content.introMarkdown: Prove that the two rings are isomorphic.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first map that is named without checking its relation or its denominator-unit condition.

An isomorphism requires two well-defined maps and identity composites, not a resemblance between symbols.

Check $6u-1$, check that $6$ is a unit, and state what each composite fixes.

## Independent localization proof

A complete localization argument has four visible parts: the multiplicative set, the fraction relation, the unit created in the target, and the universal factorization.

Do not replace the construction by the phrase “allow denominators.” The allowable denominators and the equality rule are the mathematical content.

content.title: Construct a new principal localization
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $A_{\bar x}\cong k[x,x^{-1}]$ and identify the kernel of $A\to A_{\bar x}$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first point where $\bar y=0$ is asserted without multiplying by the newly available inverse, or where the kernel is guessed without a normal form.

The calculation is the first precise example of localization forgetting boundary-supported information.

Derive $\bar y=0$, build the two maps, then decompose a general residue class to prove the kernel equality.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-25, source lines 798 to 806.

**Resource version:** J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, version 4.01.

**Exact locator:** §5 “Rings of fractions,” pp. 18–19: the fraction equivalence relation, Proposition 5.1 universal property, and Example 5.2 principal localization in J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, version 4.01.

**Reading purpose:** Compare the lesson's construction and universal-property proof with the syllabus-named concise reference.
Day 2 specializes the construction to a polynomial ring and proves that inverting $a$ produces a Laurent-polynomial ring.
Day 1 is complete when equality, arithmetic, the canonical kernel, and the universal property can all be stated without assuming a domain unless one is given.

activities.title: Test equality of fractions with zero divisors
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ and $S=\{1,[2],[4]\}$. Compare $[1]/[1]$ and $[3]/[1]$ in $S^{-1}A$.

Decide whether the two fractions are equal by applying the definition exactly.

Compute their cross-difference and exhibit, or rule out, an annihilating element of $S$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The cross-difference and every possible multiplier in the finite multiplicative set are checked correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response uses the localization equivalence relation rather than informal cancellation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The cross-difference is $[1]-[3]=[4]$. The only possible multipliers are the three elements of $S$: $[1][4]=[4]$, $[2][4]=[8]=[2]$, and $[4][4]=[16]=[4]$. None is zero in $A$. Therefore no element of $S$ annihilates the cross-difference, and the two fractions are not equal. Checking only one multiplier would not have been enough.

activities.title: Compute a localization kernel
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z$ and localize at $f=(1,0)$.

Determine the kernel of $A\to A_f$ and identify the resulting ring.

Use powers of $f$ to test the kernel, then define an explicit isomorphism.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel and the explicit target ring are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument connects annihilation by a denominator power to the structural isomorphism.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $f^n=f$ for $n\ge1$, an element $(m,n)$ maps to zero exactly when $f(m,n)=(m,0)=(0,0)$, so the kernel is $\{0\}\times\mathbb Z$. The map $A_f\to\mathbb Z$ given by $(m,n)/f^k\mapsto m$ is well-defined and inverse to $m\mapsto(m,0)/1$. Hence $A_f\cong\mathbb Z$: localization discards the second factor.

activities.title: Transfer the universal-property proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\mathbb Z[x]$, $f=2x$, and let $\varphi:A\to\mathbb Q(t)$ send $x$ to $t$.

Determine whether $\varphi$ extends to $A_f$ and, if it does, compute the image of $(x+2)/(2x)^3$.

Check the unit hypothesis before applying the forced fraction formula.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The unit condition and the fraction image are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response checks the hypothesis before invoking universality.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The element $\varphi(2x)=2t$ is nonzero and therefore invertible in the field $\mathbb Q(t)$, so the extension exists uniquely. It sends $(x+2)/(2x)^3$ to $(t+2)/(2t)^3=(t+2)/(8t^3)$.

activities.title: Prove an inverse-adjoining presentation
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\mathbb Z$ and $f=6$. Compare $\mathbb Z_6$ with $\mathbb Z[u]/(6u-1)$.

Prove that the two rings are isomorphic.

Define maps in both directions by their action on the generators and verify both compositions.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both maps and both identity checks are valid.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The quotient and localization universal properties are used in the correct directions.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Send the class of an integer $n$ to $n/1$ and the class of $u$ to $1/6$; the relation $6u-1$ maps to zero, so this gives $\alpha:\mathbb Z[u]/(6u-1)\to\mathbb Z_6$. Conversely, the image of $6$ in the quotient is a unit with inverse $u$, so the universal property gives $\beta:\mathbb Z_6\to\mathbb Z[u]/(6u-1)$. Both composites fix the integer classes and the chosen inverse of $6$, hence are identities.

activities.title: Construct a new principal localization
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=k[x,y]/(xy)$ and let $\bar x$ be the class of $x$.

Prove that $A_{\bar x}\cong k[x,x^{-1}]$ and identify the kernel of $A\to A_{\bar x}$.

Use the relation $\bar x\bar y=0$, the fact that $\bar x$ becomes a unit, and explicit maps.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The localized relation, two maps, and exact kernel are all correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response shows how making one element invertible erases the component supported on its vanishing locus.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In $A_{\bar x}$, multiplying $\bar x\bar y=0$ by $\bar x^{-1}$ gives $\bar y=0$. Thus the localized ring is generated by $\bar x$ and its inverse. The map $k[x,x^{-1}]\to A_{\bar x}$ sending $x$ to $\bar x/1$ is surjective. Conversely, $A\to k[x,x^{-1}]$ sending $\bar x$ to $x$ and $\bar y$ to $0$ respects $xy=0$ and sends $\bar x$ to a unit, so it extends to the inverse map. An element of $A$ has a unique form $p(x)+yq(y)$ with $p\in k[x]$ and arbitrary $q\in k[y]$; after localization the second summand dies, so the kernel is the ideal $(\bar y)$.

lessons.title: From polynomial fractions to Laurent polynomials
lessons.summary: Prove the syllabus isomorphism between a localized polynomial ring and a Laurent-polynomial ring, including well-defined maps, surjectivity, and uniqueness.
objectives: Prove the syllabus isomorphism between a localized polynomial ring and a Laurent-polynomial ring, including well-defined maps, surjectivity, and uniqueness.

content.markdown:
## A Laurent exponent is a recorded denominator

Inverting the variable $a$ in a polynomial ring permits finitely many negative powers of $a$ while leaving the other variables polynomial. The result is the Laurent-polynomial ring

$$\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},y,z].$$

Here $y$ and $z$ are dummy indeterminates in the syllabus's ring exercise. They are not the later normal-jet coordinates, which are introduced only after the boundary behavior has been studied.

## Use the universal property twice

Day 1 proved that a map out of $A_a$ is forced once the target makes $a$ invertible. Week 8 supplied the discipline of checking both compositions. Today combines those ideas to prove an actual ring isomorphism rather than merely writing matching notation.

## What the target ring contains

A Laurent polynomial in $a$ is a finite sum $\sum_{n=m}^N a^n p_n(y,z)$ with $m\in\mathbb Z$. Only the exponent of $a$ may be negative; $y^{-1}$ and $z^{-1}$ are not present unless they are separately inverted.

Equivalently, every element can be written $a^{-r}P(a,y,z)$ for some $r\ge0$ and $P\in\mathbb C[a,y,z]$.

content.title: Find a common Laurent denominator
content.introMarkdown: Write $h$ as one element of the form $P(a,y,z)/a^r$ with polynomial numerator.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first exponent that remains negative after multiplying by the proposed denominator.

The common-denominator normal form connects Laurent polynomials with localization fractions.

Locate the most negative exponent of $a$, negate it, and multiply every term by that power.

## The forward map is forced

Let $P=\mathbb C[a,y,z]$. The inclusion $P\hookrightarrow\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},y,z]$ sends $a$ to a unit. The universal property therefore gives

$$\Phi:P_a\longrightarrow\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},y,z],\qquad \Phi\!\left(\frac{F}{a^n}\right)=a^{-n}F.$$

Because every Laurent polynomial has a common power of $a$ as denominator, $\Phi$ is surjective.

content.title: Prove surjectivity from finite support
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $h$ lies in the image of $\Phi$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first claim that an infinite or unspecified denominator clears all negative exponents.

Surjectivity depends on Laurent polynomials having finite support.

Name the least occurring exponent and construct the preimage from it.

## Complete worked model

Compare $P_a$ with $L=\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},y,z]$.

Construct $\Psi:L\to P_a$ and prove that $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are mutual inverses.

### Strategy

Define the inverse on the Laurent generators, verify the inverse relation, then check both composites on generating sets.

### Hypotheses

The element $a/1$ is a unit in $P_a$ with inverse $1/a$.

### Intermediate claims

Define $\Psi(a)=a/1$, $\Psi(a^{-1})=1/a$, $\Psi(y)=y/1$, and $\Psi(z)=z/1$. The relation $aa^{-1}=1$ is preserved.

### Justification

The composite $\Psi\Phi$ fixes every $F/a^n$, since it sends $a^{-n}F$ back to $F/a^n$. The composite $\Phi\Psi$ fixes the four Laurent generators $a,a^{-1},y,z$, hence fixes every Laurent polynomial.

### Conclusion

$$\mathbb C[a,y,z]_a\cong\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},y,z].$$

content.title: Audit the inverse proof
content.introMarkdown: Write the analogous inverse maps and verify both compositions.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first composite checked only on the polynomial subring while omitting the inverse generator.

Fixing $t$ and $u$ does not determine a Laurent-ring map unless the image of $t^{-1}$ is also controlled.

Include $t^{-1}$ in the generating set and check a general localized fraction in the other direction.

## Uniqueness of Laurent normal form

Because $P=\mathbb C[a,y,z]$ is a domain, the canonical map $P\to P_a$ is injective. Consequently, if $F/a^r=G/a^s$, then $a^sF=a^rG$ in $P$.

A Laurent polynomial also has a unique coefficient expansion by the monomials $a^iy^jz^k$ with $i\in\mathbb Z$ and $j,k\ge0$. This is stronger than merely knowing that one common-denominator expression exists.

content.title: Prove uniqueness after clearing powers
content.introMarkdown: Prove $F=0$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first cancellation of $a^N$ without naming that the polynomial ring is a domain.

Localization is injective here because no nonzero polynomial is killed by a power of $a$.

Write the annihilation equation supplied by fraction equality, then invoke the domain property.

## Independent Laurent-ring isomorphism

The syllabus statement is a theorem with a proof, not a notation convention. The proof must establish existence and uniqueness of the Laurent representation or, equivalently, construct inverse maps.

The variables $y,z$ in this ring calculation remain algebraically independent. No claim about the later global coordinates on $X$ has been made.

content.title: Prove a three-variable localization theorem
content.introMarkdown: Prove $R_g\cong k[r,r^{-1},s,t]$ and explain why inverting $r^2$ also inverts $r$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first assertion that $r$ is invertible without exhibiting its inverse, or the first composite that omits $g^{-1}$.

Localizing at a power and localizing at its base element produce the same principal open set, but that fact requires proof.

Compute $r(r/g)$, then verify the inverse maps on the Laurent and localized generators.

## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-25, source lines 798 to 806.

**Resource version:** J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, version 4.01.

**Exact locator:** §5, Example 5.2 and Proposition 5.3, pp. 19–20: principal localization, its fraction normal form, and the presentation A[X]/(1-hX) ≅ A_h in J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, version 4.01.

**Reading purpose:** Connect the explicit Laurent-polynomial proof with the universal inverse-adjoining presentation.
Day 3 applies the Laurent chart to the two supplied equations of $X$ and proves the resulting coordinate-ring isomorphism.
Day 2 is complete when the Laurent target, both maps, both composites, and the boundary between dummy variables and later normal-jet coordinates are all explicit.

activities.title: Find a common Laurent denominator
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $h=a^{-3}y^2+2a^{-1}z+a^4yz-7$.

Write $h$ as one element of the form $P(a,y,z)/a^r$ with polynomial numerator.

Choose the smallest nonnegative common denominator exponent and compute $P$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The smallest exponent is $r=3$. Multiplying by $a^3$ gives $P=y^2+2a^2z+a^7yz-7a^3$, so $h=(y^2+2a^2z+a^7yz-7a^3)/a^3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The least common power and numerator are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response uses finiteness of the Laurent support to choose one denominator.

activities.title: Prove surjectivity from finite support
activities.promptMarkdown:
Take an arbitrary $h=\sum_{n=m}^N a^np_n(y,z)$ in the Laurent ring.

Prove that $h$ lies in the image of $\Phi$.

Handle separately the cases $m\ge0$ and $m<0$, and display a preimage.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: An explicit preimage is supplied for every Laurent polynomial.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses the finite lower bound of the exponent support.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $m\ge0$, then $h\in P$ and $h=\Phi(h/1)$. If $m<0$, put $r=-m$. Then $F=a^rh=\sum_{n=m}^N a^{n+r}p_n(y,z)$ has only nonnegative powers of $a$, so $F\in P$, and $h=F/a^r=\Phi(F/a^r)$. Hence $\Phi$ is surjective.

activities.title: Audit the inverse proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Replace $P$ by $k[t,u]$ and invert $t$.

Write the analogous inverse maps and verify both compositions.

Your proof must state what happens to $t^{-1}$ and to a general fraction.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both maps and both composite checks are complete.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof identifies generating sets on each side and verifies the inverse relation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The forward map $k[t,u]_t\to k[t,t^{-1},u]$ sends $F/t^n$ to $t^{-n}F$. The reverse map sends $t$ to $t/1$, $t^{-1}$ to $1/t$, and $u$ to $u/1$; it is well-defined because $(t/1)(1/t)=1$. The first composite sends $F/t^n$ to itself. The second fixes $t,t^{-1},u$, which generate the Laurent ring. Thus the maps are inverse.

activities.title: Prove uniqueness after clearing powers
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $F/a^r=0$ in $P_a$, where $F\in P$ and $r\ge0$.

Prove $F=0$.

Use the general equality rule and the fact that $P$ is a domain.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The equality rule and domain hypothesis are used correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response assigns injectivity to the absence of $a$-torsion rather than to notation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Equality with $0/1$ means that $a^N F=0$ in $P$ for some $N\ge0$. The polynomial $a^N$ is nonzero, and $P$ is a domain, so $F=0$. Thus the canonical map is injective and a nonzero polynomial cannot disappear merely by inverting $a$.

activities.title: Prove a three-variable localization theorem
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $R=k[r,s,t]$ and localize at $g=r^2$.

Prove $R_g\cong k[r,r^{-1},s,t]$ and explain why inverting $r^2$ also inverts $r$.

Construct inverse maps and identify an explicit inverse of $r$ in $R_g$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The inverse of $r$, both maps, and both composites are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response derives the stronger unit statement from the element actually inverted.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In $R_g$, the element $r$ is a unit because $r\cdot(r/g)=r^2/g=1$; its inverse is $r/g$. Hence the inclusion $R\to k[r,r^{-1},s,t]$, which makes $g=r^2$ invertible, extends to $\Phi:R_g\to k[r,r^{-1},s,t]$. Conversely, sending $r^{-1}$ to $r/g$ defines $\Psi:k[r,r^{-1},s,t]\to R_g$. The composite $\Phi\Psi$ fixes $r,r^{-1},s,t$, and $\Psi\Phi$ fixes $R$ and $g^{-1}$, so both are identities. Therefore the rings are isomorphic.

lessons.title: Solve the defining equations after inverting a
lessons.summary: Solve the two supplied equations in the localized quotient and prove the exact chart isomorphism by constructing both ring maps.
objectives: Solve the two supplied equations in the localized quotient and prove the exact chart isomorphism by constructing both ring maps.

content.markdown:
## Turn two relations into two solved variables

Set

$$F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,\qquad G=ad+bc-1,$$

and let $R=\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(F,G)$. The syllabus labels the common-zero locus by $X$. On the chart where $a\ne0$, the class of $a$ is invertible, so $G$ determines $d$ and then $F$ determines $e$.

The calculation proves a statement about the localized quotient $R_a$. It does not yet prove a global affine-space isomorphism, because every division by $a$ excludes the divisor $a=0$.

## Keep quotient equality visible

Week 22 established that $F=G=0$ means equality of residue classes in $R$. Day 2 established how powers of $a$ become legal denominators. Every solved formula today is therefore an identity in $R_a$, not a literal identity in the ambient polynomial ring.

## Solve the linear relation first

In $R_a$, the relation $G=0$ gives $ad+bc=1$. Multiplying by $a^{-1}$ yields

$$d=\frac{1-bc}{a}.$$

The order matters: $G$ is linear in $d$, and its coefficient is exactly the element that has become a unit.

content.title: Solve a related localized relation
content.introMarkdown: Solve for $r$ and verify the formula in $S_p$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first division performed before stating that its denominator is a unit in the localized ring.

The formula is legal only on the chosen principal open chart.

Write the quotient relation, name the unit, multiply by its inverse, and substitute back.

## Substitute before solving the second relation

Insert $d=(1-bc)/a$ into $F=0$. Then

$$abd=b(1-bc)=b-b^2c,$$

so

$$a^2e=1+b-2b^2c,\qquad e=\frac{1+b-2b^2c}{a^2}.$$

The coefficient of $e$ is $a^2$, also a unit after localizing at $a$.

content.title: Audit the two substitution signs
content.introMarkdown: Locate the first algebraic error and give the correct numerator.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first lost minus sign or the first failure to recognize that $cb^2=b^2c$.

A single sign error changes the chart map and invalidates both defining equations.

Write $abd$ on one line, negate it on the next, and only then collect commutative monomials.

## Complete worked model

Let $P=\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},b,c]$ and $R=\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(F,G)$.

Prove $R_a\cong P$.

### Strategy

Map the free chart coordinates into $R_a$, build the reverse map from the solved formulas, verify the relations, and check the generators in both composites.

### Hypotheses

In $R_a$, $a$ is a unit. In $P$, define $d_0=(1-bc)/a$ and $e_0=(1+b-2b^2c)/a^2$.

### Intermediate claims

The inclusion of $a^{\pm1},b,c$ gives $\alpha:P\to R_a$. Substitution gives $ad_0+bc-1=0$ and $a^2e_0-abd_0+cb^2-1=0$, so the ambient map sending $d\mapsto d_0$ and $e\mapsto e_0$ descends and localizes to $\beta:R_a\to P$.

### Justification

The composite $\beta\alpha$ fixes $a^{\pm1},b,c$. The composite $\alpha\beta$ fixes $a^{\pm1},b,c$ and sends $d,e$ to the solved expressions, which equal their original classes by $G=0$ and $F=0$ in $R_a$.

### Conclusion

$$R_a\cong\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},b,c].$$

content.title: Verify the reverse map completely
content.introMarkdown: Verify separately that both $G$ and $F$ map to zero.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first defining relation declared zero without an explicit substitution calculation.

A proposed map out of a quotient exists only when every defining relation maps to zero.

Evaluate $G$ first, then list the two substituted terms in $F$ before collecting them.

## What has and has not been proved

The isomorphism $R_a\cong\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},b,c]$ proves that the chart where $a$ is invertible has three algebraically independent coordinates $a,b,c$, with $a\ne0$.

It does not prove $R\cong\mathbb C[a,b,c]$. The formulas for $d$ and $e$ contain $a^{-1}$ and $a^{-2}$, so they do not define polynomial functions on the missing divisor $a=0$.

The later coordinates conventionally called $y$ and $z$ are designed to repair this boundary problem. They are previewed here only as a destination, not used as established global coordinates.

content.title: Reject a global overclaim
content.introMarkdown: Explain exactly why the conclusion does not follow from the displayed isomorphism.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first use of a localized formula at $a=0$ or the first claim that a dense/open isomorphism determines the boundary.

The entire later normal-jet construction exists because the missing divisor contains information not visible after localization.

State the domain $a\ne0$ beside every divided formula and separate the chart conclusion from the global theorem.

## Independent solved-chart proof

The proof pattern is reusable: order the equations so that each next coefficient is a unit; solve; define the reverse map; check every relation; then verify both composites.

Dimension language is not a substitute for the maps. The exact coordinate formulas are the certificate.

A genuinely analogous target proves the method was understood rather than copied from $X$.

**Reading purpose:** Place the explicit quotient calculation inside the standard localization and ideal-extension framework.
Day 4 translates the localized coordinate ring into the geometric principal open subset $X_a=D_X(a)$.
Day 3 is complete when the two solved formulas, the reverse-map relation checks, both composites, and the failure of the global inference are all explicit.

activities.title: Solve a related localized relation
activities.promptMarkdown:

Solve for $r$ and verify the formula in $S_p$.

Derive the formula from the residue-class relation and substitute it back.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The solved expression and verification are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The relation is $pr=1-q^2$ in $S$. Since $p$ is a unit in $S_p$, multiplying by $p^{-1}$ gives $r=(1-q^2)/p$. Substitution gives $p(1-q^2)/p+q^2-1=1-q^2+q^2-1=0$, so the formula satisfies the relation.

activities.title: Audit the two substitution signs
activities.promptMarkdown:
Starting from $F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1=0$ and $d=(1-bc)/a$, a draft claims $a^2e=1-b$.

Locate the first algebraic error and give the correct numerator.

Expand the term $-abd$ separately and combine both $b^2c$ terms.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $abd=b(1-bc)=b-b^2c$, the term $-abd$ is $-b+b^2c$. Hence $0=a^2e-b+b^2c+cb^2-1=a^2e-b+2b^2c-1$. Therefore $a^2e=1+b-2b^2c$, not $1-b$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both signs and the doubled $b^2c$ term are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response isolates the substituted product before rearranging.

activities.title: Verify the reverse map completely
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use $d_0=(1-bc)/a$ and $e_0=(1+b-2b^2c)/a^2$ in $P$.

Verify separately that both $G$ and $F$ map to zero.

Show every cancellation; do not cite the solved formulas as their own proof.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both relation images are expanded and vanish exactly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response proves well-definedness before using the quotient map.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $G$, $ad_0+bc-1=(1-bc)+bc-1=0$. For $F$, $a^2e_0=1+b-2b^2c$ and $abd_0=b(1-bc)=b-b^2c$. Therefore $a^2e_0-abd_0+cb^2-1=(1+b-2b^2c)-(b-b^2c)+b^2c-1=0$. Thus both relations lie in the kernel, so the reverse map descends to the quotient.

activities.title: Reject a global overclaim
activities.promptMarkdown:
A proof concludes from $R_a\cong\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},b,c]$ that $R\cong\mathbb C[a,b,c]$.

Explain exactly why the conclusion does not follow from the displayed isomorphism.

Name the excluded locus and identify the denominators in the solved formulas.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The excluded divisor and both denominator obstructions are identified.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes a principal-open chart from a global coordinate theorem.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Localization at $a$ describes only the principal open subset where $a$ is invertible; it removes the divisor $a=0$. The formulas $d=(1-bc)/a$ and $e=(1+b-2b^2c)/a^2$ may have poles there and therefore do not define a polynomial inverse on the whole space. A separate extension or gluing argument is required to recover the boundary, so the localized isomorphism alone cannot imply the global one.

activities.title: Construct an analogous two-equation chart
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $T=k[p,q,r,s]/(pr+q-1,\ p^2s-r-q^2)$. Localize at $p$.

Prove $T_p\cong k[p,p^{-1},q]$ by solving for $r$ and $s$.

Give both formulas, verify both relations in the target, and explain both composites.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both solved formulas, relation checks, and composite arguments are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response transfers the triangular solve-and-verify method to a nonidentical system.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: From $pr+q-1=0$, $r=(1-q)/p$. The second relation gives $p^2s=r+q^2$, so $s=(1-q+pq^2)/p^3$. Let $L=k[p,p^{-1},q]$. The inclusion of $p^{\pm1},q$ gives $L\to T_p$. Conversely send $r$ and $s$ to the displayed expressions. Then $p(1-q)/p+q-1=0$, and $p^2(1-q+pq^2)/p^3-(1-q)/p-q^2=0$, so the reverse map is well-defined. One composite fixes $p^{\pm1},q$; the other also recovers $r,s$ from the two relations. Hence the maps are inverse.

lessons.title: Principal open sets and the chart X_a
lessons.summary: Identify localization at a function with the principal open set where that function does not vanish, and state the geometric content of the solved chart without importing later global geometry.
objectives: Identify localization at a function with the principal open set where that function does not vanish, and state the geometric content of the solved chart without importing later global geometry.

content.markdown:
## The denominator names the visible region

For an affine algebraic object with ring $A$, the principal open set

$$D(f)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A:f\notin\mathfrak p\}$$

is the region where $f$ is invertible. Its ring is $A_f$. Over complex points, this says simply: retain exactly the points where the polynomial function $f$ is nonzero.

The general affine-variety and coordinate-ring dictionary is taught later. This lesson uses only the principal-open statement required by the syllabus.

## Convert algebra to a pointwise condition

Day 3 proved the localized ring isomorphism. Week 4 established inverse images and set-builder notation, while Week 22 established quotient relations. Today interprets the already-proved algebraic chart on the set of points with $a\ne0$.

## Why primes avoiding f correspond to the localization

A prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset A$ extends to a proper prime of $A_f$ exactly when $f\notin\mathfrak p$. If $f\in\mathfrak p$, then the extended ideal contains the unit $f/1$ and becomes the whole ring.

Conversely, contraction sends a prime of $A_f$ to a prime of $A$ that avoids every power of $f$. These operations are inverse.

content.title: Classify primes visible after localization
content.introMarkdown: Identify which prime ideals of $\mathbb Z$ correspond to primes after inverting $6$.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first prime retained despite containing a factor of the inverted element.

A localization removes every prime at which the denominator vanishes.

Test whether $6$ belongs to each prime ideal, then list the survivors.

## Complex points of a principal open

If $V\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ is cut out by polynomial equations, then

$$D_V(f)=\{x\in V:f(x)\ne0\}=V\setminus V(f).$$

Adjoining $f^{-1}$ deletes the points where $f$ vanishes because no complex number can be both zero and invertible.

content.title: Write a principal open as a set
content.introMarkdown: Describe $D_V(x)$ both by equations and by a one-parameter chart.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first chart that includes $t=0$ or checks only one composition.

The principal open remembers both the original equations and the nonvanishing condition.

Write $t\in\mathbb C^\times$, then compute both pointwise composites.

## Complete worked model

Let $X$ be the common-zero set of $F$ and $G$ supplied in Day 3.

Identify $X_a$ and give its explicit pointwise chart.

### Strategy

Restrict to $a\ne0$, use the solved formulas to define a forward map, and recover the free coordinates by projection.

### Hypotheses

$a\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $b,c\in\mathbb C$.

### Intermediate claims

Define $\Phi(a,b,c)=(a,b,c,(1-bc)/a,(1+b-2b^2c)/a^2)$. Day 3's substitutions prove that this point satisfies $F=G=0$. Define $\Psi(a,b,c,d,e)=(a,b,c)$ on $X_a$.

### Justification

The composite $\Psi\Phi$ is immediate. If a point lies in $X_a$, the two relations force exactly the displayed values of $d$ and $e$, so $\Phi\Psi$ returns the point.

### Conclusion

$$X_a=D_X(a)\cong\mathbb C^\times\times\mathbb C^2,$$

content.title: Verify both pointwise composites
content.introMarkdown: Prove both composites are identities and name the relation used to recover each eliminated coordinate.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first recovered coordinate asserted without citing the relation or the nonzero denominator.

The chart is a two-sided isomorphism only on the stated principal open.

Write the domain of each map, then solve $G$ and $F$ in that order during the second composite.

## Principal open is not the same as a small analytic neighborhood

The set $D(f)$ is Zariski open and usually large: it removes the entire zero locus of one function. It is not an unspecified small ball around a point.

The inverse function theorem from Week 17 produces a local analytic or differentiable graph near one regular point. Localization instead gives algebraic formulas valid simultaneously at every point of the principal open.

content.introMarkdown: State one conclusion each method gives and one conclusion it does not give.

### Use the feedback before continuing

Locate the first use of “local” that leaves its topology or domain unspecified.

Later arguments use both notions, and confusing them changes the strength of a theorem.

Write $D(x)$ beside the localization formula and a neighborhood of $(1,1)$ beside the analytic statement.

## Independent principal-open identification

To identify a principal-open chart, give the nonvanishing condition, solve only by legal units, define both directions, and check both compositions.

A ring presentation and a pointwise chart are complementary evidence. Neither is replaced by saying that the number of free symbols looks correct.

Find the first place where $u=0$ is allowed, the relation is not checked, or one composite is omitted.

**Resource version:** MIT 18.721 Algebraic Geometry notes, 26 January 2022.

**Exact locator:** §2.6 “Localization,” Proposition 2.6.1 and §§2.6.2–2.6.3, pp. 57–58: adjoining an inverse, identifying Spec(A_s) with the open locus where s does not vanish, and principal opens as a basis in MIT 18.721 Algebraic Geometry notes, 26 January 2022.

**Reading purpose:** Compare the explicit chart of $X_a$ with the standard principal-open correspondence in an official university text.
Day 5 proves by counterexample that the chart $X_a$ cannot determine how the deleted divisor $a=0$ is restored.
Day 4 is complete when $X_a$ is identified as the principal open $D_X(a)$ with an explicit two-sided chart, while Zariski-open and analytic-local conclusions remain distinct.

activities.title: Classify primes visible after localization
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider $\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb Z[1/6])$, the spectrum obtained by inverting $6$ in $\mathbb Z$.

Identify which prime ideals of $\mathbb Z$ correspond to primes after inverting $6$.

Use the condition that the prime must avoid every denominator.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Exactly the primes avoiding the denominator are retained.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response applies the extension–contraction criterion rather than using numerical intuition alone.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The prime ideals of $\mathbb Z$ are $(0)$ and $(p)$ for primes $p$. A prime survives in $\mathbb Z[1/6]$ exactly when it does not contain $6$. The ideals $(2)$ and $(3)$ contain $6$ and disappear; $(0)$ and $(p)$ for primes $p\ne2,3$ avoid $6$ and correspond to primes of the localization.

activities.title: Write a principal open as a set
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb C^2:y-x^2=0\}$ and take $f=x$.

Describe $D_V(x)$ both by equations and by a one-parameter chart.

State the excluded value and give mutually inverse point maps.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $D_V(x)=\{(x,y):y=x^2,\ x\ne0\}$. The map $\mathbb C^\times\to D_V(x)$, $t\mapsto(t,t^2)$, has inverse $(x,y)\mapsto x$. The two composites are identities because points of $V$ satisfy $y=x^2$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The set description, excluded value, and two point maps are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.title: Verify both pointwise composites
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the maps $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ above.

Prove both composites are identities and name the relation used to recover each eliminated coordinate.

Check the free-coordinate composite first, then recover $d$ from $G$ and $e$ from $F$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both composites and the equation used for each recovery are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb C^\times\times\mathbb C^2$, projection gives $\Psi\Phi(a,b,c)=(a,b,c)$. Conversely, let $(a,b,c,d,e)\in X_a$. Since $a\ne0$, $G=0$ gives $d=(1-bc)/a$. Substituting this into $F=0$ gives $e=(1+b-2b^2c)/a^2$. Therefore $\Phi\Psi(a,b,c,d,e)$ recovers all five coordinates and equals the original point.

activities.title: Separate two meanings of local
activities.promptMarkdown:
For $xy=1$, compare solving $y=x^{-1}$ on $D(x)$ with applying the implicit function theorem at $(1,1)$.

State one conclusion each method gives and one conclusion it does not give.

Name the domain of validity for both formulas.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Localization gives the algebraic formula $y=x^{-1}$ on the whole principal open $D(x)$, which here is the entire hyperbola because $x$ never vanishes there. The implicit function theorem gives a unique analytic graph only in some neighborhood of $(1,1)$. It does not by itself produce a single global algebraic formula on all of $D(x)$, while localization does not assert metric closeness or analytic estimates near a chosen point.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The two domains and conclusions are accurately separated.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response distinguishes principal-open algebra from point-local analysis.

activities.title: Identify a new principal open chart
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $Y=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb C^3:uv-w^2-1=0\}$ and localize at $u$.

Prove $Y_u\cong\mathbb C^\times\times\mathbb C$ by explicit point maps and identify its localized coordinate ring.

Use $u,w$ as free coordinates, solve for $v$, and give both algebraic and pointwise conclusions.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The solved formula, point maps, composites, and localized ring are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response proves the chart in both geometric and algebraic language.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: On $u\ne0$, the equation gives $v=(w^2+1)/u$. Define $\Phi(u,w)=(u,(w^2+1)/u,w)$ from $\mathbb C^\times\times\mathbb C$ to $Y_u$, and let $\Psi(u,v,w)=(u,w)$. Substitution shows $\Phi$ lands in $Y_u$; $\Psi\Phi$ is the identity, and the defining equation forces $\Phi\Psi$ to recover $v$. Algebraically, $\mathbb C[u,v,w]/(uv-w^2-1)$ localized at $u$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb C[u,u^{-1},w]$.

lessons.title: The missing divisor and localization synthesis
lessons.summary: Prove that a localized isomorphism does not determine the deleted divisor, reconstruct the complete Week 25 chart argument, and retrieve the exact 1-, 3-, 8-, and 16-week proof tools.
objectives: Prove that a localized isomorphism does not determine the deleted divisor, reconstruct the complete Week 25 chart argument, and retrieve the exact 1-, 3-, 8-, and 16-week proof tools.

content.markdown:
## The open chart cannot see what was deleted

Localizing at $a$ deliberately erases information supported on $a=0$. Two globally different rings can therefore have isomorphic localizations at $a$.

This is not a technical annoyance. The later construction of global coordinates on $X$ must recover exactly the boundary information that the simple formulas with $a^{-1}$ and $a^{-2}$ cannot see.

## Use a counterexample before the synthesis

First compare two explicit rings whose $a$-charts agree but whose global algebra differs. Then retrieve Week 9 at sixteen weeks, Week 17 at eight weeks, Week 22 at three weeks, and Week 24 at one week. Each review uses the earlier proof object in a new localization context.

## A concrete failure of global reconstruction

Let $A=\mathbb C[a]$ and $B=\mathbb C[a,t]/(at)$. After inverting $a$, the relation $at=0$ forces $t=0$, so

$$A_a\cong\mathbb C[a,a^{-1}]\cong B_a.$$

Globally, the rings are not isomorphic. The ring $A$ is a domain, whereas in $B$ the nonzero classes of $a$ and $t$ multiply to zero. Geometrically, $B$ contains an extra component supported on $a=0$ that disappears from the principal open.

content.title: Prove the boundary counterexample
content.introMarkdown: Prove the localizations are isomorphic and the original rings are not.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first global nonisomorphism claim made without a preserved invariant, or the first localized relation used before $a$ is made a unit.

The example is the formal reason that the $a\ne0$ chart cannot determine the divisor $a=0$.

Derive $t=0$ in the localization, then compare zero divisors in the original rings.

## Complete worked model

Let $C=\mathbb C[s]$ and $D=\mathbb C[s,t]/(s^2t)$.

Prove $C_s\cong D_s$ but $C\not\cong D$.

### Strategy

Use the unit $s$ to eliminate $t$ after localization, then exhibit a nonzero nilpotent in the global ring $D$.

### Hypotheses

The class of $st$ is nonzero in $D$ because $st\notin(s^2t)$.

### Intermediate claims

In $D_s$, $s^2t=0$ and $s^2$ is a unit, so $t=0$ and $D_s\cong\mathbb C[s,s^{-1}]$. In $D$, $(st)^2=s^2t^2=t(s^2t)=0$.

### Justification

Thus $st$ is a nonzero nilpotent in $D$, whereas the polynomial ring $C$ is reduced and has no nonzero nilpotents.

### Conclusion

The same principal open may arise from a reduced line or from a global object with an invisible boundary thickening.

content.title: Explain why the nilpotent is genuinely nonzero
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $st\ne0$ but $(st)^2=0$, and explain why localization at $s$ kills it.

content.markdown:
### Use the feedback before continuing

Find the first claim that the class is nonzero merely because its displayed polynomial is not the zero polynomial.

Quotient equality is ideal membership, and the boundary phenomenon depends on that exact distinction.

Test membership in $(s^2t)$, then square the class and finally use $s^{-2}$ in the localization.

## Deliberate review: Week 9 fibers of a linear map

The source object is the affine-fiber formula $x_0+\ker T$. The new context treats multiplication by an invertible coefficient as a linear map over the Laurent base ring.

content.title: Describe a localized singleton fiber

activities.promptMarkdown:

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In $B_a$, $a$ is a unit, so $at=0$ implies $t=0$. Thus $B_a$ is generated by $a^{\pm1}$ with no remaining relation and is isomorphic to $\mathbb C[a,a^{-1}]=A_a$. Globally, $A$ is a domain. In $B$, the classes of $a$ and $t$ are nonzero but have product zero, so $B$ is not a domain. Domainhood is preserved by ring isomorphism; hence $A\not\cong B$.

activities.title: Explain why the nilpotent is genuinely nonzero
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $D=\mathbb C[s,t]/(s^2t)$ with the class of $st$.

Prove that $st\ne0$ but $(st)^2=0$, and explain why localization at $s$ kills it.

rubric.label: Mathematical result

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If the class of $st$ were zero, then $st$ would lie in the principal ideal $(s^2t)$, so $st=h(s,t)s^2t$ for a polynomial $h$. Cancelling $st$ in the domain $\mathbb C[s,t]$ would give $1=hs$, impossible. Hence $st\ne0$ in $D$. Its square is $s^2t^2=t(s^2t)=0$. After localizing at $s$, the relation gives $t=s^{-2}(s^2t)=0$, so $st$ also becomes zero.

activities.title: Present a Laurent ring as a quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider $\theta:\mathbb C[u,v]\to\mathbb C[u,u^{-1}]$ with $\theta(u)=u$ and $\theta(v)=u^{-1}$.

Prove that $\theta$ descends to an isomorphism $\mathbb C[u,v]/(uv-1)\cong\mathbb C[u,u^{-1}]$.

Check the relation, prove surjectivity, construct the reverse map, and verify both composites.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Descent, surjectivity, the reverse map, and both composites are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response applies the quotient universal property before claiming an isomorphism.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $\theta(uv-1)=uu^{-1}-1=0$, the map descends to $\bar\theta$. Its image contains $u$ and $u^{-1}$, so it is surjective. Conversely, in the quotient the class of $u$ is a unit with inverse the class of $v$, so define $\psi(u)=\bar u$ and $\psi(u^{-1})=\bar v$. The composite $\bar\theta\psi$ fixes $u,u^{-1}$, while $\psi\bar\theta$ fixes $\bar u,\bar v$. Hence the maps are inverse.

The numerator $1+b-2b^2c$ is also weight zero, and $a^{-2}$ has weight $-2$, so $e=(1+b-2b^2c)a^{-2}$ has weight $-2$. These agree with Week 24.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Construction: $A_f$ consists of fractions $x/f^n$. Two such fractions are equal when some further power of $f$ annihilates their cross-difference, and $A_f$ is universal for maps that send $f$ to a unit. Laurent ring: the universal maps sending $a^{-1}$ to $1/a$ and a fraction $P/a^n$ to $a^{-n}P$ are inverse, so $\mathbb C[a,y,z]_a\cong\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},y,z]$. Solved quotient: in $R_a$ the equation $G=0$ gives $d=(1-bc)/a$, then $F=0$ gives $e=(1+b-2b^2c)/a^2$; substituting these formulas kills both relations and gives $R_a\cong\mathbb C[a,a^{-1},b,c]$. Principal open: the corresponding point maps identify $X_a=D_X(a)$ with $\mathbb C^\times\times\mathbb C^2$. Missing divisor: $\mathbb C[a]$ and $\mathbb C[a,t]/(at)$ have isomorphic localizations at $a$ but are not globally isomorphic because only the second has zero divisors. Therefore the localized chart does not determine how $a=0$ is restored.

lessons.title: Homogeneous coordinates and well-defined equations
lessons.summary: Define the projective line as nonzero coordinate pairs modulo common rescaling and prove exactly when a polynomial equation is well defined on those classes.
objectives: Define the projective line as nonzero coordinate pairs modulo common rescaling and prove exactly when a polynomial equation is well defined on those classes.

content.markdown:
## A projective point is a direction, not a chosen vector

The pair $(T,S)$ and every nonzero scalar multiple $(\lambda T,\lambda S)$ describe the same direction in $\mathbb C^2$. Projective geometry records that direction as one point $[T:S]$.

This quotient keeps the points that disappear when one divides by a coordinate. It also creates a proof obligation: any equation imposed on $[T:S]$ must have the same truth value for every representative.

## Reactivate binary forms and quotient reasoning

Week 10 supplied the monomial basis of homogeneous binary forms, and Week 15 interpreted those spaces as symmetric powers. Today introduces a new quotient: nonzero vectors are identified under common rescaling, so every definition on a projective point must be independent of the chosen representative.

## The quotient definition

Define

$$\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)=\bigl(\mathbb C^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\bigr)/\sim,$$

where $(T,S)\sim(T',S')$ when $(T',S')=(\lambda T,\lambda S)$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times$. The zero vector is removed because it does not span a one-dimensional subspace.

## Why homogeneous equations descend

If $F(T,S)$ is homogeneous of degree $d$, then

$$F(\lambda T,\lambda S)=\lambda^dF(T,S).$$

Because $\lambda^d\ne0$, the statement $F(T,S)=0$ is unchanged by rescaling. The numerical value of $F$ is not projectively invariant; its zero set is.

## Complete worked model

Consider the equation $T+S^2=0$ on coordinate pairs.

Prove that it does not define a subset of $\mathbb P^1$.

### Strategy

Find one nonzero pair satisfying the equation and a scalar multiple that does not.

### Hypotheses

The pair $(-1,1)$ is nonzero and satisfies $-1+1^2=0$.

### Intermediate claims

The equivalent representative $(-2,2)=2(-1,1)$ gives $-2+2^2=2\ne0$.

### Justification

Equivalent representatives must have the same membership status for a condition to descend to the quotient. Here they do not. The failure occurs because the two terms have different degrees and acquire different powers of the scaling factor.

### Conclusion

The equation $T+S^2=0$ is not a well-defined projective equation.

## The line through the vector

The class $[T:S]$ can also be read as the one-dimensional subspace $\mathbb C(T,S)\subset\mathbb C^2$. This interpretation makes the equivalence relation structural: every nonzero vector on the same line spans the same subspace.

It also explains why projective points are not obtained by identifying arbitrary pairs. Only common nonzero scaling is allowed.

## Independent well-definedness proof

The phrase “homogeneous coordinates” is not permission to manipulate ratios without conditions. A complete proof starts from the equivalence relation and shows how the proposed expression transforms.

For a zero locus, a nonzero scalar factor is harmless. For a numerical function, the same factor usually prevents the value from descending.

lessons.title: The two affine charts of the projective line
lessons.summary: Construct both standard affine charts of the projective line, derive their reciprocal transition, and locate the point omitted by each chart.
objectives: Construct both standard affine charts of the projective line, derive their reciprocal transition, and locate the point omitted by each chart.

content.markdown:
## Division creates a chart, not the whole space

When $S\ne0$, a projective class has the unique representative $[t:1]$ with $t=T/S$. When $T\ne0$, it has the unique representative $[1:s]$ with $s=S/T$.

Each normalization turns part of $\mathbb P^1$ into an affine line. The two parts overlap, and together they cover the projective line because a nonzero pair cannot have both coordinates zero.

## Reuse localization's domain discipline

Week 25 made division conditional on invertibility. A chart coordinate is similarly conditional: $T/S$ exists only on $S\ne0$, and $S/T$ only on $T\ne0$. Writing the domain beside the ratio prevents the point at infinity from disappearing.

## The chart where S is nonzero

Set $U_S=\{[T:S]:S\ne0\}$. Multiplying by $S^{-1}$ gives

$$[T:S]=[T/S:1]=[t:1].$$

The coordinate $t=T/S$ identifies $U_S$ with $\mathbb A^1$. The missing class is $[1:0]$.

## The complementary T-chart

Set $U_T=\{[T:S]:T\ne0\}$. Multiplying by $T^{-1}$ gives

$$[T:S]=[1:S/T]=[1:s].$$

The point $[1:0]$ lies in this chart and has coordinate $s=0$. Conversely, $[0:1]$ is the single point omitted by $U_T$.

## Complete worked model

Work on $U_S\cap U_T$, where both $T$ and $S$ are nonzero.

Derive the change of coordinates between $t=T/S$ and $s=S/T$.

### Strategy

Write the same projective point in both normalized forms and use the nonzero overlap condition.

### Hypotheses

On the overlap, $t\ne0$ and $s\ne0$. The point has representatives $[t:1]$ and $[1:s]$.

### Intermediate claims

From the definitions, $ts=(T/S)(S/T)=1$.

### Justification

Both divisions are legal on the overlap. Hence $s=1/t$ and $t=1/s$. Starting from $[t:1]$, multiplying by $t^{-1}$ gives $[1:t^{-1}]$, which is the second chart representation.

### Conclusion

The transition maps are mutual reciprocals on $\mathbb C^\times$.

Every projective point has a nonzero representative $(T,S)$. Therefore at least one of $T$ and $S$ is nonzero, so

$$\mathbb P^1=U_S\cup U_T.$$

This proof is short because it uses the defining exclusion of $(0,0)$. It is not a picture-based claim.

lessons.title: The projective root of a binary linear form
lessons.summary: Prove that every nonzero binary linear form $aT+bS$ has the unique projective root $[-b:a]$, with the case $a=0$ handled without division.
objectives: Prove that every nonzero binary linear form $aT+bS$ has the unique projective root $[-b:a]$, with the case $a=0$ handled without division.

content.markdown:
## The affine formula is only one chart

Solving $aT+bS=0$ as $T/S=-b/a$ assumes both $S\ne0$ and $a\ne0$. The homogeneous pair $[-b:a]$ avoids both hidden divisions and remains meaningful whenever $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$.

The syllabus's decisive boundary case is $a=0$. Then nonzeroness of the form forces $b\ne0$, the equation is $bS=0$, and the root is $[1:0]$.

## Keep coefficients and point coordinates separate

The coefficients $(a,b)$ determine the linear form. The variables $(T,S)$ represent a point of $\mathbb P^1$. The proposed root $[-b:a]$ swaps the coefficient order and changes one sign because $a(-b)+b(a)=0$.

## Verify the coordinate-free formula

Assume $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$. Then $(-b,a)\ne(0,0)$, so $[-b:a]$ is a projective point. Direct substitution gives

$$a(-b)+b(a)=0.$$

This proves existence without selecting a chart.

## The boundary a=0

If $a=0$ and $L$ is nonzero, then $b\ne0$. The equation $L(T,S)=bS=0$ forces $S=0$. A projective point with $S=0$ must have $T\ne0$, and every such pair represents $[1:0]$.

The affine expression $-b/a$ fails here because it chose the wrong chart. The projective root does not fail.

## Complete worked model

Let $L=aT+bS$ be nonzero and suppose $[T:S]$ satisfies $L(T,S)=0$.

Prove $[T:S]=[-b:a]$.

### Strategy

Split on $a\ne0$ and $a=0$ so every division is licensed.

### Hypotheses

At least one of $a,b$ is nonzero, and $(T,S)$ is a nonzero pair.

### Intermediate claims

If $a\ne0$, then $T=-(b/a)S$. The root cannot have $S=0$, because that would also force $T=0$. Hence $[T:S]=[-b:a]$. If $a=0$, then $b\ne0$ and the previous boundary argument gives $[T:S]=[1:0]=[-b:0]$.

### Justification

The first case uses only legal division by $a$ and the nonzero-pair condition. The second uses division by $b$, not by the vanishing coefficient $a$.

### Conclusion

Every nonzero binary linear form has exactly one projective root, namely $[-b:a]$.

## Rescaling the form does not change its root

The forms $L$ and $\mu L$ with $\mu\ne0$ have the same zero set. Their coefficient pairs $(a,b)$ and $(\mu a,\mu b)$ produce

$$[-\mu b:\mu a]=[-b:a].$$

Thus the root depends on the projective coefficient class $[a:b]$, not on a chosen scalar normalization of the form.

## Independent theorem proof

A publication-ready proof of the linear-root theorem must state that $L$ is nonzero. If $a=b=0$, every projective point is a zero and the formula $[-b:a]=[0:0]$ is undefined.

The theorem therefore has a sharp hypothesis, a coordinate-free existence check, and a two-case uniqueness proof.

lessons.title: Dehomogenization in both charts
lessons.summary: Dehomogenize a binary form in both standard charts, transport roots across the reciprocal overlap, and detect the root at infinity with its multiplicity.
objectives: Dehomogenize a binary form in both standard charts, transport roots across the reciprocal overlap, and detect the root at infinity with its multiplicity.

content.markdown:
## One homogeneous equation, two ordinary polynomials

For a degree-$d$ binary form $F(T,S)$, the $S$-chart polynomial is $f(t)=F(t,1)$ and the $T$-chart polynomial is $g(s)=F(1,s)$.

On the overlap, homogeneity gives $g(s)=s^df(1/s)$ and $f(t)=t^dg(1/t)$. The second polynomial records the root that the first chart calls infinity.

## Keep the chart name beside the substitution

Day 2 proved that $t=T/S$ belongs to $S\ne0$ and $s=S/T$ belongs to $T\ne0$. Day 3 showed why a root calculation that divides by $a$ can miss $[1:0]$. Today uses both charts systematically rather than repairing an omitted case afterward.

## Two dehomogenizations

Write $F(T,S)=\sum_{i=0}^d c_iT^{d-i}S^i$. Then

$$f(t)=F(t,1)=\sum_{i=0}^dc_it^{d-i},\qquad g(s)=F(1,s)=\sum_{i=0}^dc_is^i.$$

A finite root $t_0$ corresponds to $[t_0:1]$. The point $[1:0]$ is a root exactly when $g(0)=F(1,0)=c_0=0$.

The **projective root divisor** is the formal sum $\sum_p m_p[p]$, where $p$ runs through the distinct projective roots and $m_p$ is the multiplicity of the corresponding root in either chart. “Formal sum” means that the symbols $[p]$ record root locations with integer weights; the roots are not being added as coordinate pairs.

## The overlap identity

For $s\ne0$, homogeneity of degree $d$ gives

$$g(s)=F(1,s)=s^dF(1/s,1)=s^df(1/s).$$

Thus a nonzero $s$ is a root of $g$ exactly when $t=1/s$ is a root of $f$. The factor $s^d$ clears the denominator; it does not create an overlap root because $s\ne0$ there.

## Complete worked model

Let $F(T,S)=S^2(T-S)(T+2S)$, a binary quartic.

Determine the multiplicity of the projective root $[1:0]$ and the remaining roots.

### Strategy

Use the $T$-chart, where $[1:0]$ has coordinate $s=0$, and factor the dehomogenization.

### Hypotheses

$g(s)=F(1,s)=s^2(1-s)(1+2s)$.

### Intermediate claims

The coordinate $s=0$ is a root of multiplicity two. The other roots are $s=1$ and $s=-1/2$.

### Justification

Root multiplicity in this affine chart is the exponent of the corresponding linear factor. Translating back gives $[1:0]$ twice, $[1:1]$, and $[1:-1/2]=[-2:1]$.

### Conclusion

The projective quartic has four roots counted with multiplicity, including a double root at infinity.

## Homogenization reverses the process

If $p(t)=c_0t^d+c_1t^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d$ has degree at most $d$, its degree-$d$ homogenization is

$$P(T,S)=S^dp(T/S)=c_0T^d+c_1T^{d-1}S+\cdots+c_dS^d.$$

If the actual degree of $p$ is smaller than $d$, then $P$ is divisible by $S$; the missing degree is recorded as multiplicity at $[1:0]$.

objectives: Write a complete projective-root argument that keeps representative-independence, chart domains, roots at infinity, and multiplicity logically separate.

content.markdown:
## A robust proof survives the missing chart

This week replaced one affine ratio by a global method: define the projective class, prove homogeneous vanishing is well defined, use both standard charts, and isolate the coordinate origin that represents infinity.

Next week the resultant will detect whether two binary forms share a projective root. That criterion is meaningful only because this week's root notion includes $[1:0]$.

## Retrieval remains labelled

The four review blocks return to Weeks 10, 18, 23, and 25 at exact intervals of sixteen, eight, three, and one weeks. They are not new instruction. Each earlier object is used with greater independence or in a new projective context.

## Audit a false affine argument

A common incomplete claim is: “The root of $aT+bS$ is $-b/a$.” It omits the chart coordinate, assumes $a\ne0$, and says nothing about the boundary $a=0$.

The repaired statement is global: a nonzero form has root $[-b:a]$; in $U_S$ this has coordinate $t=-b/a$ when $a\ne0$, while for $a=0$ it is $[1:0]$, the origin of $U_T$.

## Complete worked model

Let $F(T,S)$ be a nonzero homogeneous binary form of degree $d$ over $\mathbb C$.

Explain how to determine its full projective root divisor.

### Strategy

First prove that vanishing descends under rescaling. Then compute in each affine chart and reconcile the overlap by reciprocals.

### Hypotheses

$F(\lambda T,\lambda S)=\lambda^dF(T,S)$ for $\lambda\ne0$. The standard charts $U_S$ and $U_T$ cover $\mathbb P^1$.

### Intermediate claims

The polynomials $f(t)=F(t,1)$ and $g(s)=F(1,s)$ describe the roots in the two charts. On the overlap, $g(s)=s^df(1/s)$. The multiplicity of $[1:0]$ is the order of vanishing of $g$ at $s=0$.

### Justification

Homogeneity makes the zero set representative-independent. Chart normalization is unique. The reciprocal identity prevents double counting and transports multiplicities at nonzero overlap coordinates.

### Conclusion

Factoring both chart polynomials and identifying reciprocal nonzero roots yields every projective root, including infinity, with total multiplicity $d$.

content.markdown:
## Eliminate the root without solving for it

Let $L=aT+bS$ be a binary linear form and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$ a binary quadratic. We want one polynomial in their coefficients that detects whether they share a projective root.

The resultant does this by converting a possible polynomial relation between $L$ and $Q$ into the singularity of a square linear map. This is elimination: the coordinates $[T:S]$ disappear, but the existence of a common root remains encoded in the coefficients.

## Reactivate three exact tools

Week 11 represented polynomial multiplication by matrices in ordered monomial bases. Week 13 interpreted a zero determinant as singularity of a square linear map. Week 26 proved that a nonzero linear form has the unique projective root $[-b:a]$, including the case $a=0$.

Today combines those tools. Keep the domain basis and codomain basis visible: a correct determinant with an unexplained coefficient order is not yet a reliable resultant calculation.

## The Sylvester map in degrees one and two

Let $V_j$ denote the vector space of binary forms of degree $j$. Define

$$\Phi_{L,Q}:V_1\oplus V_0\longrightarrow V_2,\qquad (A,r)\longmapsto AL+rQ.$$

The dimensions are $2+1=3$ and $3$, so the map has a square matrix. A vector in its kernel is exactly a relation $AL+rQ=0$ with $A$ linear and $r$ scalar.

## Build the matrix column by column

Use the ordered domain basis $((T,0),(S,0),(0,1))$ and codomain basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$. Their images are

$$TL=aT^2+bTS,\qquad SL=aTS+bS^2,\qquad Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2.$$

Thus

$$M(L,Q)=\begin{pmatrix}a&0&c\\ b&a&d\\ 0&b&e\end{pmatrix}.$$

The first two columns come from multiples of $L$; the third comes from $Q$.

## Complete worked model

Let $L=T+S$ and $Q=(T+S)(2T-S)=2T^2+TS-S^2$.

Construct $M(L,Q)$ and exhibit a nonzero kernel vector without expanding its determinant.

### Strategy

Use the visible factorization to rewrite $Q$ as a linear multiple of $L$, then translate that relation into a source vector $(A,r)$.

### Hypotheses

$Q=(2T-S)L$, and the Sylvester map sends $(A,r)$ to $AL+rQ$.

### Intermediate claims

Choosing $A=-(2T-S)$ and $r=1$ gives $AL+rQ=-(2T-S)L+Q=0$.

### Justification

The source vector is nonzero because $r=1$. Hence the kernel is nontrivial, the square matrix is singular, and its determinant is zero.

### Conclusion

A common factor creates a multiplication relation, and the Sylvester matrix records that relation as singularity.

## Definition and convention boundary

For the displayed ordered bases, define

$$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=\det M(L,Q).$$

Changing basis order may multiply this determinant by $-1$. The course fixes the displayed convention so that the exact formula is stable. Its zero locus does not change, because $\det M=0$ if and only if $-\det M=0$.

A complete Sylvester construction has four visible steps: declare the map, declare both ordered bases, compute every basis image, and only then take the determinant.

Do not begin by memorizing a $3\times3$ array. The map explains why the array has its shape and why a kernel relation matters.

content.markdown:
## The formula is a derivation, not a slogan

The mathematical target is the identity

$$\operatorname{Res}(aT+bS,cT^2+dTS+eS^2)=a^2e-abd+cb^2.$$

Today derives it from the fixed matrix. Every sign can be traced to one cofactor, so a remembered but unverified expression is unnecessary.

## Reactivate cofactor expansion

Day 1 produced $M(L,Q)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&0&c\\b&a&d\\0&b&e\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Week 13 established cofactor expansion and the alternating sign pattern. Expanding along the first row exposes only two nonzero terms.

## Expand along the sparse row

Using signs $+,-,+$ along the first row,

$$\det M=a\det\begin{pmatrix}a&d\\b&e\end{pmatrix}+c\det\begin{pmatrix}b&a\\0&b\end{pmatrix}.$$

The middle contribution is zero because the first-row middle entry is zero.

## Evaluate the minors

The two minors are $ae-bd$ and $b^2$. Therefore

$$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a(ae-bd)+cb^2=a^2e-abd+cb^2.$$

The three terms use two coefficients from $L$ and one from $Q$. This observation will become the bidegree calculation on Day 4.

## Complete worked model

$L=2T-S$ and $Q=3T^2+4TS+5S^2$.

Compute the resultant from both the determinant and the coefficient formula.

### Strategy

Construct the numerical matrix, expand its sparse first row, then substitute the five coefficients into the derived polynomial.

### Hypotheses

$(a,b,c,d,e)=(2,-1,3,4,5)$ and $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&0&3\\-1&2&4\\0&-1&5\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

### Intermediate claims

The determinant is $2(10+4)+3(1)=31$. The formula gives $2^2\cdot5-2(-1)4+3(-1)^2=20+8+3=31$.

### Justification

Both calculations use the same ordered-basis convention and agree term for term.

### Conclusion

$\operatorname{Res}(2T-S,3T^2+4TS+5S^2)=31$.

## Audit sign and placement errors

Two tempting wrong formulas are $a^2e+abd+cb^2$ and $a^2c-abd+eb^2$. The first loses the determinant's alternating sign. The second exchanges the leading and trailing coefficients of $Q$ without changing the basis convention.

A fast audit uses boundary forms. If $L=T$, then the unique projective root is $[0:1]$ and the formula reduces to $e$. If $L=S$, it reduces to $c$. These checks pin the positions of $c$ and $e$.

lessons.title: Why the resultant detects a common projective root
lessons.summary: Prove for a nonzero binary linear form and binary quadratic over $\mathbb C$ that the resultant vanishes exactly when they share a projective root, including the root at infinity.
objectives: Prove for a nonzero binary linear form and binary quadratic over $\mathbb C$ that the resultant vanishes exactly when they share a projective root, including the root at infinity.

content.markdown:
## Evaluate the quadratic at the linear root

Week 26 proved that a nonzero $L=aT+bS$ has the unique projective root $p_L=[-b:a]$. Substituting that representative into $Q$ gives

$$Q(-b,a)=cb^2-dab+ea^2=a^2e-abd+cb^2.$$

Thus the resultant is not an unrelated coefficient trick: it is the quadratic evaluated at the canonical root vector $(-b,a)$.

## State the hypotheses before the equivalence

Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $L$ be nonzero, so $[-b:a]$ is defined and is its unique projective root. Let $Q$ be homogeneous of degree two. Homogeneity makes the statement $Q(p_L)=0$ independent of the nonzero representative chosen for $p_L$.

## The evaluation identity

Direct substitution yields

$$Q(-b,a)=c(-b)^2+d(-b)a+ea^2=cb^2-abd+a^2e.$$

After reordering terms, this is exactly $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. No division by $a$ or $b$ occurs.

### Use the feedback before continuing

Repair this particular case by following the task in order and writing every required check: Substitute $T=-b$, $S=a$, retain the mixed-term sign, and compare with Day 2.

## The forward and reverse implications

Because $p_L=[-b:a]$ is the only projective root of $L$, the forms share a projective root exactly when $Q(-b,a)=0$.

Combining this statement with the evaluation identity gives

$$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=0\iff L\text{ and }Q\text{ have a common projective root}.$$
