content.title: Week 57, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Polynomial regularity of $z$.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain Global polynomial representatives, Normal jets, and Ideals and quotient rings, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **First and second normal jets: The identities $b-1=ay$ and $c-1+\tfrac32ay=a^2z$ define corrected first and second normal coefficients along $a=0$.**
- **Localization: $A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.**
- **Torus weights and gradings: A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.**
- **Polynomial and binary form: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of polynomial regularity of $z$

Reconstruct and synthesize polynomial regularity of $z$.

### Global polynomial representatives

A regular function on an affine variety $X$ is represented by an element of its coordinate ring. To extend a fraction, prove that it equals a polynomial residue class modulo the defining ideal.

**Concrete example.** In the coordinate ring of $X$, $b-1=a(2bd-ae)$, so $(b-1)/a$ agrees on $a\ne0$ with the global polynomial $2bd-ae$.

**Boundary case.** Cancelling $a$ in the ambient polynomial ring would be invalid on $a=0$ and would not prove a global extension.

### Normal jets

$b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

**Concrete example.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

**Boundary case.** The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

### Ideals and quotient rings

$A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.

**Concrete example.** Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.

**Boundary case.** Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain An explicit affine-space isomorphism, The normalized factorization threefold, Coordinate rings, and Normal jets, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Global polynomial representatives: A regular function on an affine variety $X$ is represented by an element of its coordinate ring. To extend a fraction, prove that it equals a polynomial residue class modulo the defining ideal.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Ideals and quotient rings: $A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.**
- **Affine varieties: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.**
- **Localization: $A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.**
- **Torus weights and gradings: A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of affine-space miracle capstone

Reconstruct and synthesize affine-space miracle capstone.

### An explicit affine-space isomorphism

An isomorphism $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ consists of polynomial maps $\Phi:\mathbb A^3\to X$ and $\Psi:X\to\mathbb A^3$ whose two compositions are identity maps.

**Concrete example.** Coordinates $(a,y,z)$ together with the supplied polynomial formulas for $b,c,d,e$ give a candidate $\Phi$, while $y=2bd-ae$ is part of $\Psi$.

**Boundary case.** A birational formula valid on $a\ne0$ is not yet an affine isomorphism because it may fail on the boundary divisor.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Concrete example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Boundary case.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

### Coordinate rings

$\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.

**Concrete example.** $X\cong\mathbb A^3$ follows from an explicit isomorphism of coordinate rings.

**Boundary case.** A rational expression with a denominator is not automatically a global regular function.

### Normal jets

$b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

**Concrete example.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

**Boundary case.** The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

content.title: Week 59, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Read the derivation as a mathematician.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain Classifying claims and evidence, Mathematical proof, and The Keller map, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **An explicit affine-space isomorphism: An isomorphism $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ consists of polynomial maps $\Phi:\mathbb A^3\to X$ and $\Psi:X\to\mathbb A^3$ whose two compositions are identity maps.**
- **Functions and maps: A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.**
- **The normalized factorization threefold: $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.**
- **Étale maps: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.**
- **Marked-root incidence: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of read the derivation as a mathematician

Reconstruct and synthesize read the derivation as a mathematician.

### Classifying claims and evidence

An algebraic identity is checked in a ring, a local claim on neighborhoods, a global claim over all points, and a topological claim with properties such as compactness or properness.

**Concrete example.** A nonzero Jacobian establishes a local property; a separate fiber calculation is needed for global injectivity.

**Boundary case.** Using a local theorem as evidence for a global conclusion is a category error, even when every local calculation is correct.

### Mathematical proof

A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.

**Concrete example.** Let $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$. If $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y$, then $f$ and $g$ are mutual inverses.

**Boundary case.** Testing an identity at many numerical points is evidence, not a proof of a polynomial identity.

### The Keller map

$G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ is obtained by composing the affine chart of $X$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$.

**Concrete example.** $\det DG=-1$ while the map is generically three-to-one.

**Boundary case.** A constant nonzero Jacobian does not itself provide a global polynomial inverse.

**Analogous problem.** Verify that $b=1+ay$ follows from the identity $y=2bd-ae$ on the displayed threefold.

content.title: Week 60, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Reconstruct the five-dimensional map.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain The five-dimensional coefficient–resultant map, Resultant, Étale maps, and Tangent spaces and differentials, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Classifying claims and evidence: An algebraic identity is checked in a ring, a local claim on neighborhoods, a global claim over all points, and a topological claim with properties such as compactness or properness.**
- **Polynomial and binary form: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.**
- **Projective roots: A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.**
- **Inverse function theorem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. If $DF_x$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $x$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $F(x)$ such that $F|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.**
- **Tangent spaces and differentials: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Jacobian and total derivative: For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.**
- **Affine varieties: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of reconstruct the five-dimensional map

Reconstruct and synthesize reconstruct the five-dimensional map.

### The five-dimensional coefficient–resultant map

From a linear form and a quadratic form, record the four coefficients of their product together with $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. This defines a polynomial map from affine five-space to affine five-space.

**Concrete example.** Its differential combines $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$ with the derivative of the resultant.

**Boundary case.** The four coefficient functions alone define a map to affine four-space and necessarily retain at least one infinitesimal kernel direction.

### Resultant

$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

**Concrete example.** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.

**Boundary case.** The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Concrete example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Boundary case.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

### Tangent spaces and differentials

$dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

**Concrete example.** When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

**Boundary case.** Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:

- **Polynomial and binary form: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.**
- **Projective roots: A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.**
- **Inverse function theorem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. Suppose two polynomials $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ have the same coefficient for every monomial. Then $P-Q$ has every coefficient equal to zero, so $P-Q$ is the zero polynomial. Therefore $P=Q$.

## Exact task being assessed

Write a complete proof of this exact target, with explicit hypotheses, justified implications, and exceptional cases: For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, derive the four coefficients of $LQ$ and $\rho=a^2e-abd+cb^2$. Prove that $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\rho)$ is étale on $\rho\ne0$ by the tangent-kernel and resultant-weight argument, then use a determinant only as a consistency check.

## Task-specific reference

### The five-dimensional coefficient–resultant map

**Definition used.** From a linear form and a quadratic form, record the four coefficients of their product together with $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. This defines a polynomial map from affine five-space to affine five-space.

**Valid case.** Its differential combines $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$ with the derivative of the resultant.

**Boundary.** The four coefficient functions alone define a map to affine four-space and necessarily retain at least one infinitesimal kernel direction.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

### Resultant

**Definition used.** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

**Valid case.** $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.

**Boundary.** The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

### Étale maps

**Definition used.** For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Valid case.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Boundary.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

### Tangent spaces and differentials

**Definition used.** $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

**Valid case.** When $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, the kernel is $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

**Boundary.** Dimension counting alone does not identify the kernel vector.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

## Reference solution or decisive derivation

Expand $LQ$ to obtain the four coefficient formulas and compute the resultant. The tangent-kernel argument identifies the one lost scaling direction, and the resultant derivative detects it, proving étaleness without the determinant expansion; the determinant is then only a consistency check.

## Passing standard for this response

The proof must begin from the stated hypotheses, establish the exact conclusion, justify every nontrivial implication, and treat every exceptional case.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can complete and interpret this exact verification: For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, expand $LQ$ and compute $\rho=a^2e-abd+cb^2$. Then verify that the relative-scaling tangent is killed by multiplication but detected by $d\rho$ when $\rho\ne0$.

## Why this matters

Exact computation can certify an algebraic claim, but only when you state what was computed and why that evidence reaches the conclusion.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Classifying claims and evidence: An algebraic identity is checked in a ring, a local claim on neighborhoods, a global claim over all points, and a topological claim with properties such as compactness or properness.**
- **Polynomial and binary form: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.**
- **Projective roots: A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.**
- **Inverse function theorem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. If $DF_x$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $x$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $F(x)$ such that $F|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.**
- **Tangent spaces and differentials: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Jacobian and total derivative: For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.**
- **Affine varieties: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Use exact computation as evidence

Carry out this exact symbolic or logical verification: For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, expand $LQ$ and compute $\rho=a^2e-abd+cb^2$. Then verify that the relative-scaling tangent is killed by multiplication but detected by $d\rho$ when $\rho\ne0$. Show every transformation, state what the result proves, and name one stronger claim that does not follow from this calculation alone.

A reproducible calculation has three parts: define the objects exactly, show the transformation, and interpret the output.

**Evidence boundary.** Exact expansion can prove a polynomial identity because coefficients can be compared. A finite list of numerical substitutions cannot prove that identity for every input.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain A smooth threefold by base change, The normalized factorization threefold, Fibers and base change, and Étale maps, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **The five-dimensional coefficient–resultant map: From a linear form and a quadratic form, record the four coefficients of their product together with $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. This defines a polynomial map from affine five-space to affine five-space.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Functions and maps: A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.**
- **Affine varieties: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.**
- **Inverse function theorem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. If $DF_x$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $x$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $F(x)$ such that $F|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.**
- **Tangent spaces and differentials: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of reconstruct the threefold $x$

Reconstruct and synthesize reconstruct the threefold $x$.

### A smooth threefold by base change

Étale morphisms are stable under base change. Pulling an étale map back along a smooth subspace gives an étale source over that subspace and preserves the expected dimension.

**Concrete example.** Fixing the normalized resultant and one coefficient cuts the five-dimensional target to a three-dimensional affine subspace; its inverse image is $X$.

**Boundary case.** Counting two equations inside affine five-space does not prove smoothness unless their differentials have the required independence.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Concrete example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Boundary case.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Concrete example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Boundary case.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Concrete example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Boundary case.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Verify the affine-space coordinates.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain Polynomial inverse verification, The normalized factorization threefold, Ideals and quotient rings, and Normal jets, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **A smooth threefold by base change: Étale morphisms are stable under base change. Pulling an étale map back along a smooth subspace gives an étale source over that subspace and preserves the expected dimension.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Polynomial and binary form: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.**
- **Localization: $A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.**
- **Torus weights and gradings: A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of verify the affine-space coordinates

Reconstruct and synthesize verify the affine-space coordinates.

### Polynomial inverse verification

To prove polynomial maps are inverse on $X$, substitute one formula into the other and reduce each coordinate difference modulo the defining ideal of $X$.

**Concrete example.** For $y=2bd-ae$, substitution into the forward chart and reduction by the two equations returns the original coordinate $y$.

**Boundary case.** Numerical checks or verification only on the dense chart $a\ne0$ do not prove the polynomial identities on all of $X$.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Concrete example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Boundary case.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

### Ideals and quotient rings

$A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.

**Concrete example.** Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.

**Boundary case.** Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

### Normal jets

$b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

**Concrete example.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

**Boundary case.** The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

For Polynomial inverse verification, The normalized factorization threefold, Ideals and quotient rings, and Normal jets, use each supplied definition to verify the supplied example. For each boundary case, name the first defining condition that fails. State every domain and hypothesis that your verification uses.

## Task-specific reference

### Polynomial inverse verification

**Definition used.** To prove polynomial maps are inverse on $X$, substitute one formula into the other and reduce each coordinate difference modulo the defining ideal of $X$.

**Valid case.** For $y=2bd-ae$, substitution into the forward chart and reduction by the two equations returns the original coordinate $y$.

**Boundary.** Numerical checks or verification only on the dense chart $a\ne0$ do not prove the polynomial identities on all of $X$.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

### The normalized factorization threefold

**Definition used.** $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Valid case.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Boundary.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

### Ideals and quotient rings

**Definition used.** $A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.

**Valid case.** Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.

**Boundary.** Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

### Normal jets

**Definition used.** $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.

**Valid case.** $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.

**Boundary.** The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

A correct answer explicitly matches the valid case to the definition and names the first failed condition in the boundary case.

The answer must apply the supplied definition to the supplied case and explain the boundary failure in complete sentences.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can complete and interpret this exact verification: Use the full forward chart $\Phi(a,y,z)=(a,b,c,d,e)$: $b=1+ay$, $c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z$, $d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz$, and $e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z$. Use the inverse-coordinate candidates $y=2bd-ae$ and $z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$. Differentiate the displayed forward formulas with respect to $a,y,z$ and compute the determinant of the $(a,d,e)$ coordinate minor at $a=0$. Explain why its nonzero value checks local invertibility there but does not replace the two global composition identities.

## Why this matters

Exact computation can certify an algebraic claim, but only when you state what was computed and why that evidence reaches the conclusion.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **A smooth threefold by base change: Étale morphisms are stable under base change. Pulling an étale map back along a smooth subspace gives an étale source over that subspace and preserves the expected dimension.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Polynomial and binary form: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.**
- **Localization: $A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.**
- **Torus weights and gradings: A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

Carry out this exact symbolic or logical verification: Use the full forward chart $\Phi(a,y,z)=(a,b,c,d,e)$: $b=1+ay$, $c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z$, $d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz$, and $e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z$. Use the inverse-coordinate candidates $y=2bd-ae$ and $z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$. Differentiate the displayed forward formulas with respect to $a,y,z$ and compute the determinant of the $(a,d,e)$ coordinate minor at $a=0$. Explain why its nonzero value checks local invertibility there but does not replace the two global composition identities. Show every transformation, state what the result proves, and name one stronger claim that does not follow from this calculation alone.

## Why this matters

Retrieval exposes what remains usable without prompts. Repairing the earliest error is more valuable than rereading a complete solution.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **A smooth threefold by base change: Étale morphisms are stable under base change. Pulling an étale map back along a smooth subspace gives an étale source over that subspace and preserves the expected dimension.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Polynomial and binary form: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.**
- **Localization: $A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.**
- **Torus weights and gradings: A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

This section is review, not a new introduction. Close your notes before answering.

- **Week 61: Reconstruct the threefold $X$.** Retrieve this target: For $X=\{a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,ad+bc=1\}$, prove smoothness and dimension $3$, identify the strata $a=0$ and $a\ne0$, and prove that the normalized product map is the base change of the étale coefficient-resultant map.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain The explicit Keller map $G$, The Keller map, Jacobian and total derivative, and The normalized factorization threefold, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Polynomial inverse verification: To prove polynomial maps are inverse on $X$, substitute one formula into the other and reduce each coordinate difference modulo the defining ideal of $X$.**
- **The normalized factorization threefold: $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.**
- **Étale maps: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.**
- **Marked-root incidence: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.**
- **Vector spaces and dimension: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of derive the polynomial map $g$

Reconstruct and synthesize derive the polynomial map $g$.

### The explicit Keller map $G$

Let $\Phi:\mathbb A^3\to X$ be the polynomial chart and let $H:X\to\mathbb A^3$ record the selected cubic coefficients. The Keller map is $G=H\circ\Phi$.

**Concrete example.** The derivative satisfies $DG=D H_{\Phi(a,y,z)}\,D\Phi_{(a,y,z)}$; the established local isomorphisms make its determinant the stated nonzero constant.

**Boundary case.** Calling a map a Keller map requires an explicit polynomial formula and constant nonzero Jacobian, not merely a factorization through smooth spaces.

### The Keller map

$G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ is obtained by composing the affine chart of $X$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$.

**Concrete example.** $\det DG=-1$ while the map is generically three-to-one.

**Boundary case.** A constant nonzero Jacobian does not itself provide a global polynomial inverse.

### Jacobian and total derivative

For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.

**Concrete example.** For $F(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $DF=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Boundary case.** A symbolic determinant calculation without a theorem statement does not establish global behavior.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Concrete example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Boundary case.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Derive the polynomial map $G$.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can complete and interpret this exact verification: Use the full forward chart $\Phi(a,y,z)=(a,b,c,d,e)$: $b=1+ay$, $c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z$, $d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz$, and $e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z$. Use $G_1=a-\frac32a^2y+a^3z$, $G_2=\frac12y-3az+6ay^2-6a^2yz+\frac92a^2y^3-3a^3y^2z$, and $G_3=-2z+4y^2-6ayz+7ay^3-6a^2y^2z+3a^2y^4-2a^3y^3z$. Compose the chart with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$, collect the three polynomial coordinates, and verify that they equal the displayed $G_1,G_2,G_3$ formulas. Compute $\det DG$, then identify the two differential factors in the chain rule that explain why the determinant is constant.

## Why this matters

Exact computation can certify an algebraic claim, but only when you state what was computed and why that evidence reaches the conclusion.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Polynomial inverse verification: To prove polynomial maps are inverse on $X$, substitute one formula into the other and reduce each coordinate difference modulo the defining ideal of $X$.**
- **The normalized factorization threefold: $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.**
- **Étale maps: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.**
- **Marked-root incidence: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.**
- **Vector spaces and dimension: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Derive the polynomial map $G$.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can retrieve this week's argument and the scheduled ideas from weeks 62, 60, 55, 47, then repair the first error you find.

## Why this matters

Retrieval exposes what remains usable without prompts. Repairing the earliest error is more valuable than rereading a complete solution.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Polynomial inverse verification: To prove polynomial maps are inverse on $X$, substitute one formula into the other and reduce each coordinate difference modulo the defining ideal of $X$.**
- **The normalized factorization threefold: $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.**
- **Étale maps: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.**
- **Marked-root incidence: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.**
- **Vector spaces and dimension: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Deliberate review

This section is review, not a new introduction. Close your notes before answering.

- **Week 62: Verify the affine-space coordinates.** Retrieve this target: Using the forward and inverse formulas from Week 58, verify both polynomial compositions by hand and in the quotient ring. Explain what a zero Gröbner normal form and a nonzero Jacobian determinant each verify, and why neither alone replaces both global identities.
- **Week 60: Reconstruct the five-dimensional map.** Retrieve this target: For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, derive the four coefficients of $LQ$ and $\rho=a^2e-abd+cb^2$. Prove that $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\rho)$ is étale on $\rho\ne0$ by the tangent-kernel and resultant-weight argument, then use a determinant only as a consistency check.
- **Week 55: The boundary $a=0$.** Retrieve this target: At a point $(0,1,1,d,e)$ of $E=X\cap\{a=0\}$, linearize both defining equations in the normal parameter $a$. Solve the first-order terms to obtain $b=1+2ad+O(a^2)$ and $c=1-3ad+O(a^2)$, and explain the coefficient $-3/2$ in the corrected coordinate.
- **Week 47: Point-set topology.** Retrieve this target: For locally compact Hausdorff spaces, prove that a proper map has compact inverse images of compact sets and explain the converse criterion. Then state precisely why the same compactness language cannot be transferred unchanged to the Zariski topology.

For each item, state the claim, the decisive reason, and one error that would make the argument invalid.

### Worked proof: an exact polynomial identity

Suppose two polynomials $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ have the same coefficient for every monomial. Then $P-Q$ has every coefficient equal to zero, so $P-Q$ is the zero polynomial. Therefore $P=Q$.

content.title: Week 65, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Fibers and noninjectivity.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain Fiber cardinality and noninjectivity, Fibers and base change, Marked-root incidence, and Properness and nonproperness, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Linear equivalence and the determinant chain: If $F_{\mathrm{orig}}=B\circ G\circ A$ for invertible linear maps $A,B$, then $DF_{\mathrm{orig}}=B\,DG\,A$ and $\det DF_{\mathrm{orig}}=\det(B)\det(DG)\det(A)$.**
- **Functions and maps: A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.**
- **Affine varieties: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.**
- **The projective line: $\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Fibers and base change: The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of fibers and noninjectivity

Reconstruct and synthesize fibers and noninjectivity.

### Fiber cardinality and noninjectivity

The fiber of $F:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $F^{-1}(y)$. If it contains two distinct points, then $F$ is not injective; a generic fiber count describes this on a dense target set.

**Concrete example.** A square-free binary cubic has three distinct marked roots, hence three distinct normalized factorizations and three corresponding preimages.

**Boundary case.** The nonzero Jacobian proves that these preimages are locally separate; it does not collapse them into one global point.

### Fibers and base change

The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.

**Concrete example.** A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.

**Boundary case.** Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

### Marked-root incidence

A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.

**Concrete example.** Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.

**Boundary case.** A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

### Properness and nonproperness

Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.

**Concrete example.** A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.

**Boundary case.** Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

**Analogous problem.** Verify that $b=1+ay$ follows from the identity $y=2bd-ae$ on the displayed threefold.

**Conclusion.** The last expression vanishes by $ad+bc=1$, so $b=1+ay$ in the coordinate ring. The quotient-ring reduction is the required global check.

## What you need first

- **Functions and maps: A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.**
- **Affine varieties: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.**
- **The projective line: $\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **Fibers and base change: The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.**

content.title: Week 66, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Final examination and exposition.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can explain Proof synthesis and mathematical exposition, The Keller map, Étale maps, Marked-root incidence, and The normalized factorization threefold, test an example against the definition, and identify one boundary case.

## Why this matters

A proof cannot be clearer than its definitions. Today prevents later algebra from hiding a domain error or a missing hypothesis.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Fiber cardinality and noninjectivity: The fiber of $F:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $F^{-1}(y)$. If it contains two distinct points, then $F$ is not injective; a generic fiber count describes this on a dense target set.**
- **The normalized factorization threefold: $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.**
- **Étale maps: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.**
- **Marked-root incidence: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.**
- **Inverse function theorem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. If $DF_x$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $x$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $F(x)$ such that $F|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.**
- **Tangent spaces and differentials: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **The projective line: $\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.**
- **Fibers and base change: The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Learn the language of final examination and exposition

Reconstruct and synthesize final examination and exposition.

### Proof synthesis and mathematical exposition

A complete exposition states the target, fixes notation, cites each theorem with its hypotheses, proves intermediate claims before use, and distinguishes local, global, algebraic, and topological conclusions.

**Concrete example.** A final proof of $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ displays both polynomial maps, checks both compositions, and then explains how the normalized product map becomes the stated affine map.

**Boundary case.** A chain of correct formulas is not a readable proof when the objects, logical transitions, or scope of the conclusion remain unstated.

### The Keller map

$G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ is obtained by composing the affine chart of $X$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$.

**Concrete example.** $\det DG=-1$ while the map is generically three-to-one.

**Boundary case.** A constant nonzero Jacobian does not itself provide a global polynomial inverse.

### Étale maps

For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.

**Concrete example.** $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.

**Boundary case.** Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

### Marked-root incidence

A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.

**Concrete example.** Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.

**Boundary case.** A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

### The normalized factorization threefold

$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.

**Concrete example.** The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.

**Boundary case.** Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Final examination and exposition.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can use the definition-first method from the worked example to complete this related task: Use $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e)\in\mathbb C^5:a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$. Use the full forward chart $\Phi(a,y,z)=(a,b,c,d,e)$: $b=1+ay$, $c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z$, $d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz$, and $e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z$. Use the inverse-coordinate candidates $y=2bd-ae$ and $z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$. Prove $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ by writing the supplied polynomial chart and inverse, checking both compositions, and explaining why two-sided polynomial inverses establish an isomorphism. State how these coordinates place the normalized product map $(L,Q)\mapsto LQ$ on affine three-space.

## Why this matters

A stable method separates mathematical decisions from calculation. You will use the same route with less support on the proof page.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Fiber cardinality and noninjectivity: The fiber of $F:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $F^{-1}(y)$. If it contains two distinct points, then $F$ is not injective; a generic fiber count describes this on a dense target set.**
- **The normalized factorization threefold: $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.**
- **Étale maps: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.**
- **Marked-root incidence: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.**
- **Inverse function theorem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. If $DF_x$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $x$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $F(x)$ such that $F|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.**
- **Tangent spaces and differentials: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **The projective line: $\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.**
- **Fibers and base change: The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a method before working alone

First study this complete worked problem from the same mathematical family.

Then apply the same order of decisions to this related but different problem: Use $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e)\in\mathbb C^5:a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$. Use the full forward chart $\Phi(a,y,z)=(a,b,c,d,e)$: $b=1+ay$, $c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z$, $d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz$, and $e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z$. Use the inverse-coordinate candidates $y=2bd-ae$ and $z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$. Prove $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ by writing the supplied polynomial chart and inverse, checking both compositions, and explaining why two-sided polynomial inverses establish an isomorphism. State how these coordinates place the normalized product map $(L,Q)\mapsto LQ$ on affine three-space.

Use this four-step method:

1. Name the objects and their domains.

2. Rewrite the target using the relevant definition.

3. Perform one justified algebraic or logical step at a time.

4. Check the result against the original hypotheses.

### Complete worked solution

**Analogous problem.** Verify that $b=1+ay$ follows from the identity $y=2bd-ae$ on the displayed threefold.

**Objects and relations.** Work modulo $a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $ad+bc-1$.

**Calculation.** $b-(1+ay)=b-1-2abd+a^2e$. Replace $a^2e-abd$ by $1-cb^2$ to obtain $b-bc b-abd=b(1-bc-ad)$.

**Conclusion.** The last expression vanishes by $ad+bc=1$, so $b=1+ay$ in the coordinate ring. The quotient-ring reduction is the required global check.

**Why this solution is complete.** It states the objects and restrictions before calculation, justifies the decisive transformation, and returns to the original hypotheses at the end.

Prove $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ by writing the supplied polynomial chart and inverse, checking both compositions, and explaining why two-sided polynomial inverses establish an isomorphism. content.title: Week 66, day 4: Transfer and interpret
content.markdown: Build a proof-ready understanding of this week's focus: Final examination and exposition.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can complete and interpret this exact verification: Prove the normalized product map $(L,Q)\mapsto LQ$ is noninjective by starting with a cubic having three distinct roots, constructing the three distinct resultant-one factorizations associated with the three marked roots, and checking that all three have the same product.

## Why this matters

Exact computation can certify an algebraic claim, but only when you state what was computed and why that evidence reaches the conclusion.

## What you need first

Before starting, retrieve these earlier ideas from memory:
- **Fiber cardinality and noninjectivity: The fiber of $F:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $F^{-1}(y)$. If it contains two distinct points, then $F$ is not injective; a generic fiber count describes this on a dense target set.**
- **The normalized factorization threefold: $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$.**
- **Étale maps: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.**
- **Marked-root incidence: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.**
- **Inverse function theorem: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. If $DF_x$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $x$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $F(x)$ such that $F|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.**
- **Tangent spaces and differentials: $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.**
- **Resultant: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.**
- **The projective line: $\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.**
- **Fibers and base change: The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.**
- **Coordinate rings: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.**
- **Normal jets: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.**
For each one, say the definition and one example. If any item is unclear, open its Forge concept page before attempting the checkpoint.

## Use exact computation as evidence

Carry out this exact symbolic or logical verification: Prove the normalized product map $(L,Q)\mapsto LQ$ is noninjective by starting with a cubic having three distinct roots, constructing the three distinct resultant-one factorizations associated with the three marked roots, and checking that all three have the same product. Show every transformation, state what the result proves, and name one stronger claim that does not follow from this calculation alone.

A reproducible calculation has three parts: define the objects exactly, show the transformation, and interpret the output.

**Evidence boundary.** Exact expansion can prove a polynomial identity because coefficients can be compared. A finite list of numerical substitutions cannot prove that identity for every input.

  - Boundary to check: A chain of correct formulas is not a readable proof when the objects, logical transitions, or scope of the conclusion remain unstated.
- **The Keller map:** $G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ is obtained by composing the affine chart of $X$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$.

  - Boundary to check: Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

## Deliberate review

This section is review, not a new introduction. Close your notes before answering.

- **Week 65: Fibers and noninjectivity.** Retrieve this target: For $C=T S(T-S)$, construct the three resultant-one factorizations obtained by marking each projective root. Prove they are distinct points with the same product, then compare with cubics of root types $2+1$ and $3$ while keeping fiber cardinality, ramification, and nonproperness separate.

Prove that its three marked roots give three distinct normalized factorizations $C=LQ$ with resultant $1$, and that coprimality makes the normalized product map locally invertible at each factorization.
